Uniform Title: *Stutikusumāñjali* Author: Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa Editor: Premavallabha Tripāṭhī
Description: Hymns in praise of Śiva in thirty-eight chapters.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: April 6, 2012.
Publisher: Sanskrit Book Depot Publication Year: 1939 Publication City: Benares
Country of Publication: India.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Composed by the great Kashmiri poet, the illustrious Jagaddharabhaṭṭa.

Victorious is He who is full of compassion and devoted to the upliftment of the wretched; who illuminates the world with the splendor of His body, which is filled with the discernment of the knowledge of Brahman; who destroys the threefold suffering with His peaceful and compassionate gaze; and who gladdens all with His sweet speech, as if sprinkled with the essence of nectar.
The Guru.

May that true Guru named Hariharānanda protect me from the fear of worldly existence— he to whom the Goddess of Speech, abandoning her restlessness, remains for a very long time like one mute, having placed her finger upon his lotus-face and fixed her devotion upon the streams of nectar-like honey flowing from the lotus of his mouth, while ceasing the sounding of her lute.

Where is that Jagaddhara, the poet-empire of poets, by whose composition even Śiva was struck with awe? Where am I, devoid of discernment, and where is devotion to Śiva? Therefore, this [attempt of mine] is indeed nothing but a mockery.
What indeed is the use of this wretched state of my mind? If only the compassionate, smiling glance of the True Guru were to fall upon me, what great misery could possibly remain?
By meditating on his lotus feet, even the mere mention of the fear arising from the delusions created by Māyā—the source of birth within the various cosmic eggs—is no longer heard.
May that certain compassionate deity bestow auspiciousness upon me, by whom compassion has been extended even toward one devoid of learning and virtue.

May this Sarasvatī, with her first hymn— consisting of fresh, pure, unimpeded, life-giving, and sin-removing verses capable of quelling the Lord’s fatigue— be able for a moment to restrain His mind. 1-1.

Just as the river Sarasvatī is able to detain the mind for a moment with her waters— which are refreshing, pure, unimpeded, sin-destroying, capable of quelling fatigue, and ever-new life-givers— so too may this Sarasvatī [of mine] detain the mind of my Lord (Śrī Sadāśiva) for a moment with these hymns— which are refreshing, pure, unimpeded, life-giving, sin-destroying, capable of quelling fatigue, and ever-new.

Possessing the stable virtues of her master and flowing with a natural grace that rains nectar upon the ears, may this Sarasvatī cause your mind to abandon its habitual restlessness for a moment. 1-2.
May this beloved Sarasvatī, adorned with beautiful style, faultless, radiant with virtues, charming with excellent meters, and endowed with aesthetic flavor, delight the mind of her lord. 3.

May this pure Sarasvatī of the Conqueror of Smara enter the mind of the Lord of Beings— she who is praised for having obtained excellent boons, whose complexion is bright and clear, and who remains stainless despite the turbulence of the dark rainy season.
Instantly awakened by my own intellect through devotion, this Sarasvatī, desiring to propitiate the Lord in order to obtain her desired boon, has become Sarvamaṅgalā.

We worship that supreme, imperishable Light, which, vibrating as "Oṃ," is the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) within the chest; it is the ultimate state that contains within its womb the entirety of all speech.

We worship that Great Light which is the existent, the imperishable, the supreme state "Om" in which all speech is condensed within its womb; which, throbbing in our chest as the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), resounds within the heart;
which cannot be turned back by the sun, the moon, or the great light [of fire], and by which [all else] is instantly (or suddenly) illuminated.
It attains an inner peace that dispels darkness; we worship that Great Light.
We worship that Light by which the internal darkness— which was not dispelled by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by the great light— is instantly brought to peace.

We worship that One Reality which, though single, shines manifoldly as both consciousness and matter, like the sky within the hollows of the *kīcaka* reeds, or like the orb of the sun reflected in the waves.
Great! || 8 ||

We worship that Light which, though one, shines manifoldly within both the conscious and the unconscious—like the sky within the hollows of the *kīcaka* reeds, or like the orb of the sun within its waves;
it is beyond the reach of words harsh with logic, witnessed solely at the moment of one’s own direct experience, and free from the turmoil of all mental constructs. We worship that Supreme Lord.
Great! || 9 ||

We worship that Supreme Lordly Light, which is beyond the reach of words sharpened by logical analysis (*anvaya-tarka*), which has as its sole witness the occasion of one’s own direct experience, and in which the turmoil of all conceptual constructions has been stilled;

we worship that Light by which the world— though consisting solely of its own manifestation— is made to appear as diverse through *māyā*, just as a brilliant rainbow appears in the cloudless sky due to the sun.
The Great One. || 10 ||

We worship that Great Light which, consisting solely of its own self-manifestation, appears as the world differentiated by Māyā— just as a variegated rainbow is manifested by a streak of cloudless light from the sun—
and which, hidden within the deep cavern of the heart-cave, illuminates the interior of all the three worlds.
Its stable position was maintained by the vital breaths emerging from the openings of its caves, ravines, and chasms. || 11 ||

We praise that wondrous lamp which they declare to be devoid of all ten stages, free from arising and decay, devoid of form, independent of any support, stainless, and beyond the range of the senses. (12) [A *yugma* is said to consist of two verses; a *viśeṣaka* of three; a *kalāpaka* of four;
and more than that is known as a *kulaka*.]

We praise that [Supreme Self], whom the possessors of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñānin*) declare to be the lamp— hidden within the deep chamber of the heart’s cave, illuminating the interior of the three worlds, maintaining a steady presence through the vital breath emerging from the openings of the mountain caverns and valleys; who has abandoned all states of existence, whose arising is inexhaustible, who is devoid of form, who does not depend on a wall [for support], who is stainless, beyond the range of the senses, and wondrous.
We praise that Lord of the Universe, the Consort of Umā, by whose lotus-feet, having attained unimpeded union with their pollen, the grains of rice possess a wondrous freedom from dust.

We praise that Lord of the Universe, the Consort of Umā, by the dust of whose lotus feet— possessing the glory of a continuous lineage of excellence— the devotees, having attained unimpeded yoga, assume a wondrous state free from passion (*nīrajaskatā*). He is adorned with the beautiful crescent moon, has formed a bond of friendship with the serpents, and has accepted as his enemies the dense clouds of the rainy season.
We praise the blue-throated one, who is the object of great wonder.

We praise the Blue-throated One, who is adorned by a beautiful crescent moon following him in succession, who has formed friendships with serpents, and who has entered into enmity with the thick clouds;

we praise him with great curiosity— him who, while contemplating the worlds by his mere will, though he is one who accepts the service of those dear to him, has become one who accepts the service of those who are not dear, having as his minister his own sovereign power.
We praise Śiva. 15.

We praise that Śiva, whose companion is his own power (Svaśakti), who— though he had previously been one who accepted only agreeable offerings while nourishing the worlds according to their desires— has now become one who accepts even disagreeable offerings;
he who is cherished by the hand-drum (mṛdaṅga) of the lotus-dweller (Brahmā), worshipped by the lotus-eyes of Padmanābha (Viṣṇu), and colored by the rays from the crown of Padmabandhu (the Sun).
We praise the divine pair of lotus feet. || 16 ||

We worship that Lord who bears a pair of feet radiant with the garlands upon the heads of the lords of the immortals, a chest brightened by ashes, and a crest-ornament illuminated by the rays of the moon.
We worship that Lord who bears a pair of feet radiant with the garlands upon the heads of the immortals, a chest radiant with ashes, and likewise a crest radiant with the rays of the moon;
He who, on His head, bears a smile as white as a mass of foam and possessing a splendor as beautiful as the rays of the moon— a smile that removes the suffering of embodied beings.
And he who [worships] the slender form of Siddhasindhu; || 18 ||

[The compound *aviṣādam* is analyzed as follows: *aviṣādam* means "one in whom despair (*viṣādaḥ*) does not exist" (*yasya saḥ tam*). *Viṣādam* means "one who eats poison (*viṣam*, i.e., *kālakūṭa*). [The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: He who bears upon his head the celestial river (*siddhasindhu*), which possesses a splendor beautiful like the rays of the moon, whose smile is as white as a mass of foam, which removes the suffering of embodied beings, and which is vast;

and he who bears a body that possesses a splendor beautiful like the rays of the moon, whose smile is as white as a mass of foam, which removes the suffering of embodied beings, and which is slender—he is [the one to be praised]. (Note: The text provides a partial analysis of the term *aviṣādam*, contrasting it with *viṣādam*, which is derived from *viṣa*—meaning either "despair" or the specific poison *kālakūṭa*.)
[This is connected with the following verse: "I take refuge in him who possesses such despondency. (The connection is with the subsequent verse:

"Whose mind would not be filled with curiosity at the thought that even a servant is capable of acting [thus]? For he does not possess the nature of Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, nor the character of Vicitravīrya. (19)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: Whose mind does he not inspire with curiosity? (The meaning is: rather, he inspires the minds of everyone with curiosity. He whom, though possessing the physical form of Śantanu, one does not perceive as Bhīṣma, and whom one does not perceive as Vicitravīrya—I take refuge in that undepressed Viṣāda, as before.

I take refuge in that Viṣāda (Sorrow), who rendered Yama—who was rushing forward with his physical form—formless; and who likewise made Darpaka (the God of Love) devoid of pride. I take refuge in that Viṣāda (Grief), who is free from dejection, who—like a Lord—rendered the embodied Yama, as he was rushing forward, formless and irresistible; and who likewise rendered Darpaka (Kāma) devoid of pride. I take refuge in Śaṅkara, who is covered by the sky, supported by the waters upon his head, and adorned by living beings, serpents, and snakes. *Anvaya:* Aham tam aviṣādam viṣādam āśraye, yaḥ puras āpatantam savigraham yamam avigraham ayamam vyadhāt, tathā yaḥ darpakam adarpakam vyadhita. [He] is covered by the garment of space, [he is] supported on his head by the waters of life, and [he is] adorned by enjoyments, serpents, and snakes. I take refuge in Śaṅkara.
We worship the one who brings about auspiciousness. || 21 ||
We worship Śaṅkara, the bringer of auspiciousness, who is enveloped by the sky-like expanse of his matted locks, who rests upon living waters at his head, who is adorned by serpents and their coils,
who is graced by fire, illuminated by the white-rayed moon, and resplendent with the shining sun.
We worship the three eyes of the All-pervading Lord. || 22 ||

We worship the three eyes of the Lord: the one on the forehead adorned with the flaming fire, the one on the left illuminated by the cool-rayed moon, and the one on the right resplendent with the blazing sun;
the three eyes of the Lord, which bestow fearlessness upon those who take refuge in them, assume his own true nature, and possess a union of all intense and complete splendors, like pure stars.
And I bow to the three-pointed crest of the trident. || 23 ||
I praise the three eyes of the Lord, which possess the nature of bestowing fearlessness, which bear the union of all unrestrained flames, and which have pure stars;
and I praise the triple-pointed crest of his trident.
[The goddesses] whose root-cheek regions are moistened by streams of tears flowing from the casket of their closed eyes, [worship] the God who is adorned with a digit of the moon.
The virtuous here praise him who wears the ear-ornament as "Śaṅkara, Śaṅkara. || 24 ||

In this place, virtuous ones—whose roots of the cheeks have been bathed by streams of tears gushing forth from the casket of their closing eyes—worship the God who wears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, crying out, "O Śaṅkara! O Śaṅkara!
I was indeed deluded; at that time of calamity, struck by a great confusion of directions, I wandered falsely along wrong paths. Now, having rested in the ever-new Nandana grove...
But now Śiva’s grief comes upon me; it shall be my end.
Anvaya: At this time of slaughter, being struck by confusion regarding the directions, I have indeed wandered falsely along great by-paths;
but now, having rested in the Nandana garden of Śiva’s pleasure grove, that exhaustion of mine comes to an end.
For even by the Goddess of Speech—who is accustomed to dwelling with the swan that is my vehicle, beautiful as the rays of the full moon—rest is found in our minds, though they are defiled.
The playful grace of that fortune of the Lord whose crest is the moon is victorious. || 26 ||

Victorious is the good fortune of the Lord whose crest is the moon, that even the Goddess of Speech—who is accustomed to dwelling upon the swan of his arm, which is as beautiful as the rays of the full moon—should find rest within our impure minds.

Having abandoned him, who is worthy of the heart, those who praise him become successful, their enjoyments of the earth being both desirable and unsurpassed; yet they do so while leaving behind him who is truly suited to the mind.
O you who have maintained self-restraint! Alas, those whose enjoyments are vast will find no way to go to the next world. 27.

O mind, observer of restraint! Is it not improper for you to abandon that which is desirable—adorned by those with unimpaired enjoyments (*ahīna-bhoga*) and likewise praised by the wise—and thereby go elsewhere (*paratra*), to make songs about the earth and sky (*mahī-nabha-gā*)?

For one who attains dignity in the world through great virtues and meditates upon Him who is the crest-jewel of the Lord of the Night (*īramaṇa-śekhara*), there arises a dignity devoid of pride (*gaurava-ndhya*). Therefore, [meditate] upon Him together with Umā...
Now, my unclouded mind has been directed toward a hymn of praise for Him who has displayed equal and great splendor. 28.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the speech (*gauḥ*) of a person who meditates upon Him whose crest is the moon becomes infallible (*anandhyā*), therefore, having attained dignity through virtues that are weighty in this world, I have now directed my unclouded mind toward the praise of Him (*Śiva*), who has performed great sports together with Umā.

Blessed are those who, recognizing the human world to be difficult to attain and easily won only through immediate merit, and having obtained discernment (*viveka*)—the sole friend that quells all calamities—[devote themselves to Him].
Some praise the swan, who bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, with words that are pure, sweet, and drenched in devotion. || 29 ||

Considering this world of living beings— which is difficult to attain again and is easily won through the merit of past deeds— to be such, some fortunate ones, having found the singular friend that quells all misfortunes— discrimination (viveka)— immediately praise with pure and sweet words the Swan, who bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. Indeed, a poem that is empty within, devoid of merit, sapless, and lacking in creative genius, though it may resemble a land-lotus, is not pleasing to the wise.
There too, may the Lord, whose intoxication is intensified by devotion arising from a deep-seated attachment to the sandy banks of his own ears, deign to perform this blameless act.

[Objection: "Surely this poem—which is empty within, devoid of poetic qualities, tasteless, and lacking in creative structure, resembling a land-lotus—will not be pleasing to the hearts of the wise. [Reply:
Even so, the Lord ought to place upon the shore of his ears this irreproachable poem, which is refined by devotion arising from the deep continuity of passion.

Or rather, this speech— which rains down drops of nectar, possesses the luster of the moon, and bestows intense bliss— will surely bring the Lord of Girijā’s life, who is as sensitive as a moonstone, to a state of melting.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: Or rather, this speech of mine—which rains down drops of nectar, possesses the luster of the moon, and bestows intense bliss—surely brings the Lord of Girijā’s life, who is like a moonstone, to a state of moisture. Thus ends [the hymn] to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the illustrious Kashmiri great poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the first hymn is titled "The Introduction to Praise.
The second hymn:
*Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Self, whose sole form is the ultimate reality; to Śambhu, who is divided by unreal distinctions manifested through His own will.* (1)
Oṃ. Salutation be to Śambhu, the Supreme Self, whose single form is the ultimate reality, who appears as the manifold unreal distinctions through his own will.
Salutation to Śiva, who is endowed with the complete pacification of all afflictions, and who shatters the bonds of worldly existence that are difficult to untie due to the three qualities.

Salutation to Śiva, who brings about the complete pacification of all afflictions through their underlying tendencies, and who shatters existence—the difficult-to-unravel knot of the three qualities (guṇas). Salutation to him whose feet are fashioned by the crowns of all the gods; salutation to him whose actions grant joy through the playful creation of the city of the world.
Salutations be to Śiva, whose feet are fashioned by the crowns of all the gods in succession, and whose deeds grant the joy of playful sport in the construction of the city of the universe.
Salutations to him whose crest is adorned by a fragment of the beloved of the night (the moon), and who knows how to sever the exhaustion born of the despair caused by the darkness of suffering.

Salutation be to Śrī Śiva, whose head is adorned with the crescent moon— the beloved of the night— and who knows how to sever the exhaustion born of the despair caused by the darkness of worldly suffering.
Salutation to the self-existent one, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree for all mental constructions and intentions, and who possesses a mass of beautiful blossoming buds.

Salutation be to the Self-existent One, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree for the conceptualization of all mental constructions that follow their logical sequence, and whose mass of blossoming buds is as beautiful as the digit of the moon.

Salutation to him who has compassion for the multitude of living beings overcome by darkness, and whose eyes are illuminated by the splendor of the light of the white-rayed moon and the great-rayed sun.

Salutation to the one who has compassion for the multitude of beings overwhelmed by the darkness of saṃsāra; salutation to the one whose eyes are illuminated by the splendor of the great light of Śveta-bhānu.
Salutation to Bhava, who brings joy to those distressed by the sound of "huṃ" uttered by Śamana, and who rains down nectar upon those agitated by the forest-fire of worldly existence.

Homage to Bhava, who gladdens those distressed and trembling with the *huṃ* sounds of the *anvaya-śamana* (the subduer of lineage), and who rains down nectar upon those agitated by the forest-fire of worldly existence (*bhavadāvāgni*).

Homage to the bull-bannered Lord (*vṛṣalakṣman*), the physician who cuts through the heavy fever of the pride of the intoxicated Kandarpa, and who destroys the incurable diseases of worldly existence.

Salutations to the one marked by the bull (Śiva), who cuts through the heavy fever of pride caused by Kandarpa (the god of love) that has been subdued by his power, and who is the physician for destroying the incurable diseases of worldly existence;
salutations to the wearer of the skull (Kapālin), who protects against the terror and affliction of birth, old age, and death, and who is tender with the contact of the nectar of compassion. 9.

Salutations to the Skull-Bearer (Kapālin), who protects [beings] from the fear and distress of birth, old age, and death through his lineage; who is tender with the contact of the nectar of compassion;
salutations to the ocean of the nectar of grace, which is naturally free from obstacles; to the kinsman of those afflicted and tormented by the heat of the desert of saṃsāra. 10.

Salutations to the ocean of the nectar of grace, which is naturally and effortlessly free from obstacles; salutations to the kinsman who provides relief to those tormented by the heat of the desert of saṃsāra.
Salutations to Mahākāla, who is beautified by the deep resonance of his thundering voice that flows with thick nectar, and who dispels the exhaustion of the summer heat of worldly existence.
Salutation to Mahākāla, who is resplendent with a deep resonance that flows like a dense stream of nectar, and who dispels the exhaustion of summer born from the heat of Bhīṣma;

salutation to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), whose majesty transcends speech and mind, and whose form is beyond qualities, yet possesses the three qualities, the eightfold powers, and infinite attributes.

Salutations to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), whose majesty transcends both speech and mind; who is the embodiment of the three qualities, the eightfold qualities, infinite qualities, and yet devoid of qualities.
Salutations to the Swan (Haṃsa), the traveler of the sky, the destroyer of long-standing evils, whose own splendor has dispelled all darkness.

Salutation be to the Swan, who brings an end to the long-standing faults of transmigration, who moves through the sky, and who has dispelled all darkness by the majesty of his own splendor. Salutation to that Conqueror of Smara, who bears the beauty of gold, of the moon, of the son of Gaṅgā born from fire, and of refined gold.
Homage to him who, by means of his golden moon—the son of Gaṅgā born from fire—bears the splendor of the sun; homage to the conqueror of Smara!
Homage to Śambhu, who bestows grace upon his devotees even through the graceful bending of his own limbs, and who has paralyzed the pillar-like arms of the enemy of Jambha! 15.

Salutations to Śambhu, who bestows grace upon his devotees even through the manner of breaking his own limbs in accordance with [the devotee's] lineage; salutations to him who paralyzed the pillar-like arms of Jambhāri (Indra).
Salutations to the peerless one, worthy of honor, the instructor of the path of justice, the foremost of all, the most generous, the blessed, and the Lord. (16)
As the sages contemplated the unprecedented beauty of your unclothed body, a certain agitation arose within their wives;

for even by performing worship once upon the broken secret parts, liberation is surely attained—yet for you, who gives birth to the goals of human endeavor, that very thing becomes something indecorous.
Salutations be to the Master, who is honored for his lineage that is peerless, who instructs in the path of justice, who is preeminent, generous, and blessed.
Salutations to him who has withdrawn Time, whose splendor is like that of black iron, whose mass [of hair] is washed by the Gaṅgā, and who finds no decline in his arts. 17.

Salutations to Śiva, who has withdrawn time through his succession [of manifestations], whose luster is like that of black iron, whose matted locks are washed by the Gaṅgā, and who never suffers the loss of his digits;
salutations to the Lord who is praised by the victorious Indra, by Viṣṇu the pervader of the worlds, by the powerful Brahmā, and by the primordial Brahman.
Salutations to the Lord who is praised by the victorious Viṣṇu, the most powerful one, and by the primordial Brahmā;
salutations to Him who presides over the lotus-throne, which has the principal mountains for its petals, the golden mountain [Meru] for its pericarp, and the serpent Ananta for its stalk. 19.

Homage to Him who occupies the lotus-throne, whose petals are the mountain ranges of the lineage, whose pericarp is the golden mountain [Meru], and whose stalk is infinite. Homage to that Lord Paṅkajanābha (the Lotus-navelled One), who manifests even without a cause within the one whose navel is a lotus. 20.
Homage to that all-pervading Lord whose navel is a lotus, who acts even without a cause;

homage to Him whose navel is a lotus! Homage to Him whose body is half-moon, whose crown is adorned by the crescent moon; homage to Him who possesses the white splendor arising from the white conch-shell! 21.
Homage to the one whose body is half-mooned by his lineage, homage to the one who has made the crescent moon his crown; homage to the one whose white splendor arises from the white [elephant] Abhaya;
homage to the Master who worships Vināyaka—who delights Vinatā, who has the fierce face of a serpent-form, and who is gazed upon with a look. 22.
Homage to the Lord who gazes with his eye upon Vināyaka, who delights the daughter of Anvaya (Pārvatī) and possesses a fierce face in the form of an elephant;

homage to the source of existence, whose ear is Brahmā, Hari, and the Three-eyed One (Śiva), and who, having the bull as his emblem, is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world. (23)
Salutation to the bull-bannered Lord, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, who is the progenitor of Anu, Yama, Brahmā, Hari, Tryambaka, and Śravaṇa;

salutation to that Supreme Light which, though undivided, appears divided—just as gold exists within its ornaments such as the *karṇikā*, or water within the oceans and other bodies of water. || 24 ||
Salutation to that supreme light which, like gold in its various ornaments or water in the oceans and other receptacles,

remains undivided within all things that are divided; salutation to that Lord Pinākin, whose nature is a vow to protect those beset by every calamity, and upon whom— though he is the one and only refuge— no celestial being, even though great, entertains any further desire.

Salutations to that Pinākin, whose power alone provides refuge for even the great celestial beings, so that no desire arises in them for anything else; to him who is devoted to the vow of protecting those beset by every calamity.

That which was placed in the Creator during the act of world-creation, that which is established in the Creator as the cause of its preservation, and that which is withdrawn into the Creator at the time of dissolution—salutations to Him.
Salutation after salutation to that supreme, great glory. || 26 ||

Salutations again and again to that Supreme Light, which was deposited by the Blessed One in one half during the process of creating the world, established in another half during its maintenance, and borne within the third half during its dissolution. Salutations to Him who brought about the destruction of the enemy of the stars (Rāhu); salutations to Him whose splendor is like that of the stars resting in the three worlds; salutations to Him whose meritorious deeds save the world. Salutations! Salutations! Salutations! Salutations! Salutations!
Homage to the one who has the King of Stars (the Moon) as his crown. || 27 ||

Salutations to the one who has produced the enemy of Tāraka through his lineage; salutations to the one whose splendor as a savior rests in the three abodes; salutations to the one whose meritorious deeds save the world; salutations again and again to the one who wears the king of stars upon his crest.

Salutations, salutations to you whose crest is the nectar-rayed moon; salutations, salutations to you, the bestower of the attainment of immortality; salutations, salutations to you who hold the jar of nectar in your hand. Salutations.
Salutations to you, whose self is Amṛtabhairava. || 28 ||

(He, O Supreme Lord! Salutations again and again to You whose crown is the moon of nectar; salutations again and again to You who bestow the attainment of immortality; salutations again and again to You who hold the vessel of nectar in Your hand;

salutations again and again to You whose very self is Amṛtabhairava. Salutations to You whose movement reaches the furthest limit beyond darkness; salutations to You whose power is differentiated throughout all the paths (adhvan); salutations to You whose forms are both sequentially arranged and unified; salutations!
For the liberation of devotion offered to the one who abides in peace. || 29 ||

Salutations to Him whose activity reaches the furthest limit beyond the darkness of succession; salutations to Him whose power is differentiated throughout the entire path of existence; salutations to Him whose forms are both sequential and simultaneous, whether manifested individually or as a whole;
salutations to Him who bestows liberation upon those who have offered devotion to the state of peace.
Salutations to Śabara, the supreme one who grants victory and triumph; salutations to Hara, the remover of the accumulation of all stains.
Salutation to Bhava, whose majesty is bold in curing the world's ailments; salutation to Śiva, who has revealed auspiciousness through his most excellent boons. || 30 ||

Salutations to the excellent Śabara, who bestows victory upon those seeking lineage; salutations to Hara, who removes the accumulation of all stains; salutations to Bhava, whose power is preeminent in curing the world’s ailments; salutations to Śiva, who has manifested auspiciousness through his most excellent boons.
Thus ends [the hymn] composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*, dedicated to the Blessed One...
In the *Stutikusumāñjali* of Maheśvara, this is the second hymn, consisting of salutations.
The third hymn:

[Salutations] to that one who is eternal, unobscured, whose sole measure is his own self-experience, the abode of bliss, the unique seed for the sprout of the world, and who is beyond all limitations such as direction, space, time, and calculation.
May the Great One, who is difficult to overcome, grant us great auspiciousness. || 1 ||

May that Great Light bestow peace upon us— eternal in its continuity, unobscured, having as its sole authority its own self-experience, the abode of bliss, the unique seed for the sprout of the universe, and incapable of being crushed by the grasp of all things such as direction,
space, time, and their divisions; in which this world arises, like a mass of clouds in the sky, like a multitude of waves in a lake, or like the radiance of the moon in the thousand-rayed sun.
And may that Śāmbhava [state] dissolve for the sake of the increase of our sovereign power. || 2 ||

May that power of Śambhu lead to our prosperity—that power in which this entire world arises and dissolves, like a mass of clouds in the sky of the Absolute, like a multitude of waves in a lake, or like the light of the moon in the thousand-rayed sun;

he who, performing the sport of the maintenance, dissolution, and creation of the three worlds, assumes through his own effects the forms of Hari, Hara, and Dhruviṇa; that God who transcends the speech and mind of all people.
May Śakti grant you eternal and imperishable auspiciousness forever. || 3 ||

May that Lord—who, through his activity, performs the sport of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds; who is the state of Hari, Hara, and Dhruhiṇa; and whose power transcends the speech and mind of all people—grant you eternal and imperishable auspiciousness.
Indeed, this entire collection of causes, such as the Puruṣa, atoms, karma, and time, becomes capable of fashioning the manifold universe only by his grace.
May the sole Great Lord of the three worlds protect you! || 4 ||

Logical connection (*anvaya*): This entire collection of causes—such as primordial matter, atoms, karma, and time—is powerless; he, by whose grace it attains proficiency in the construction of the manifold universe, that sole Great Lord of the three worlds may protect you.
Before whom alone, who possesses knowledge and action independent of all instruments, the entire universe shines forth as he beholds the world.
May that Supreme Lord grant you the supreme gain, appearing like an *āmalakī* fruit in the palm of his hand. || 5 ||

May that Supreme Lord, before whom the entire manifold universe flashes forth like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, nourish your supreme gain— he who, possessing the power of knowledge independent of causal instruments,
gazes upon the world; he who, of immeasurable majesty and unsurpassable glory, sports with Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others as if with mere balls.
May the beloved of the Daughter of the Himālaya mountains, the destroyer of Death himself, diminish your sins. || 6 ||

May He—the immeasurable Lord who sports with Purandara, Padmasadman, Padmāpati, and others as if with balls; the crusher of Kṛtānta; whose majesty is insurmountable; the Beloved of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain—lighten your sins.
May that Abode, whose footstool is made rosy by the mass of rays from the crest-jewels of all the gods bowing in service, grant prosperity.
May the Lord, whose beautiful form causes the deer-marked moon to appear as if it were a mountain peak turned tawny, be auspicious to you.

May the Lord, whose footstool is reddened by the mass of rays from the crest-jewels of all the gods who attend upon him in succession, whose form is as sweet as the moon that makes the mountain peaks tawny, nourish your abode.
His lofty body is adorned with the graceful curves of armlets fashioned by serpents, and he bears the Gaṅgā, which flows with leaping waves and touches the courtyard of the sky.
May He, the all-pervading One, who bears the destruction of the amorous gestures of Cupid—whose own movements have been rendered motionless—grant you swift and unswerving spiritual impulses.

May the Lord of Anvaya, who possesses a lofty form that bestows unbroken movement upon you— his limbs displaying the grace of armlets fashioned by serpents, his body touching the Ganges as it flows through the courtyard of the sky with leaping waves, and having brought about the destruction of the restless god of love—

graciously accept your prostrations. He who, through the skillful instruction of the methods of ritual circles, mandalas, water-pots, mantras, mudras, meditation, worship, praise, and recitation, [bestows liberation].
May that Teacher of the Three Worlds, who bestows enjoyment, liberation, subduing of passions, and grace upon those who bow before him, delight you.

May that Teacher of the Three Worlds delight you— he who, through the method of instruction consisting of the fire-pit, the mandala, the circle, mantras, mudrās, meditation, worship, praise, recitation, and so forth, bestowed grace that grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who bowed before him;
he whose splendor was as bright as the pure frost of a vast autumn cloud, radiant with a mass of shimmering ashes and a luster like the moon.
May that auspicious form, with its throat as dark as a bee and resembling the autumnal moon adorned by its spot, bestow welfare upon you. || 10 ||

May the body of Śambhu bestow auspiciousness upon you—a body as white as the abundant autumnal clouds and frost, radiant with a mass of shimmering splendor, possessing a luster bright like a bee-black throat, and resembling the autumn moon adorned with its spot.
By means of the infallible method taught by Him, men attain prosperity through the riches of heaven and liberation; may that Lord protect you.
May it be the ground of confidence for the attainment of the fruits of all actions, for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goals. || 11 ||

May that Lord—who, having taught the infallible means by which [devotees], upon attaining it, become masters through the splendors of heaven and liberation; who is the ground of confidence for the realization of the fruits of all actions—be for the fulfillment of your desires.

He is served by the wise with flowers that are free from their roots, yet possessed of buds, capable of quelling the heat of those who bow before him, devoid of withered leaves, and yielding immediate fruit.
May Sthāṇu, with his wondrous form, be for your prosperity.

May Sthāṇu, distinguished by a wondrous form that is rooted in continuity, free from buds, capable of quelling the suffering of those who bow before him, devoid of fallen leaves, yielding immediate fruit, and worshipped by the wise, be for your prosperity.
He bears a body rendered pure by bathing in the celestial river and service to the sacred fire, such that all suspicion of blemish is removed.
May the Lord of the twice-born, worshipped by the Supreme Lord and free from the persistence of defects, bring about the pacification of darkness and heat for you. 13.

May the Lord of the Twice-born (the Moon), who bears a body purified by bathing in the celestial river of his lineage and by serving the sacrificial fire—thereby free from even the suspicion of blemish—who is devoid of attachment to faults, and who is worshipped by the Lord (Śiva), bring about the pacification of darkness and heat for you.
He whose son is the illustrious Dhanada (Kubera), whose hand is overflowing with the water of charity, and who is obediently situated near him; he who rests upon the head [of Śiva].
May that Lord, who is a cloud raining down gold, protect you with his hand outstretched. 14.

May that Lord Kanakavarṣaghana—who has a glorious son whose hand is overflowing with the water of charity; who has the wealthy Dhanada obedient at his side; and who is sought for refuge upon the head by the King with outstretched hand—protect you all!
In that place, the sun and moon dwell together without envy, as do fire and water, and the nectar and the hālāhala poison, under the new king.
May that Śarva-form, presided over by Him, become radiant for the attainment of your desires. || 15 ||

Anvaya: May that body of Śiva, presided over by a radiant and youthful king—in which the sun and moon dwell together without envy, as do fire and water, and ambrosia and the hālāhala poison—be for the fulfillment of your desires;
he who is the speaker and the one who brings joy, the Lord of the Vedas, who bears upon his chest a hand marked with a lotus, and who [bears the crescent moon] upon his head.
And bearing the daughter of Himavat upon his body, may he who exists as threefold be auspicious for your welfare. || 16 ||

May that Śiva—who, as the All-pervading Lord, is the speaker of the Vedas in the form of Brahmā and their bringer of bliss; who, as Viṣṇu, bears upon his chest and hand the mark of the lotus; and who, as Rudra, carries upon his head and body the daughter of Himavat—may he, manifesting in these three ways, be for your welfare.

May the three-eyed Lord, the enemy of Tripura, who is honored by the three worlds, grant you the removal of the threefold afflictions through his three prongs; the attainment of the three aims of life through his three eyes; the dissolution of the three impurities through the water of the three streams; and the destruction of the three stains. (17)
May the three-eyed face of the Enemy of Tripura, worshipped by the three worlds, grant you the removal of the threefold afflictions;
may his abode in the three realms grant you the attainment of the three goals of human existence; and may the water of the triple-streamed Ganges grant you the destruction of the three impurities.
Blessed are those whose lotus-eyes remain half-closed for a long time through the experience of the bliss of the nectar of beholding him.

May that Śiva, who bestows auspiciousness upon you, be ever present—He who bears, as it were, the very breaking of the contact with the rays of the sun and moon that fall within the range of the path of vision.

May that Śiva be the bestower of auspiciousness upon you—he who, by the nectar-like bliss of his vision, causes the lotus-eyes of the fortunate ones to remain half-closed for a long time, as if through the touch of the rays of the sun and moon within the range of the path of seeing;
he who, pacifying Time with his mere glance, made his white fame successful in its endeavor and a source of supreme wonder. Śvetaṃ yaśaḥ (His white fame).
May that Śiva protect you, who, by pacifying both the wicked and the virtuous, makes his time meaningful. || 19 ||

May that Lord Śiva protect you—he who, creating the highest wonder through his lineage, pacifies Time by his mere glance; he who made the white [Kāla] fruitful in his efforts, while quelling the white fame of the wicked, fulfills the purpose of Time for the virtuous.
May that mass of matted hair protect you, which is tawny and bears a friendship with the fire on its forehead, wherein the serpent attains a state of aesthetic unity with the flame.
May the Lord of the Pramathas manifest that state of being which, though even his enemies are equal [to him], is free from resentment. || 20 ||

May that tawny matted lock (*jūṭa*) of the Lord of the Pramathas spread for you a state of freedom from resentment even toward your enemies—that lock which bears friendship with the fire of the forehead, wherein the serpent attains a state of aesthetic unity (*sāmarasya*) with the flame; may it protect you.
May he protect you, upon whose head even today the waters of the celestial river (*Surasindhu*), embraced by the rows of flames from the fire of his eye, remain.
The moon attains a beauty as if it were situated in the midst of the lovely Ocean of Milk, enveloped by the flames of the submarine fire. || 21 ||

May he protect you— he upon whose head the moon, embraced by the waters of the celestial ocean licked by the flames of the fire from his eye, even today possesses a splendor as if situated in the midst of the lovely milk-ocean enveloped by the submarine fire’s crest.
May he protect you— he whose weight of foot-dust turns the foreheads of the virtuous into a tablet of ash, upon which the Creator writes the letters of their destiny.
"His lotus-feet shall be worshipped by the garlands of crowns belonging to the lords of the earth; thus he shall become [renowned] upon the earth. || 22 ||

May that Śiva protect you—he who, on the forehead-plates of the virtuous made dusty by the weight of the dust from his feet, inscribes these letters: "On this earth, there shall be a man whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the garlands of crowns of kings.

May the crescent moon of Śiva grant you auspiciousness—reddened by the scattering of rays from the jewels of the serpents in his matted locks—and may the Goddess grant it too, as she is perceived through the notion of the fresh nail-marks upon it.
She covers her breasts with the hem of her garment as she makes her way across.

May that crescent moon of Śiva’s consort, reddened by the scattering of rays from the jewels of the serpent in her matted locks, grant you auspiciousness—she whom the Goddess conceals with the hem of her garment on the slope of her breast, mistaking it for the mark of a fresh nail-scratch.
May that nipple of the Goddess’s breast, which dwells in the half-body of the Moon-crested Lord, lead to your attainment of nectar; for it approaches the golden pedestal of the worshipful Madana.
Possessing the beauty of a sapphire linga established upon its back.
May that beauty of the emerald *liṅga* installed upon the surface of the golden pedestal worshipped by Madana—
which resembles the nipple on the breast of the Goddess who dwells in half the body of the Moon-crested Lord— be for your attainment of immortality.
May those [braids] of the Subduer of Cupid, which bear the imprint of Mount Mandara encircled by the waves of the Ocean of Milk, lead you [to liberation].
May those rays of the sun, which cause the waves of the perfected river to manifest in double density, cross over your sins. || 25 ||
May those rays of the sun, which bear the likeness of Mount Mandara encircled by the waves of the Ocean of Milk upon the matted locks of Anaṅgadamana,
and which possess the dense ripples of the celestial river manifested twice over, dispel your sin.
That ladder which ascends toward the station most exalted as the birthplace of the prosperity of the three worlds— [may it lead you upward].
May that daughter of Jahnu’s son, who is the crest-jewel of the moon, the banner of victory, and the daughter of [the sage] Anihanu, protect you. 26.

May the daughter of Jahnu protect you—she who is the ladder for ascending to the most exalted station, the very earth that gives birth to the prosperity of the three worlds; she who is the Vaijayantī banner on the crest of the moon-crested Lord.
May the skull of Bharga’s head grant you bliss, its entire cavity fixed by the fire-piṭaka of his forehead, as it cooks the body of the Time-Fire.
A vast multitude of living beings goes toward his state as a kitchen. || 27 ||

May the skull of Bharga’s head grant you prosperity— that very skull which, with all its apertures pinned by the fire-stake of his forehead-eye, became the kitchen for him who, in the form of the fire of Time,

cooks the vast multitude of living beings. And may the lunar orb, the waters of the celestial river, the nectar-sustaining golden jar held in his hand, and the affectionate play of his glance [grant you well-being].
May your laughter and smiles serve to pacify the heat of Śambhu. || 28 ||

May these—the lunar light of Śambhu, the waters of the celestial river, the life-giving nectar from the golden pitcher held in his hand, the affectionate play of his eyes, and his white smile—serve to allay your fever.
[These are present] upon his head, which is white as the celestial river, like a crescent moon; upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa, his white mount; and even upon his body, which is as radiant as frost.
May this manifestation of Śiva, consisting of a union of similar elements, nourish you. || 29 ||

May this harmonious assemblage of Śiva protect you: upon his head, white as the ocean of milk, is a pale crescent moon; on the peak of Mount Kailāsa is his white mount; and upon his body, radiant as frost, is this ash.

Furthermore, the digit of the moon possesses the luster of refined gold, while in his hand, beautiful with young coral, he holds a skull; and upon his copper-red lip is a white smile—this is a wondrous combination!
May the grace of the one whose head bears the moon bring you well-being. || 30 ||

May this wondrous arrangement of the moon-crested Lord bring you well-being: his matted locks possessing the luster of refined gold, his hand—beautiful with its young coral-like fingers—holding a skull, and his copper-red lips bearing a white smile.

May she, whose complexion is most pure, who is worthy of worship by the Lord of the Gods whose every desire is fulfilled, and who is as meritorious as the speech of the best of poets, grant you supreme prosperity.
May the multitude of particles from the dust of the feet of the one whose crest-jewel is the young moon [Śiva] be for your [protection]. || 31 ||

May the multitude of dust-particles from the feet of the one whose crest-jewel is the young moon—the dust which possesses a most pure luster through its connection [to him], which is worthy of worship by the Lord of the Gods whose every desire is fulfilled, and which is meritorious—grant you supreme welfare, just as the speech of the best of poets does. May that chest of his protect you, which is variegated by the splendor of the dark-blue hue of the great sapphire on the hood of the formidable Lord of Serpents, who has been made into a necklace; may it conceal... [the world].
The mark of the musk-deer of the musk-patch upon the tips of the breasts of the daughter of the Lord of Men [Kṛṣṇa], which belongs to the Moon-crested One [Śiva].

May the chest of the Moon-crested Lord protect you—variegated by the shimmering reflection of the intense sapphire-blue hue of the lordly hood of the serpent king, which has been made into a decorative border; and where the mark of musk on the tips of the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King is concealed.
May the throat of the Blue-throated One, possessing a luster dark as a garland of fresh blue lotuses, be for your wisdom. He who...
Through its union with the coils of Vāsuki, white as a *ketakī* flower, it assumes the beauty of the vault of heaven split open by the mass of its body. || 33 ||

May that throat of the Blue-Throated One (Śiva) be for your good fortune—the throat which, through its union with the coils of Vāsuki white as the *ketakī* flower, assumes the beauty of the celestial vault streaked by the flow of the Gaṅgā; which possesses a luster dark as a garland of fresh blue lotuses;
and who, possessing incomparable grace, fondles upon his head like a child the Son of the Milk Ocean who has taken up residence at the soles of his lotus feet.
May that Lord, an ocean of compassion and beloved of his devotees, grant you joy. || 34 ||

May that Lord, the ocean of compassion and beloved of those who take refuge in him, grant you joy— he who, with incomparable grace, caresses upon his own head the young son of the Milky Ocean, who has taken up residence at the base of his own lotus feet.

She whose beauty is enhanced by royal swans and peacocks, and who immediately attains clarity when the thick veil of clouds has vanished— just as the autumn at the beginning of the season following the end of the rains.
May the eye of Śambhu, which brings to fruition the desired results, be for your welfare. 35.

May the eye of Śambhu grant you the ripening of desired fruits— its beauty enhanced by the king of swans and fire, having just cast off its veil of clouds, it attains clarity like the sky at the beginning of autumn following the end of the rainy season;

may that body of the Supreme Lord, which conceals the submarine fire within while the moon has arisen, and which is graced by the embrace of the celestial river, be like the Ocean-born goddess (Lakṣmī), [bestowing] elephants, horses, and jewels.
May He, who brings about the attainment of glory for those with well-disposed minds, grant you the nectar of His vision.

May the gaze of the Supreme Lord—which conceals the sun and fire while revealing the risen moon, which is as beautiful as the embrace of the celestial river, and which bestows upon the wise the fortune of elephants, horses, and jewels—be for your immortality like the body of the ocean.

For therein the fire does not desire even a spark without extending its tongue; the sun, having lost its luster, does not approach it night after night; and even the waning moon does not resort to it.
May those three eyes of the enemy of Tripura, which are the abode of Śrī, be for your prosperity. || 37 ||

May those three eyes of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) be for your prosperity—those three abodes of glory which the sun does not approach night after night when its rays have departed and it no longer desires even a grain of light by stretching out its tongue; nor does the waning moon ever resort to them.

Therein, the sun never experiences the northern solstice even in the winter season, nor does the moon suffer the loss of its digits even during the dark fortnight, nor does its radiance ever grow dim.
May the three eyes of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), which contain fire by day, protect you there. || 38 ||

May those three eyes of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) protect you—those in which the sun does not undergo its northern course even in the winter season, where there is no shedding of rays from the cool-rayed moon even during the dark fortnight, and where the fire does not carry a diminished luster even by day. [May that Goddess protect you], resorting to whom the sun (the jewel of the sky) possesses a beautiful radiance; who rendered the fire of the end of desire (Kālāgni) devoid of its heat; and who is the earth of nectar born from the moon.
May those glances of Śarva, whose body is auspicious, be for your welfare. || 39 ||

May those glances of Śarva’s body—which possess a splendor delightful to behold; which the sun, the jewel of the sky, has resorted to; which, being tireless, rendered the God of Love and Death devoid of their power; and which are the earth for the nectar born of the moon—grant you auspicious prosperity.
May they nourish you, [the glances] of him who was agitated by the fear of interrupting the affectionate confidence of Gaurī when she was shy at their first union.
The mind of the one adorned with serpents felt remorse at that moment, having burned the body of Darpa who had performed his duty.

May the mind of the serpent-adorned Lord Śiva—distressed by the fear of breaking the intimacy of his affectionate confidence with Gaurī, who was shy at their first union; a mind feeling remorse for having burned the body of Darpa (Kāma) to accomplish the task of that moment; a mind whose matted locks hold fragments of skulls, whose hand holds the moon, the nectar-water, and the simple poison in his throat, and who undergoes prostration before Indra and the other gods—may that mind nourish your hearts. His departure... [is also there].
And may that Hara, who removes the miserable state of even a cow, always protect you. || 41 ||
May that Hara—who has fragments of skulls upon his matted locks, who holds the moon in his hand, and whose throat is graced by straight poison;

who is bowed down by Indra and other gods, yet moves about with a bull; and on whose head the earth shines like a wreath of flowers, while he himself rests upon the serpent Śeṣa as an armlet—may he forever remove your misfortunes. May he, upon whose... [the earth shines].
May Sarasvatī, whose every word is no different from a stream of the Lord’s nectar, destroy all your misfortunes. 42.

May the speech of that Lord— which shines upon his arm like the serpent Śeṣa supporting the earth upon his head, and which is no different from a cascade of nectar— destroy all your misfortunes. He whom the glorious Kalpavṛkṣa tree could not satisfy, whom one cannot reach even by meeting the essence of elixirs, and who is not obtainable even through the most profound yogic practices— he [is that Lord].
May that grace bestowed by Hara, which is not common to others, remove your sin. || 43 ||

May that extraordinary grace bestowed by Hara remove your sin—that grace which the glorious Kalpavṛkṣa tree could not provide for its attainment; having encountered which, there is no longer thirst for the essence of elixirs (*rasāyana*); and which cannot be obtained even through the oblations of profound yoga.
For liberation is indeed the supreme goal of human endeavor, and those who know its inner nature perceive nothing else as an obstacle to it. What more need be said? Let that alone suffice.
May your devotion to the crest-ornament of the crescent moon, composed of nectar, be unbroken. || 44 ||

For liberation is indeed the one supreme goal of human endeavor; yet, since even those who know it perceive obstacles within it, may that very devotion to Him—whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon—be forever unbroken for you. He, in whom the peacock of Guha sports with the flickering tongues of the serpent of worldly existence, and he who draws the trunk of the elephant-faced god, and he who is the lion of the Daughter of the Mountain King... [He is].
And may that abode of Śambhu grant you prosperity—that abode where the buffalo, the son of the Sun (Yama), takes delight in the neighing of the horses of the Sun. || 45 ||

May that abode of Śambhu grant you splendor—that abode where Guha and his peacocks find joy through the flickering of the tongues of the serpent of worldly existence; where the lion of the Mountain King’s daughter and the elephant-faced one find joy through the dragging of each other's trunks; and where the buffalo of the Sun’s son finds joy through the neighing of the Sun’s horses. May it bestow its light upon you.

May that third eye of Śambhu, whose flood cannot be surpassed even by the waters of the Ganges in eclipsing great splendor, spread for you prosperity and bliss—that eye in which that Kāma, the conqueror of the three worlds, became one whose desires were shattered; and in which that Kāla, when his time had come, attained the insignificance of a moth.

*Anvaya:* *yasmin sa tribhuvanajayī kāmaḥ bhagnakāmaḥ jātaḥ; yasmin prāptakālaḥ sa kālaḥ śalabhalaghutām [lebhe]*... *Translation:* In which [eye] that Kāma, the conqueror of the three worlds, became one whose desires were shattered; and in which that Kāla, when his time had arrived, attained the insignificance of a moth... [may that third eye of Śambhu spread for you prosperity and bliss].*
May that third eye of Śambhu, at the mere mention of whose greatness the current of the Gaṅgā loses its power, spread for you beloved and supreme welfare.
O Lord! I do not behold your face, which delights the three eyes and mocks the full moon, even though I am your servant.
O Lord! I know that even such a state of union as this has been bestowed by you out of compassion, yet it appears to me like a mockery.

May that God—who made Darpaka (Kāma) a fuel for the fire of his wrath; who rendered Yama, the end-maker of the worlds, one who knows how to sever the very root of pride; and who is capable of leading away every instance of the loss of intellect—may he spread fearlessness for you on the path without obstacle. (47)

May that Lord— who made Kāma a fuel for the fire of his wrath, who made Yama the bringer of death to the worlds, and who is capable of bringing to an end all the decline of the intellect of the wise— spread unimpeded security for you on the path.

May the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the Destroyer of Smara, protect you— He whose row of upward-pointing toe-nails, reddened by the mass of filaments falling from the *mandāra* garlands on the heads of the prostrate lords of gods and demons, appears like a line of planets accompanied by their satellites, out of envy for the moon (the lover of the dark-headed Śyāmā).

**Anvaya:** *śiraḥśyāmākāmukamatsareṇa sopagrahāṇāṃ grahāṇāṃ paṅktiḥ prahvasurāsureśvaraśiro...* *(The construction continues with the comparison of the toe-nails to the line of planets, which are "accompanied by satellites" [sopagrahāṇām] due to the envy of the moon, who is the lover of the dark-headed Śyāmā.)*

May that Destroyer of Smara, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, protect you— he whose feet are resorted to by the Mandara garland under the guise of his upturned rows of nails, which are tawny with the mass of filaments dripping from it.

May those feet of that Lord, which are worshipped by the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn with Mandāra, Kunda, and Kumuda flowers, and which are not dull because they extinguish the heat of the impurities of sin, grant you prosperity.
May this hymn bestow joy upon you, like the Mandākinī river. || 49 ||
May the praise of that Lord—which the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn offer with the Mandāra, Kunda, and Kumuda flowers—be not in vain;
like the Mandākinī, may it bestow joy upon you by quelling the heat of the impurity of sin.
May he whose body is smeared with ashes, who is mounted upon a bull as white as frost and rests upon the shoulders of the mountain of moon-white Jyotīrasa stone, be for your welfare.
The God, the beloved of Kātyāyanī, whose pure luster is like that of a young swan sporting upon a magnificent white lotus blooming in the midst of the great ocean of milk. || 50 ||

May the Lord, the beloved of Kātyāyanī—whose form is smeared with sacred ashes; who is mounted upon a bull as white as frost, resting upon the shoulders of the moon-white Jyotīrasa mountain; whose pure luster is like that of a young swan sporting upon a beautiful lotus blooming in the midst of the great ocean of milk—be for your welfare.

May Mṛḍa protect you—the God who is the protector of those burdened by fear, the Lord of both the conscious and the unconscious, the destroyer of the afflictions of the virtuous who praise Him, the bestower of equality with Himself upon His devotees, and the doer of harm to the wicked; He who is the ground for the accomplishment of enjoyment and liberation for His servants, and whose play is manifested in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.

May the God Mṛḍa protect you—he who is the protector of those terrified by worldly succession, the Lord of both the conscious and the unconscious; the destroyer of the suffering of virtuous people who praise him; the one who grants equality with himself to his devotees; the doer of harm to the wicked; the ground for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation for his servants; and he whose play is manifested through the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.

May that Dhūrjaṭi bestow upon us abundant blessings— he by whom the entire universe was brought under his command through the Sudarśana discus obtained from Kṛṣṇa, who, renowned for victory throughout the three worlds, had devoutly employed his eye in the ritual worship of the Lord’s lotus feet, just as Kṛṣṇa himself did with the Sudarśana.

May that Dhūrjaṭi grant us abundant blessings— he by whom the entire universe was brought under his command through Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna), who, like Viṣṇu, had obtained the Sudarśana [discus] from him; and who, like Viṣṇu, was served with devotion by Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna), the son of Vāsava, whose fame for victory is renowned throughout the three worlds, as he fixed his eyes upon the ritual of worshipping his lotus feet according to the *Anvaya* lineage.
May the row of lunar mansions belonging to the Blessed One—consisting of Śrīkaṇṭha with Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, and Bharaṇī; Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, and the two Bhadrapadas; Punarvasu joined with Citrā and Viśākhā;
Aṣāḍhā joined with Mūla and the hand of Akṣata; and Maghā adorned by Vaiśravaṇa—grant you prosperity, like a protective guardian of the stars. (53)

May the form of the Blessed Śrīkaṇṭha—joined with Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Bhadrapadā; conjoined with the Vasus (Dhaniṣṭhā), Citrā, and Viśākhā; fashioned from Akṣata, Hasta, Mūla, and Āṣāḍhā; adorned with Maghā; and resting upon Vaiśravaṇa (Śatabhiṣaj)—grant you prosperity like a garland of lunar mansions.

"Shatter the joints and bonds of the mountains; swell with the mass of waters of the ocean; crush the surface of the earth, which possesses the elegance of rolling upon the broad hoods of bursting serpents;
pound the sky, where the clusters of stars shriek as they are split by your mighty slap! Thus begins your fierce twilight *tāṇḍava* dance—may the illustrious Bhairava protect you! (54)

Break the joints and bonds of the mountain ranges that follow in succession; [here, having applied the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre loṭ loṭo hisvau vā ca taddhvamoḥ* and following the rule *samuccaye'nyatarasyām*, the substitution of *hi* for the third person singular imperfect occurs in the sense of conjunction; thus the form *bhinddhi* (from *abhidat*) is obtained.

The same should be understood in what follows. Make the ocean swell, so that the surface of the earth—its excellence enhanced by rolling upon the broad surfaces of the hoods of the expanding serpent—may expand.
May the illustrious Bhairava protect you—he who has commenced a fierce twilight *tāṇḍava* dance, [exclaiming] "Crush the sky! Shatter the family of the noisy stars with a full-blown slap!

Grind it into a ball!"—and may there be prosperity for you through his performance, wherein the skulls that serve as his ornaments resound with the roar of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) held upon his head, while he utters a mocking laugh.

May the body of the Lord protect you— his form which follows the playful movements of peacocks that have rushed out from caves at the sound of deep-sounding kettledrums struck by the dancing Tumburu and Nārada; his body whose ornaments of skulls mimic the sound of laughter through mouths resonating with the roar of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) held upon his head, as it is imitated by the cries of those peacocks.

May that Moon, whose greatness increases in due sequence, be for our prosperity— he who first took his station upon the surface of the foot, then attained the support of the hand, thereafter reached the state of being held in the beloved lap through the power of being placed within the auspicious gaze, and finally achieved the great majesty of being borne upon the crest of the head.
May you have the favor of your master. || 56 ||

By whose grace—the grace of Śrī Śiva—the moon first took its place at his feet; then it obtained the support of his hand; thereafter it attained the favor born from the power of being established within his auspicious gaze; and finally it reached the great majesty of ascending to his head—may that grace of the Lord, whose greatness increases in this sequence, be for your prosperity!

May this ancient poet bring you joy— the source of the emergence of that powerful poetry whose manifestation consists of faultless steps with footfalls laden with gold, whose form is charming through the freedom of unrestrained movement of a white cow, and which is intent upon the composition of a poetic structure of celebrated and wondrous creation.

May that ancient poet be for your delight— he whose single cow, with its flawless gait manifested by the placement of feet laden with gold, possesses a charming form through the freedom of its unrestrained movement, and who, through his exertion in composing a collection of celebrated and wondrous works, is the source of the emergence of powerful poetry.

May the well-spoken verses from the hymns of praise of the Teacher of the Three Worlds nourish you—verses more beautiful even than the moon, more captivating to the heart than the nectar of the innocent chatter of young women, and more enchanting even than a pearl necklace; verses that flow as a complete nectar for the ears, even when uttered by the tongues of children with disheveled hair.

**Anvaya:** *rākendoḥ api sundarāṇi, bālāṅganāmugdhālāpakathāmṛtāt api hṛdayagrāhīṇi, hārāt api param...* **Translation:** More beautiful even than the moon, more heart-captivating even than the nectar of the innocent conversation of young women, and even more exquisite than a pearl necklace... [may these words nourish you].

May the well-spoken verses of praise for the Teacher of the Three Worlds nourish you— verses that captivate even the ears of children with their lofty crests, yet flow as nectar to fill the ears of the wise. May the golden-hued sprout-like arm of the Daughter of the Mountain, clinging to the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha which possesses the luster of a fresh sapphire polished on a whetstone, protect you.
Beholding which, the six-faced Śikhin (Kārttikeya) does not abandon his fierce tāṇḍava dance, due to the delusion that it is the flickering of lightning embracing a rain-cloud. 59.

May that sprout-like arm of the Daughter of the Mountain protect you from the fear of worldly existence— she who, having observed her lineage, does not abandon her fierce *tāṇḍava* dance even when mistaken for a flash of lightning clinging to a water-laden cloud by the six-faced Fire-god; she whose golden luster is fixed upon the neck of Śiva, which possesses the brilliance of a fresh sapphire polished on a whetstone.

May that praise of Śiva bring you well-being— the praise of Him whose body serves as the very ornament of creation, whose fame acts as the ear-ornament for the women of the quarters, whose splendor is like heaven itself, and whose words act as a rain of nectar for the virtuous who have withered under the fire of ill times.

May that praise of Śiva bring you peace—that praise whose majesty is seen in these [beings]: some with bodies serving as ornaments for creation; some whose fame serves as ear-ornaments for the women of the quarters; some whose splendor is like heaven itself; and some whose speech acts as a rain of nectar for the virtuous who are withered by the fire of ill times.

Thus ends the third hymn, titled "Benediction," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*. [The Fourth Hymn]

May that enchanting form of Hari and Hara grant you auspiciousness—that singular abode for experiencing the bliss of brotherly affection among the conch, the kaustubha gem, the moon, poison, and nectar; wherein truth and dharma have established their unimpeded foundation. 1.

May that captivating form of Hara, which is established in the unobstructed state produced by the truth of the Noble Path (*anvaya-satya-dharma*), and which is the sole abode for experiencing the bliss of brotherly affection toward the conch, the Kaustubha gem, and the moon—the very nectar of immortality—grant you prosperity.
[That form] which, in the act of binding a floral crest (*āpīḍa*) and upon the bed, highly prizes his body as possessing the full splendor of enjoyment... where...
May that enchanting form of Hara, which causes the King of Serpents to rejoice exceedingly, bestow auspiciousness upon you. || 2 ||

May that body of Hara, which steals away all else, bestow auspiciousness upon you— that body which the King of Serpents rejoices in most exceedingly, highly esteeming it as his own form, possessing the full splendor of enjoyment both in the act of binding the *āpīḍa* (turban) on one side and upon his bed on the other;
a body whose half is white like the moon and the *umā* flower with its lotus-petal ornaments, while the other half is honored by the beauty of jasmine blossoms, possessing the luster of bees.
May that auspicious form of Harihara, which attains a unique splendor when drunk by the oyster-shell-like eyes of Animiṣā, bestow grace upon you. || 3 ||

May that enchanting form of Hara and Hari bestow auspiciousness upon you—a form that attains a unique beauty by being drunk from the pearl-oyster shells of their unblinking eyes: one half, white as the moon, worshipped by Umā with blue lotus petals; likewise, the other half, possessing the luster of gold, worshipped by Śrī with jasmine flowers.
Therein lies a wonder: clouds bearing bodies filled with the *jhāṅkāra* sound of the ocean of the sky, which is the flame of the fire of their eyes, carry water resting upon their hair.
May that captivating form of Harihara, characterized by the fleeting flash of a steady lightning bolt, bestow auspiciousness upon you. || 4 ||

May that enchanting form of Hara grant you auspiciousness— that form in which clouds resting upon his hair, their bodies filled with the rumbling of the ocean and the flames of the fire of his eye, bear the wonderful occurrence of steady lightning and laughter;

and [may it grant auspiciousness] to him whose limbs are distressed by the shrinking of his movements out of fear of the narrowness caused by the half-lotus dwelling in his navel, as he desires to divide his body in half.
May that auspicious form of Hari and Hara, wherein even Druhiṇa [resides], bestow blessings upon you. || 5 ||

May that enchanting form of Hara grant you auspiciousness— the form in which even Brahmā, the progenitor, having his limbs distressed by the contraction of his movements due to the fear of being crowded within the lotus of his navel (which was but half its size),

desired to divide his own body in half; and where Agni blazes with even greater intensity, perceiving both the Sun and the Moon situated before his eyes as a single, undivided form, while his own body is but a half.
May that body of his, which has attained lightness yet remains captivating and removes all obstacles, bestow auspiciousness upon you.

May that body of Harihara grant you auspiciousness— that body in which fire, though it has entered [the mouth], blazes even more intensely out of anger upon perceiving the sun and moon residing in his eyes as possessing unbroken forms, and perceiving its own body to be but half;
in which the lotus, though virtuous, sensitive, fruitful, and rooted, has fallen from the hand in that abode of sovereignty, while the conch remains.
May that enchanting form of Hari and Hara, which maintains a mode contrary to that [of the world], bestow auspiciousness upon you. || 7 ||
In that abode of sovereignty, the lotus—possessing qualities, sensitive to beauty, and complete with its stalk—fell from his hand;
whereas the conch, possessing the opposite characteristics, remained in his grasp. May that form of Harihara bestow auspiciousness upon you.
And where the waters of the celestial river, emerging from the tips of his feet, ascend unimpeded to his head—that which is both most wonderful and beautiful.
And may that auspicious form of Hari and Hara, which is unrestrained, bestow grace upon you. || 8 ||

Anvaya: May that body of yours—which, in one place, has its feet extended into the exceedingly wonderful, beautiful, and unrestrained waters of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) which flow without hindrance, and in another place, ascends the head—being itself exceedingly wonderful, beautiful, unrestrained, and captivating like Hara, grant you auspiciousness.
Thus ends [the hymn] composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddhara, accompanied by the commentary named *Śrī Premamakaranda*. Regarding the Blessed Maheśvara...
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the fourth hymn is titled "The Octet of Auspiciousness.
The fifth hymn:
She who is intent on removing the distress of those in need, as gracious as a shimmering wave, like the celestial river Ganges, and as cooling as the essence of nectar—
Her speech, like a digit of the moon, takes refuge solely in Śiva; she is victorious, like the Goddess Īśvarī herself. || 1 ||

Victorious is the speech of the true poet, which takes refuge solely in Śiva; like compassion, it is intent on removing the suffering of those who have fallen into distress; like the celestial river, it is beautiful with its surging waves; like a digit of the moon, it is cooled by the essence of nectar; and like the Goddess herself, it has Śiva as its sole refuge.

Victorious are those poets who bear in their hearts that Goddess of Speech, upon whose head the King of Serpents rests as his crown while supporting the earth like a garland, and in whom that Lord of Speech dwells.

Victorious are those poets who bear in their hearts that Goddess of Speech, upon whose head the Lord of Serpents wears the earth like a garland, and whom the Lord of Eloquence (Bṛhaspati) serves as his turban;
for they gather the flowers of well-spoken verses from the creeper of speech that has grown in the garden of their own mouths— verses that are blessed, pure, fragrant, and entwined with excellence.
They place these descriptions of the virtuous like ear-ornaments upon the ridges of their ears. || 3 ||

Fortunate are the poets who, having gathered the pure, fragrant, virtue-laden, and exquisitely colored flowers of well-spoken verses from the creepers of speech that have grown in the garden of their own mouths, place them as ear-ornaments upon the ears of the virtuous;
they do so with words enriched by compositions beautiful with a flow of honey-drops falling unrestrainedly from the ears of the wise. Fortunate are these good poets.
They, too, bring them joy with their sincere expressions of wonder and words of praise. || 4 ||

Fortunate are those good poets who delight the ears of the virtuous with words enriched by compositions beautiful with drops of honey flowing without restraint; they [the virtuous] also delight their ears with cries of "well done! arising from genuine aesthetic wonder. Victorious are certain poets whose voices are charming through the composition of continuous and faultless literary works; even when not yet fully savored, their work causes wonder in the ear.
The sweet speech was indeed made, like nectar itself. || 5 ||

Victorious are those certain poets whose speech is charming due to its skillful composition and seamless connection of syntactical links; their sweet expression, even when its aesthetic flavor has not yet been fully relished, produces a wonder like nectar as soon as it is placed upon the ear.
Victorious are those great poets, like sea-faring merchants who have beheld the further shore of the infinite great ocean of literature.
I perceive that the virtuous perfume their mouths in assemblies with the delicate fragments of cloves from the garlands of well-spoken verses.

I consider those great poets to be victorious, like sea-faring merchants who have reached the further shore of the infinite ocean of literature; for with the delicate fragments of cloves from the blossoms of their well-spoken verses, the virtuous scent their mouths in the assemblies.
On the stage-ground of the tip of the tongue, the Goddess of Speech herself is devoted to the festive dance of the playful performance of that true poet.
The necks, crowned with earrings and adorned with arched eyebrows, attain the status of masters in the instruction of dance for those who are skillful.

The Goddess of Speech herself, ever devoted to the festive dance of graceful play upon the stage of the tip of the tongue of a poet who possesses a lineage of excellence, becomes the preceptor for the art of dancing before those fortunate ones whose heads are crowned with the earrings of their arched eyebrows.

What is the use of the poetry of that poet whose verse does not cause the head of his opponent to reel when it strikes his heart? And what is the use of the arrow of that archer which does not make another’s head whirl when it has struck his chest?
Harlots, parasites, and the like attract the wealthy merely for the sake of their bellies, making them vessels for even a single grain of wealth;
whereas the lords of poets, skilled in composing series of eloquent verses drenched with devotion to the one adorned by serpents [Śiva], attract those who are mature.
Those such as courtesans and parasites, who have made themselves mere vessels for the crumbs of wealth obtained through their lineage and bellies, win over only monasteries;
whereas the lords of poets, skilled in composing series of well-spoken verses drenched with devotion for the one adorned by serpents, win over the truly mature.
Blessed is that certain great poet, a performer of the poet’s task, who resembles the moon of Kārtika in removing the suffering of the world, and whose [works] they sing.
It is like the wonderful life-story of the one whose crest is the young moon, which purifies the three worlds and is the work of a master artist.
