Succession: There is some fortunate and excellent poet whose poetic work—which dispels the suffering of the world, which resembles the moon of the month of Kārtika, and which purifies the three worlds—is sung by the wise like the life-story of the virtuous Śiva, the one who bears the crescent moon on his crest.
One shines as the jewel that adorns the three worlds and the friend of the assembly of the virtuous; the second is the Sun of Poetry. They proclaim the excellence of his greatness.
Even the mountains performed the act of grasping his feet with their heads.
The lineage of his descendants is the jewel that adorns the three worlds; he alone is the sun who shines in the sky, while his poetry shines upon the earth.
Even the kings of the world, bowing their heads, proclaim the excellence of his greatness.
His speech, flowing like nectar from his mouth with its curved elegance adorned by the beauty of frost and pearls, is like the celestial river Ganges upon the head of a mountain.
Or like the crescent moon of Hara, she dwells within him; let us bow to that excellent poet. || 11 ||

We bow to that good poet in whose mouth dwells well-spoken verse— flowing like the nectar of logical connection, possessing the beauty of a necklace of frost, and graced with elegant, curved inflections— just as the celestial river Ganges dwells upon the head of Hara, or as the crescent moon rests upon the head of Hara; [and we bow to] the intellect of the virtuous, which by its very nature has attained excellence through its qualities, and which maintains its first, innate transformation.
And by the grace of the one whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon, his speech meets with no obstruction whatsoever.

The intellect of the virtuous, having attained growth through its inherent qualities and being pure by nature, and the speech of poets— both bearing their first natural transformation— never encounter any obstruction whatsoever by the grace of the Moon-crested Lord.

The eloquent utterance of poets, whose words are profound and filled with the composition of grace arising from the remembrance of the feet of the One who has the Moon as his crest-ornament, sustains [this state].
The playful sound of the golden anklets of the Goddess of Speech, as she dances upon the stage of the lotus-face. || 13 ||
The eloquent speech of poets, whose words are overflowing with the grace of recollecting the feet of the moon-crested Lord (Śiva),
bears the playful resonance of the golden anklets of the Goddess of Speech dancing upon the stage of their lotus-like faces.
When poetry is contemplated, the eyes— half-closed in rapture— spontaneously abandon their flickering restlessness and assume its smooth serenity.
Leaving aside their innate [beauty], the creeper-like eyebrows of the accomplished ones, the foremost among poets, [shine forth]. 14.
When the eminent poets who compose with refined intellects contemplate their own poetry, their half-closed eyes abandon their natural restlessness;
yet their creeper-like eyebrows, casting off their smoothness, seize that very restlessness.
Victorious is that certain unprecedented ripening of merit performed in the past, white as frost and a pearl necklace, which now—
It reflects back in the pure, well-composed verses of good poets, which are like the rays of the young moon adorning their crowns.

Victorious is that unprecedented ripening of the merit previously accumulated by the lineage of true poets—a merit as white as frost and a necklace of pearls—which now reflects within these stainless hymns of praise adorned with crescent moons;

which, having been tasted by the wise, reveals the expansion of consciousness through the dancing of the eyebrows grown thick by the power of reflection upon subtle truths. [The wise], having savored that [merit]...
Victorious is that [speech] of the elephant-like poets, which bears upon its face the nectar of well-spoken verses. || 16 ||

Victorious is the nectar of the eloquent sayings of the elephant-like poets, which those of refined intellect, having tasted it, bear upon their faces a blossoming of consciousness signaled by the dancing of their eyebrows as they contemplate the perception of subtle meanings;
even those who understand nothing more than mere words and meanings drink it with their ears like deer drinking a melodic strain.
With the expansion of all their faculties restrained, they become as if fixed in a painting; let us praise that voice of the supreme poet.

We praise that speech of the lord of poets, which even those who do not understand even a mere word or its meaning become like deer— drinking it in with their ears as if it were a melodic chant (*mūrcchanā*), their entire range of sensory faculties stilled,
remaining as if fixed in a painting; for it captivates the heart of a deer, so what need is there to mention conscious beings?
Where can such a virtuous man be found, whose pair of creeper-like eyebrows the lords of poets regard with the grace of two swarms of bees fluttering over the lotuses of his eyes? (18)

Where can that noble man be found, whose pair of creeper-like eyebrows—possessing the grace of two swarms of bees fluttering over the lotuses of his eyes—is observed by the lords of poets as they display their own compositions?
Is even the essence of musk, with its vast abundance of fragrance, truly essential? And does even a garland of jasmine not flourish [without it]?
Joy flows forth if the Goddess who bestows the flow of honey grants her favor.

Sequence: If the Goddess of Speech pours forth a flow of honey, then what is the use of the vast abundance of fragrance from the musk deer? At that time, even the essence of that [musk], though essential, becomes utterly worthless; even a garland of *saumanasa* flowers does not produce joy (*saumanasya*).
May this work of the poet, which is skilled at severing the exhaustion manifest on the desert path of worldly existence, be victorious—that by which [all else] has been made to be forgotten.
The path presided over by Yamunā is well known to us as the Vaibudhasaindhava.

May this poetic work prevail, which is skilled in severing the exhaustion of those traveling the path of the demon Māra that is cyclic existence; for by it, even our well-known path to the divine Sindhava (the ocean) has been made to forget its fame, as it is now presided over by Yamunā.
It is like the mountain Ekapiṅgala, which was always brought to the state of being a dwelling place by the Destroyer of Madana (Śiva)—a mountain profound, pure, and cool with floods of nectar.
Within the mind, internal objects flash forth; without meritorious deeds, where can such a person be found? || 21 ||

In whose mind—pure, profound in its logical consistency, and cooled by a flood of nectar—the Destroyer of Love has eternally made his abode, objects of meaning flash forth within as if in Lake Mānasa; where can such a one (the good poet) be found except through meritorious deeds?

From him, as he gazes upon them, there flow forth rays of light, pure as the waves of the celestial river, bestowing grace upon all who behold them, like rays of speech that distill the essence of nectar.
This lord of the twice-born, the sole ornament of all the quarters, is victorious. || 22 ||

Pure like the waves of the ocean of the day of the lunar fortnight (Anvaya), bestowing clarity upon the vision of whoever beholds them, and emitting the essence of nectar— may that Lord of the Twice-born (Brahmin) be victorious, whose rays spread in all directions, and who is the sole ornament of the universe.

Victory to him who is devoted to the praise of Śaṅkara, by whose side even a light syllable attains gravity when it comes into conjunction with a heavy syllable refined by supreme meaning, even if it stands at the end of a foot.
Whose heart would not find joy upon attaining a life of pure conduct and a good reputation? (23)

Whose heart does not attain joy upon reaching this *Suśloka*, which is adorned with logical sequence (*anvaya*) and ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), whose syllables—even those light ones at the end of a line—attain heaviness through their conjunction, which possesses pure meter (*pariśuddhavṛtta*), and is dedicated to the praise of Śaṅkara?
For here indeed the majesty of Sarasvatī prevails among the virtuous; she is the physician who heals the three worlds when they are obscured by the sprouting of *māyā* and delusion. She manifests...
[That which leads] to the removal of the exhaustion, suffering, and affliction produced by the calamities resulting from the continuous bondage of old age, death, and disease. || 24 ||

Indeed, that power of Sarasvatī which belongs to the virtuous and which is proclaimed here as the physician for the three worlds—hidden though it be by the sprouts of illusion and delusion—is capable of removing the exhaustion, affliction, and calamity born from the continuous bonds of old age, death, and disease.
Victorious is that certain transformation of the poets’ speech, which bestows upon those who contemplate it some indescribable excellence of wonder; for when it is released...
But when [He is satisfied], thoughts arise [in the mind] that He is nectar, the supreme good, the beloved abode, and the highest station. (25)
Victorious is that certain consummation of the poets' speech which, bestowing upon those who contemplate its logical connection some indescribable excellence of aesthetic wonder,

gives rise in the mind— once it has been created— to such thoughts as: "This alone is nectar," "This alone is the supreme good," "This alone is the beloved abode," and "This alone is the highest station."

Victorious is the grace of the Goddess of Speech, whose form is the nectar of the poetry of the most eminent poets; it is as sweet as the essence of fresh ambrosia and liquid sandalwood paste, its beauty capable of pacifying the onset of the distressing delusions of wandering through the desert of worldly existence, having rendered the conditions of misfortune mild like a slow-dripping stream of honey. (26)

Triumphant is the grace of the Goddess of Speech— flowing with the honey of logical consistency, diminishing the adventitious afflictions of misfortune, beautiful for its power to soothe the onset of distress from wandering in the desert of worldly existence, as delicious as the essence of fresh sandalwood paste upon the earth, possessing a body of nectar in the form of the poetry of the most eminent poets.
With eyes moistened by abundant tears rising from the outpouring of intense bliss...

The faultless words of poets, moist with nectar, grace the faces of the fortunate—faces where the sandy banks of the forehead ripple as the creeper-like brows move gracefully, and the cheeks are covered with the blossoming flowers of rising horripilation. (27)

The faultless and nectar-drenched words of poets bring about for the fortunate: a face with eyes moistened by abundant tears rising from a flow of intense bliss; a forehead-sandbank shimmering with the playful undulation of the creeper-like eyebrows; and cheeks made to blossom with clusters of bristling horripilation.
For the fortunate, these words flow as nectar in the heart, become clusters of *mallikā* flowers as ornaments in the ear, and turn into strings of pearls upon the sandbank of the throat.

The words— which possess a delightful surge like the breaking waves of the milk-ocean tossed by mountains, and which contain the narrative composition of the adornment of the regions beloved by Śyāmā— melt as nectar into the hearts and ears of the fortunate.

Upon the sandy banks of the throats of the fortunate, there arise—under the guise of their speech—the clusters of blossoms that are the ornaments of the *valanmallikā* flower, appearing as if they were strings of pearls.
These emerge from the mouth of the Lord of Caṇḍī, who dwells within the pericarp of the heart and whose heat is dispelled by the awakening nectar of his well-spoken words.
Are these the luster of the jewels in his matted locks? Are they the filaments of the flowers in his garland? Or are they the rays of the moon upon his crown?
Are these the waves of the river of the gods? || 29 ||

Do the lusters of the jewels in the crown-serpent of the Lord of Caṇḍī—who dwells in the lotus-heart of those whose fever is dispelled by the nectar of their own well-spoken words under the guise of speech in the mouths of the fortunate ones—rise up? Or do the needle-like filaments of the flower-garland rise up?
Or do the rays of the moon upon his crest rise up? Or do the waves of the celestial river rise up?

That joy which arises from the sweet hymn of praise to Śambhu— which is akin to nectar, which produces intense bliss, which holds the moon (the bearer of nectar), which is like the full moon, which has a mature flow, which is naturally cool, which is a waterfall from the celestial river Gaṅgā, which is filled with deep love, which removes the fever of passion, and which is found in the lips of the unrestrained Rāmā— is not to be found elsewhere.

That joy which arises from the sweet engagement in the praise of Śambhu—which is like nectar to the ears—does not exist even in the full moon that holds the nectar-ray and causes intense bliss; nor does it exist in the natural coolness of the cascading waters of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) with its full flow. Likewise, it does not exist in the lips of the unruly Rāmā (Rati), which remove the fever of love and are filled with deep passion.

To whom on earth is a true poet not praiseworthy—his speech being full of vitality, sweet, clear through its lucidity, pure in its refinement, endowed with distinct expression and figurative power, distinguished by appropriate styles and meanings, adorned with ornaments, grounded in proper meters, mature, free from discordance, possessed of virtuous conduct, and extraordinary? Just as such is the sequence of his own well-spoken verses. (31)

Whose poetic sequence—endowed with *anvaya* (coherence), vigor, sweetness, clarity through lucidity, purity of refinement, distinguished by its style (*rīti*) through the manifestation of denotation and suggestion, adorned with appropriate meanings, established in the proper meters (*vṛtta*), possessed of maturity, free from discordance, following good conduct, and being extraordinary—is not praised on earth? (The meaning is: it is praised by everyone.)

If the Blessed Goddess Vāgīśvarī, who is capable of performing benefit for both oneself and others, has been obtained by some through their former merits like a wish-fulfilling creeper, yet she remains difficult to attain again;

then what sin, other than a curse, could bear fruit in the mire of arrogance for those ignorant ones who, struck down by evil desires, show contempt for the instructions given by those who know that Truth?

If the divine Goddess of Speech is obtained—even through the remnants of former merits—like a wish-fulfilling creeper, then she, who is capable of bringing benefit to oneself and others, becomes difficult to find again. When she is cast away into the mire of arrogance by the ignorant, who are struck down by false hopes and disregard the instructions of those who know the truth, what fruit does she bear other than a curse and sin? (The meaning is that she bears nothing but that.)
Sporting with confidence, her graceful steps refined by art, languid in her charm, and possessing a noble form envied for no reason by her enemies,

she— she whose eyes are like Gaurī’s— cries out piteously with tears, having been cast into the blind well of proud kings by those seized by the crocodiles of desire under the guise of eloquent words, as if by fishermen. 33.
A cow—sporting with confidence in her lineage, with graceful steps, languid in her charm, and of noble form—is suddenly and without cause eyed with arrogance by enemies (bad poets).
Seized by the crocodiles of desire, she is cast like fishermen into the dark well of proud kings; such a cow weeps piteously with the guise of eloquent verses.

She sighs hotly, scratches the ground, and offers no word of affection for her beloved lord through her eloquent verses; she rests her cheek upon the palm of her hand. Seized by a heavy fever of heart, Sarasvatī has been driven by wretched fate to become a vessel for the shame of praising a king who has displayed such cruel anger in vain.

Brought to a state of shameful indignity by base poets— whose hopes are destroyed by their addiction to even a fragment of wealth— who vainly display hymns to a miserly king out of anger, the Goddess of Speech, overcome by the fever of her heart, sighs hotly, scratches the ground, fails to offer praise for the beloved Lord through her eloquent verses, and rests her cheek upon her palm.
When the Goddess of Speech is brought to ruin in an improper place by those of ruined intellect, she leads only to reproach, defeat, great suffering, or sin.
But when bestowed upon the worthy in a fitting place, she brings about renown, prosperity, peace of mind, service to others, and ultimately,
the attainment of liberation.

But when it is spent in the proper place by the virtuous, it serves to bring renown to the good, their prosperity, the peace of their minds, the benefit of others, and ultimately, the attainment of auspiciousness.
How can these words not captivate the heart, which is so fondly addicted to the play of tasting the nectar of the various treatises composed by former poets?

But for certain wise ones who are eloquent in uttering words of praise for the Lord, these [teachings] will become objects of longing on earth for those like me, who are touched by the afflictions of existence. (36)

How can these words of mine captivate the hearts of the wise— hearts that are spoiled by the sport of tasting the nectar of various treatises composed by ancient poets? Furthermore, how will they become objects of longing for certain people on earth like myself, who are touched by the afflictions of worldly existence and who are intent upon uttering words of praise for the Lord?

Thus ends the sixth hymn, titled "Praise of the Poet and the Poetry," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flower-Praises) to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
Victorious is Hara, whose lotus-feet have the rays of their toenails made thick by the sprouting luster of the crest-jewels of all the foremost gods;
he who, with the threefold light fashioned by his three wide eyes, has dispelled the pervasive darkness of the three worlds.

Victorious is Hara! His lotus-feet have the rays of their nails made thick by the sprouts of light from the crest-jewels of all the foremost of the sky-dwellers; he triumphs, having dispelled the pervasive darkness of the three worlds with the triad of splendors fashioned by his three wide eyes.
Victorious is he whose intense pain from the heat of the fire of his fierce eye has been extinguished by the sprinkling of the waters of the celestial pool!
Hara is the benefactor of the three worlds, endowed with the majesty and power of a brilliance that is incomparable, unique, and blazing with inconceivable conduct. || 2 ||

Victorious is Hara, whose intense heat and agony were extinguished by the sprinkling of water from the celestial pool of the lineage of gods; who, through his inconceivable conduct, bestows benefit upon the three worlds with the majesty of a blazing, peerless, and radiant power;
and who triumphs, his beautiful throat embraced by the lovely creeper-like arms of the Daughter of the Mountain, its dark splendor intensified by the shimmering poison.
Hara is one whose joy in dancing is offered by the peacocks of Guha, who are intoxicated by the delusion of seeing the unfailing clouds shimmering as they are overtaken by circles of lightning.

Victorious is Hara, whose lovely throat is embraced by the graceful vine-like arms of the Daughter of the Mountain, its dark splendor intensified by the shimmering radiance of the poison; he who inspires joy through the dance performed by the peacock of Guha, who is intoxicated by the illusion of a magnificent cloud encircled by flashes of lightning. Victorious is he, capable of releasing the noose of the Destroyer—which is terrifying with its hoods bristling with the mass of flames from the incessantly surging poison—by means of his noble [glance].

Hara is one whose heart is sprinkled with the essence of the flowing stream of the rasa of compassion, and who acts as a helmsman for those who have entered the ocean of calamity to carry them across.

Victorious is Hara, whose heart is drenched by the flow of the essence of noble compassion; who is capable of releasing the noose of Kṣapaṇaka—terrible with its hooded crest and the mass of sparks from the weapon of incessantly surging poison-fire; and who is the helmsman for crossing the ocean of calamities for those who have sought refuge in him.

Victorious is he who is praised by the hosts of gods and demons, who are filled with an abundance of joy and a sense of fearlessness obtained upon the vomiting of the poison that had issued from the ocean.
Hara is he who deluded Brahmā and Vāsudeva with the great majesty of his blazing linga, which rose from the depths of the netherworld and was impossible to surpass. || 5 ||

Victorious is Hara! He is praised by the hosts of gods and demons who are filled with an abundance of joy and a sense of security attained from swallowing the ocean-born poison; he has deluded both Brahmā and Viṣṇu by the great majesty of his blazing, insurmountable *liṅga* rising from the netherworld.
Victorious is he who, having crushed the fickle god of love burning with the fever of immense pride, has shattered the desire for worldly enjoyment.

Hara, whose throat was forcibly constricted by the Daughter of the Mountain as she trembled at the swaying of the single tawny mountain [Kailāsa] shaken by the circle of the ten-faced one's arms; || 6 ||

Victorious is Hara, whose neck was forcibly entwined by the Daughter of the Mountain—she who trembled at the shaking of Mount Ekapiṅga by the circle of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa’s arms; he who shattered the desire for worldly enjoyment, having crushed the fickle God of Love burning with the fever of immense pride awakened by his incomparable valor.
Victorious is he whose acts of restraint and grace are celebrated as the means of pacifying and countering the Asuras blinded by the excessive weight of their unassailable and surging arrogance.
Hara is the cloud of universal dissolution who effortlessly swallows the terrible forest fire of the three cities that strikes fear into the three worlds.

Victorious is Hara, whose acts of restraint and favor are celebrated for his consoling of the Asuras who were blinded by the excessive pride of their swelling power; he is the cloud of dissolution that playfully swallowed the three worlds as they were terrified by the fierce forest fire of Tripura.
Victorious is Mādhava, the consort of the wise Mādhavī, the thunderbolt that destroys sin, the ocean of the nectar of compassion, and the sole raft across the great sea of worldly existence.

Hara is the wind that scatters the grass of misfortune, the wish-fulfilling gem for the hearts of those who seek his favor, and the one who performs the play of creation and dissolution for the entire universe.

Victorious is Hara— the thunderbolt that destroys the sins of his followers, the son of Mādhavī who possesses perfect wisdom, the ocean of the nectar of compassion, the sole raft across the great sea of worldly existence, the wind that scatters the straw of misfortune, the wish-fulfilling gem for the hearts of his devotees, and the one who performs the sport of the creation and dissolution of all the worlds. Thus ends [the hymn] to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the illustrious Kashmiri Great Poet Śrī Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the sixth hymn is named "The Octet to Hara.
The seventh hymn:
Like sleep at the end of the night, like the childhood of a new bride, like the tremulous glance of one who is startled, like the celestial river, and like the narrative of Śambhu—
May the speech of the Lord of Poets bestow upon you the bliss of contentment. || 1 ||

May [the glory of Śiva], like the sleep of the sons of Anvaya, like the childhood state of a new bride, like the startled glance of the celestial river, like the story of Śambhu, and like the speech of the lords of poets, bestow upon you ultimate bliss (*nirvṛti*)— that is, the supreme good consisting in the cessation of all suffering. May the splendor of the Supreme Lord, which is the cause of extraordinary delight, the serenity of the mind, and witnessed by one’s own experience alone, shine forth within your hearts.
It is like the secret meaning of the words of a skilled poet. || 2 ||

May that supreme splendor of the Lord— which is the cause of extraordinary bliss, which gladdens the mind, which has its sole witness in one's own experience, and which is like the secret of a great poet’s words— be revealed within your hearts. That very splendor, from whose bow the infallible (Acyuta) arrow suddenly fell, fierce with its crest, like a flame from a fire, and which, as Bhairava, formerly turned cities into non-cities.
May that non-existence which shatters all fears be existence for you.

May that Bhava, the source of existence, who became Bhairava— the terrible one— who formerly rendered cities cityless with his fierce arrows discharged from his bow— those arrows which were "Acyuta" (unfailing) because they fell from his bow (cāpa), and which were "Śikhāvataḥ" (possessing crests) and "Ugra" (terrible) by virtue of their flames— may he shatter your fears. May he, the Lord of the three worlds, whose favor consists in allowing the Bull (Vṛṣa) to place its feet upon his back during the mounting of the Bull, shower nectar through his speech.
May Vṛṣākapi remove your distress. || 4 ||

May that Vṛṣākapi, the Lord of the three worlds— who, as the Bull upon whom he mounts, receives the placing of his feet in every house— and who showers nectar with his speech, remove your distress. May that Lord,
whose two feet the subduer of Pāka (Indra), whose commands are ever blazing, constantly worships, look upon us with a gaze purified by grace.
The destroyer of the god of love brought about the destruction of the obstacle to his ritual action. || 5 ||

May that Lord, the subduer of the god of love (Anaṅgaśāsana), whose two feet the subduer of Pāka (Indra) always worships and whose teachings are kindled by tradition (Anvaya-iddhaśāsana), grant us the destruction of calamities with his glance pure with grace. He whose son is the conqueror of armies (Camūrjayan), the destroyer of fear (Bhījanaka), the golden-hued (Anaka), the remover of fatigue (Klahahā), the great and most glorious (Mahāmahāḥ), and who bears matted locks as red as the rising sun (Tarunāruṇāruṇāḥ).
May Śrī, who is auspicious and free from fear, grant you fearlessness.

May he—the son of her who is the source of all, he who does not conquer the armies of the Bhīṣmas, Duryodhanas, and Karṇas; he who removes fatigue, possesses great luster, and bears matted locks as red as the rising sun, distinguished by his auspicious radiance—grant you prosperity free from fear.

Indeed, O Lord, your glance has surely fallen upon me, bringing grace moist with the nectar of compassion, honored, beneficial, and destroying all that is harmful. Therefore, by me, whose sins have been destroyed through the light of your presence, [I am transformed].
Praise has been offered with a heart full of extraordinary aspiration. || 7 ||

Anvaya: O Śambhu! Has a gracious, beneficial glance, moist with the nectar of compassion, been surely cast by you upon me? Indeed, for this reason, with an exceedingly hopeful heart, I have offered this hymn of praise to you—a hymn that dispels the disease of worldly existence. Fearing the torments of old age, sickness, and death, men who are free from envy abandon in vain the glorification of Him who is the ornament of the moon, which is like a rain from a cloudless sky.
Why do they run after elixirs? || 8 ||

Why do men— who are free from envy toward their kin, yet terrified by the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death— run in vain for the sake of elixirs (*rasāyana*), abandoning the praise of the One who is the crest-jewel that produces nectar, which is like rain from a cloudless sky? Just as even a very minute gem [neutralizes] potent poison, as even a small fire consumes a great mass of grass, and as even a young lion [overcomes its foes],...
Just as a slender lamp dispels a mass of darkness, so does the body [dispel] the herd of elephants.

Just as even a small dose of medicine overcomes a violent disease, and even a tiny amount of nectar removes the fear of consumption, so too, O Lord, even an atom of praise certainly dispels even long-standing sin in an instant. (10)

The logical sequence is as follows: just as even a very subtle gem dispels potent poison; just as even a slender fire dispels a vast mass of grass in an instant; or just as even a young lion drives away a herd of elephants; just as even a tiny lamp dispels a heavy burden of darkness;
just as even a small medicine dispels a frenzied disease; and just as even a little nectar dispels the fear of death—even so is that which is atomic.
A hymn of praise to the Lord, composed in whatever language it may be, certainly dispels even a long-standing sin in an instant.

A sequence of words characterized by profound grace through its intense composition and mastery of the Vaidarbha style, necessarily attains unbreakable beauty once it has reached the Lord who is worthy of all virtues.

The sequence of words belonging to the fortunate poet—possessing the profound grace of an effortless composition and the mature mastery of the Vaidarbha style—certainly bears imperishable beauty upon reaching a powerful lord worthy of its virtues.

For just as a woman of noble family is [worthless] without character, as a wise person is without discernment, and as sacred scripture is without the understanding of its true meaning; so too is this speech without a worthy master.
Just as the earth is [unbearable] without the great serpent.
Just as the sky is without the friend of the lotus (the sun), or as the night is without the moon, just as an assembly is without a circle of wise men, or as prosperity is without modesty; || 13 ||

Just as wisdom is without fruit without compassion, and as the status of a householder is without a good son, even so is Sarasvatī pitiable without the application of your hymn, O Lord who has the moon as his crest-jewel. 14.

The logical sequence is as follows: just as a noble lady is pitiable without virtue, just as a wise person is pitiable without discernment, just as sacred learning is pitiable without the understanding of its true meaning, just as the earth is pitiable without a serpent-like king, just as the sky is pitiable without the sun, just as the night is pitiable without the moon, and just as [a gathering] is pitiable without a circle of refined people; so too is it with this.
An assembly is lamentable without discipline,

just as prosperity is lamentable without wisdom, and just as the state of a householder is lamentable without a virtuous son, even so is the Goddess Sarasvatī (Speech) lamentable without the employment of this hymn to the one whose crest is the moon.

Even the goddess Ramā is not pleasing to my mind, and even Kṣamā (Forgiveness) is unable to console me; for me, the only remedy is the eloquent Sarasvatī, who is devoted to the Blessed One and is full of vitality in shattering the affliction of worldly existence. || 15 ||

Even Queen Anvaya-Ramā is not so pleasing to my mind, nor is Queen Kṣamā capable of winning me over; rather, for the shattering of the affliction of worldly existence, only the singular, divine, and eloquent Sarasvatī is capable. That mountain, which is insentient, fond of its base location, and whose heart is wounded by hundreds of various external conditions, is that upon whose foot-base he is long served.
Even by the lords of sages, he is regarded as one whose mind is pure. || 16 ||

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "That mountain (*Kailāsa*), though insentient, fond of a base location, and its interior pierced by hundreds of diverse external adjuncts (*upādhi*), has a pure mind and is long frequented at its foot by the lords of sages; this is the emergence of fruit from the great cosmic tree whose essence is the refuge of Gaurī’s Lord"—this is the connection with the verse to be cited hereafter.

That serpent, who by nature abides on a path censured by the righteous, who is soiled and moves crookedly—he, though possessing a massive body, is a great serpent adorned with earrings and a crest-jewel. 17.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: That serpent which by nature dwells on paths censured by the virtuous, which is soiled and crooked in its movement—even he has become a great serpent (*mahābhujaṅga*) adorned with earrings and a crest-jewel, possessing a vast hood; this is the emergence of fruit from the great wish-granting tree whose essence is refuge in the Lord of Gaurī. The connection is to be understood as before.

Although the moon, consisting of mere digits, is by nature hollow and accustomed to constant contact with dull matter, it bears a body that is free from stain, composed of nectar, radiant, and devoid of the rising of defects. (18)

This is the emergence of fruit from the great wish-granting tree (kalpamahāmahīruha) whose very nature is its reliance upon Gaurīśvara; what conscious person indeed would not strive to reach it for their own welfare? (19)
(An *sandānitaka* verse:

Although the moon—composed of digits, naturally insignificant, and accustomed to constant association with the dull-witted—is by nature so base, yet that very moon bears a body that is free from blemish, composed of nectar, devoid of the rising of defects, and radiant; for it has become the very self of the great wish-granting tree of the world, which takes refuge in the Lord of Gaurī.
Indeed, what conscious person with a desire for their own welfare would not strive to reach this [place] which takes refuge in Gaurīśvara?
(The meaning is: rather, everyone indeed would.
[It is superior] even to a roadside tree that dispels the fatigue of wandering in the great desert scorched by the summer heat—a tree from which the flood of the Yamunā’s waters has met.
Even from the flooding caused by the weight of the waters of the three paths. || 20 ||

Even more than from the sequence of words that are both clear and profound, filled with the very essence of Sarasvatī’s grace; and even more than from the playful embrace of a woman whose breasts are marked with musk and thick saffron. (21)

Flowing with the liquid essence of the nectar of intense bliss, this unfailing sound "Namaḥ Śivāya" causes wonder in my heart, which is distressed by worldly existence, as it resounds throughout this entire path of the universe. 22.

(Tilaka) Even from a tree by the roadside—which dispels the exhaustion of wandering in the great desert scorched by the summer heat—there arises, upon this long path of the world where I am afflicted by suffering, the resonance: "Obeisance to Śiva! in my heart.

Even from the flooding mass of waters of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) joined by the currents of the Kaliṅga maidens; even from the clear and profound movement of its steps, nourished by the essence of the Sarasvatī’s auspiciousness;
even from the graceful embrace of women whose breasts are marked with thick musk and saffron—it flows forth as an abundant, unfailing distillation of the nectar-essence of bliss.

[He] amazes [me] more than all these [others]. Reflecting that life alone is life, supporting that the earthly alone is the earthly, and contemplating that splendor alone is true existence—when shall I take refuge in Śaṅkara alone as my Śaṅkara? || 23 ||

Constantly reflecting on life as merely a succession of births, considering earthly sovereignty as nothing but worldly power, and realizing that prosperity is indeed transitory (meaning it perishes in an instant)—when shall I take refuge in Śaṅkara alone?
It would be better even to have an inferior body, provided it is a supreme means for the propitiation of Hara; but never one that celebrates the festival of serving those who destroy sacrifices.
Liberation, which strikes down [bondage], falls outside the scope of logical reasoning. || 24 ||

For it is a logical consequence that even an inferior body would be better if it were a means for the worship of Hara, which is a festival for serving the Destroyer of Kṛtānta; whereas liberation, which strikes down [the body] and falls outside of reason, would not be better.
Where are the two feet of great merit, which clearly provide assistance by approaching the abode of Nīlakaṇṭha? And where are [the benefits of] rubbing with unguents, anointing, and so forth?
The two hands are engaged in offering worship to the Enemy of Tripura and in performing libations. || 25 ||

Where, O Lord, is this tongue of mine that day after day engages in the festival of uttering Your name; and where is this head of mine, which is adorned by the shimmering pollen-dust of the lotus feet of the Mountain-Daughter’s Lord? (26)

Where is the eye that has long harbored the longing to behold the beauty of the very form of the Moon-crested Lord? And where is the ear purified by the continuous hearing of the wondrous deeds of the Enemy of Darpa? (27)

Where is the mind that has shaken off the delusion of manifold conceptual constructions through the practice of meditating on the Three-eyed Lord, and where is this liberation, which is indeed not a path at all for those who possess the full abundance of the pleasures of serving the Enemy of Smara? 28.

Knowing this, the wise, freed from fear, even while relying on a meditative absorption that cuts through desire, highly value their body as having manifest utility for bowing to the Lord, praising Him, contemplating Him, and worshipping Him. (29)

(These five form a *kulaka*: Where are your two feet, which possess great virtues and provide manifest assistance by approaching the abode of the Blue-Throated One (*Nīlakaṇṭha*) for [the devotees]? And where is this liberation (*apavarga*), the pathless [state] that is the ultimate wealth of the bliss of serving the Enemy of Smara? [It is not attained] by means of ointments, rubbing with unguents, or cosmetic applications.
Where are my hands, ever intent on offering worship to the Enemy of Tripura? And where is my tongue, which has begun this festival of chanting the Lord’s name day after day?

Where is my head, adorned by the shimmering streaks of pollen from the lotus feet of the Daughter of the Mountain’s Lord? And where is my sight, whose longing to behold the beauty of the Moon-crested One’s form has long been fulfilled?
Where is the Veda, purified by the diverse and wondrous conduct of the enemy of Darpaka (Śiva), which has been heard continuously?

Where is the mind, fixed in meditation on the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva) to dispel the turmoil of manifold conceptual constructions? And where is this liberation, the pathless way to the total abundance of the bliss of serving the Enemy of Smara (Śiva)? Knowing this, the wise, casting off fear, have resorted to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that cuts through mental anguish.
They hold their bodies to be of great value when they find clear utility for bowing to the Lord, praising Him, meditating upon Him, and worshipping Him.
For those who know the inner truth, liberation is indeed the sole supreme goal of human endeavor; yet they perceive that very liberation as being obstructed [by worldly desires].

O you who shatter the god of love, what auspicious thing do you consider more unfortunate than propitiating Him—[that] for whose sake one undergoes most difficult exertions that result in the loss of wealth?
You weary yourself in sacrifices performed for the sake of attaining specific goals.

O friend! O unfortunate one! What auspicious thing do you consider to be other than propitiating the Destroyer of Love? For the sake of which you weary yourself in sacrifices that must be accomplished through extremely difficult exertions that result in the loss of wealth.
These splendors of the sacrificial fires, as pure as snow, arise from the grace of the Lord; yet you perform them merely with the desire for a libation.
The sin of harming living beings who are objects of compassion. || 31 ||

Anvaya: O unfortunate one! Out of a mere desire for self-satisfaction, you commit the sin of harming living beings who are objects of compassion; yet these splendors of theirs, as pure as snow, arise from the grace of their Lord.
O friend! Your exertion toward the acquisition of wealth through accepting gifts, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and so forth, passes away like the wind, and it destroys your very life.
Ah! You have been impelled for the sake of the sacrifice. || 32 ||

Friend! For you, who are weary of acquiring wealth through accepting gifts, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and so forth, your life passes away like the wind; alas, it destroys your effort, your gesture, and your desire for the worship of Śrī Śiva.

Therefore, [seek refuge] in the Self-born One (Svayambhū), the source of bliss, the abode of those who have attained their desired prosperity by themselves, which is free from affliction and untainted by sin.
Devote yourself to the festival of serving his lotus feet.
(To be recited in a circular manner:

Therefore, O friend! Devote yourself to the festival of serving the lotus feet of the Self-born One—the abode of riches sought after by oneself, free from affliction, undiminished by sin, the source of bliss, and the primary cause of all prosperity.

What person of sound intellect would not daily honor the bliss of serving the lotus feet of Hara, which are tender yet free from affliction, which shatter the "huṃ" of the invincible messengers of Death, and which are a fire to the fuel of misfortune, and which remove all infirmities? (34)

What wise person indeed would not daily revere the happiness of serving the lotus feet of Hara— a happiness that is tender with its lineage of non-affliction, indestructible by the roar of the invincible messengers of Death, which drives away the fire of fuel-like worldly existence, and removes all disease? [They do so] in those places frequented by hundreds of deer slow from rumination, cooled by the spray of the Ganges, and beautiful with the growth of precious fruit-bearing sprouts.
They have established their dwellings in the caves of the snowy mountains.

Blessed are those who, possessing the wealth of concentration and having cast off the bonds of attachment to riches and the like, perceive within themselves the infinite Lord—the supreme light from which the vast web of conceptual constructions dissolves—by means of their purified intellect. (36)

Fortunate are those whose wealth is concentration, who have made their home in the caves of the snowy mountain— caves resorted to by hundreds of deer sluggish from chewing their cud, cooled by the spray from the headwaters of the Bhāgīrathī, and beautiful with sprouting, precious fruit-stalks.

Having shaken off with their intellect the bonds connected to wealth and the like, those who study meditative absorption behold within [the heart] the supreme light, the infinite Lord, as the web of manifold conceptual constructions dissolves. Fortunate are those who worship the one whose crest is the young moon, their minds terrified by the "hum" of the staff-bearers at the gates of royal palaces.
In the bowers of young creepers on the sandy banks of the celestial river, frequented by wise men whose minds are stilled through dispassion; || 37 ||
Fortunate are those whose minds are made timid by the "huṃ" sounds from the mouths of gatekeepers in the palaces of kings;

they worship the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) in the bowers of young creepers on the sandy banks of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), which are crowded with wise men whose minds are tranquil through dispassion.
The virtuous remember Him who is eager for service upon the crest of the crescent moon, while dwelling on the banks of the heavenly stream.
Of those calamities arising from the transgressions of foolish kings, who were arrogant with the intense intoxication swelling from even a slight fraction of the Goddess of Fortune; || 38 ||

The virtuous, who are ever eager to serve the crest of Śiva—the moon—recall on the sandy banks of the celestial river those calamities of being trampled by the foolish kings who were intoxicated with the pride of their abundant and swelling wealth.
This honey-faced poison snatches away life at that very moment; this unwholesome thing, when consumed, causes pain to the body in its final digestion. This...
In an instant, it causes that wealth which was acquired here through foul and violent deeds to fall into a pit covered with heaps of grass. || 39 ||
Therefore, abandoning the ostentatious display of vanity on earth born from the favor of kings whose pride has been shattered by the emergence of their own meager power,
the wise resort to that crest-jewel of the moon, who delights in dwelling upon the sandy banks of the celestial river.
(These two verses form a pair.
Here, the wealth acquired by men through impure and excessive deeds is like poison with a honeyed face; it snatches away life at that very moment.
This unwholesome thing, when consumed, causes the body pain upon its digestion. That wealth which has been amassed through impure and excessive deeds—[that is what is described].
This cave, covered with heaps of grass, provides shelter from below in an instant; for this reason, the wise— who delight in dwelling on the sandy banks of the celestial river—
abandon the ostentatious display born of the favors of kings whose pride is swollen by their meager earthly power, and instead take refuge in Him who has the moon as His crest-jewel.
What is the use of further worthless transformations of fortune involving harsh objects, or what is the use of further desires for heavenly enjoyments that end in the bitterness of a fall?
I believe that for men who are distressed by the calamities and fears of worldly existence, there is nothing else worthy of being desired except devotion to Bhava, the Blessed Lord.

By that [merit], the virtuous perform the service of the lotus-feet at the head of the Moon with minds solely devoted to that addiction, maintaining a bond of faith through their immersion and emergence in the celestial river— which casts away calamities and misfortunes with hands charming as its far-reaching, restless waves.

What is the use of many worthless objects of sense that are harsh? What is the use of the worthless transformations of wealth? Or what is the use of desires for the enjoyments of heaven, which are tasteless at their end—for men who are terrified by the calamities and fears of worldly existence, there is nothing except devotion to the Blessed Lord Bhava?
I believe there is no other blessing worthy of praise; for that reason (due to the aforementioned cause), the virtuous—
whose minds are solely devoted to the fervent desire of serving the lotus-feet upon the head of the Moon-Holder—
extend their bond of faith toward the repeated immersion and emergence in the celestial river, which dispels the heat of calamity with hands as charming as its far-reaching, playful waves.

Thus ends the seventh hymn, titled "Rejoicing in Service," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*.
The Eighth Hymn.

Victorious are the feet of the verse concerning Śambhu—which, like a virtuous mountain, is resorted to by Fortune; which, like Hari or the Sun, possess radiant splendor; and which both adorn and purify the worlds. (1)
Victorious are those auspicious quarters of the verse concerning Śambhu, which belong to the auspicious [poet] Anvayaśambhu; for like the quarters of Mount Meru,
like the feet of Hari who is the refuge of Lakṣmī, and like the rays of the radiant sun, they both adorn and purify the worlds.

Victorious are those praises of Dhūrjaṭi, whose movements are as delightful as the breaking waves of the celestial river; they which separate one from the mire of worldly impurity and unite one with ever-shining virtue. 2.
Victorious are those hymns, whose movements are as delightful as the rippling waves of the celestial river, which separate the devotee from the mire of worldly impurity and unite them with eternal,

radiant, and auspicious well-being; they are the medicinal elixirs that heal the speech, mind, and body scorched by the fierce forest fire of saṃsāra, and they bring mastery over the powers of wealth, enjoyment, and liberation.
The acts of praising, meditating upon, and worshipping Śambhu are victorious. || 3 ||

Victorious are the praises, meditations, and worship of Śambhu— the medicinal herbs that heal the speech, mind, and body scorched by the terrible forest fire of cyclic existence, and the magical charms for the rites of attaining prosperity, liberation, and power.

[They bring about] the supreme placement upon the head of the Moon (the mine of defects), the severing of the head of Brahmā, the constant union of Kubera, and the reduction to ashes of the God of Love.
The ten directions were brought under control by Tripura, the wielder of the noose, and Smara, as was the ten-necked one. || 4 ||

Victorious is that unrestrained and unimpeded sovereignty of the Lord, by which—sporting as it were with autonomy—he established his residence upon the head of the Moon; he brought about the severing of the heads of Brahmā; he effected the non-separation (friendship) of Śiva and Kāma; he caused the reduction to ashes of the Three-eyed One, the Wielder of the Noose, and Smara; and he brought the ten directions under the control of the Ten-headed Rāvaṇa. Thus it triumphs.
The connection [of this verse] is with the eighth verse that is yet to be spoken.

[He recounted] the brilliance of Śauryānala’s fire-fan; Rāma’s warding off of Indra’s mace-like arms; King Marutta’s golden [shower]; and Acyuta’s gift of the Sudarśana discus for seven days and a year. || 5 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: That unimpeded sovereignty of the Lord (*īśvara*) is victorious—[that sovereignty] by which [independence], through the axe-fan, He produced the brilliance of Rāma’s fire of valor;
by which He produced the obstruction to Indra’s club-like arms in the city of King Marutta for seven days; by which He produced a golden rain;
and by which He performed the surrender of the *Sudarśana* [discus] to Acyuta. The connection is to be understood as before.
The casting out of the noose from the neck-sands of Śveta by Samavartin; the plucking out of the eyes of Bhaga; the granting of the Ocean of Milk to the sage Upamanyu;
and the creation of obstacles for Dakṣa while he was consecrated for the sacrifice.

By that very sovereignty (by which), he performed the casting away of the noose from the sandy neck of Śveta; he performed the granting of the Ocean of Milk to the sage Upamanyu; he performed the creation of obstacles in the sacrificial rites of Dakṣa when he was consecrated for the sacrifice;

he brought about the humiliation of Andhaka by making him mount the trident, the seizing of the jaw of Pūṣan, and the favor toward Arjuna; and he granted fearlessness to Nandīśvara from the son of Ravi (Yama).
It crushes the pride of those women who consider themselves sages by means of the "serpent-like" style.

Victorious is that sovereignty which, by means of its autonomy, brought about the defeat of Andhaka through his mounting upon the trident; which brought about the seizing of the jaw of Pūṣan and the favoring of Arjuna; which granted fearlessness to the sages from the son of the Sun; and which, by crushing the pride of the serpent-like [demons] who considered themselves sages, destroyed the arrogance of those women who fancied themselves to be celestial nymphs.
Or rather, what more need be said? Having assumed the forms of Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and Śiva, he has performed the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds as if in play;
thus, the unimpeded and absolute sovereignty of the Lord triumphs.

(Quintet) Or rather, what more need we say? Victorious is that unrestrained and unimpeded sovereignty of the Lord, by which, as if playing in its freedom, having assumed the forms of Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and Hara, it performed the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds.
From whose throat, though it be the seat of most terrible poison, there arises for those who bow before him speech that is a life-restoring medicine;
and whose gaze, though fierce with the brilliance of a blazing, dense fire, showers down only the potent liquid of nectar.
(Anvaya:
To him from whose throat, though it be the seat of most terrible poison, there arises for those who bow down speech that is the life-restoring medicine (*sañjīvana-auṣadha*);

and whose gaze, though fierce with the brilliance of the tongues of blazing, dense fire, rains down nothing but the unfailing nectar-fluid for those who bow down—[to him, the remover of the distress of those who take refuge, I bow].
"I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord"—this is the connection with the twenty-fifth verse at the beginning.
Even His face, though terrible and formidable with fangs, assumes the grace of one who shatters the fear of those who have sought refuge;
and the particles of ash from His body attain the splendor of a mass of camphor powder upon those who have taken shelter at His feet. (10)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: [I take refuge in that Lord] whose face, though terrible with fangs and dark like a blue lotus, assumes the aspect of one who shatters the fear of those who have sought refuge;
and the particles of whose bodily ashes, upon those who have taken shelter at his feet, assume the beauty of a mass of camphor dust.
(The connection is to be understood as before).

Even for him, the black serpents that serve as his arms rejoice as if they were garlands of blue lotuses; moreover, his head, when bent and struck by the wind, attains the stainless beauty of a conch shell—an auspicious sign—when it bows down.

I take refuge in that Lord, whose serpent-arms—even though they are black serpents—delight Pārvatī as if they were garlands of blue lotuses; moreover, when moved by the wind, his severed head, resting upon his body, assumes the beauty of a stainless auspicious conch for those who bow before him.
On his limbs, which are smeared with the thick blood from the elephant-hide, some woman, out of playful curiosity, [applies] auspicious silken garments on the banks of the Yamunā.

She drew him, who was staying in a bower of lovely *mañjula* and *vañjula* trees, by the hand with her silken garment (*dugūla*). She displays such grace that even in those distressed by the heat of passion, the skull resting upon his hand assumes the beauty of a fragment of the nectar-filled lunar orb. 12.

I take refuge in him whose limbs, though smeared with thick mire of blood, sport in the guise of auspicious silken garments; in whose hand even a skull-bowl assumes the grace of a vessel of nectar for those distressed by suffering;
whose cremation ground, purified by contact with the dust of his feet, surpasses Śrīśaila, Naimiṣa, and other sacred sites; and through whose praise, one's well-being remains unimpaired.
The rim of the skull acts like a row of lotuses for the wise. || 13 ||

I take refuge in Him, by the touch of whose foot-dust even the cremation ground becomes pure and surpasses holy sites such as Śrīśaila and Naimiṣa; by the mere praise of whom the row of skulls on the neck of Śiva brings about complete well-being for the virtuous like a cluster of lotuses; and who, with His head bowed, sits comfortably upon the lap of the Lord of the Gods, fanned by the palm-leaf fan of the hand of Rāma—the enemy of the Lord of Laṅkā—while the *Śatarudriya* and other hymns [are recited].
The wise one praises with mantras in a sweet voice. || 14 ||

I take refuge in that God whom the Creator praises with a sweet voice through mantras such as the *Śatarudriya*, while he sits comfortably, asleep on the lap of Anvaya-Surabhartṛ, his head resting upon a palm-leaf fan waved by the hand of the enemy of the Lord of Laṅkā;

he by whom the three worlds were swallowed in sport, and by whom even Indra, Mukunda, Aruṇa, and the Moon were devoured; he whose blazing fire from the large eye in his forehead— [...is the one I seek for protection.]
That Kāla became like a moth in a mass of flames. || 15 ||

I take refuge in that Lord, by whom—through whom time playfully licked the three worlds with its tongue—the very Purandara, Mukunda, and Ravīndu were swallowed; and who [himself] became like a moth in the series of flames from the fire of the great, blazing eye upon his forehead.

He who, perceiving the white fortnight as the cause for the moon’s rise and Time as the bringer of destruction for one who has taken refuge in his sight, quickly [bestows] white [purity] through his compassion made clear.
Having favored him with a glance, he brought his adversary to peace by that very glance alone.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "I take refuge in him who, having understood that the rising of the moon—which has resorted to its bright fortnight—is the cause [of its waxing], and likewise having understood that the time and the fortnight are the causes of the moon's waning; and therefore, having favored the opposing side—the time—with a glance purified by compassion, brought that very adversary to peace by his glance alone"—as before.

The wheel of that king, who wielded the bow of the lord of mountains, had its fierce, flaming tongue flickering at its tip as it licked the sky; having been made into an arrow by his speech, it became the instrument of destruction for the ancient [enemy] on the front lines of battle.

I take refuge in him, the wielder of the bow of the king of mountains (the Himalayas), by whom—on the front lines of battle—the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu), whose sky was licked by the fierce tongues of fire flickering from the tip of his mouth, was made a mere arrow;

and likewise, the Ring-bearer (Vāsuki), whose sky was licked by the fierce tongues of fire flickering from the tip of his mouth, was made a mere string, thereby becoming the instrument for the destruction of the cities. I take refuge in him.
He who, having transformed the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) into an arrow and the two sovereigns of the lunar dynasty (Rāma and Rāvaṇa) into the wheels of a chariot,
caused tears born of both joy and grief to flow from the women of heaven and the underworld alike.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "I take refuge in that All-pervading Lord, who, in the battle of Tripura, having turned his discus-weapon into the form of arrows, and having turned the two friends known as the Moon and the Sun into the state of chariot wheels, caused tears consisting of both joy and sorrow to flow from the eyes of the women in the celestial abode and in the netherworld."

Who that has accomplished their desires would not feel joy and passion in their heart upon receiving that glance of his—the very offering of which caused Kāma to forget both joy and passion in his own heart, even though he had already ascended to the height of pride? (19)

Having received that glance of the Lord—which, though its pride was mounted by lineage, caused even Kāma to forget both *prīti* and *rati* when offered to his heart—what devotee, having attained their desires, would not bear *prīti* and *rati* in their heart? The rest is as before.

[He is] one who has taken up residence in the forest depths, whose body bears a praiseworthy form despite being in the guise of a hunter, following the path shown by Kṛṣṇa, and enduring the intense heat of the vast [forest].
Dhanañjaya alone, having set foot within the range of his vision, shone forth with splendor.

I take refuge in him, by whom Dhananjaya himself—following the path shown by Krishna, possessing a body praised for its great heat and majesty, and having adopted a life in the forest—shone with splendor as soon as he came within the range of vision of that Lord, even though he was in the form of a hunter.

It is fitting that the nectar of the moon, the nectar of the moonstones, the waters of the celestial ocean, and so forth, remove the heat from the mind; yet it is the skull-mālā of funeral ashes clinging to his body [that does so].
Even [substances] such as hālāhala poison and fire are indeed pleasing to the heart. || 21 ||

It is fitting that the nectar of the moon of lineage, the nectar of the moon, the waters of the celestial ocean, and so forth, dispel the heat (the torment born of the activities of creating the three worlds) within his mind;

yet this is truly marvelous— that even the skull-garland, the funeral ashes clinging to his limbs, the Halahala poison, serpents, fire, and the like, become nothing but delightful to his heart— to him I go for refuge.

The body of a worm, that of a centipede, has entered the ear; seen, it produces pain and ill fortune for people. But the solar form, indeed, possesses a thousand feet; when stationed in the eye, it removes the fear of death for those who take refuge in it.

A centipede, having entered upon hearing the *anvaya* (the sequence of words), is seen by people to be the very form of a worm that creates misfortune and pain for them. But surely, the solar body with a thousand feet, which resides within his eyes, removes the fear of death for those who take refuge in him—(in him I seek shelter).
Having heard the piteous words of the distressed, he, an ocean of compassion, [is showered] by the masses of droplets from the celestial river whose waters are shaken by his head.
It doubles the luster of the supreme pearls resting upon the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King, which are nestled in his lap. || 23 ||

[I take refuge in Him] who is an ocean of compassion; having heard the piteous words of the distressed, He—by means of the showers of droplets from the celestial river [Gaṅgā] flowing from His head shaken with mercy—doubles the pearls clinging to the tips of the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King as they rest upon His lap. [He is the one] from whom flows nectar that emits an exceedingly pure radiance, having dispelled the thick darkness of faults by means of intense devotion.
His complexion was pure and radiant, his speech reached to the ends of his ears, and his eyes were wide. || 24 ||

I take refuge in Him whose speech— dispelling the thick darkness of intense faults through profound devotion, possessing an exceedingly pure radiance, endowed with distinct syllables, and reaching to the very ends of the ears— and whose eyes vomit forth nectar;
[and] when those whose heads are purified by friendship with the dust of His lotus feet, and who are firm in truthful speech, do not become worthy vessels [for such grace].
Of those displays of fierce frowns accompanied by haughty anger, and of the terrifying threats from the gaping mouths of formidable black warriors; || 25 ||

Those whose heads are purified by friendship with the pollen of the lotus-feet of [the Buddha], and whose speech is steady and truthful— those fortunate ones do not become objects for the terrifying threats of the fierce faces of the arrogant soldiers of Time, nor for the displays of eyebrows knit in violent anger;
[I take refuge in him].

Bearing pure eloquence that flows as nectar for the ears—eloquence that is crooked yet possesses unyielding virtues and is vast—the poets and panegyrists sing of him, whose fame and pure learning increase for those who have taken refuge in him. (26)

The poets, whose lineage and learning are perfectly pure, who bear a great, crooked, and unbroken-stringed *sūkti* that flows as nectar for the ears and is ever-pure; and likewise, the lute-players, who bear a great, crooked, and unbroken-stringed lute that flows as nectar for the ears and is ever-pure— they sing the glories of that Lord whom the devotee has taken refuge in.
The connection is: "I take refuge in the All-pervading Lord.

For the servant of Him, there is at the proper time a wife whose face is radiant with a tilaka-mark blooming from the edge of her brow—overcome by the multitude of arrows of the god of love intoxicated with pride—and a blossoming garden grove delightful with the warbling of sweet-throated cuckoos, both of which become worthy of enjoyment. (27)

I take refuge in him, at whose feet his servants find that the garden grounds—overcome by clusters of arrows from the intense intoxication [of spring], resplendent with the beauty of forehead-marks blooming on the faces of women, and delightful with the warbling of cuckoos—are fit to be enjoyed when the time is right;
and in whom those whose minds are undistressed dwell, having reached a consensus to pacify the suffering of those fallen into calamity; he who is Kātyāyanī, Compassion, and Art.
Her gaze is as gentle as the moon, and her speech is like the river Sarasvatī. || 28 ||

I take refuge in that Lord, in whom dwell— unwearied in mind— the Goddess Kātyāyanī, Compassion, the tender digit of the moon, the gracious eye, the celestial river Gaṅgā, and Sarasvatī; who, through their esteemed power to pacify the distress caused by the calamities of worldly existence,
possess waters as white as the moon, like those of the Ocean of Nectar, which are capable of removing the abundance of suffering, and which fashion, intoxicate, and purify [the soul].
And their glories fully revive the worlds. || 29 ||

I take refuge in that Lord, whose fame— white as the moon and capable of removing the mass of all afflictions— completely sustains, gladdens, purifies, and enlivens the worlds like the waters of the celestial ocean;
[and which fame is] like camphor for those distressed by the frying pan of the hardships of an evil age, and for those whose minds are filled with intense pride.
Oh!

How wonderful that his deeds shatter the longing for a multitude of abundant drops of cool sandalwood paste for those whose minds are tormented by the fierce pride of the cauldron of this evil age’s distress (I take refuge in that Lord).

Upon the sandy banks of the lotus ponds, the wise lords of the quarters sing His deeds—a song filled with the "gu-ma-gu-ma" humming of female bees who have taken their pleasure in the nectar of full-blown lotuses. (31)

I take refuge in that Lord whose deeds the lords of the quarters— endowed with the wisdom of logical inference— sing upon the banks of lotus ponds, accompanied by the humming songs of female bees who have taken to the nectar of full-blown lotuses.

The goddess Kamalā herself, the bestower of boons, dwells upon his lotus-face— which is adorned with a radiant, manifest halo, possesses long eyes, broad ear-lobes, and a neck that rises without restraint— as if out of a desire to conquer her own abode, the lotus.

The Goddess of Speech herself dwells upon his face—which is praised for its symmetry, clearly radiant with a mass of curls, possessing long eyes, broad ear-lobes, and a neck that rises without restraint—as if out of a desire to conquer Kamalā, who resides in a lotus; [the connection is: "I take refuge in that Lord, the remover of the distress of those who seek shelter."

I take refuge in that Lord, the remover of the distress of those who seek shelter, who has the young moon as his crest-jewel; he whose playful speech is never in vain toward his fallen kinsmen, and who is ever near to offer consolation through both immersion and emergence from the waters. 33.

(An *kulaka* of twenty-five verses) — I take refuge in that Lord, who is the remover of the distress of those who seek his protection; who possesses the unfailing splendor of speech in consoling those near death and those already deceased; whose kinsmen have attained [liberation]; who has the young moon as his crest-ornament.
I take refuge in that God, by whom— under the guise of the thousands of jewels flashing from the hoods of the lordly serpents upon his crown—
the fire of his forehead shines as if it has released a thousand sprouts drenched by the waters of the celestial river.

I take refuge in that God, whose forehead-fire— sprinkled by the waters of the celestial river— shines as if it were a thousand sprouts released under the guise of the thousands of jewels flashing from the hoods of the lordly serpents upon his crown;

he whose foot-base is resorted to by the highest hosts of gracious attendants, who bears the celestial river upon his head, whose form is accompanied by frost (or snow), and who is served by venomous serpents.
I take refuge in Guha, who is exceedingly dear to the Lord of the Mountains, for the sake of quelling the heat within my heart. || 35 ||

For the sake of quelling my distress, I take refuge in the Lord of Mountains, whose foot-base is resorted to by the supreme hosts of his followers, who bears the celestial river upon his head, whose form is accompanied by the frost of the Ganges, who is frequented by serpents on his ridges, and whose caves are exceedingly charming. He who, in order to remove [the burden of] the ocean of milk, bears it at his foot, holds the jar of nectar in his hand, and carries the noble celestial river upon his head.
I take refuge in Him, the root of the three impurities consisting of māyā, which is the subtle karma that brings about bondage. || 36 ||

I take refuge in Him who, as it were, bears upon the soles of His feet the ocean of milk to remove the three impurities—the root of the *māyā* of subtle karma for all living beings; who holds in His hand the jar of nectar-water; and who bears on His head the noble celestial river.

He whose river-like Ganges, like a garland of flowers, rests in His matted locks; who wears the moon upon His head like a decorative ornament; and who [bears] the Goddess, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness.
He bears a gracious look, as if pleased; I take refuge in that Lord. || 37 ||

I take refuge in that Lord, in whose matted locks the river Saumanasī shines like a garland; who bears upon his head the Kaumudī as if it were a decorative crest; and who, being pleased, carries the Goddess—who bestows boons and fearlessness—as if she were his very glance.
He alone is the one who [bears] Gaurī, the mother of the elephant-faced god, the daughter of Himavat, who instantly purifies the three worlds, as well as Kātyāyanī and the celestial river.
The all-pervading Lord sustains [the world]; I go for refuge to that moon-crested one who bestows liberation. || 38 ||

I go for refuge to that moon-crested Lord who bestows liberation, the all-pervading One who alone instantly purifies the three worlds, and who bears upon Him the daughter of the Himalayas, Kātyāyanī Gaurī, the mother of the elephant-faced god, and the celestial river.
[He is] somewhere the one who rescued the sacrificial horse by severing its head, and elsewhere the deer resting upon His lap; He is the lord of medicinal herbs, yet He is also cruel.
In one place I take refuge in the Kirāta, who finds sole delight in the slaughter of deer; in another, I take refuge in the Lord Vāta, whose chariot is the wind.

I take refuge in the Lord who is thus: in one place, he whose head is severed from the body of the sacrificial beast; in another, the Lord of Herbs (the Moon) resting upon his lap with a deer; in another, a cruel hunter whose sole delight is the slaughter of deer; and in another, the Wind-god whose vehicle is a deer.

Though possessed of unrestrained faults, he is endowed with long-reaching virtues; though embraced by the coils of a serpent, he is ever associated with the fire of asceticism; and though engaged in the vow of a Kāpālika, he is the ultimate refuge.
I take refuge in the Lord, the crest-jewel of the foremost of the twice-born, who is without goad.

I take refuge in that unrestrained Lord, who—though possessed of fierce defects—is endowed with long-reaching virtues; though entwined by the coils of serpents—is attended by the presence of the risen fire; though engaged in the vow of a Kāpālika—is the crest-jewel upon the head of the King of Brahmins.

Furthermore, I seek refuge in Śiva, the fierce Lord of the Universe, who holds a skull-fragment in his hand, and who, while bearing on his body a woman whose limbs are broken by the god of love, remains the sovereign of all.
I take refuge in the Lord who is Hara, Aghora, the Unborn, Sadyojāta, and a treasury of wonders. || 41 ||

I take refuge in the Lord, the ocean of wonder— the pervasive Śiva, who is both the fierce Hara and the non-terrible Aghora, the unborn Sadyojāta, the sovereign of the universe, who holds a skull in his hand, who supports the world, and who has brought about the dissolution of the limbs of the bodiless God of Love. On this most treacherous path of worldly existence, I, a coward, seek refuge in that sole hero who subdues the thieves of passion, anger, and the like.
The Lord of unsurpassed power, the crest-jewel of the lineage of the Night-maker (the Moon). || 42 ||

In this most perilous path of worldly existence, I, being fearful, take refuge in the Lord—the sole hero who subdues the thieves of passion and anger, possessed of unsurpassed power, and the crest-jewel upon the brow of the night’s lineage.
Is Kailāsa indeed more weighty than mountains such as Meru and Mandara? It is the Lord of Mountains alone who is the world’s sole preceptor.
That which bestows fearlessness, is free from confusion, devoid of doubt, possesses a beautiful mark, is stainless, and serves as an ornament. || 43 ||

What is the use of mountains such as Meru and Mandara? Kailāsa alone is the most preeminent, for upon its fearless, unconfused, doubt-free, well-peaked, and stainless lap—the central region—Girīśa, the sole teacher of the world, adorns himself. Having transgressed the command of the Son of the Unborn (Viṣṇu), who else would reach the point of desiring to worship another's command? For, having abandoned the forest...

The camel, its mouthful filled with leaves of fresh ginger, resorts only to pits abounding in thorns. [In this instance, although the word "uṣṭra" (camel) is harsh to the ear, it is not a defect because it pertains to a specific context. || 44 ||
Transgressing the teaching of the doctrine born of no other [source], some rare fool reaches the firm resolve to worship another teaching;
for indeed, having abandoned a forest full of fresh *nāgara* leaves, a camel resorts only to a pit filled with a mass of thorns.

Service rendered to Śitikaṇṭha, even when undertaken for another purpose, inevitably bears fruit like a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatikā). Indeed, a flame of a lamp, though lit for the sake of another, reveals a multitude of objects to that other person as well. // 45 //

Service rendered to Śitikaṇṭha, even when undertaken for another purpose, inevitably bears fruit like a wish-fulfilling creeper for the world. Just as a flame of a lamp, though kindled for the sake of another, reveals a multitude of objects even to that very person who lit it; so too, if that Blessed One is worshipped—even if merely for the sake of a livelihood—he surely dispels the ripening of one's sins. Whoever...
It floats upon the waters of the celestial river; indeed, it becomes a cleanser of sins that wards off the heat of the summer season.

Logical connection: If that Blessed One, even when worshipped by someone merely for the sake of a livelihood, removes the ripening of that worshiper’s sins; for even he who floats upon the waters of the celestial river solely to dispel the heat of summer becomes cleansed of sin.

Even those who perform devotion to Bharga when appointed by others cast off the misery of worldly existence; for even a nurse employed merely to provide breast milk becomes the vessel for all enjoyments and the bliss of repose for a child.
Even those who, though appointed by others for other purposes, practice devotion to Bharga, they too cast off the misery of worldly existence—this is observed:
even a nurse employed merely for the sake of an infant's milk becomes a vessel for the enjoyment of every pleasure and ease;
likewise, even a rite of service performed out of hypocrisy toward the Conqueror of Cupid certainly bestows the intoxication of supreme bliss.
For a courtesan, what pleasure is there even in a contrived dress made white with cosmetic ointments, garlands, and fine silks? (48)

Even a ritual of service performed toward the Conqueror of the Bodiless (Kāmadeva) out of mere hypocrisy certainly bestows an abundance of joy; for does not even a feigned attire—white with unguents, garlands, and silken garments—worn for the sake of another bring happiness to the women of the brothel?
(Indeed, it surely does.)

Therefore, approach the All-pervading Lord in whatever manner possible; for even if liberation does not occur, will your sins not be dissolved? If one who plunges by his own will into the inner lake of nectar does not sink, would he not surely emerge unsullied? (49)

Therefore, O connoisseurs! Whether it be by your own will, at the instigation of another, due to some circumstance, or even out of hypocrisy—take refuge in the All-pervading Lord alone. If liberation does not come to you, why then do your sins not dissolve?
If one who falls by his own will into a pool of nectar does not sink within it, would he then rise up unsprinkled?

How can that Lord be described, for whom the effortless bestowing of the ocean of milk, the unrestrained raining down of gold, the uprooting of the noose of the serpent held by the enraged God of Death, and even the wondrous act of swallowing the fierce Kālakūṭa poison, were all merely acts of play? (50)

How can that Lord— who treats with ease the effortless bestowing of the ocean of milk from his lineage (in the city of King Marutta), the unrestrained raining of gold (by King Śveta), and even the wondrous deeds such as the uprooting of the noose of the hooded serpent released by an enraged Kṛtānta and the swallowing of the fierce Kālakūṭa poison— be described by us whose eyes are but of flesh?

When this Lord Maheśvara, moving according to his own will, causes the creeper-like brow to quiver by chance, the gods and asuras—who are arrogant due to their persistent rivalry with the dense boastfulness of having obtained the favor of his command—engage in heated quarrels during their service.
In the act of praising the greatness of this God, who are we? (51)

When this Great Lord, acting according to his own will and at his pleasure, causes the creeper-like brows to quiver, the gods and demons— intensely embroiled in a rivalry fueled by boasting over the acquisition of favors and commands through his service— engage in conflict while still possessing their fiery energy; yet, in the act of praising the majesty of this God Maheśvara, who are we?
He who, through his eight manifestations consisting of the Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, Ether, Mind, Moon, and Self, sustains the world as both its enjoyer and its object of enjoyment—
