what can we say of that Great Lord, who, being independent, sports with his own vast expansions such as Brahmā, Indra, and others, as if with dice?

What can we say of the majesty of that Great Lord, who— being both the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment— sustains the world through his eightfold manifestations consisting of the Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, Ether, Mind, Moon, and Self; and who, being independent, sports with his own vast attendants, such as Brahmā, Indra, and others, as if with mere game-pieces?

Thus ends the eighth hymn, titled "Taking Refuge," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmad Jaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
[The Ninth Hymn begins.]
This is the fulfillment of the radiance of lamps by means of the light of the sun; this is the filling of the ocean with the waters of mist.
That we, whose vision is limited, should attempt to offer praise to You—saying even "O Bhava, O Bhava"—is merely the impulsive rashness of our speech, constrained as it is by fixed conventions. 1.
Anvaya: O Bhava! That which is undertaken as the rashness of praising you by those like us—people of limited vision—with restricted words, is merely a mockery;
it is like the filling of the ocean with the rays of the sun augmented by the multitudes of lamps, or the filling of the sea with the waters of mist. (The sense is that it is for mere derision.)

O Hara, it is this speech of mine that offends you—this naturally loquacious tongue, so fond of sounding, which, though it has reached the highest maturity, still desires to seize you by force as its Supreme Lord. (2)

Anvaya: O Lord! Although this [my speech] has not attained supreme maturity, being naturally talkative and full of passion, it desires to seize You, the Supreme Person, as if by force; in this matter, O Hara, it is this audacity of my words alone that offends. Or rather, for one who has taken refuge in You, there exists some indescribable greatness that is difficult to attain, such that even one like me is not [unworthy]; for in whomsoever [that greatness resides], even if it be slow and according to its own will— (Note: The final sentence fragment "svacchandamandamapi yatra" appears to be an incomplete thought or a transition to another verse, likely referring to the power of devotion which acts spontaneously and gently.)
Your bull places his foot there, for the earth indeed becomes made of gold in that place. || 3 ||

Alternatively: O Lord! For one such as me who has taken refuge in you, even that kind of praiseworthy greatness is certainly not difficult to attain; for wherever your cow, even if she places her foot slowly and at her own will, that ground becomes made of gold. Bhīṣma, the causeless enemy, has made this mind—which was bound by despair even more than by poison—full of agitation; I shall lead this disease of delusion to its utter destruction.
O Lord, by the consumption of the elixir of your praise, [may I be healed]. || 4 ||

Sequence of meaning: O Lord! This disease of delusion (*mohāmaya*), more terrifying even than poison and having no cause [other than ignorance], has rendered my mind afflicted by sorrow and full of agitation. Therefore, O Master! By the practice of the elixir (*rasāyana*) of Your hymn of praise, I shall bring this [disease] to its end.
This hymn of Yours, O Girīśa, which issues the command of fresh nectar-like instruction, is some kind of unprecedented Guru; it immediately manifests before me.
By the power of the sequence of its transition, the Goddess of Speech [is manifested] through that which is difficult to transcend.

O Lord of the Mountains! Victorious is this certain hymn of yours, which acts as a teacher imparting the instruction of fresh intoxication; for by the power of its sequence of transmission, the Goddess of Speech suddenly flashes before my eyes.
It has no desire for flavorful elixirs, nor for the nectar from the mouth of a woman with a moon-like face whose senses are unrestrained; yet it persists in its insistence to dwell in your presence.
O enemy of Andhaka, exert your effort upon this mind of mine.

O Enemy of Andhaka! This longing of my mind is not for the flavorful elixir (*rasāyana*), nor is it for the nectar from the face of the unrestrained moon-faced woman; rather, it finds its persistent attachment (*nirbandha*) in your presence. Therefore, O Lord, make this mind of mine free from attachment—that is, liberated from the bond of *māyā*.

Neither does the city of Śakra shine with greater splendor to me, nor does the mountain of gold (Meru) pour forth such joy; I know that the forest alone is the supreme refuge, wherein there may be the bliss of worshipping the lotus-feet of Hara.

O Hara! To me, the city of Indra does not appear superior; nor does the Golden Mountain (Meru) sprinkle the nectar of joy upon me, O Lord! I consider that very forest to be the supreme refuge where there may be the bliss of worshipping Your lotus feet.
She, who previously wandered helplessly among the flowers and the sprout-like arms of the lovely-eyed women due to the power of longing, [now...]
The river of vision reveals the creeper of devotion to You, which is thirsty for the enjoyment of its fruit.

O Lord! That swarm of bees which was formerly my eye—helpless under the influence of longing for flowers—wandered excessively among the sprouts of the arms of the small-eyed one, now that it has become wrinkled, manifests a thirst to enjoy the fruit of the wish-fulfilling creeper of devotion to You.
Was it fashioned by pressing the crescent moon of Your crown? Or perhaps by the water of the river that takes refuge at Your head? Or else...
O beloved one, with the flooding nectar from the jar held in your hand, may you bring peace to the fever of suffering of those who are devoted to you.

Anvaya: O Supreme Compassionate One! Was this devotion of your devotees fashioned by you by crushing the crescent moon of your crown for the sake of quelling their worldly suffering? Or was it fashioned by the waters of the river that takes refuge at your head? Or was it fashioned by the immersion in the nectar of the digit held in your hand? (The meaning is: if it were not so, how could it be the remover of the threefold suffering of living beings?)

O Lord of wondrous deeds, this speech of mine, having firmly rooted its passion in the nectar of the songs of Your exploits, has cast aside all other paths; like a doe, it truly cannot bear to move even a single step further. 10.

Anvaya: O Master! This speech of mine, which has firmly rooted its affection in the nectar-songs of Your wondrous deeds and has cast aside all other paths, is like a doe that truly cannot move even a single step from one place to another.

jury for all eternity, a jury for all existence, a jury for all non-existence, a jury for all reality, a jury for all unreality, a jury for all truth, a jury for all falsehood, a jury for all knowledge, a jury for all ignorance, a jury for all wisdom, a jury for all folly, a jury for all virtue, a
The proclamation of the nectar of the words of the king of good poets triumphs over the nectar of your deeds. || 11 ||

Victorious is the proclamation of the nectar of your deeds, O Lord! It is a consolation for those distressed by the fear of Yama; it is the resuscitation for those who have perished from the agony of the forest fire of worldly existence; it is the support for the nectar-like words of the kings of great poets.
Indeed, the Ocean of Milk is but a wave-tossing gift, and liberation is merely a favor granted out of fear of the most formidable Time; even renunciation lasts but seven days.
What noble deed of yours is not praiseworthy, like a rain of gold? || 12 ||
The Ocean of Milk is indeed as fickle as a wave; [the gift of] the young sage Upamanyu was liberation from the most terrifying fear of Death;
[the favor of] King Śveta was a rain of gold for seven days; and [the generosity of] King Marutta in his city was renunciation—O Lord! What noble deed of yours is not worthy of praise?

O Lord, this heart of mine—though accustomed to passion, fickle by nature, and inherently impure—now bears the likeness of a bee overflowing with the weight of joy, having taken refuge at the lotus-feet of Your Majesty. 13.

Anvaya: O Lord! This heart of mine—which is associated with passion (*rajas*), fickle by nature, and inherently impure—having developed partiality toward the lotus-feet of Your Honor, bears the beauty of a bee (*bhṛṅga*) overflowing with the weight of joy.

You are Vāmadeva, yet you are *dakṣiṇa* (right-handed/favorable) toward those who seek refuge; you are Śaṅkara (the Auspicious), yet you dwell everywhere as the enemy of Smara (Kāma); and you are Ananta (Infinite), yet you are the cause of the pacification of even the most extreme anger.
I take refuge in the one who has inconceivable movement and is the sole cause of peace. || 14 ||

O Śaṅkara! I take refuge in you, whose course is inconceivable—you who are Vāmadeva yet are gracious toward those who seek shelter; who dwell everywhere yet are the enemy of Smara; who are the cause for the cessation of death yet are the sole cause for the eternal cessation of all affliction.
You are pleased in one place, bestowing brilliant light; in another, you grant the obstruction of dense coverings. What can we do in this matter?

For the Lord of great and venerable majesty, there is indeed no such thing as limitation, whether it be of the sky or of the Lord. [Regarding the phrase "the two worshipped here," when it is said "of the Lord and of the sky," there is no fault even in including a portion of the sky, because the sky is of one essence with the venerable Lord Śiva, and thus that portion was already indicated previously. || 15 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! In one place You bestow pure light and are gracious; in another, You grant the obstruction of dense veils.
Therefore, what can we do here? Indeed, there is no fixed destiny for the Lord, whose great majesty is most exalted, nor for the sky.

[We offer] a mind intent on removing the torment of prostrate suffering, speech devoted to the vow of granting fearlessness to those who are afraid, and this body, dependent upon service for the benefit of the world.
And who else but you, O supremely compassionate one, bears such a body? (16)

O Lord! Who else but You—supreme and most compassionate—is there who bears this mind ever intent on removing the distress and suffering of those who bow before You, this speech ever inclined toward the vow of granting fearlessness to the terrified, and this body entirely devoted to the service of the world?
My mind did not sink into despondency; it attained no other state than grace; it abandoned neither its proper reflection nor its outward activity; it found no opening anywhere [to escape].
O Blessed One, this supreme awakening is not understood by me, for it has been separated from you alone. || 17 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! This very mind of mine, held in separation by You alone, has fallen into despondency; it has not attained supreme clarity. It has abandoned appropriate reflection and has not ceased its outward wandering. Thus, this mind has found no opening anywhere (indeed, it has found openings everywhere), and it does not attain the highest awakening.

That it unwearyingly obscures the inner self, that its transformations of passion are never stilled, and that the darkness made manifest by the crown of the deer-bannered god blinds and deafens us—what excessive consequence is there in this? I cannot fathom it.
O you whose crown bears the deer-marked one! It is only natural that internal darkness—which is unappeased, restless, and clearly manifest—should blind [the mind];
however, that it should deafen [the person] as well—is this not an excessive consequence? I cannot conceive how such a thing could be.

Having reached the dwelling within the corners of the eyes of women who are restless in their playful charms, that [darkness] shatters even the minds of the wise; yet here it is, having entered the stainless heart.
"Alas! How is it that the Mind-born (Cupid) does not pierce my very vitals? || 19 ||

O Lord, does a living being perceive one who dwells there as if he were non-existent, or what else could this be? Victorious is that all-conquering grace of yours, by which even one who has been consumed [by fire] regains his pride upon attaining it once more.
(These two verses form a pair. Anvaya:
That Mind-born One (Manobhū), having found his dwelling within the corners of the eyes of women unsteady with play—where does he not shatter even the high-minded? Fie upon him!
This very Mind-born One, having entered even my stainless heart, why does he not pierce every vital organ? (The meaning is: he certainly pierces them. O... [Addressing the beloved].
O Master! That [Manobhū] perceives you—who are indeed dwelling there [in my heart]—as being non-existent; is this so?
Or rather, what else could it be? Even though he has been consumed by fire, having obtained your grace, he again bears pride; thus, that all-conquering grace of yours reigns supreme.

Her limbs, which serve as the auspicious stage for the dancer Ananga (the God of Love), bear a beautiful cosmetic paste made from a mixture of sandalwood, musk rubbed with moonlight, camphor, and saffron; they possess the delicate softness of freshly sprouted plantain leaves. (21)
O Lord! She who bears a body adorned with an auspicious unguent of sandalwood paste, musk, camphor, and saffron;
whose limbs possess the tenderness of a rising young plantain leaf; who is the auspicious stage for the dance of the God of Love;

whose face is like a full-blown lotus; whose arms are like blossoming *śirīṣa* flowers; and whose eyes are like fresh blue lotuses—she has fashioned this irresistible Brahma-missile for my destruction.
as if with the flowers of the flower-armed god by means of the spring month.

With a face like a fully blossomed lotus, arms adorned with a garland of blooming *śirīṣa* flowers, and eyes like fresh blue water-lilies— (therefore,) for the benefit of the Flower-Armed One (*Puṣpāyudha*), she was as if fashioned by Mādhava with flowers as an unimpeded *brahmāstra* (the weapon of Brahmā; note that the term *brahmāstra* here maintains its original gender, as in the expressions "the Vedas are the authority" or "the Śrutis are the authority").

Addressing him as "O Lord," "O Taker of my life," and "O Compassionate One," she spoke with words tender with affection and feigned anger; revealing all her hidden feelings through intense passion, she captivated him with playful expressions that were beyond the reach of ordinary speech. (23)

O Lord! O taker of my life! O you who are supremely compassionate!—thus speaking with affectionate anger and with words exceedingly tender, she captivated his mind with amorous gestures beyond the reach of speech, thereby revealing her entire hidden state of intense passion; or rather, what else could it be? For the heart of this innocent woman was pierced by the flood of arrows from the wrathful and pitiless five-arrowed god of love as she embraced him firmly. Of the simple folk... [the rest of the verse follows].
Having overcome her innate modesty, she offered the nectar of her lower lip, thick with longing. || 24 ||

Or rather, what more shall we say? Pierced in the heart by the flood of arrows from the enraged and merciless Five-Arrowed One, the innocent woman—having overcome her natural modesty and having firmly embraced [you]—offers the nectar of her lips, thick with longing.
[She offers it to you who are] eternally satiated by the fulfillment of the rasa of devotion to you, which is like the great flood of nectar produced during the churning of the ocean.
For one whose senses have been withdrawn and who has attained the bliss of samādhi, even that fawn-eyed woman does not captivate anything beyond you.
(These five form a *kulaka*.
Even though she was such a fawn-eyed woman,

he had withdrawn his senses and was eternally satisfied by the breaking of his fast upon the nectar of devotion to Your Lordship— the very essence of the great flood of nectar arising from the churning of the ocean which had been seized [by him].
[The Lord] does not seize [the devotee] who has attained the bliss of samādhi and is intent upon You; He is unable to bring such a person under His sway.
Where is the sustenance of forest trees, which are shaken by the playful Malaya breezes and provide for themselves with fallen fruit?
And where is the wretched face of base kings standing before one whose mind reels with the remembrance of Hara? || 26 ||

For one whose mind reels with the remembrance of the lineage of [his] service to Śambhu, sustenance comes from the fruits that have fallen of their own accord from the forest trees shaken by the Malaya breeze blowing in sport; where then is the wretched face of base kings?
O Lord, my eyes exist for the beholding of Your form, my speech for the delight of chewing upon Your deeds, and my faculty of hearing for the task of listening to Your stories.
My other senses also desire to go to the state of being without Karna. || 27 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! My other senses desire to attain the state of being eyes in the act of beholding Your form; my other senses desire to attain the state of being speech in the play of relishing Your deeds; and my other senses desire to attain the state of being ears in the task of hearing Your sacred narrations.

O Blessed One, that prosperity of the accomplished which consists of umbrellas, chowries, and white garments is but a trifle compared to Your grace; yet even greater than that for the virtuous is the attainment of equality with You—such that their bark becomes clothing and the forest becomes their dwelling. (28)
Anvaya: O Blessed One! That splendor consisting of umbrellas and chowries which belongs to the accomplished (kṛtins) is but a very small favor from you;

for the virtuous (santaḥ), however, the favor greater than even that is your likeness (tvatsāmyam). Greater even than that (tvatsāmyāt) is this favor, namely, that bark is their garment and the forest is their dwelling.

If my two hands are ever again anointed with the dust of your lotus feet, my speech is ever proud of relishing your deeds, and my mind is ever devoted to the vow of remembering the multitude of your virtues—then, alas, I am truly blessed! (29)

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! If my two hands are smeared with the dust of Your lotus feet, if my speech is proud of relishing Your deeds, and if my mind possesses the vow of remembering the multitude of Your qualities—then, indeed, I am blessed! (Note: *Bhūyaḥ* is an adverbial modifier meaning "exceedingly" or "to a great degree.")

O Blessed One, though you subsist on alms, though you possess nothing, though your dwelling is an ancient cremation ground, and though you are naked; O Giver of Boons, what more need be said? Even with a body as coarse as ashes, may you, the All-pervading Lord, be mine in every birth. (30)

O Lord! Even if you are one who subsists on alms, even if you possess nothing, even if your dwelling is an ancient cremation ground, and even if you are clothed only by the directions—what more can I say?
O Giver of Boons! O Devourer! Though your body is rough with ashes, may You alone be my sovereign lord in every birth.
I beg for nothing else: let my residence be on the king of mountains named Kailāsa, which is inhabited by You. Or rather, O Lord, what is there that does not belong to me?
There are other friends for you as well: the gavayas, the monkeys, and the deer. || 31 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! I do not beg anything else from you, who are compassionate; rather, let my dwelling be on that king of mountains named Kailāsa where you reside. O Blessed One! Are those who are my friends not there, and are there not others as well—Gavayas, Kapis, and Kuraṅgas?

Those objects of sense which were once the domain of my speech, wherein I experienced a treacherous thirst that scattered poison— may she, with the nectar-like essence of her radiant and flickering sidelong glances, nourish me with that very nectar.
In those very objects where I experienced thirst as if scattering poison, those objects are now beyond the reach of words.
Therefore, O Lord, favor me with the nectar-essence shining from the placement of the corners of Your radiant and tremulous eyes.
Without devotion to You there is no grace of Yours, and without Your grace there is no devotion to You; for whom is this not like the sprouting of a seed?
For the sake of prosperity, there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect. || 33 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Without devotion to You, Your grace does not occur; likewise, without Your grace, devotion to You does not occur. Like the seed and the sprout, for whose prosperity does this mutual relationship of cause and effect not exist? If the mind is peaceful through restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), what is the use of others? If speech is pleasant and beneficial, what is the use of praises and flattery? If compassion exists, what [is the use of other virtues]?
If there is devotion to Bhava through vows, fire-offerings, and gifts, what is the use of longing for other pleasures? || 34 ||
The logical sequence is as follows: if the mind is peaceful, then what is the use of other restraints? If speech is pleasant and beneficial, then what is the use of praises and flatteries?
If there is compassion, then what is the use of vows, fire-offerings, and gifts? Likewise, if there is devotion toward existence, then what is the use of desires for other forms of pleasure?

By some of dull intellect, the happiness of the celestial realms was consumed as morsels of conceptual thought, and liberation was merely perceived through the lens of various scriptures; furthermore, nectar was drunk with the shells of their ears, yet this very devotion to Śiva has been tasted directly before their eyes. (35) *Anvaya:* By some of dull intellect (*vikalpakavalaiḥ*), the happiness of the celestial realms was consumed (*bhuktam*); liberation (*muktiḥ*) was merely perceived (*ālokitā*) through the lens of various scriptures (*vividhaśāstradṛśā*). Furthermore...

But by us, through the vision of various scriptures and with the hollowed shells of our ears as vessels, this very nectar—devotion to Śiva—is drunk; indeed, liberation is right before our eyes, having been tasted. Long-standing sins become like days of intense heat, the loss of strength is like that of river water in autumn, and sufferings are like the insults of the wicked.
Alas, these [sorrows] are unbearable; I am powerless. O You who are without refuge, have compassion for me! || 36 ||
O Lord! My sins become as long as days of intense heat; my strength wanes day by day like the water of a river in autumn;
and my sorrows, like insults from the wicked, become unbearable. Alas! I am exhausted; have compassion for me, who am without refuge.

Let discernment (viveka) indeed touch the mind with coldness—like a haughty kinsman rebuking one in times of misfortune—but delusion (moha), like the summer sun bringing frost to destruction, causes it to burn away its very essence, even as it brings knowledge (vidyā) to ruin, O Nidāgha. || 37 ||

Though censured by the adversity of my lineage, may my discernment—like a proud kinsman—not touch my heart that has grown callous. But delusion, like the summer sun, brings knowledge to destruction as frost does in the heat of midsummer, and thus afflicts the mind.
Therefore, do not allow it to reach its ultimate end with such speed; show mercy for as long as the crescent moon of the evening first day of the lunar fortnight remains visible.
I am ruined by this sin, since she has been constrained for me by your son. (38)
Therefore, O Lord! As long as this body of mine does not swiftly reach its end— like the digit of the moon on the evening of the first day of the lunar fortnight—
and as long as I have not been destroyed by that very sin through which Your grace was withheld from me, so long do You show mercy toward me.

The host of Death’s soldiers approaches, free from trembling—those very ones we tremble at when we fix them in our minds; O Giriśa, in that situation, your compassion alone is the one refuge, for it leads even those who have fallen into a state of trembling to the arising of auspiciousness.
O Giriśa! That host of the soldiers of Death, which we tremble at when we contemplate in our minds, approaches now free from its own trembling;
O All-pervading Lord, in that matter, Your compassion alone is my refuge. Who does it not lead to becoming a vessel for the dawning of auspiciousness?
For even though You were free from desire, You brought forth a son, Kumāra, making him Māra by turning him into a moth for the fire of Your eye. That [compassion] of Yours is for the sake of others.
Do not destroy with such haste that which is renowned even among children; give me, therefore, this word.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! That you, though free from desire, having made Māra a moth for the fire of your eyes, brought forth Kumāra—that [deed] of yours is renowned as being for the sake of others even among children; therefore, come with speed and do not abandon me; give me your word. My enemies, who have dealt me a great blow, are robbing me of my very life-force and stealing away my pure necklace of discernment (*viveka*); may your compassion, which provides protection, be present here.
Having withdrawn [from the battle], alas, I am ruined in the presence of the crest-jewel of kings! 41.

Anvaya: O Hara! Enemies (the six internal ones, such as desire and the rest), having dealt a mighty blow, are carrying away my very everything—my discernment (viveka)—just like thieves; in this matter, your protective grace has failed to effect its rescue. Alas! Even before Rājaśekharamaṇi, I am ruined.

The pigeon seeks its dwelling in the temple; the merchant-fisherman (aśaṅkapota) finds his livelihood in the ocean; and the many-legged ant (anekapa) constantly carries prosperity upon its back; therefore, O Lord, I resort to devotion for you, just as the frog-pigeon resorts to a lake. 42.
O Lord! The pigeon seeks its dwelling in the temple; the merchant on the sea frequents his ship without fear;
the elephant constantly bears prosperity upon its back; for these reasons, like a small frog approaching a lake, I approach You with devotion.

Never before has such fortitude been attained by Vāsava, even when surrounded by his army, nor by Bala on earth after he had drunk the Soma juice— such as this fresh joy that comes from one who has taken refuge in you.

Anvaya: O Lord! That fresh fortitude which belongs to one who has sought refuge in You with his own being—that fortitude was never obtained in heaven by Vāsava (Indra), surrounded as he was by his army known as Vāsava (the host of the eight Vasu deities); nor was it obtained on earth by Bala, who had drunk the Soma juice.

O Great Bull among men, for whom do you not bestow auspicious peace with that speech which is difficult to obtain even in heaven, which is the terrifying abode of destruction for Time, and which possesses a splendor equal to that of the Fearless One (Amitābha) toward those who bow before it? (44)

O Great Bull among men! That speech of yours which is difficult even for Brahmā in heaven to obtain, and which is the abode of destruction for terrible Time— by that auspicious speech, possessing a splendor equal to the drum of fearlessness for those who have performed prostrations, whom do you not bestow peace upon?

O destroyer of the great Kali age, you who are peaceful yet appear afflicted, you who have rendered the vast Kali age into the Kṛta age; she gazes with longing at you as you shine like a nectar-filled bud of the moon.

Anvaya: O you who have destroyed the great Kali age! O you who have rendered the vast Kali age as if it were the Kṛta age! That virtuous man whom you behold, though he is distressed, shining yet languid—that young woman, beautiful like a digit of the moon consisting of nectar, gazes upon him with longing (with eyes moist with affection).

She is like a string of pearls abandoned by its lord, Śiva; she is like your own assembly of attendants deprived of its leader, Vināyaka; she is like the Goddess of Speech forsaken by you, the Lord of all.
By whom could she be imagined as being capable of enchanting the heart? || 46 ||

Anvaya: O Śiva! By whom can speech, abandoned by you—the Lord of all—be considered capable of enchanting the heart? It is like a string of pearls deprived of its central gem (*nāyaka*), or like the assembly of your own attendants (*gaṇasabhā*) when separated from their leader (*vināyaka*).

The mind of one who is fit for it attains peace through the concentration of renowned honor; yet, by that very [absence of you], the inner mind bears great distress. [Only such a person] touches upon pure intelligence.
Even there, you, who are easily prone to arrogance, do not show compassion toward those who are likewise easily overcome by pride. || 47 ||
Anvaya: O you of celebrated pride! Your mind bears distress within because of that mental anguish (*ādhi*) which is appropriate for one who has attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
One who is stained by the smearing of dust touches a pure intellect; yet even there, you—who are easily accessible to such smearing—do not approach with compassion.
Let there be many things of a fortunate nature in this world as you wish; however, for me, only two things are objects of longing: [the one] beautiful with the ripeness of word and meaning.
Or is it the unbroken devotion of the poet-king Girvāṇa toward the Mountain of the Celestial River (the Himalayas)? 48.

Anvaya: O father! Let there be many things in this world—such as moon-faced women, moonlight, sandalwood, and gardens—that possess a charming nature; yet for my longing, there is only this pair: either the speech of a king of poets, exquisite in its refinement of word and meaning, or unyielding devotion to the Lord of the Celestial River (the Ganges).

O Lord Aghora, just as a cakora bird is delighted by masses of moonlight, as a lotus bud by the radiance of the sun, and as a young peacock by divine waters, so too is there no satisfaction for you through hymns of praise.

Anvaya: O Lord! O Aghora! By your divine waters, as by moonlight-rays for the *cakoraka* bird, or by the radiance of the sun for the lotus bud, or by your hymns of praise for the young peacock—whose joy does this not produce?
Where is your state, which transcends all speech and mind; and where is the mind whose movement falters due to the veil of worldly existence? Thus [he addresses] the one who is filled with terror.
Pure devotion has driven me forward; therefore, this praise offered for your sake is true devotion. || 50 ||

Where is your life-story (character), which transcends all speech and mind, and where is this mind of mine, whose movement falters due to the veil of worldly existence? For this reason, your purifying devotion has rescued me from my terror; therefore, I have offered this hymn of praise to you with true devotion.
We bow down to You and yet dispute variously; we feel shame and yet indulge in impurities; we long for evil words and yet endure them.
And we are consumed by misfortunes for the sake of the belly. || 51 ||

For the sake of our bellies, we bow down to the wicked along with the disputants; we engage in various disputes and feel shame [in some instances]; we indulge in impurities and strive after them in manifold ways; we endure the evil words of the base, and we are consumed within by misfortunes [sins acquired through evil deeds]—alas, what misery!

We know full well that this human state, obtained after long ages of merit yet so transient, is easily regained; and yet, alas, we who are destined for whatever may come do not strive to accomplish our own welfare. 52.

We certainly know that this human state, obtained through long-standing virtuous deeds, is both fleeting and unstable, and is not easily attained again. (And yet,) we do not strive to accomplish our own welfare—alas! we are truly those who live for whatever may happen by chance (*yadbhaviṣya*). Therefore, while these people—who are addicted to the pleasures of enjoyment, who have not completed their duties, and who are utterly helpless—are still here, [the time to act] has surely arrived before the fisherman comes and suddenly seizes the fish.
Death forcibly carries away those who are without refuge in an instant. || 53 ||

Be gracious for now; have compassion for us intensely. O Moon-Bearer, forgive our loud lamentation; do not abandon us! Speak yourself, O Blessed One, ocean of mercy: whom else shall we go to for refuge when we have been forsaken by you? (54)
(These two verses form a pair.

Therefore, before death—like a fisherman coming suddenly and unexpectedly to forcibly seize us in an instant, like whales—takes us away by sheer force while we are helplessly addicted to the pleasures of sensory enjoyment, with our tasks unfinished and without refuge, O Moon-bearer! be gracious to us and show us compassion.
Raise a loud cry! Forgive me; do not abandon me! O Blessed One, you alone speak as an ocean of compassion:
abandoned by you, to whom else shall we go for refuge?
If it is said that death is inevitable for one who is born, was that not transgressed by Śveta and by the one who delights the Lord whose crest is the moon? If even they were conquered by him—
For us, whose austerities are slight, he is indeed impossible to ward off by means of vast penances.

Therefore, O Lord whose crest is the moon, if it is true that death is inevitable for one who is born, then why was that [death] not [prevented] by Śveta and Nandin? (56) [Yugma] O Lord, may my life-breaths depart through Your grace at the conclusion of my worship, while I am intensely embracing Your footstool with unwavering devotion, my eyes closed under the guise of sleep.
Anvaya: O Śītakaraśekhara! Since death is certain for one who is born, [if so,] then why was that [death] not [prevented] by Śveta and Nandin?

Is he [Death] surpassed? If you think that he has been conquered by those two through their vast austerities, whereas for us, who possess only meager penance, he remains truly irresistible—then, O Lord! by your grace, at the conclusion of my worship, may my life-breaths depart as I embrace your footstool with intense fervor, my eyes closed under the guise of sleep, while I am possessed of unyielding devotion.

By this [comparison], what is meant? Are serpents not possessed of firm coils, or do they not partake in the expansion of the play of crookedness? Yet, how can they—diminished in sequence and devoid of the artful arrangement of words—ever aspire to imitate the nectar of well-spoken verses? (57)

Therefore, O Lord, casting aside this terrifying pride—which is wanton in its pretense of using serpents as ear-ornaments—please skillfully transform these words, pregnant with affectionate service, into ornaments for Your ears. (A yugma) Anvaya: O Śiva! Are these snakes (so dear to You) bearing tight coils, or are they partaking in the expansion of the play of crookedness?

[They] do not exist [though they do indeed exist]; however, since these [verses] are gradually diminished and lack the artful composition of words (*padagumpha*), how can they aspire to emulate the nectar of my well-spoken verses? For my nectar of well-spoken verses possesses dense construction and partakes in the expansion of the play of *vakrokti* (poetic deviation);
whereas these are not only gradually diminished and lacking in word-composition, but rather possess proper sequence and are endowed with the appropriate arrangement of words.

The meaning is that my well-spoken nectar possesses a distinct excellence over [the words of] the serpents. Therefore, O Lord! Abandoning this terrifying [serpent]—this ear-ornament of the snakes, which is perverse in its playful arrogance—please skillfully make these words of mine, filled with affectionate courtesy, your own ornament.
O Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Death himself, alas, since I have spoken these words to you, who are the sole kinsman of the world, as if you were without kin... [O Lord].
O ocean of compassion, show mercy to me as I praise you from my heart. (59)

Anvaya: O Lord! by me, who am without kinsmen, these words were spoken before You, the sole kinsman of the world—O Destroyer of Death! O Ocean of Compassion! O Śaṅkara! Alas! please lend Your ear to that piteous speech of mine as I praise You.

Does that agony—which makes one who sees blind, one who possesses self-conceit free from pride, and even one with wide ears deaf—not cause the wicked to dance like the Goddess of Fortune? Therefore, O Blessed One, forgive my transgressions. (60)

The agony that makes one who sees blind, brings low one who is proud, and deafens even one with wide ears— that same agony, like the fortune of wicked kings, why does it not make this wretched person dance? Therefore, O Blessed One, forgive these transgressions (consisting of improper and incoherent prattle).
Fearing that this unrestrained rogue, whose strength is insurmountable, who blazes within like Death itself, who is free from hesitation and possesses no small pride,
might maintain his fixed wrath even toward our wondrous and eloquent discourses sanctified by the life of Śaṅkara, we shall awaken him.

We address you—O Kṛtānta—who, though your mind is purified by the wonderful sayings of Śaṅkara’s life-story, remains stubbornly angry even toward us; who are unrestrained, wicked, possessed of invincible strength, burning within, free from hesitation, and filled with no small pride.

Desiring to reconcile you, we speak this truth which is fresh, harsh, without scales [of deceit], beneficial for the future, wholesome, satisfying, faultless, and nourishing to freedom from anger—for your own welfare, O Kṛtānta.
And whatever we say, listen to it with focused attention. || 62 ||

O Kṛtānta! You who wish to make peace with us—heedfully attend to that which we say to you: it is true, beneficial, measured, fresh and firm, free from splinters, wholesome for the future, satisfying, faultless, and devoid of the nourishment of anger.
Elsewhere, O unrestrained Kīnāśa of evil intent, display your "huṃ" roars and destroy our pride; do not [disregard] even those who have made the moon-crested Lord their protector.
I think you will surely rebuke me; this hope of yours is already as good as destroyed.

Anvaya: O unrestrained one! O Kīnāśa! O you of evil intent! Show your "huṃ" sounds elsewhere; do not destroy your pride, thinking, "I shall revile even those who have made the Moon-crested Lord their protector. This hope of yours is utterly destroyed—it is nothing but contemptible.

O mind, you whose longing is aroused by the tremulous eyes of that fickle-eyed woman! Why do you dance upon beholding the greatness of her who possesses steady love? What, do you think you will sport with her? Alas, abandon this wretched inner hope! She has indeed been turned into a stone tied around the neck in the ocean of worldly existence.

O Dīnadamana, you have always been wayward; nevertheless, O terrible Kāla, surely you must abandon this vain and wicked hope against the Disposer (Vidhi). Do you think, alas, that you will forcibly strike down this man as if he were helpless—this one renowned throughout the three worlds as the servant of Śaṅkara and the sole vessel of the Lord’s love?

Since that great Lord, though their offenses were grave, inflicted punishment upon them yet again showed them favor, we are his servants; therefore, even when we speak what is beneficial to your enemies, you consider it anger.
O Time! Even though you have committed an offense, that Great Lord, who is supremely compassionate, has again shown favor toward you;
we are His servants. Therefore, when we speak for the welfare of even your enemies, do you think with anger, "They speak such words out of malice toward me"?

O wicked, ill-behaved Kāla, long ago you obtained from Purāri the punishment for your own insolence; hearing of that, even the hearts of the steadfast tremble—how then can you venture upon that very same act again?

O ill-behaved one! O rogue! O Death! Having heard that very punishment for your own insolence which you previously received from Purāri, even the hearts of the steadfast tremble; why then do you again attempt that same thing?
Place quickly the noose of the wind-eater (Śeṣa) in your hand; O snare for men, there is no room here for your anger among those who are free from worldly attachment.
O Time, you who cause fear to the cowardly—what can you do against those who have taken refuge in Śaṅkara? 66.

Anvaya: O Puruṣapāśa! Place the noose of Pavanaśana quickly upon your hand; here there is no room for your anger, O you who cause fear to the cowardly! O Kāla! What do you do toward us, who have taken refuge in Śaṅkara among those free from worldly attachment? Employ your own man against others; do not let anger sprout toward the servants of Śaṅkara. Have you forgotten?
O you whose weapon is the venomous serpent, that roar of "Hūṃ" uttered by you is the drum that awakens unimpeded wrath.

O Kāla! Employ your own man [Yama] against others [those devoid of devotion to Śaṅkara]; do not let the wrath of the servants of Śaṅkara sprout. O you whose weapon is the serpent! Have you forgotten that roar of Hara, which is the drum for awakening unrestrained fury?
For it was for the sake of protecting a single devotee that you were formerly consumed by the Enemy of Tripura.

Though he may be utterly intent on wrath, with a deep and terrible *huṃkāra* like the roar of clouds that threatens all people, what can Yama—even with staff in hand—do to me, who am completely shielded by the armor of devotion to Śarva’s feet?
O Kīnāśa! O fool! O unrestrained one! O thoughtless one! O cruel one! O merciless one! If you, without cause and without regard for others, act thus toward those who have no refuge...
Why do you harbor anger? What do you intend to do against those who have taken refuge in Maheśvara?

O destroyer! O fool! O unrestrained one! O thoughtless one! O merciless one! O pitiless one! O you who show no consideration! If you direct causeless wrath toward those who have no refuge, then what do you intend to do with those who have taken shelter in Maheśvara? By creating unceasing enmity toward those who are not your kin, you vainly assume a haughty neck like that of Yama, even toward those distressed by grave offenses.
For the virtuous are not even capable of inflicting harm upon the base. || 69 ||
Anvaya: O Yama! You, creating unceasing hostility toward those who have no kinsmen and no refuge, bear this state of having your neck uplifted in vain;

for the virtuous are not capable of inflicting harm even upon the lowest of men when they are distressed by grave offenses. Since you are able to strike living beings with violence, having obtained the favor of your Lord, the Father of the Lord of Destruction (Śiva), that must surely be the result of your past deeds.
What is your manly prowess, O End-maker, in regard to that fruit which is a difficult evil and hard to overcome? (70)

O Antaka! Having obtained the grace of the Lord, the father of Pramathānātha, that you are able to strike living beings with violence—that is merely the fruit of the past misdeeds of those very beings, which are difficult to overcome. What manly prowess is there in that for you?
Is it not a mere truth that people praise you as Dharmarāja and Kāla, [calling you] a thorn [to the wicked] without cause? Do people not [do so]?
They declare the owl to be a bird of ill omen, though it is the very treasury that is the root of all world-wide misfortune.

Anvaya: O Kāla! Is it indeed true that people praise you—who are a thorn without cause—as the "King of Dharma" (Dharmarāja)? (And this is observed: Do people not praise the owl—the root-treasury of misfortune for the world—as the "bird of auspiciousness"? And why do weeping Kāpālikas, the funeral-priests, and the twice-born praise you as the "Lord of Life" (Jīviteśa), O Antaka? For that is entirely fitting, since you are the Supreme... Translation: O Kāla! Is it truly the case that people praise you—who are a causeless thorn—as the "King of Dharma" (Dharmarāja)? (Indeed, this is seen: Do people not praise the owl—the very source of inauspiciousness for the world—as the "bird of auspiciousness"? And why do weeping Kāpālikas, the funeral-priests, and the twice-born praise you as the "Lord of Life" (Jīviteśa), O Antaka? For that is entirely fitting, since you are the Supreme...
He is a friend to them, while he is an enemy without cause to his enemies and no friend to others.

Anvaya: O Antaka! That it is fitting for weeping women (*rudatyaḥ*), Kāpālikas, corpse-burners (*śavadahaḥ*), gurus, and twice-born ones (*dvijāḥ*) to praise you, O Lord of Life (*jīviteśa*), saying "O Lord of Life!"—is indeed appropriate; because you are their supreme friend, whereas to others you are a causeless enemy and a foe. Therefore, they address you as "Lord of Life"—that is, the master and leader of life, O taker of life!
(Thus they praise:

"O son of the Sun, those most compassionate teachers who, for the sake of others, undergo the toil of rites such as the *apamārjana*, *bhūta-yajña*, *niryāṇa-karma*, the final *iṣṭi*, and the propitiation of Śiva (*śivakriyā*), praise you as 'the God of Faith' (*śrāddhadeva*). (73)

Anvaya: O son of the Sun! Those most compassionate preceptors who, through rites such as the *apamārjana*, *bhūta-yāga*, *niryāṇaka*, *carameṣṭi*, and *śivakriyā*, labor for the sake of others, praise you as "Śrāddhadeva.

For your father, the Sun, does not abandon his domain—whether it be good or bad, whether it be the end of darkness or the path of righteousness; therefore, he is the Equal One (*Samavartin*). You, however, are equal toward both the virtuous and the wicked.
Even at the stroke of death, they immediately praise you, O Samavartin, the Ender.
Having displayed anger toward you, he who bestowed grace [upon you] now desires to bestow that same grace even upon your servants. Why then do you employ me in this?
For you are praised by those who know the vital points (*marmavit*) as being impartial (*samavartin*) even though you act with partiality (*viṣamavartin*).
(Yugma) Anvaya: O Antaka! Your father, Arka (the Sun), while bringing darkness to its end, did not [leave] any region—whether auspicious (*santa*) or inauspicious (*asanta*)—unseen.

Therefore, the Sun, who revolves with equanimity, becomes [the god] Samavartin; you, however, strike out equally toward both the virtuous and the wicked, and for this reason people immediately praise you as Samavartin. Thus, even though you are one whose course is uneven—and who, being devoid of discrimination between the good and the bad—nevertheless, you are praised by those who know the vital points as "Samavartin.
(But) that Śambhu, having manifested his wrath, has bestowed grace upon you; and since you now desire to bestow grace even upon his servants, [you are truly worthy].

If that is so, what do you say to me in this regard? You honor those whose foreheads are whitened by the nectar of the lotus feet of the One who wears the stainless moon upon His crest; yet you, O knower of policy, treat me with contempt.
Do not treat me thus, for if you are wrathful, you are merely a man of Rudra’s lineage, and thus a Raudra.

Anvaya: O Knower of Policy! You are a man; therefore, O Raudra! if you protect your own seal of pride (*svamānamudrām*), then do not insult those men whose foreheads you grace with the nectar of the lotus-feet of Him who bears the stainless moon upon His crest. Since you are *Śamana* because of your subduing the pride of the wicked, or rather, since you are *Yama* because of your restraining the base, I consider that [your name] is for the purpose of quelling my own intoxication.
The power belongs to you alone; it is you whom those devoted to existence must control. (77)
Anvaya: O Antaka! That you are Śamana because of subduing the pride of the wicked, or that you are Yama because of restraining the lowly—let that be otherwise.
But I consider this: that those who possess devotion to Bhava are able to subdue your very intoxication or to restrain you yourself;
for, O cruel Antaka, you exert yourself excessively against even those intent on the praise of Śarva, despite their being free from arrogance. This is destined to happen.
May you, moreover, bring about the destruction of the arising fire from the forehead of Bhairava, who is fierce with the terrors of future existence.

O cruel one! O you who are excessively arrogant! O Death! That you act so insolently even toward those intent on praising Śarva—that shall bring about your own defeat, arising from the fire of the fierce forehead-eye of Bhairava, whose future power is terrifying.
Or what else? O son of the Sun, do you wish to perform that broad-mouthed laughter at the refuge of the Lord? Do not do it, for it will not be so.

O you who are free from fear! O you with the formidable face, son of the Sun! What more need be said? Do not seek to mock those who have taken refuge in the Lord; for that Great Lord, who is affectionate toward his dependents and full of grace, will not tolerate your impropriety. (Anvaya: O Viśaṅka! O Viśaṅkaṭāsya Arkaja!! What else shall we say? Since you desire to make a laughingstock of those who have sought refuge in the Lord, do not do so;
for this Maheśa, who is compassionate toward his dependents and gracious, does not forgive what is unbecoming of you. (Kālopālambhakulakam)

Like the surface of a forehead adorned with a sectarian mark, like a forest grove graced by the agitation of a bride’s sidelong glances, and like the night beautified by the moon— the mark of the dust of Brahmā— Śambhu bears splendor through the *Vasantatilaka* meter as his poetic ornament.

Like the forehead of a bride adorned with a *tilaka* shaken by her side-glances, or like a forest grove graced by a deer-marked [moon], this petition to Śambhu composed in the *vasantatilaka* meter bears a beauty like that of the night. The *kuravaka* tree [blooms] through embraces, the *tilaka* through side-glances, and the *aśoka* through the strikes of feet accompanied by the tinkling of anklets.
Through the falling of mouthfuls of wine from the women, the Bakula tree attains full bloom in this season filled with the spirit of spring.

[O King,] since your garments have frayed hems, your youth has faded, your faculties are impaired, and your mind is incapable; since there is distress in your limbs due to the lack of respect shown by worthless, wicked lords; since your residence is useless, your human birth is in vain, and this body carries a treasury devoid of all virtue—take compassion in your heart upon these words.
And [this is] stated in the Śruti. || 81 ||
O Master! For one who bears a garment with frayed ends and an age devoid of its early stages;
for one who bears a collection of senses incapable of their own functions and a mind devoid of patience;
there arises distress—meaning wretchedness—from the humiliation of worthless and wicked lords, as well as from limbs that have become worthless and weak.

Listen to these words of mine, who am bearing the agitation of decline (due to exhaustion) and the high fever of old age (accompanied by trembling), who am maintaining a house that has become useless (meaning impoverished), and who am carrying a human birth that has become entirely futile (meaning meaningless), as well as this body devoid of auspiciousness (lacking the blessing of the means to liberation) and a treasury devoid of prosperity (destitute of gold). And in your heart, cultivate compassion.

I am indeed ignorant and dull-witted; I am not capable of composing charming flatteries by which I might become an object of Your compassion. However, having taken this cry of a distressed, helpless, and miserable man into Your ears, come quickly and place Your foot upon the head of me, the unfortunate one.

O Lord! First of all, I, being ignorant and consequently dull-witted, am not capable of composing those charming and flattering words by which I might become an object of Your compassion. However, having taken to Your ears the lamentation of one who is distressed, helpless, and miserable, come quickly and place Your foot upon my head, for I am so unfortunate.

Thus ends the ninth hymn, titled "The Lamentation of the Wretched," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*.
The Tenth Hymn.

Victorious is the praise of the one whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon—the moonlight for the cakora-bird of the mind, the solar radiance for the lotus-face of the virtuous, and the path for the raining peacock of the ears. (1)

Victorious is the moonlight for the cakora-birds of the hearts of the virtuous, the splendor of the sun for the lotuses of their faces, the path for the rain of peacock-feathers upon the ears, and the praise of the crescent-moon crest of Śiva.
Victorious is the ever-fresh spring for the creeper of devotion, produced from the ripened fruit of the tree of merit, and the kinsman to those distressed by the calamities of misfortune.
The nectar from the mouth of the bride that is the eloquent speech of a skilled poet.
This hymn is a boat for crossing the great ocean of existence; it is the deep roar of the peacock-cloud that is the preeminent sage; it is a flow of nectar that removes the burning heat of the heart;

and it is the ornament of the moon, the delighter of the night-lotuses. (Yugma) It is the fresh springtime for the creeper of devotion; it arises from the ripened fruit of the tree of merit; and it is a kinsman for those distressed by the calamities of misfortune.

Victorious is this hymn—the nectar from the lips of the bride that is the eloquent speech of the good poet; the raft for crossing the great ocean of worldly existence; the deep roar of the clouds that are the eminent masters; the liquid nectar for removing the burning heat of the heart; the ornament of the moon who delights the night-lotuses.
It is sweeter than the face of a moon-faced woman and more refreshing than the waters of the celestial Ganges. Victorious is it, purified by the praise of the Lord of the Three Worlds!
It is the elixir of the essence of the eloquent verses of true poets. || 4 ||

Victorious is the elixir of the aesthetic essence of the eloquent verses of true poets— sweeter even than the face of the moon-faced woman, more refreshing than the waters of the celestial river, and sanctified by the praises of the Lord of the Three Worlds.

Victorious is this sprout of sandalwood that delights the heart, which shines with the ever-fresh humming of bees and is capable of quelling the heat of wandering through the desert of worldly existence.
Devotion to Śaṅkara is unbreakable.

Victorious is the unyielding devotion to Śaṅkara, which is beautiful with the ever-fresh humming of bees, capable of quelling the heat of wandering through the desert of worldly existence, and a sprout of sandalwood that delights the heart. Now, having seen even a newly sprouted shoot of discernment that had somehow taken root in the mind, suddenly shattered by a flood of various calamities— [The verse continues: ...it is instantly crushed like a lotus stalk struck by the thunderbolt of a cloud. Therefore, O friend, abandon all distractions and, with a focused mind, practice this supreme devotion to Śiva, which is the sole means for the attainment of liberation. Otherwise, one will surely fall into the ocean of worldly existence, which is difficult to cross. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Devotion," in the *Śivabhaktikalpalatā*, a work composed by the illustrious Śrīmad Appayadīkṣita, the son of the venerable Śrīmat Rāmakṛṣṇa Dīkṣita, who was himself the son of the venerable Śrīmat Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita. I address the Teacher of the World.

Now, having observed that even a fresh sprout of discernment—which had somehow (with great difficulty) taken root in my mind for a moment—has been shattered by the flood of manifold calamities, I immediately petition the Teacher of the World:

O Haṃsa, you who are renowned throughout the world, devoted to compassion, and who have assumed a form dedicated to the welfare of others; why do you not take up residence within the lotus of my heart?
[He is] the refuge for those seeking shelter from calamities. || 7 ||

Anvaya: O Haṃsa! Though world-renowned as one devoted to compassion, who has assumed a form for the welfare of others, why do you, having taken your station in the lotus-heart of those like me seeking refuge, not destroy our calamities?
If you were to establish your presence in the heart, how could the abundance of misfortune spread? If that were not to spread, how could it ever take hold?
Even wise people [are led astray] by improper actions. || 8 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*): O Lord! If you were to establish your presence within the heart, then how could this flood of calamities spread? And if it did not spread, then how could even a wise person become attached to improper actions?
Here, by these outbursts of calamity—which seize the mind with vast and towering attachments—if one does not fall into cowardice, dependence, and fruitlessness...
And a person should associate with the wicked. || 9 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O All-pervading Lord! If, in this world, people whose minds are seized by the demon of excessive possessions due to the emergence of great calamities were not to succumb to cowardice, dependence, fruitlessness, and wickedness, then who could endure the torment of the deformity of miserliness arising from the intoxication of even a fragment of worldly power, once they have abandoned the mental delight born of the addiction to worshipping Your lotus feet? This is the connection with the verse that follows.
The same applies hereafter:

if one would not resort to the company of the virtuous—that abode of abundant compassion which is an antidote to the serpent of calamity—then one's heart possesses the splendor of a moonstone melted by the touch of the moonbeams' pleasant rays. (10)

If the heart of a person—which is a constant abode of abundant compassion due to its addiction to the company of virtuous people—does not possess the splendor of a moonstone melted by contact with the pleasant touch of the moonbeams, then [the following would occur]; the connection is as before.
Those oppressed by the long summer heat of spreading and unrestrained misfortune would desire the arrival of wealth, if it were like the arrival of the clouds.
Like thirsty deer, they were full of longing. || 11 ||
If those who seek your favor— people in need, tormented by the long summer heat of unobstructed misfortune and therefore parched with thirst—
did not long for the arrival of wealth as deer long for the coming of the clouds, then who indeed would turn away from serving the lotus-feet of Your Honor?
This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) as before.

If women here, whose waists ripple with the waves of three folds and are made beautiful by full, firm breasts, did not steal the mind with their side-long glances while abiding in the joy of love; [then this place would be truly delightful]. 12.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: if, in this world, these women—who possess full and firm breasts and whose waists ripple with the folds of a triple furrow—should not captivate the mind while they hold their lovers in delight, then [the following would be true], as before.
[This is so] in this world crowded with the thieves of the powerful senses, terrifying with the fierce serpents of sense-objects, and unbearable like a long-lasting forest fire of misfortune.
In consciousness overwhelmed by the darkness of dense delusion.

Even those of refined intellect, as they hasten along the path of worldly existence, have their selves carried away by the force of powerful karma; were it not for these adversaries—Lust, Pride, and the rest—who would strike at the opportune moment. (A yugma) [This occurs] in this world crowded with the thieves of the powerful senses, terrifying with the fierce serpents of sense-objects, and unbearable like a long-lasting forest fire of misfortune.

For one who runs along the path of worldly existence with consciousness obscured by the thick darkness of delusion, whose self is carried away by the force of powerful karma—even for such a person of refined intellect, if these adversaries, headed by Madana and Māna, did not strike at the opportune moment (the moment of meditating on Śrī Śambhu), then all [the benefits] would be as described before.
The drum signaling the commencement of Madana’s world conquest. || 15 ||

If, in the springtime, the drum-roll for the onset of Love’s world-conquest—intensified by the warbling of cuckoos eager to devour rows of fresh mango leaves—were not able to terrify people, then [the rest] would be as before.

If, in the spring, the humming songs of bees intoxicated by drinking honey were not there to take away the longing of one who desires even a fragment of pleasure... [then everything else would remain as before].
They would not capture this deer of the mind. || 16 ||

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Hara! If these [trees], whose songs are the humming of bees intoxicated by the passion for drinking honey in the springtime, do not capture this deer of my mind—which longs for the experience of even a fragment of pleasure—then [the consequence would be] as stated previously.
They are bent low by the weight of their breasts in the form of fresh clusters of blossoms, and their hands are the sprouts made to dance by the breeze. If they...
The creepers, whose sweet voices consist of the humming of bees, shall rival the binding of the [lovers'] limbs. || 17 ||

If the creepers— those amorous women with breasts bent down by clusters of fresh blossoms, hands in the form of sprouts dancing in the breeze, and voices sweet with the humming of bees— did not succeed in binding the deer of the mind, then [the summer would be unbearable], as before. If, during the dense season of the clouds, the dust-covered quarters did not bring intense heat to the minds of the proud lovers, as if it were the month of Śuci (Jyeṣṭha), with its young rays incessantly touching them...
The Lord of the Day (the Sun) desired to encompass it. || 18 ||

If the Lord of Day (the Sun), desiring to embrace closely the green quarters still bearing their pollen with his youthful rays, were not to bring intense heat during the scorching season (summer)—as if into the pure minds of the proud—then all [would be well], as described before.

And if these deer-eyed women, with their broad hips, thighs, and breasts, and with garments fluttered by the heavy and restless wind, were not present at the arrival of the clouds... [then all would be well].
And they shattered the quarters of the sky and destroyed all steadfastness. || 19 ||

Anvaya: If, at the arrival of the clouds, these deer-eyed women—with their broad, firm thighs and heavy breasts, and with garments disarrayed by the forceful, heavy wind—did not become like the quarters of the sky, which have broad, dense clouds for their hips and breasts, and whose garments are tossed about by the forceful, heavy wind, and which shatter one's composure;

then [the rest follows as before]. (Note: *Pṛthulasajjaghanorupayodharāḥ* is a punning compound where *pṛthula-sajja-ghana-uru-payodharāḥ* refers to the women’s broad, ready, dense, and heavy breasts, while *pṛthula-sajja-ghana-uru-payodharāḥ* refers to the quarters of the sky having broad, ready, dense, and vast clouds.)

O lady with arched brows, if the rivers did not recall for you in autumn the abode of bathing— where the lotus-faces were accompanied by fragrant scents and laughter, and which possessed the graceful charm of lovely swans— then they would not have reminded you of it.
If, in autumn, the rivers— the abodes of bathing— possessing lotus-faces with fragrant smiles and bearing the graceful movements of charming swans,

were not to cause [men] to remember those women with arched brows who likewise possess lotus-faces with fragrant smiles and bear the graceful movements of charming swans at the place of bathing, then [the consequence would be] as stated previously.

If Dīrghatamas had not encountered the unbearable, fierce winds in the month of Sahas (Mārgaśīrṣa), even the nights would have served as a cause for recollecting the firm, warm, and large breasts of young women. 21.

In the winter season, when the winds are fierce and difficult to endure and the nights are exceedingly long, if they did not serve as a cause for remembering the firm, warm, and large breasts of young women—then [the situation would be as described] previously. If the sun, its radiance dimmed by the rising of thick clouds, were not present outside; and if one were distressed by suffering both in body and in mind during the heat...
Even a person whose passion has been aroused may become indolent. || 22 ||

When the winter season was agitated by the distress of the birds' flight, and when the minds of all people were agitated by the distress of vices such as hunting, and when the sun— the treasure-house of light— had its radiance dulled by the rising of dense clouds; even a person whose passion for asceticism had taken root would become indolent, and so on, as described previously.

Having once again attained this body—which is difficult to obtain and capable of rescuing one from all calamities—he beheld it as being like a drop of water trembling upon the leaf of a young lotus-stalk shaken by the wind. (23)

O Bhava! Who, having abandoned the mental disposition of being addicted to the worship of your lotus feet, would here endure the torment of the base transformations of pride swelling from even a fragment of worldly prosperity? (24) [Yugma; a group of eighteen verses]. *Anvaya*: O Lord! (If the aforementioned transformations such as desire and the like were not powerful,) then again, O Bhava! here—

Having obtained this body—which is capable of rescuing one from every calamity yet difficult to attain, and which resembles a drop of water trembling on a young lotus leaf shaken by the wind—who would endure here the torment of the base transformations of pride swelling at the prospect of a mere fragment of worldly power, while abandoning the benevolence born of devotion to worshipping the lotus feet of Your Honor? This great darkness, consisting of clouds, rises up, obscuring the intense light of the sun; yet that time of death, though possessed of dense strength, has arrived. Therefore, O Swan, depart from here!
Set your foot upon the mind. || 25 ||
Anvaya: O Haṃsa! This great darkness consisting of my sins rises up; that Time of dense power has also arrived;
therefore, take your place (remain) here in my mind.
Thus, while the great darkness of delusion rises up, concealing within [the heart] the infinite joy, may you, whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire, [dwell] in my heart.
This announces his absence. || 26 ||

Anvaya: O Ananta! This great darkness of delusion (*moha-mahātamaḥ*) which rises within [the heart] concealing joy—this very darkness in the hearts of those like me proclaims the absence of You, whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire.
Indeed, O Maheśa, the waves of worldly existence (*bhava-ūrmi*) are not able to cause the mind presided over by You to wander; for a forest protected by the lord of lions cannot be disturbed.
Are the monkeys anywhere capable of destroying it? || 27 ||
O Great Lord! Indeed, these waves of worldly existence are not able to cause the mind of Your devotee, which is presided over by You, to wander.
For it is observed that monkeys are never capable of destroying a forest protected by the king of beasts.

It is better to dwell at the foot of a tree on the sandy banks of a forest river, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, and clothed in unrestrained bark garments, than to live without devotion to Śiva.
The state of being the Lord of the Thirty-three [gods]. (This is an interpolation. The sequence:

It is better to dwell at the foot of trees on the banks of rivers in the forest, subsisting on fruits, roots, and water, clothed in unrestrained garments of bark—provided one possesses devotion to Śiva; even the state of being the Lord of the Thirty-three is not better without it.

Misfortune perishes and is seen to vanish; power quivers and the intellect attains steadfastness. For one whose mind is intent on the act of praise, who upholds the Śruti and Smṛti, peace of mind finds its firm standing. || 28 ||

Anvaya: O Maheśa! When You behold [the devotee], misfortune perishes, power flashes forth, the intellect attains steadfastness; likewise, in one who possesses discernment and honors the Śruti and Smṛti, supreme bliss (nirvṛti) finds its abode in the act of Your praise.
How many living beings here in this ocean of worldly existence do not glitter like bubbles and then dissolve? Yet, has any single person been born again in this world whose birth is truly desirable?
He who is a servant of Śiva. || 29 ||

In this ocean of worldly existence, how many living beings do not shine like bubbles and then dissolve? Yet, whoever in this world is a servant of Śiva, he alone has become one whose birth is truly desirable.
He is as if made of the pure particles of dust from the Lord’s feet, which have been instantly cast down upon the throne by those who possess devotion.
Those like me have placed their feet even upon the heads of the gods.

By good fortune, through us—pure devotees who have suddenly cast our bodies upon the pedestal—the foot of the Blessed One has been placed even upon the heads of the gods, as if by the particles of dust from his feet.

Victorious is that jewel, which provides a support free from mockery for those falling into the treacherous ocean of calamity, and which brings about the destruction of all inauspiciousness in the world! Ah, how wonderful!
The service of Śiva. || 31 ||

Oh, for those beings falling into the treacherous ocean of calamity, that which serves as a support—though appearing like a mockery—is the jewel of service to Śiva, which brings an end to all worldly inauspiciousness; it triumphs! It triumphs, being composed of nectar, the abode of all auspiciousness, the destroyer of misfortune, and capable of pacifying the sufferings of birth, old age, and death.
Worship of the Blessed One is a great medicine. || 32 ||

Victorious is the great medicine named the worship of the Blessed One—capable of pacifying the afflictions of birth, old age, and death inherent in the cycle of existence, the eradicator of misfortune, the abode of all auspiciousness, and composed of nectar. This is an alchemical elixir (*rasāyana*) that requires no preparation; it is inexhaustible bliss without the need for sensory enjoyment; it is nectar obtained without churning the ocean.
That which is imperishable is the service of the Lord.

That service to the Lord which is imperishable is itself an unaccomplished elixir (*rasāyana*); it is an inexhaustible happiness devoid of [worldly] enjoyment; and it is nectar obtained without churning the ocean. What is the use of other fruitless snares of worldly existence—the ostentation of elephants, horses, chariots, and garments? Let my addiction to serving the lotus feet of the Blessed One be my wealth until the end of time. (34)
What is the use of these other fruitless snares of worldly existence—the grand displays of elephants, horses, chariots, and garments?
Let my addiction to serving the lotus feet of the Blessed One be my inexhaustible wealth.
Let that woman carry away my loveliness; let nectar be nectar, or honey be honey. But let there be the nature of ultimate bliss.
Serving the adornment of the moon, the lover of the night, is our very purpose. || 35 ||

Let the well-known beloved woman possess her loveliness; let nectar remain nectar (which bestows immortality); or let honey be honey (the product of bees). But for us, only the service of the ornament of the night’s lover [the moon] shall be the abode of bliss. I, with a single-minded heart day and night, my envy toward the god of love slightly subsiding, having understood the insurmountable ways of the Blessed One, [worship] the ornament of the autumnal sky.
I take refuge. || 36 ||

Having understood that the Blessed Goddesses are difficult to overcome, and with my pride, passion, and envy subsided, I take refuge day and night, single-mindedly and with devotion, in the one who bears the crescent moon as his ornament.
I pray to this ocean of the nectar of compassion, the crest-jewel upon the head of the young moon; may he [protect] me in birth after birth.
"May your body become a means for worship. || 37 ||
I pray thus to him, the ocean of the nectar of compassion, the crest-jewel of the young moon: "In birth after birth, may my body become a means for the worship of you.
May that stainless ornament, which bears upon it a certain most enchanting mark like the unbridled god of love himself, adorn my face.
The name of Śiva is free from all affliction.

May that name of Śiva—which bears an indescribable, utterly captivating chisel-mark that is unrestrained—become an ornament upon my mouth; for it is stainless and free from all affliction. O heart, contemplate a pure state of being; O inattentive one, maintain a firm resolve! You, who are powerless, shall thus attain happiness.
What is indestructible without the service of Śiva? || 39 ||
O heart! Cultivate a state free from turbidity; O inattentive one! Bind yourself with firm resolve; O powerless one!
What imperishable happiness do you seek other than the service of Śiva?
O mind, through your current thirst for the flavors of worldly existence, you abandon your mental elevation, which lies beyond the commands of the Destroyer of Madana.
You look toward a means that is both a source of desire and a downfall.
O mind! Now, through thirst for the flavor of worldly existence, you abandon the loftiness of your own nature; what infallible remedy do you look for beyond the command of Madana?
[Look] at the grove, whitened by *mādhavī* creepers stirred by the wind and entwined with rows of trees.
In the lotus that purifies the six-legged bee seated within its stainless and tender calyx; || 41 ||

O Madana, having subdued her with passion, take this bride—who is won over by you—to your lord; he, whose mind is intent on uplifting the helpless, will bring about for you the ultimate cessation of sorrows. (A yugma) [In the verse:
In the place whitened by *mādhavī* creepers stirred by the wind and curved by rows of trees...
In this pleasure grove, where the lotuses—purified by the feeding of bees seated within their tender, unblemished buds—are full of passion, you young wives have been brought under the sway of love.
Cast aside your husband and worship Him alone; He, whose intellect is intent on rescuing the defenseless, brings an end to your supreme sorrow.
Abandon delusion, return to your own true state, give up your grief, and embrace the possession of honor.
Day after day, be intent on drinking the elixir of the remembrance of the lotus feet of Hara. 43.

O mind! Abandon delusion; resort to your own true state (your proper limit); cast off grief; relinquish the possession of pride; daily devote yourself to the drinking of the elixir that is the remembrance of the lotus feet of Śiva;
and, my dear friend, abandon that which is improper—that curse of the fickleness of women’s eyes—since you, ever turned outward, do not even attain the mental delight of remembering Śaṅkara.
It should be abandoned. || 44 ||
O mind, ever turned toward the external! Alas, that you consider it virtuous to lead yourself to the curse of fickleness caused by the eyes of women—that indeed is what you deem good—is the meaning.
That you lead even the mental state born of the remembrance of Śaṅkara to a state of worthlessness—that is improper (meaning:
unfit). If you can endure the fear of the frown of the enraged soldiers of Time, which is difficult to overcome, then resort to that medicine for the incurable disease of worldly existence.
The one who delights the one adorned with serpents. || 45 ||

O mind! If you consider the fear of the frown of the enraged soldier of Time to be difficult to overcome, then resort to the one who delights the serpent-adorned Lord [Śiva], for he is the medicine for the incurable disease of worldly existence.
If you desire to cultivate friendship with yourself, if you wish to cast off the bond of sin, and if you seek to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
This service to the Lord is the maker of iron. || 46 ||

O mind! If you desire to act with friendship toward yourself, if you wish to avoid the bondage of sin, and if you seek to cross the ocean of worldly existence, then take refuge in the service of the Lord, which bestows happiness.
O fool! If, as a result of some past good deed, a treasure has fallen into the palm of your hand—a treasure capable of removing all calamities—do you not take hold of it?
How could there be pointlessness? || 47 ||

Anvaya: O wretched mind! If, as a result of the ripening of good karma, a treasure has fallen into the palm of your hand, then, O fool, why do you lead that [human birth]—which is capable of removing all calamities and is fit for the worship of Śiva—to futility?

O mind, you lead it away from the joy of worshipping the Conqueror of Cities (Śiva), though it is renowned for its stainless character, lineage, and learning, and is expert in discerning between the real and the unreal.
[That] human birth which... (The *kulaka* on the instruction for the mind in ten verses):

O Mind! Why do you lead away that human birth—which is renowned for its stainless conduct, lineage, and learning, and is expert in discerning between what is beneficial and what is harmful—from the bliss of worshipping the Conqueror of Cities?

O Hara, come to the state where the curse has been pacified; with your speech—which resembles the ocean, its seal sounding with the impact of waves slow and languid from their circling—grant me a true boon.
O Hara! Come; with a voice that resembles the ocean—sealed by the sound of blows from its slow and sluggish, wandering waves—grant us a true boon that puts an end to the state of calamity.
Be gracious, O Ocean of Compassion, accept the request of your devotee in accordance with his supplication. Render assistance; act firmly.
The mind is slightly inclined toward rescuing those who are without refuge. || 50 ||

Anvaya: O ocean of compassion! favor the requests of your devotee; accept his words in accordance with his devotion. (Please) assist us; make your mind, which is intent on rescuing the helpless, firm even slightly. Your head is broad, your body is embraced by the celestial river (Gaṅgā), and your heart is possessed of auspicious compassion; O Blessed One, how can there be composure when [the world] is so greatly afflicted?
Even at the place of the openings of my ears, my words do not enter.

Sequence: O Lord!
