Your broad (vast) head is occupied by the celestial river; your broad (noble) heart is occupied by compassion; your broad (extensive) body is occupied by Śivā (the Daughter of the Mountain). Then, even though your ears are exceedingly large, why is there no capacity (retention) for my words?
"O Hara, my mind—tormented by the weight of its passion for you and yet incapable of the task of pleasing you—is turned away from flattery and makes known its own distress. (52)

Anvaya: O Hara! Because she is tormented by the weight of her devotion to you and is incapable of the task of pleasing you, my mind—turning its back on flattery—presents its own distress. "You are the dearest to my mind, yet she, though possessed of virtues, does not enter your heart"; thus, O Maheśa, afflicted by separation from you, she experiences an indescribable state.
The torment of desire. || 53 ||

Anvaya: O Maheśa! You are the most beloved of my mind; yet that [mind], though virtuous, does not enter your heart. Thus, being distressed by separation from you, she suffers some indescribable torment of love. O Bhava, let there be the happiness of your embrace; but as for the matter of enjoying your company, what talk can there be? For me, who desires nothing more than even a mere sight of you— [The implied conclusion: ...how could I possibly endure this state of suffering? Therefore, grant me your vision.
Why do you disregard your intellect in this manner? || 54 ||

O Bhava! Let there not even be the pleasure of an embrace from her—that is, my mind; for what talk can there be of enjoying her? Yet, why do you thus disregard my mind, which longs for nothing more than the mere sight of you? It has not become crooked through intentional effort, nor has it attained an innate impurity; why then do you carry my mind, distressed by its intense passion for you?
Toward a harsh disposition. || 55 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! This [mind] has not become excessively crooked, nor has it attained its innate impurity;

then why do you harbor a harsh disposition toward my intellect, which is tormented by dense passion? Or, if you discard my most innocent mind because it has reached a state of transformation, what else can be said than that it is merely fainting from being overwhelmed by thick delusion?
This ruthlessness of yours [is not fitting]. || 56 ||

[Anvaya: Now, if you say, "She has reached this state of transformation," and thus abandon my most deluded understanding, then what else shall I say? She is utterly swooned by dense delusion; let her proclaim your cruelty. This mind is exceedingly fickle, reeling with the intoxication born of union with the destroyer of the bodiless one (Kāma), and it bears a river possessing the splendor of a jar of nectar.
O you whose crest-jewel is the moon, purify! || 57 ||

O Maker of the Jar of Nectar! O Bearer of the River of Light! O You who have the Moon as Your Crest! Purify this fickle mind of mine, which is excessively agitated by the delusion of union with the Cupid-like fire of worldly passion.
It is distressed by the exhaustion of wandering in the desert and parched by the most treacherous heat of sense-objects; therefore, become my Lord and gladden my heart completely.
The nectar of remembering your feet. || 58 ||

O Bhava! My heart—afflicted by the exhaustion of wandering through the desert of worldly existence and parched by the most treacherous heats of the objects of the senses—is being thoroughly drenched by the nectar of remembering Your feet. O Hara! Lift up me who am enslaved by the serpent-nooses of sense-objects, submerged in the great ocean of worldly existence, helpless, and crushed by the massive boulder of dense delusion.
Me, who have come for refuge. || 59 ||

O Hara! Lift me up, who have come to you for refuge—me who am enslaved by the serpent-noose of sense-objects, submerged in the great ocean of worldly existence, devoid of self-mastery, and oppressed by the massive rock of dense delusion;
me who am being carried away by the unrestrained soldiers of Yama, helpless and having sought shelter at your feet; look upon me with a gaze overflowing with the nectar of profound compassion.
O crusher of Madana, look upon me! || 60 ||

O crusher of Madana! Look upon me with a gaze overflowing with the nectar of intense compassion—me who am being carried away by the unrestrained soldiers of Yama, helpless and having sought refuge at your feet.
When, indeed, shall I behold your moon-like face, which has the proclamation of fearlessness as its pretext for manifesting the flow of nectar, and which possesses the moon of an unfailing smile?
Darkness will turn into auspiciousness. || 61 ||

O crusher of Madana! For me who beholds the moon of your face—whose nectar-fluid is manifest under the guise of the proclamation of fearlessness, and whose moonlight is the unfailing smile—when indeed will my darkness come to rest? O Lord, do you not bear compassion in your heart for the young moon, the lord of the twice-born, whose body is tormented by intense heat; do you not bear it upon your head?
Like a waterfall of liberation. || 62 ||
O All-pervading Lord! Why do You not bear compassion in Your heart—like the river of the gods upon Your head—to protect the young Lord of the Twice-born, whose body is tormented by intense heat?

Place within Your heart that compassion which flows with nectar, which is capable of destroying the calamity of suffering for those who bow before You, and which dispels the state of perpetual darkness.
Like a digit of the moon upon his head. || 63 ||

O All-pervading Lord! Place upon my head that compassion—which is capable of destroying the calamities of those who bow before You, which dispels the dense darkness of the cycle of existence, and which flows with nectar—just as the crescent moon rests upon the head of Śiva. O Lord, carry within Your heart that beloved Compassion, which bestows the attainment of all desired goals in abundance, which cuts through the forest fire of worldly existence, and which is unfailing; and bear it upon Your body.
Like the daughter of the king of mountains. || 64 ||

O All-pervading Lord! Bear in Your heart that beloved Mercy—which bestows the attainment of all desired goals beyond measure, which cuts through worldly suffering, and which is unfailing—just as You bear the Daughter of the Mountain King upon Your body.
For even the wish-fulfilling gem is of the nature of crystal and insentient; even the Kalpa tree is fashioned from hard wood; and indeed, even a cow has reached the state of a beast.
By good fortune, they become like a wish-fulfilling cow for the virtuous, bestowing their desired fruits. || 65 ||

But you, O Lord, though the sole Great Sovereign of the three worlds, though possessed of sufficient power, and though an ocean of perfect compassion—even for me who am crying out piteously yet deceived by fate, you have become indifferent even toward my mere sight. (Yugmam) The lineage of crystal is the *cintāmaṇi* jewel; the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*), though insentient, is fashioned from hard wood; and the cow of plenty (*kāmadhenu*)—[is likewise insentient].
Even those who have fallen into the state of animals become givers of desired fruits through the good fortune of the virtuous. O Lord!

You, though the sole Great Sovereign of the three worlds, though possessed of sufficient power, and though an ocean of perfect compassion, have nevertheless abandoned all regard even for the mere sight of me, who am wailing piteously yet deprived by fate.
For a long time he stood at the edge of the door, intent on watching for an opportunity; he endured the contempt shown by the angry gatekeeper with his mouth agape.
Having made his face wretched before petty lords whose vision is blinded by the pride of a mere fragment of wealth—who indeed has not endured such humiliation? (67)

Pride has withered away; though the body is slender, it suffers most intensely; the mind wanders in the whirlpool of delusion, and fortitude sets. Even the mention of afflictions does not reach the path of cessation; in this far-extended realm of existence, the intellect runs about in vain. (68)

Thus, O Master, alas! entering this vast thicket of delusion—so treacherous due to the onslaught of hundreds of irresistible calamities—a person who finds no other friend capable of providing consolation becomes an object of contempt for you, the ocean of compassion. (69)
(Tilaka) [Anvaya:
With the intent of waiting for an opportunity, we stood for a long time at the entrance of those petty lords whose vision was blinded by pride in their meager wealth;
right there, we endured the insults administered by their angry and talkative gatekeepers. Thus, in this manner, we have remained wretched before these petty lords.
Having made [this] my face, what humiliation indeed has not been endured? O Lord! My pride is withered; my body is emaciated and suffers exceedingly;

my mind wanders in the whirlpool of delusion; and my fortitude sinks toward its end. Even the mention of afflictions does not reach the path of cessation; my intellect runs in vain through this far-stretching world of existence. Alas! O Master! Such is it.

Entering this vast and dense forest of delusion, made treacherous by the onset of hundreds of irresistible afflictions, and finding no other protector, kinsman, or friend capable of offering solace, this person— such as I am— is not a fit object for Your contempt, O Ocean of Compassion; he does not deserve to be treated with disdain.

Alas, here in this world, those of ruined intellect, whose vision is blinded by the thirst for mere fragments of wealth, endure the humiliation born of the thick knitting of the eyebrows of misers— misers whose minds are deluded by the Goddess of Fortune who has dissolved into the cool lotus petals resting upon the trembling tips of fresh lotus shoots.

But I, bearing on my head—purified by the pollen from the fresh lotus-feet of the Lord and heavy with the weight of supreme devotion—shall worship the Lord of Beings while manifesting a frown, out of the impetuosity of an overflowing mass of joy, becoming a vessel for the manifestation of the Lord’s own frown. (Yugma) O wretch! Here, those of ruined intellects have their eyes blinded by the thirst for mere fragments of wealth.

Miserly people endure humiliation arising from the frequent knitting of brows before those whose minds are bewildered by the shifting lotuses submerged in the cool water at the base of trembling lotus leaves; I, however, bearing upon my head— purified by the pollen of the fresh lotus-feet of the Lord and made heavy by the grasp of supreme devotion— shall,
through the impulse of an overflowing abundance of joy, assume a frown that serves as the very vessel for the manifestation of the Lord of Beings’ own brow-knitting.

When shall we, whose limbs are emaciated by fatigue yet who disregard the calamities and afflictions of worldly existence, find satisfaction in the blissful essence of serving the feet of Hara at the waters of the celestial stream— waters fragrant with the mass of flowers from the branches on its banks and resonant with currents stumbling over clusters of mountain rocks?

When shall we—who are characterized by limbs exhausted by toil in the waters of the celestial river, which are fragrant with the abundance of flowers from the branches along its banks and whose currents are made resonant by stumbling over clusters of mountain rocks; who, for that very reason, have disregarded the calamities and afflictions of worldly existence—find satisfaction through the essence of the bliss of serving the feet of Hara? When shall we, bearing upon our heads the pair of lotus-feet of the Moon-crested Lord, experience intense joy as the miseries of our burning heat diminish and fall away?
By the waves of the celestial river, variegated with the waters of the Yamunā, the heap of fuel that is the bondage of worldly existence is turned to embers. || 73 ||

When will the mass of fuel that is our bondage to worldly existence— belonging to us whose distress and misfortune have been diminished by the intense joy of placing the pair of lotus feet of the Moon-crested Lord upon our heads—
be turned into charcoal by the waves of the celestial river, variegated like the waters of the Yamunā? [When shall it happen] for one who,
possessing the merit of spiritual excellence, has his senses stilled by dense bliss and is hidden somewhere at the root of a tree on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī?

The fortunate one, having taken refuge in the sole beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain Lord in all His aspects, rejoices in his own self and attains the tasting of the nectar of the bliss of tranquility.

Having attained that one beloved of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains in every aspect, his senses stilled by intense bliss, fortunate and possessing the merit of spiritual skill, rejoicing in his own self, he remains hidden at the root of some tree on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī and attains the taste of the nectar of the happiness of tranquility (*śama*).
Who indeed would be able to bend the neck of one who is uplifted by the weight of pride in noble lineage, virtues, fame, and wisdom, so as to humble it in an assembly? They [the wise] act thus.
This momentary, playful disregard would not occur if these enemies, the senses, were not capable of leading one astray. || 75 ||

[The connection: O Master! While you repeatedly practice a sportful disregard [toward them], if these enemies—the senses—were not capable of deluding [a person], then what man indeed would be able to bend his neck—which is already uplifted by the weight of pride in his noble lineage, virtues, fame, and wisdom—in the assembly? The meaning is: "No one at all."

To whom is pride not dear? To whom is a state of existence dependent on looking to the faces of the wicked pleasing? To whom does a head bowed down by the weight of shame appeal? Nevertheless, with our hearts full of arrogance toward a master who has been rendered a slave by his enemies, we serve petty, modern-day lords who are intoxicated by the pride of wealth.

To whom is following the will of others not dear? To whom does a state of existence dependent on watching the faces of the wicked bring pleasure? To whom is a head bowed down by the weight of shame due to begging agreeable? However, while our master’s heart is full of passion, we—enslaved by internal enemies such as desire and the like—serve petty, contemporary lords who are intoxicated by the pride of wealth.
That we stand paralyzed at the gates of kings when rebuked by their staff-bearers; that we are consumed by the arrogant, harsh outbursts of those favored by wealthy monarchs;
and that we insult the divine Speech through the sins of false flattery—all this is but the manifestation of the mere turning of Your curved face.
(261) That we stand here paralyzed at the gate of the kings of the lineage, rebuked by the staff-bearers;
and that we are consumed by the harsh outbursts of proud and wealthy monarchs, through the sins of false praise directed toward the divine Speech.
O Lord! We indeed disregard all that as merely the manifestation of the movement of Your curved face.

Having seen the face of the deer-eyed one—its cheeks marked with a pale-red hue, its eyes reddened with tears, and its bimba-like lips quivering, provoked by her first offense—our minds have now become filled with love, wonder, humility, bashfulness, longing, and fear.
It is both weary and at peace for us. || 78 ||

Having seen the face of the fawn-eyed one— its cheeks streaked with a natural rosy hue, its eyes reddened by tears, and its bimba-like lips quivering— as it was provoked by our first offense, our minds became filled with love, wonder, humility, shame, longing, and fear; yet now, having been sprinkled with the nectar of devotion to Śiva, they have become both weary and tranquil.

That momentary, great, and stable joy born of meditating upon you diminishes the small, fleeting pleasure arising from sense objects—what wonder is there in this? But this is truly marvelous: that the vast and unstable flood of tears born of worldly suffering is surely pierced by the minute and transient tear of joy arising from meditation on you. (79)

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! That momentary, trivial pleasure born of sense-objects is dwarfed by the stable and great joy arising from meditation upon You—what wonder is there in this? It means nothing at all. But rather, that the constant and very great tears born of sorrow for You are pierced by the fleeting, subtle tear of joy from meditating on You—that is truly marvelous!

O Great Lord, release me with Your compassionate glance; comfort me, who am blinded by ignorance, friendless, devoured by those called "senses" which are actually demons, and cast into the deep pit of the great darkness of delusion by treacherous inner foes. I cry out as one who has come for refuge, my fortitude gone, the very abode of all calamities. Grant me relief from my terror.

O Great Lord! Do not abandon me, who have come to you for refuge—blinded by ignorance, friendless, devoured by demons called the senses, cast into the deep pit of the great darkness of delusion by wicked inner enemies, crying out, deprived of fortitude, and the abode of all calamities. Console me, who am filled with terror, with your compassionate glance.
That Your glance, though capable of uplifting the entire universe and whose sole nature is to protect the defenseless, disregards me in my distress—that is the power of my own wicked karma.
When the Goddess, filling the earth with divine nectar held in Her breasts, does not let even two or three drops fall into the mouth of the peacock, what can be said against the heavens? (81)

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Although Your vision is capable of uplifting the universe and has as its sole nature the protection of the helpless, that it neglects me in my distress is the result of my own wicked karma. And this is indeed fitting: while the Goddess pours nectar from her breasts to fill the earth, if not even two or three drops fall into the mouth of the peacock in the sky, then what can be said against heaven?

O Lord of Caṇḍī! Release your speech—which is pure, which tirelessly pervades the inner heart overcome by fresh compassion, into which not even a trace of the suffering of the peaceful devotees who bow before you enters, and which is skillful in destroying the calamities and afflictions of the multitude of common beings who are wretched in their plea for the protection of their lives.

*Anvaya:* O, Lord of Caṇḍī! [Release] that speech which is pure within, which is tirelessly pervaded by fresh compassion, into which not even a fraction of the suffering of the peaceful people who have bowed down enters, [and which is]... [skillful in removing the harm and distress of the group of ordinary living beings who are distressed in their desire for the preservation of life].
Bearing within your heart, release that speech which is skilled in destroying the calamities of the multitude of ordinary beings who are wretched in their longing for the protection of life.

This path of worldly existence is full of vast chasms and abundant with terrors; this night of delusion, which generates confusion, is endless, and the moonlight of awakening is fading away. These [senses] carry one away...
Bestow peace; you are the lamp against the winds of calamity arising from turbulent sense-objects, the light called wisdom that directs the vision which pacifies the afflictions. 83.
This path of worldly existence is fraught with many calamities and possesses vast abysses; it is this endless night of delusion, wherein the moonlight of awakening fades away.
These turbulent winds of sense objects act as portents that extinguish the lamp known as wisdom; therefore, O Lord, direct toward us that vision which pacifies all afflictions!

My body is free from disease, my youth is fresh, my mind is refined, my birth is venerable, and even you, my Lord, are easily won through devotion. While this collection of favorable conditions—obtainable only through hundreds of meritorious deeds—does not yet fall apart, listen to this piteous cry of mine. (84)

A body free from disease, youth that is fresh, an intellect refined by culture, a venerable birth, and a Lord who is easily accessible through devotion— while this collection of conditions, obtainable only through hundreds of meritorious deeds, does not fall apart, O All-pervading One, then listen to this piteous cry of mine!
Victorious are the words of the skillful poet, drenched with the essence of nectar and possessing a luster that mimics the rays of the full autumnal moon.
These well-spoken verses possess a wondrous sequence purified by praise of the lotus feet of the Enemy of Tripura, and are as tender as blossoming jasmine buds.

Triumphant are the well-spoken words of the skillful poet— words purified by their sequence of variegated verses in praise of the lotus feet of the Enemy of Anvaya (Śiva), whose syllables are sprinkled with the essence of nectar, whose luster imitates the rays of the blossoming autumnal moon, and which are as tender as a blooming jasmine bud.
Through the pretext of the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by the honey dripping from creepers swaying in the Malaya breeze during spring, [the poet] offers this hymn to Śiva.
With their necks embraced by the arms of women whose hair-partings were terrified by the *jhaṇit* sound of Madana’s bowstring as it twangs, they dwell in the pleasure grove. || 86 ||
Those who have composed this hymn to Śiva— the authors of the *Śrīparameśvarastuti* and the sensitive listeners— dwell in the pleasure garden during the spring season;
their necks held by the arms of women terrified by the jingling of the bowstring of the roaring god of love,
they reside there under the guise of the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by honey dripping from creepers swaying in the Malaya breeze.
By the soft warbling of the sweet-throated cuckoos nestled in the rows of mango trees growing in the nearby outer gardens;
and by the humming of swarms of bees as they alight upon the blossoming jasmine flowers trembling and swaying in the turning Malaya breeze. || 87 ||
By the cries of young swans dwelling within the hollows of lotuses, startled by the agitation in the ponds caused by the striking of hidden timi-fish;
and by the shrieks of peacocks in the palace, which resounds with the clamor of a multitude of sounding paṭaha, jhallarī, mṛdaṅga, tūrya, and bherī drums. || 88 ||
By the songs of singers rendered skillful through the elixir of fresh melodies arising from throats made resonant by the sweet, wine-like essence of nectar;
and by the vibrant sounds of lutes accompanied by the sequences of notes and melodies produced by expert players, along with the resonant warbling of *kīcaka* reeds. || 89 ||
With the tumultuous clamor of the playful quarrels of parrots and mynas awakened by the hymns of throngs of bards intent on praising the virtues of the dawn;
and with the grand resonance of the jingling of golden bells and the tinkling of jeweled girdles rattled by women strolling outside. (90)

At dawn, those who praise Śambhu slowly leave their beds— their chests constricted by the weight of the breasts of amorous women languid with passion— awakened by the neighing of horses whose hooves have bruised the earth, and by the ringing of bells from the throats of elephants shaking their necks.
(An *kulaka* of five verses:
By the warbling of sweet-toned cuckoos perched upon rows of mango trees growing in the nearby outer gardens;
by the humming of swarms of bees stumbling over blossoming jasmine flowers as they sway in the turning Malaya breeze;
and likewise by the soft cries of young swans staying within the hollows of lotuses, startled by the agitation in the ponds caused by the sudden contact with dense darkness.
With the clamor of sounding paṭaha, jhallarī, muraja, tūrya, and bherī drums resounding through the palace halls;
with the songs of skilled female singers whose voices, thickened by the sweet, nectar-like essence of *vāruṇī* wine, produced melodies like a new elixir for the ear;
and with the resonant vibrations of lutes (*vallakī*) accompanied by the rising scales and sequences of notes from expert lute-players, their strings vibrating like the *kīcaka* reeds.

Gradually, sleep was dispelled by the clamor of flocks of bards intent on praising the virtues of the dawn, by the playful squabbling of parrots and mynas awakened by those hymns, by the pervasive jingling of golden bells and the tinkling of jeweled girdles rattled by women wandering outside,
and by the sounds of neck-bells on elephants whose throats were raised in awakening at the neighing of horses whose hooves had dug into the earth.
They abandon the savor of sleep.

Thus ends the tenth hymn, titled "The Lamentation of Compassion," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flower-Petals of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
The eleventh hymn:

I am blessed, for the Goddess of Speech—who flows with some kind of perfect nectar and acts as the life-giving elixir—bestows [this] upon me; like a mother whose pair of breasts overflows with affection, she protects my soul when I am distressed by suffering. (1)

I am fortunate— [I, who am] distressed by suffering, to whom the Goddess of Speech, flowing with some nectar, bestows life-restoring vitality (sañjīvana) and nourishment; she who, like a mother whose pair of breasts overflow with milk out of affection, flows with some perfect nectar for the sake of protecting the life of this child.

I am blessed, for even though I have fallen into unbearable calamity, this path of mine—upheld by your speech, which is beyond the reach of the unmeritorious, auspicious, and worthy of being cultivated by the wise—is not far from me, like the northern path leading to Mount Sumeru. || 2 ||

For one fallen into an unbearable calamity through the force of past actions, this path—maintaining its loftiness, inaccessible to those who have performed no merit, auspicious, and worthy of being frequented by the wise—is like the path belonging to Mount Sumeru; for that path also maintains its height, is not the domain of those who have done no merit, is auspicious (as *kalyāṇa* means gold, and thus refers to the golden nature of Sumeru), and is frequented by the wise (the gods).
This path likewise maintains its loftiness, is inaccessible to those who have performed no merit, is auspicious (possessing every blessing), and is frequented by the wise.
I am blessed— blessed indeed is he for whom that speech, which ought to be sought out when one has fallen into unbearable calamity, is not far removed (but rather situated very close,
even within his own mouth); blessed am I, for whom, though my vision is blinded by the darkness of delusion, that sweet-sounding and virtuous [speech] has been provided by a providence full of grace.
This Sarasvatī, assuming a crooked expression, is for the propitiation of Giriśa. || 3 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: Just as for a man whose vision is blinded by cataracts, the goddess Sarasvatī—the lute (*vīṇā*)—which possesses a melodious sound, is endowed with strings, and assumes curved bends, is prepared by a benevolent Fate for the propitiation of Giriśa; so too, for me, whose vision is blinded by the cataract of delusion, this [speech] which possesses a melodious sound and is endowed with qualities [is prepared] by a benevolent Fate for the propitiation of that very Giriśa.

I am fortunate that Sarasvatī (the Goddess of Speech), assuming a graceful and curved form, has been fashioned [by me]. I recognize her as a life-restoring elixir created by Fate for me, who had been reduced to ashes by the fire of worldly existence. This speech, whose sole object is Śiva, is like the startled glance of the newly wedded Gaurī toward the God of Love.

I perceive that this speech, which has Śiva as its sole object, is like the fresh glance from the eyes of the newly married Gaurī— timid and directed solely toward Śiva— which acts as a new reviving herb for the God of Love (Makaradhvaja) who was reduced to ashes by the fire of Bhava; likewise, this speech of mine, which has Śiva as its sole object, has been fashioned by Fate as a new reviving herb for me, who was reduced to ashes by the fire of Bhava.

I know that somehow this cow has emerged from my heart, scorched by the fire of my grief, her soft steps faltering; she will slowly enter my mind, cooled by the flowing stream of the nectar of compassion from the Moon-crested Lord.

Just as a cow, having emerged from a place heated by fire with faltering, soft steps, slowly enters a shelter cooled by the flow of a stream of nectar— cool with the discharge of a flood of water— so too this cow (my speech), having somehow emerged and arisen from my heart scorched by the fire of grief with faltering, soft steps, [enters a state] cooled by the discharge of a flood of the nectar of compassion.
"I know that even my mind will gradually enter [the heart] of the one who bears the moon upon his crest;

yet, because I am subject to the insurmountable wandering of worldly existence, I repeatedly act here with the fickleness of flattery while harboring delusion. In this matter, it is the incomparable delicacy of the husband of the daughter—who is herself desirable, unassailable, and of noble lineage—that offends."
Whatever fickle flattery I repeatedly practice here in this world, driven by innate delusion and wandering through insurmountable existences,
in that act of fickle flattery, it is only the irrepressible, desirable, and supreme delicacy of the husband of the Daughter of the Mountain (the Lord of Girijā) that is at fault.

Who would not venture to petition that Lord, who bears upon his head the celestial river Ganges, resounding with the *jhāṅkāra* of its unrestrained torrents as it cascades down, and who accepts from his devotees the consecration of the ritual pitcher? (7)

Who would not venture to petition that All-pervading Lord—the crest-jewel of the compassionate—who, though bearing upon his head the celestial river Ganges roaring with the sound of *jhāṅ* from the unrestrained torrents of its cascading flow, nevertheless accepts the ceremonial ablution from the water-pot of his devotees? (The meaning is: indeed, everyone should.)

I am already scorched by this Damuna, who blazes within my heart, born from the cause of the fierce heat of sin; how can speech emerge from my throat as it slips away, while I am liberated yet agitated by extreme fear?

[Anvaya: That fire (*damunā*), born from the cause of the intense heat of my sins, blazes within me; first of all, I have been burnt by it. Therefore, how can speech arise for me, who am freed from fear yet overwhelmed by extreme terror, and whose [voice] is failing or falling away? O wielder of the Pināka bow, O cause of deliverance from acute agony, I cry out: I am terrified! [Translation: That fire, born from the cause of the intense heat of my sins, blazes within me; first of all, I have been burnt by it. Therefore, how can speech arise for me, who am freed from fear yet overwhelmed by extreme terror, and whose [voice] is failing or falling away? O wielder of the Pināka bow, O cause of deliverance from acute agony, I cry out: I am terrified!
Listen to this for my welfare, as I am afflicted by Śiva [and] situated amidst the terrible perils of the forest of delusion. || 9 ||

Anvaya: O wielder of the Pināka bow! O cause of the crossing over of intense suffering! Therefore (for the reasons mentioned above), I, being distressed, cry out something [or other]. O Śiva! For my welfare, take heed of this lamentation of mine as I stand in the terrible peril of the forest of delusion.
O moon-bearer, O Lord, hold my cry in Your ear; who else than You is the supreme helmsman, the ultimate cause? With my head...
Carrying a fragment of a boat that is unbroken merit, whom do you not rescue from the ocean of worldly existence today? || 10 ||

O Bearer of the Moon! O Lord! Heed my cry (meaning: listen). O Supreme Cause! Who else but You is the helmsman? Carrying the fragment of the moon upon Your head, whom—possessing unbroken merit—do You not deliver from the ocean of worldly existence?

I know that the flattering and fickle words composed by impure people like us do not delight your mind; for even when performed to win over [others], O Moon-crested Lord, do the playful antics of a dog ever receive respect?
Who indeed can provide protection from the ocean of existence, which is so difficult to cross and agitated by hundreds of waves of illusion wandering in many directions?
He alone becomes the Lord who stands ever within the range of one's vision, protecting that boat—the sun—while he himself is an ocean of the nectar of compassion.

O Moon-crested One! These fawning and frivolous words composed by impure ones like us do not delight Your mind; thus, with my heart excessively distressed, I shall not become an object of derision in the world. For how could I, a fool, go to cross the ocean of existence without a helmsman, while holding onto only half of a raft? **Anvaya:** O Moon-crested One! The fawning and frivolous words fashioned by impure ones such as myself do not please Your mind. (Thus I [shall not become an object of derision].)
I understand (and this has been observed): do people pay any heed to the playful antics performed to win over a dog?
(The meaning is: they do not.
Or rather, even these innocent acts do not produce favor in you, O ocean of compassion, who are intent on wandering through the city of Indra, my lord.
Why do these playful gambols of yours not captivate your heart?

Furthermore, O Lord! It is not that even your charming deeds do not produce grace in you, who are an ocean of compassion (indeed, they do); for instance—O All-pervading One! Do the playful gambols of your childhood not captivate the heart of you who were devoted to sporting in the city of Daratpura (meaning, with the children of that region)? (The sense is: they certainly do.)

Just as the hearts of those who are treasuries of compassion are moved by the piteous, deluded words of the distressed—words whose meaning is inconsistent—it is not so moved by the elaborate display of speech, though it be adorned with compositions full of boldness and the brilliance of wit seen in assemblies. (13)

Just as the hearts of those who are treasuries of compassion melt at the humble, incoherent, and deluded words of the destitute, they do not melt at the elaborate expansions of speech, though adorned with well-composed structures and the bold confidence of one who has witnessed the assembly of the learned. You, though born from the Ocean of Milk, choose but a drop of water; you, though having the three-eyed Śiva as your eye, accept a mere lamp; and you, though the progenitor of all speech— [you remain indifferent].
Do you listen to the words of the simple-minded? What do you not do out of consideration for humble people? 14.
Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Though You are the giver of the Ocean of Milk, You accept even a single drop of milk offered by Your devotee at the time of worship;
though You possess three abodes and three eyes, You welcome a lamp; though You are the source of the speech of Brahmā, You listen to the simple words of the innocent.
O Compassionate One! What is there that You do not do out of consideration for those who are humble?

O Lord, it is indeed a marvel that even this speech of mine, though known throughout the world for its truthfulness and free from malice, has been addressed thus; yet, this is even more extraordinary—that Arundhatī, desiring to propitiate you, has spoken in such a manner. (15)
Anvaya: O King! That this speech of mine, though known by the whole world to be truthful, is not regarded as envious—this alone is a marvel! (It is a wonder!
That even when addressed in such a manner, Arundhatī, having failed to reach you, still desires only to propitiate you—that indeed is most extraordinary! (It is a great wonder!)
Though you are yourself beyond price, Gaṅgādhara, you choose the ritual bath with water and accept the drops of the *arghya* offering;

though you are the supreme light, you accept the lamp—what is there that you will not do out of consideration for humble people? Having made the Goddess who grants liberation take up residence in my own abode, the heart, you yourself have shown the way in by becoming intent upon her; yet now, she is tormented by the ever-increasing pain of separation.
"It is improper for you to maintain such composure after having been so addressed. || 16 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Having entered Your own abode—my heart—and having established Your residence therein, You Yourself have brought about the turning away of my Goddess of Speech. Furthermore, it is improper that You now disregard her, who has been afflicted by the pain of separation intensified to the point of a continuous stream, after having previously instilled such fortitude in her.

If you remember the boon granted by the daughter of the Mountain King—that "you alone shall be my beloved"—then how is it that out of love you carry the celestial river upon your garment, the crescent moon upon your head, and yet both your beloved and compassion within your heart? 17.

Anvaya: O Aparṇā! If you remember the boon granted by the daughter of the Mountain King—that "you alone shall be my beloved"—then, O Lord, why do you bear with affection the celestial river and the crescent moon upon your head, yet carry compassion in your heart as your beloved? You who pride yourself on being steadfast and profound, how can you utterly disregard her who is naturally simple and charmingly noble? Do you not know this by now, even after hundreds of times?
For you have been made to dance by that increasing compassion which is shown toward those who bow down in supplication. || 18 ||

O Lord, you who possess a naturally firm and profound dignity, why do you disregard this praise of mine, which is by nature simple and charmingly innocent? Do you not know that you have been made to dance repeatedly by the old woman—namely, Compassion—which increases with every hundred humble entreaties? This [praise], distressed by its own lack of shame, ventures to offer flatteries that are awkward due to its innocence; for you, who are spoiled by the words of Kātyāyanī.
Those [jewels], resembling pearls, do not delight your mind. || 19 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! This [my speech], tormented by distress—[the anxiety of "By what means might I become the most beloved of my Master"]—out of shamelessness attempts to offer even these faltering flatteries; yet, being comparable to [empty] liberation, they do not delight Your mind, which has been spoiled by the words of Kātyāyanī.

O Lord who has realized the ultimate truth, if you have no affection for her—who is distressed by the fever of unbearable separation—then that is only because you are unrestrained; but how could you have forgotten your firm vow to shatter all internal suffering? (20)

O Knower of Truth! O Lord! If Your unbridled (unrestrained) affection does not exist solely for this [my hymn], which is distressed by the fever of unbearable separation, then, O All-pervading One, how have You forgotten Your firm vow to shatter all internal suffering?
It is true that you bear a portion of truth in that you hold Umā as half of yourself; yet it is true that you bear compassion in your heart for those who seek your aid, which makes her dance.
O Blue-throated One, because of this [compassion], you have been reduced to the state of having a blue throat; but as for my words, you turn your face aside as if in anger.

O Blue-throated One! You truly bear a digit [of the moon]; for while you carry Umā upon one half of your body, you hold that very compassion in your heart by which [compassion] they make you dance among supplicants, thereby reducing you to the state of being "Blue-throated. Yet, O Lord, you turn your face askance toward my words as if out of anger!

You take up with your white, tossing waters the celestial river as it overflows and stumbles at your feet; yet you abandon this woman of virtuous conduct who has no other refuge—what can be said of your independent behavior?
Anvaya: O Lord! You bear upon your head the celestial river, which has overflowed its banks with white, restless waters and stumbled at your own feet;
yet you abandon this speech of mine, which is helpless, virtuous in conduct, and seeks no other refuge. What more can be said of you whose conduct is entirely independent?
What need for further words? If she is not dear to your heart, why do you dwell in her house? Why do you not dwell in my heart, living together with your beloved?
For the neglect of such [a lover] brings suffering to proud women, even more so than death itself.

What is the use of further elaboration? If this [my speech] does not reach your heart, then why do you dwell in my heart, which is her home? For to proud women, dwelling with one who loves them and yet being neglected by him is more painful than even death.

O Mother Sarasvatī, having presented my petition—distraught with affliction—to you, who possess all power, maintain your steadfast resolve; for the Goddess Śivā, the digit of the moon, and the River of the Sky (Gaṅgā) invariably show partiality toward those who are weak.

Sequence: O Mother Sarasvatī! Maintain your composure. Both the auspicious Goddess Śivā and the River of the Sky (Gaṅgā), who possess a digit of the moon, will surely show partiality toward weak women after reporting your petition—distressed by affliction—to their Lord (the Master). Even if this crescent moon is naturally curved and the celestial river is eternally rippling, the Goddess, whose heart is moist with compassion, [will surely help].
The blessed daughter of the Lord of Nagas will not treat you with intense contempt.

(Anvaya: O Mother Sarasvatī! If this Candralekhā is naturally crooked, and the celestial river is eternally surging with waves, then the blessed Goddess, daughter of the Mountain King, whose heart is moist with compassion, will not treat you with intense contempt.
O Goddess Vāṇī, I take refuge in you alone; O auspicious one, praise the Moon-crested Lord with well-spoken verses. O Mother, I shall not lead [her] away...)
Furthermore, you have become a vessel for being transgressed by foolish people who are talkative with false speech. || 26 ||
Anvaya: O Goddess! O auspicious Speech! I take refuge in you alone; do you praise the Moon-crested Lord with well-spoken verses.
O Mother, I shall not again subject you to the state of being transgressed by a fool whose speech is false and boastful.

O Goddess, bestower of boons upon those who seek refuge, O Gauri, radiant with virtues! Whatever little of this limited [knowledge] flows forth here, may it, at the proper time, reach full maturity for its worthy Master.
Be gracious enough to inform Mākūtavedin.
Just as someone might offer to their master whatever small amount of milk a cow (or milch-cow) yields, having cooked it thoroughly (well-boiled by fire), so too:

O Giver of Boons to those who have sought refuge! O Goddess Gaurī, radiant with virtues! O Gaurī!! Be gracious so that this cow (the goddess of speech) may, at the appropriate time, present whatever small measure she yields here to her Master, who understands her inner intent, after it has been well-cooked.

Though this [work] is fashioned according to my own whim, its ripening is distinguished by the unseen (adṛṣṭa), it lacks proper measure, and is not enjoyed by noble persons; nevertheless, even as the speech of a madman, it will surely be a true medicine for the poison-like disease of worldly existence. (28)

(Although) this (speech of mine), fashioned according to my own whim, possessing a ripening not seen [before], lacking in measure, unappreciated by noble persons, and necessarily the talk of a madman; nevertheless, even so, it serves as the true medicine for the uneven disease of worldly existence. Just as the celestial river, though situated upon your crown, is indeed unable to quench the fire on your forehead, so too [this speech] cannot quench the fire burning incessantly within your heart.
Even though this Sarasvatī dwells within my mouth, she burns with the fire of grief.

Anvaya: O Lord! Just as the celestial river (Siddhasindhu), though situated upon Your crown, is indeed unable to extinguish the fire of Your forehead, so too this Sarasvatī of mine, though dwelling here in my mouth, is unable to extinguish the fire of grief burning incessantly in my heart—[without Your grace].

O Lord, if the impure karma I have previously committed were indeed the cause, how could this firm devotion of mine toward You arise? And if it were due to exclusively pure karma, then why does this most unbearable fire of grief burn within my heart? (30)

Anvaya: O Lord! If indeed turbid karma alone was performed by me in the past (in a previous birth), then from where would this firm attachment of mine toward You arise? And if indeed exclusively pure karma was performed by me, then why would this most unbearable fire of grief, which burns the heart, exist within me?

In some other birth, my mind must have been full of longing after having performed the worship of the Lord; for otherwise, how could this entire human birth of mine—purified as it is by lineage, virtue, and the like—have become so utterly fruitless? (31)

Anvaya: O Lord! I know that in some other birth, having performed the propitiation of the Lord, my mind has certainly become full of longing [for You]; otherwise, how has this entire human birth of mine—though purified by lineage, virtues, and the like—become utterly fruitless?
Having long since obtained the vessel of human birth and having found You, the one adorned with compassion, as its savior, it has become overwhelmed by the burden of the desire to cross over.
I am drowning in the ocean of existence; tell me, whose mockery is this?

Anvaya: O Lord! Having after a long time obtained the vessel of human birth, and having finally attained You—who are the ornament of compassion and the savior from the shoreless ocean of worldly existence—I, for whom there arose a great conviction (and a heavy responsibility) to cross the ocean of existence, am now sinking right there; tell me, then, whose mockery (or public derision) would this be? (The implication is: it would be Yours alone.)

What is surprising in this that a master bestows grace upon servants who have been helpful, who are worthy, and who are virtuous? But the noble, even toward those who are unworthy recipients, spontaneously carry hearts drenched with the essence of the nectar of compassion.
What wonder is there if the Lord of the Universe bestows his grace upon worthy and virtuous servants who have rendered him service—upon those who are disciplined and devoted?

But the holy ones carry hearts sprinkled with the essence of the nectar of compassion even toward those who are unworthy, without any external cause. Therefore, [he is] one whose every means for attaining worldly prosperity has ceased, whose mind is weary, and whose conduct is broken by the impossible.
Honor me, who am sinking through the fear of death and tormented by misfortune, by personally bestowing upon me the gift of fearlessness. 34.

Therefore, by granting me—this wretched one who has completed all means for worldly prosperity, whose efforts have been shattered by the impossibility [of success], who desponds out of fear of death, and who is tormented by calamities—the gift of safety, honor me yourself.
He who honors you is truly wise; he is devoid of wisdom who is not released from your heart. For he who... [is yours].
One who is devoted to you attains honor for his own honor; I have taken refuge in you—why then am I, though I am Bhava, not liberated from existence? (35)

O Lord! Even that man who possesses right conduct (*nītimān*)—one intent on discerning what ought and ought not to be done—and who worships you, becomes free from calamity (*anītiḥ*, meaning devoid of distress and affliction). Likewise, he who is not released from your heart is indeed liberated;
and he who is devoted to your worship (*apacitaye*) does not undergo decay (*apacitim*). Since I have thus taken refuge in you, O Bhava, why then am I not free from worldly existence (*abhavaḥ*)?
Am I?

Sleep is difficult for me to attain at night when my mind is filled with anxiety; I pass the time in constant burning, yet I am never free from the heat of passion. O Śiva, protect me who am entirely subject to you;
why are you so merciless and harsh toward me? 36.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! For me, whose mind is filled with anxiety, sleep at night is difficult to obtain. O Blessed One! Through Your grace, being free from the burning anguish, when shall I ever pass my days? O Śiva! You must certainly protect me, who am solely dependent upon You; why are You harsh and cruel toward me?
"You ought not to abandon me, thinking 'I am a wicked and base man. What is the use of protection for one who is wise and free from fear?
Since I am unrighteous, lowly, and of impure deeds, I am therefore all the more worthy of your compassion. (37)

O Lord! Because this man is wicked and sinful, you ought not to abandon me. What is gained by protecting one who is fearless and wise? Since I am unrighteous, base, and of unholy deeds, I am all the more worthy of your compassion. Even though I have descended to a low state through my own misdeeds, O Protector, I am not a fit object for your disdain; for even a proud beast that falls is not to be despised.
For the compassionate world does not neglect even one who has fallen of their own accord into a blind well. || 38 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Although I have fallen low due to my own evil deeds, nevertheless, I am not a fit object for Your contempt; for even a proud beast—who, intoxicated by youth, falls of his own accord into a blind well—is not ignored by a compassionate person. If You think, "This fickle one has fallen from his own exceedingly high station and, being dull-natured, will wander upon many evil paths," and thus abandon him— (Translation of the provided Sanskrit verse: O Lord! Even though I have descended to a low state because of my own misdeeds, I am certainly not a vessel for Your disdain. For even a proud beast—one arrogant with the intoxication of youth—who falls of his own accord into a blind well, is not neglected by a compassionate person. Thinking, "This fickle one has fallen from his own most exalted position and, being of a dull nature, will wander upon many wrong paths," if You [abandon him]...
"Why was this very same torrent from the Ganges placed by you upon my head? (39)
If you carry this stream of the Ganges on your head with the thought, "Alas, it shall surely destroy even the suffering of those in hell," then this is truly worthy of you—
a vast ocean of the nectar of compassion who strives to shatter the pain of the helpless.

"The tongue of one such as I would break into a thousand pieces upon reaching Your head," she says; yet my vow is this: "I shall uplift the three worlds merely by the touch of Your foremost foot. (The Tilaka) Anvaya: O Lord! Thinking, "Having fallen from his own exceedingly lofty station, this fickle one of dull nature will wander upon many evil paths," [the world speaks thus].

If you abandon me thinking [I am insignificant], then why was this very stream of the Gaṅgā borne by you upon your head? Indeed, if it was borne on your head, it was for the reason that "this flood of the Gaṅgā shall destroy the suffering of those in hell. O Lord! If you carry the flood of the Gaṅgā [upon your head], then [you act] as one whose primary concern is to shatter the suffering of the helpless, an ocean of the nectar of profound compassion.

"This is indeed worthy of you; this tongue of a devotee such as I, having reached your head, shall remain in bliss like the Gaṅgā"—speaking thus, it might break into a thousand pieces. But what talk can there be of even the desire to reach your head? My vow is that by the mere touch of your foremost foot, I shall uplift the three worlds in an instant; but what need is there to mention those in hell?
[He] says:

"O Lord, if you discard me because you think, 'This moon is emaciated, excessively dull, crooked, yet possessed of arts [or digits], and a source of faults,' then why, O Master, was the moon, despite being approached by all such defects, borne upon your head? (42)

Anvaya: O Lord! If you abandon this moon on the grounds that it is emaciated, excessively dull, crooked, yet possessed of arts (kalā), and a mine of faults (doṣākara); then, O Master, why has this very moon been borne upon your head, even though he is possessed of all such defects as emaciation and the rest?

If you bear upon your head the moon—the lord of the twice-born, of tranquil form, stainless, and supposedly free from blemish—then why, despite being such as this, was I not deemed worthy by you to be supported even at the edge of the seat of your feet? (43)

It is said that this moon is of peaceful form, the lord of the twice-born, stainless, and free from blemish; for this reason, if you bear him upon your head, then why have you not resolved to hold even one such as me at the edge of the footstool? "An evil planet attains stability only through the seizure of others' property, not otherwise"—thinking thus, you abandon me, even though I am of such a nature to you.
O Lord, how have you become one who possesses the taste for being a worthy recipient of the casting of glances from the right? || 44 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! If it is because this malefic planet does not attain composure without seizing the wealth of others that you abandon me, then how has even such a one as this—the radiant Sun—become the object of your right-hand glance? If he has approached you having proclaimed his friendship and his kinship with those endowed with virtues, then he has attained your favor; whereas I, having always remained in the state of your servant alone— [The commentary on the verse follows: O Sovereign! If this evil planet does not find stability without the plundering of others' property, and for that reason you cast me aside, then why has this very [Sun], despite being of such a nature, become the recipient of your right-hand look? If he has come to you after making known his friendship and his status as a kinsman to those possessed of merit, then he has indeed attained your affection; whereas I, having eternally entered into the state of your servitude alone... [the verse concludes].
Having become devoted to serving those possessed of virtue, how could I be unpleasant to them? (45)

This is the logical sequence: if this Sun, having proclaimed his friendship with you and his kinship as one bound by virtue, has come to be dear to you, then how can I—having always entered into your service and being intent on serving the virtuous—be unpleasant to you?
If you abandon me because you have determined that I am excessively hot, foul-smelling, many-tongued, and unworthy even of touch, then even such a person as I...
How has this consumer of its own support been made by you a fit vessel for the establishment of auspicious views? (46)

If you abandon me after determining that I am excessively hot, foul-smelling, many-tongued, and unworthy even of touch, then how is it that such a consumer of its own support (fire) has been made by you a vessel for the casting of a favorable glance? For this [fire], possessing a luster like the petals of the *bandhujīva* flower, becomes the means of sustenance for the multitude of virtuous gods who act as supplicants; and through the mouth of the circle of its friends, this [fire] [consumes] the entire universe.
If you are attentive, nourish it with that in the fire. || 47 ||

O Lord, if there is no donor for me, I pray that You may incessantly grant nourishment to my mind; for I am unable to sustain my own kinsmen, and I must support the entire world through the mouths of my friends.

Therefore, know me here to be innocent; grant me a glance clear with grace and moist with the flow of nectar. Favor this wretched one, who is a fit object for compassion, with your faultless, playful movement of the eyebrows, which are as transient as a flickering flame. (Tilaka) This [Fire], possessing the beautiful luster of a Bandhujīva petal, having properly [acted] for the sake of the life of the assembly of gods, now assumes the state of a petitioner.

Through the mouth of Mitra’s orb, he nourishes the universe; for that reason, O Lord, if you are intent upon the fire [of destruction], and if I am a petitioner to constantly provide nourishment for the well-disposed, then there is no other such donor for me. Therefore, O Lord, I am unable to sustain the lives of my kinsmen and nourish the world through the agency of a friend in this matter. For that reason, O Lord, in this regard—

Know me to be innocent; bestow upon me, who am a vessel of compassion and wretched, a glance clear with favor and moist with the essence of nectar. Favor me with a compassionate heart through the movement of your eyebrows, which is vast, free from delusion, and yet transient. O Lord, if it is fitting for you to favor a pure friend like the lord of the twice-born (the moon) by granting him your stainless gaze, then do so even toward one such as I.
"You maintain an unfavorable gaze toward me"—this is the decree that has turned its back upon me.

Sequence: O Blessed One! If you favored the friend (the Sun), the pure one (Agni), and the lord of the twice-born (the Moon) by bestowing upon them your stainless glance, that is indeed fitting. But that you cast such a displeased look even upon me in this state—this is my destiny (fate) turned away from me (meaning: this is merely my own lack of fortune).

O Lord, if you think, "This one is earless, addicted to crooked ways, and double-tongued," and thus abandon me who have no other refuge; then why, O Śrīkaṇṭha, did you seize this very same serpent—who feeds only on air—upon the sandy bank of your own throat? 51.

O Lord! If you abandon me, who am without refuge, thinking, "This one is earless, addicted to crooked ways, and double-tongued," then, O Śrīkaṇṭha, why was even such a serpent (pavanāśana) taken by you onto the sandy bank of your throat?
If he remains upon the pedestal of your throat because he formerly praised you with a pair of a thousand tongues, then I have but a single tongue for your praise.
Therefore, O Great Lord, let my place be at the soles of your feet. || 52 ||

Anvaya: O Maheśa! Formerly, you were praised by this [Śeṣanāga] with his two thousand tongues (since Śeṣa possesses a thousand heads); for that reason, if he remains upon the surface of your throat, then I have but a single tongue for your praise; therefore, O Īśa!
let my place be at the very soles of your feet.

If you avoid me because you consider me to be a horned beast, devoid of discrimination, mad, and excessively timid—then how is it that even such a bull as this has been made a recipient of your grace by the mere placing of your foot? 53.

Sequence: If you think, "This horned beast is devoid of discrimination and is intoxicated," and thus avoid me out of extreme fear, then how is it that even such a bull was made an object of your grace by placing his feet [upon you]?
He carries you on his back at times; if merely by this much he were to become an object of your compassion, O Lord, as for me—
"Since I carry you within my heart every day, alas, how could I not be worthy of your compassion? (54)

(Anvaya: If this bull (*vṛṣabha*) carries you on his back only once in a while, and by that much he becomes an object of your compassion, then, O Master! since I carry you in my heart every single day (*anvaham*), oh! how am I not worthy of your pity?

If you think thus and abandon me—[thinking] "This cruel, crooked one turns his face away from the task of perceiving virtues and abandons the multitude of arrows [or seekers] who are worthy"—[then I am indeed pitiable].
O Lord, how is it that such a Pināka bow has been held by you in the palm of your hand?

If you think, "This cruel and crooked man abandons the multitude of arrows (the *mārgaṇaugha*, i.e., the collection of supplicants) that are fit for the task of grasping the string (or, grasping virtues)," and thus abandon me— then, O Master, such a person as this (namely, one who is cruel, crooked,
and turning away from the multitude of arrows [the collection of shafts] that are fit for the task of grasping the string [the act of drawing the bow]) is indeed the one who abandons them.

Why is this Pināka bow held by you in the palm of your hand? For if, even when its string has reached its highest tension, you do not abandon the Ajagava because it remains exceedingly bent, then why is it that even at a slight tension there is such excessive bending, such that I am not an object of your compassion? (56)

If, having reflected upon the fact that the string [both the bowstring and qualities such as compassion and courtesy] has reached the highest limit [both the tip of the bow and the highest number], you do not abandon the Ajagava bow [or the Ajagava-like state] which is exceedingly bent, then why am I not an object of your compassion, given that I am already excessively humble [or disciplined] even toward meager virtues such as compassion and courtesy?

O Lord, if you have abandoned me because you consider me to be excessively sharp-witted, utterly harsh, having gained entry through my guilelessness, and exceedingly painful to the touch—then for what purpose do you carry this very trident, such as it is, already in your hand? 57.

O Lord! If you enter [me] with straightforwardness while I am facing you—though I am exceedingly sharp and extremely harsh—and then abandon me upon realizing I am excessively piercing, for what purpose do you carry this trident already in your hand?

Or, if you know it is fit for the ritual action performed in battle and thus bear this three-pointed weapon with its three faces blazing like a peak, why do you not [bear one] for me who am destitute?
Since you perceive me as being of equal flavor and fit for beneficial action, you do not bestow grace upon me.

If you, knowing me to be one whose three peaks are blazing with ten million rays, capable of performing beneficial deeds, and of equal flavor (samarasa), still bear [this trident]—then do you not know me to be destitute (niḥsva), yet capable of beneficial deeds and of equal flavor, such that you do not show me favor?

If you abandon me after considering me as one who has humbled the twice-born, who has not diminished the former gods and gurus, who is intent on offering [himself] even in adversity, and who has caused a breach in [your own] lineage; [Then...]
How is it that such a festival for the eyes as this is your world-conquering youth? || 59 ||

Anvaya: O Master! If you abandon me—having humbled the twice-born, intent on offering the misfortunes of my former gods and gurus without diminishing them, and having caused a rift in my lineage—then how can such a one as I (humbled the twice-born, intent on offering the misfortunes of my former gods and gurus without diminishing them, and having caused a rift in my lineage) be a world-conquering prince who is a festival for your eyes?
(“The one who brings light to the eyes,” meaning a most beloved son.

O Lord, if you consider this Viśākha to be of pure birth and maintain a firm confidence in him, then why, O Blessed One, do I—who am likewise devoted to no other—become an object of your disregard? 60.

Anvaya: O Lord! If, considering this Viśākha to be of pure birth, you maintain a firm favor toward him, then, O Blessed One, why do I—though being such a person devoted to none other—become an object of Your disdain? If You are one who delights in seizing everything, whose face is distorted with intoxication, who is fickle as an ear-ring, and if You are corpulent, then even one such as I, O Blessed One... [The verse continues: ...even though I am such a person, O Blessed One, [why am I an object of Your contempt? For I am one who delights in the total destruction [of pride], whose face is distorted by madness, who is as fickle as an ear-ring, and who is bloated with [the weight of] all things. Even so, O Blessed One, [I remain devoted].
Why has he been appointed by you as the leader of the hosts, appearing with the face of an elephant? || 61 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! If I—who am fond of seizing everything, whose face is distorted with madness, who am fickle-eared and pot-bellied—am to be abandoned by you, then why has this elephant-faced one, even though he is such, been appointed by you to the leadership of the Gaṇas?
He always carries a trunk sprinkled with the water of ichor; if it were because of that he obtained lordship over the Pramathas, then a poor man would never be able to bestow gifts.
I am patient; O Lord, let me be a servant to your attendants.

Anvaya: O Lord! Since this one (the elephant-faced god) always carries a trunk that is sprinkled with the water of his ichor [drenched with rut-fluid and sprinkled for the sake of giving], and by virtue of that he obtained the lordship over the Pramathas; then, if I, being destitute, am not capable of bestowing gifts, let my status be nothing other than servitude to your attendants.

If I am to be abandoned by you because of my lack of service, while you treat all the planets equally as they traverse their respective zodiacal signs, then since only the sun and the moon are excluded from your path of vision, have the others been spared by you for that reason? 63.

Anvaya: O Lord! While all the planets are equally traversing their zodiacal signs (*rāśi-bhoga*), if only the two—Sun and Moon—do not abandon the path of Your vision, then by that much alone, have the others (Mars and the rest) been rejected by You? Why am I to be abandoned on account of being a non-servant?

O Lord, both of these powerful lords of the twice-born are your devotees; yet one of them removes the deep darkness of living beings. O Great Lord, if you alone are able to behold that which is veiled by him, then for that reason you are known as the one of "unequal vision."

O Lord! Both these young moons—the one moon who is the lord of the twice-born (the crescent moon on your head), and the other moon who is the lord of the twice-born (myself, a Brahmin)—are your devotees.

Of these two, the one moon situated upon your crest removes the blinding darkness of living beings; yet, if you are able to look upon the other, the lord of the twice-born (me, a child), who am shrouded by that very same darkness, then indeed, O Maheśa, you are known as one of "unequal vision."

It is fitting that your heart be moist with compassion even toward an enemy or a friend who is arrogant with faults; yet, why this prideful lack of mercy toward a wretched person who is now destitute, lacking refuge, and devoid of self-control? 65.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! If your heart is moist with compassion toward even an enemy swollen with faults or toward a friend—since you possess equal vision toward both—that is fitting. But why this arrogance of pity toward a wretched person like me, who is now without recourse and lacking self-control? This rising of the sun from the orb of the nectar-rayed moon is but the sprout of darkness; so it is for one such as you.
That the ocean of the Kaunāmbas should suddenly show such disregard for us who are without refuge. || 66 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! That disregard which exists toward us, who are like you—an ocean of compassion and the savior of the three worlds in a single moment—and who are without refuge, is like the emergence of a thunderbolt from the orb of the moon, or like the growth of darkness from the sun.
O Lord, You are the compassionate Mṛḍa, while I am afflicted by a heavy burden of great suffering; You are the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya), while I am agitated by the fear of death.
You are the Bearer of the Gaṅgā, while I am scorched by the fierce heat of worldly existence; how, indeed, could I not be an object of Your compassion? (67)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*): O Lord! You are Mṛḍa (the Gracious One), while I am afflicted by a heavy burden of manifold sufferings; you are the Conqueror of Death (*Mṛtyuñjaya*), while I am agitated by the fear of death; you are the Bearer of the Gaṅgā (*Gaṅgādhara*), while I am scorched by the fierce heat of worldly existence (*bhava*); therefore, O All-pervading One (*Vibhu*), how, indeed, am I not worthy of your compassion?
O Physician of the Universe, grant to me—one who am agitated by the feverish heat of existence and the tremors of delusion—a single portion of Sudarśana!

O Lord, though You yourself are fond of devotion, do You not suddenly perceive my suffering—my suffering as one afflicted by hunger, even though You delight in the festival of drinking for those who thirst, and though You are intent on providing shelter for those distressed by heat? (68)

Anvaya: O Lord! You, who are yourself fond of your devotees, how is it that you do not suddenly perceive the suffering of me, who am possessed by hunger [the desire to behold you]? Being one whose sole delight is in the festival of drinking [the nectar of your vision], how is it that you do not perceive the suffering of me, who am parched with thirst [agitated by the thirst to see you]? Likewise, being one who respectfully serves the clouds [the multitude of devotees], how is it that you do not suddenly perceive the suffering of me, who am tormented by heat?
O Omniscient One, you understand everything—past and future; yet this exhaustion of my fortune, O Blessed One, belongs to me alone. You know it even as it dwells within my heart;
or perhaps, though knowing my distress, you maintain your "elephant-like gaze" of indifference.

Anvaya: O Omniscient One! You perceive everything—past and future. O Blessed Lord! Yet, this destruction of my very fortune exists, such that even though [the affliction] resides within my own heart, You do not know it; or, even having known it, You maintain a "blindness like an elephant" (*gajanimīlita*). The entire world clearly knows of the fire on Your forehead, the poison in Your throat, and the trident in Your hand; but these three things situated within me...
"You alone know [the truth], yet you are not compassionate; therefore, I am slain. (70)
Anvaya: O Lord! This entire world clearly perceives the fire upon Your forehead, the poison in Your throat, and the trident in Your hand;

but You alone, as the foremost of internal witnesses, know this triad within me—the fire of grief born from separation from pure knowledge which is the cause of consolation, the poison in the form of evil karma which is sweet at first but cruel in its final result, and the trident known as old age and death—and yet You are not compassionate.
Therefore, I am destroyed.

You alone are the causeless friend of all living beings; your compassion is innate, like the radiance of the sun. But my destiny is adverse, for you do not even notice my lamentations, which have become equal to the wailing of one in a wilderness.
O Lord! You alone are the disinterested friend of all living beings; like the radiance of the sun, Your compassion is innate.

Yet, for me—whose lamentations have become like the wailing of a wilderness, who am utterly unfortunate, unworthy, and a vessel of ill-fortune, who from birth have been turned away from joy and whose speech is harsh and loud—this fate is adverse, O Great Lord, since by destiny I have obtained one who is the lowest of all men.
Misfortune did not abandon me, just as a woman of good family does not desert her husband. || 72 ||

O Maheśa! Having by fate obtained me—who am utterly wretched, unworthy, unfortunate, devoid of humor from birth, foul-mouthed, and the lowest of all beings—this misfortune did not abandon me, just as a virtuous wife does not leave her husband. O Śiva! I have wandered away from your supreme abode, which consists of nectar, possesses a blazing splendor, and removes both meditative absorption and its opposite; therefore, I am deluded.
In order to obtain riches whose foundations are as unstable as waves tossed by the Malaya breeze... 73 ||

O Śiva! For that reason, having abandoned meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which removes all unease, and having abandoned Your supreme, nectar-filled abode, I have wandered through the ten directions to acquire riches whose destruction is as fickle as waves tossed by the Malaya breezes. I have propitiated wicked lords who were as unstable as lightning, but not those who are true gurus by virtue of their abundance of virtues; alas, those [former pursuits] of mine have resulted only in great loss.
In vain have I been exhausted; alas, I am struck down by the spreading darkness of delusion!

O All-pervading Lord! By me, a fool, only fickle and wicked lords were worshipped, like fickle women; the venerable gurus, who are heavy with floods of virtues, were not worshipped. Therefore, those days of mine have gone to waste in vain! Alas! Stricken by the darkness of widespread delusion, I am exhausted.

Day after day, my craving has grown ever more expansive in my mind like a long winter night; O Lord whose eyes are the three worlds, grant me the grace of Your glance to bring an end to this blindness of despair, which is filled with delusion.
Anvaya: O Lord! In my mind, a longing as vast as a wintry night has increased its intensity day by day.
O You whose eyes are the three worlds! Bestow upon me the grace of Your glance; lead away the blinding darkness accumulated by delusion and bring it to an end.
What person indeed does not cause a paralysis of pride, expand some form of delusion, and place a seal upon their speech?
The unbearable fever of the inflammation of immense pride does not manifest as a disease consisting of suffering. || 76 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! This unbearable complication of the fever of unabated pride causes a pillar of hypocrisy to expand, spreads a certain delusion, imposes a seal upon one's speech—what malady indeed does it not propagate? Therefore, I now take refuge in You, whose hand-attainments are world-renowned and who are the crest-jewel of the lords of medicinal herbs; break Your silence and impoverish [this disease].
Drive away the sleep of delusion and the affliction of the senses quickly! || 77 ||

In this world, where there constantly arise aversion, fear, delusion, and incoherent speech, brought about by various intense afflictions that have accumulated like a feverish disorder, there is one powerful hunter who alone is able to destroy that most treacherous "malignant fever" known as saṃsāra, effortlessly and with ease. || 1 ||

Therefore, O Lord! I now take refuge in you, whose hand-accomplishments are world-renowned, the crest-jewel upon the head of the Lord of Herbs. O All-pervading One! Break the seal of my silence; dispel the sleep of delusion; swiftly drive away the affliction of the senses.
I place my trust in the fathomless waters, O Blessed One, and I grow weary even when faced with the assault of enemies; yet I do not wake when the Impartial Destroyer desires to slay me.
"What will be my fate if you show even the slightest contempt? (78)
Because you remove the blindness of delusion and ward off the intense fever of worldly existence, you alone are the skillful crest-jewel of physicians for all embodied beings.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! I am a fool; I place my trust in the fathomless waters of the ocean of worldly existence (*bhavārṇava*), and I remain indifferent even when faced with calamities brought about by enemies. Why? Because I do not remain vigilant before Yama, who is intent on destroying me. O All-pervading Lord! If you, the compassionate one, show even the slightest disregard toward me, then what recourse will I have?

"To him who gives you sound, you grant his excellence; or to him who carries intoxication, you ordain his restraint"—O you who delight in such play of reversing two syllables, why do you not direct your mind toward paying homage to him? 79.
Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! You grant a boon to him who, at the time of worship, offers you sound (or the sound of a mouth-instrument, or a lamentation/cry);

and you inflict punishment upon him who bears pride (madam). Thus, you who delight in the sport of transposing two syllables—why indeed do you not direct your mind toward me, who am offering salutation? (In this case as well, one may perform a reversal.)
(The meaning is: "It is fitting.

O Śiva, this abundance of the moon—present in your hand, on your head, in your eye, at the soles of your feet, and even in your form—is a source of relief for one distressed by heat and darkness who has come for refuge; how could it possibly become fruitless for one who has transgressed you? 80.

Anvaya: O Śiva! Since there is a moon upon your hand, your head, your eye, at the base of your feet, and even in your very form—this being such an abundance of moons for you—how could there come to be any futility in you, who have disregarded me as I have sought refuge with you, distressed by heat and darkness? (The meaning is: by quenching my heat and darkness through this abundance of moons which is entirely under your own control, please make it fruitful.)

From you, my mind has acquired crookedness from the crescent moon, yet not its nectar-like nature; heat from the upward-gazing fire, yet not its supreme brilliance; and turbidity from the flowing Ganges, yet not its profound depth—thus it has become like a winnowing basket for me. 81.

O Lord! My mind, which is intent upon meditating on you at every moment, has attained crookedness from the crescent moon, yet it has not attained the nature of nectar; it has attained heat from the upward gaze, yet it has not attained supreme radiance;
it has attained impurity from the flowing [tears], yet it has not attained depth even from you.
How can I describe the gravity of this calamity, since she, having suddenly instructed me to stand at the foot of a trunkless pillar, has rendered my flowers devoid of branches,
their existence inferable only by their absence, stripped of luster, fruitless, and bereft of fragrance?

Inference: How can I describe the gravity of this calamity, since it has suddenly appointed me to the station of a *sthāṇu* (the foot of Lord Śambhu), having taught me the state of being branchless, the condition of not being an object for flowers, the lack of luster, fruitlessness, and the absence of sap?
O God, names such as Sarvajña, Śambhu, Śiva, Śaṅkara, Viśvanātha, Mṛtyuñjaya, Īśvara, Mṛḍa, and so forth, belong to You in other contexts.
They are indeed fruitful, O Blessed One, yet you alone remain a mere trunk for me, unfortunate as I am.

Anvaya: O Lord! Your names—Sarvajña, Śambhu, Śiva, Śaṅkara, Viśvanātha, Mṛtyuñjaya, Mṛḍa, and so forth—are fruitful in other spheres; however, O All-pervading One, to me, who am of little fortune, You are merely Sthāṇu (the motionless trunk). [To You] who, toward Śveta when he was intent on offering the Sudarśana discus and toward Kṛṣṇa, possessed no discriminatory thought, You grant existence and prosperity.
"You release me among the meritorious while leaving the meritless ones behind; this is the rule that has wounded me. (84)

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord!
