You, in whom no distinction of thought arose—whether toward Śveta (the king named Śveta), who was intent on offering his beautiful vision (*sudarśana*), or toward Kṛṣṇa (Śrī Kṛṣṇa), who was intent on offering the Sudarśana discus (*sudarśana*)—that very You bestow prosperity upon the Puṇyajanas (such as Kubera and others), yet [You do not bestow it] upon me.
That you abandon those devoid of merit—this is my ruined destiny.
Having first won over the gods with offerings of elephants, horses, jewels, the *pārijāta* tree, wine, the moon, and nectar, you then took poison for yourself;
by what power of yours was that done? Where now is that compassion of yours toward me, the unfortunate one? (85)
O All-pervading Lord! Having won over the gods by offering them the jewels of elephants and horses, the glorious Pārijāta tree, wine, the moon, and nectar—
thereby securing their favor and supreme satisfaction— where now is that same compassion of yours, by whose majesty you took the poison upon yourself, toward me, who am so unfortunate?

When those arrogant Andhakas, who were skilled in the intoxication of passion, appeared before you, the sprout of the poison of wrath arose in your mind; yet, when sprinkled by her grace which consists of nectar, it produced a state of tranquility—where is that same compassion of yours now toward me, who am devoid of merit?

That sprout of the poison of wrath which appeared in your mind when the Andhakas were arrogant due to their lineage and were being consumed by the fire of passion—watered by which it produced a grace consisting of nectar; where is that mercy of yours now toward me, who am bereft of fortune?

Some [devotees] have obtained from you, O Blessed One, a boon of fearlessness held in your hand; some a boon of dense [bliss], and some a boon of nectar. Those who are lovers of your mercy have attained these.
I am merely a vessel for this spear, utterly consumed by misfortune. || 87 ||
Anvaya: O Blessed One! some devotees, seeking Your grace, have become recipients of Your boon;
some have become recipients of Your fearlessness; and some have become recipients of the thick nectar held in Your hand; but I, wounded by misfortune, have become the recipient of only the trident.

My mind, established within you, has become free from error through your presence, like the solar disc by the sun whose nature is light; yet if it were ever made turbid by darkness, it would shine only when the power of its merit is undiminished.

Alas, alas! I am greatly afflicted, utterly deluded by the suffering of old age and other ailments, and perpetually tormented by a single thorn of pain; therefore, I go to that physician renowned throughout the three worlds, the wielder of the trident (Śiva), for its pacification.
[The *anvaya* is: O Lord! Just as the solar orb (*bimba*), which possesses a luminous body, is presided over within by the Sun, and whose function is unerring—
If at any time it has been made turbid by darkness (*tamas*, i.e., Rāhu), then its greatness of merit remains undiminished and it shines forth.

Likewise, my mind— which has you as its ultimate refuge and whose activity is unerring— being presided over within by You, whose body is light, if at any time it has been made turbid by darkness (*tamas*, i.e., ignorance), then even there its greatness of merit alone shines forth undiminished.
I know that I am unable to enter your heart, which consists of nectar; for you are struck by the fierce forest fire of unbridled sorrow.
Yet, I am likewise not capable of holding you within my own heart—you who are as cool as the celestial ocean, nectar, and the moon. Shame on me! 89.
O All-pervading Lord! Struck by the forest fire of unrestrained suffering, I do not know how to enter Your nectar-filled heart;
nor am I able to hold You—who are as cool as the celestial river, nectar, and the moon—within my own heart. (Thus, in both ways) shame on me!
Wasted away, with all my virtues destroyed and my luster dissolved, I have taken refuge in You, just as the waning moon resorts to the sun; yet [my hope] is truly non-existent.
My life-force is something quite different; you would not show favor by even setting foot upon it. (90)

Wasted away, with all my luster diminished and my radiance dissolved, I am like the moon that has taken refuge in the sun—you, O Lord! If you do not show favor by setting your foot upon me, then I have no other means of survival whatsoever. Tell me, if you abandon me—who am distressed by terrible darkness, scorched by manifold afflictions, and struck down by the heavy frost of calamity—what else can I say?
May Hari, whose eyes are like the moon and fire at the end of the kalpa, remove my threefold suffering. || 91 ||

O Lord! If You abandon me—wretched as I am, distressed by terrible darkness, scorched by various afflictions, and struck down by the heavy frost of calamity—then tell me, who else is there? Who, possessing the sun, moon, and fire as his eyes, will remove my threefold suffering?

For one afflicted by the epilepsy of misfortune, there is no manifestation [of You], no intellect, no movement, no power, nor even memory; therefore, [I seek] him whose crown is the Lord of Herbs (Śiva).
"Except for you, the teacher of the three worlds, no one else will provide medical treatment for me. (92)

O Lord! For me, who am afflicted by the epilepsy of calamity—whose manifestation lacks intellect, whose movement is likewise absent, and who possesses neither power nor even memory—who else but You, the Preceptor of the Three Worlds and the one crowned with the Moon, will provide a cure?
O Śiva, You are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and so am I; Your supreme abode is void (*śūnya*) and so is mine. If You [are present] within the Cow...
"You bestow such fortitude; yet I am in distress, for you are Śiva while I am inauspicious, struck down by fate."

Anvaya: O Śiva! Just as you are *nirguṇa*—[according to the Sāṃkhyas, the state of equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is *mūlaprakṛti*; you are neither *prakṛti* nor *vikṛti*, being the *puruṣa*]—so too am I *nirguṇa* [devoid of qualities such as courtesy]. Furthermore, just as your supreme abode (*param dhāma*) is some kind of void [because the Supreme Self, whose nature is the supreme light, has its locus in the void above the cosmic egg], so too is mine.

Your supreme abode (home) is utterly empty (devoid of worldly implements), yet if you maintain your steadfastness (residence) in the cow, I too maintain my steadfastness (affection) in the cow (speech). However, alas! You are Śiva, protected by fate, whereas I am aśiva (inauspicious)!

Just as my desire found fruitlessness in you, so too was the time spent by me with you rendered fruitless; O Lord, my body’s luster has been destroyed just like yours. Alas! You are auspicious, but I am inauspicious, ruined by fate.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Just as in you, so too in me desire has met with fruitlessness; just as by you, so too by me time has been spent in vain. O God! Just like your body, my body also has its luster destroyed—this is indeed a pity. You are Śiva, while I am afflicted by fate and am not Śiva.
O All-pervading Lord, just as the serpent shines within Your heart, so too does it shine within mine, for I am solely devoted to You. Just as You are intent upon Your own dharma, so am I;
yet, alas, while You are auspiciousness itself, I have become inauspicious, struck down by fate.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Just as the serpent (Vāsuki) shines within Your heart, so too does the absence of sin (nāgaḥ = na āgaḥ = aparādhaḥ) shine within my heart, which is solely devoted to You. Just as You are intent upon Your own duty, even so am I intent upon my own duty.
But this is indeed a tragedy: O All-pervading Lord! You are Śiva (the Auspicious One), while I, afflicted by fate, am aśiva (inauspicious).

O Śiva, this distress is as appropriate for you as it is for me; O Blessed One, this gaze is as fierce for me as it is for you. Just as you are the trident-bearer, I am one whose power is destroyed by despair;
alas, you are auspiciousness itself, while I am inauspicious, struck down by fate.

Anvaya: O Śiva! Like Your form, this form of mine is suited to adversity; like Your vision, my vision too is troubled. Just as You are one whose power is unhurt by poison, so too am I one whose power is struck down by poison. Alas, however, this is the case: You are Śiva, while I, wounded by fate, am Aśiva (inauspicious).

Poison dwells in my throat as virulently as yours; like you, O Lord of Beings, I am Paśupati. My body too is consumed by a heavy, blazing fever just like yours. Alas! You are Śiva (the Auspicious), while I am inauspicious, ruined by fate.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Just as the terrible poison [Kālakūṭa] dwells in Your throat, so too does the terrible poison [in the form of envy] dwell in my throat. Just as You are the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśvara) and the Lord of Animals (Paśupati), even so am I the Lord of Beings [by implication, the foremost among the most fierce] and the Lord of Animals [figuratively, the master of the ignorant]. Just as Your body is afflicted by heavy disease...

It is blazing—[blazing with the radiance of heavy pain]—and likewise my own body is also blazing with heavy pain, [consumed by a great disease]; yet this is the tragedy: you are Śiva, while I am struck by fate and am *aśiva* (inauspicious).
Like the full orb of the moon swallowed by Rāhu, or like the body of a young woman shattered by a terrible illness.
Like a slab of sandalwood encircled by a python, or like the base of a king's feet surrounded by sycophants, [it was] encompassed. 98.

It was like the water of the great ocean of milk mixed with *hālāhala* poison; like the shore of the celestial river blocked by a great sea-monster; like the conduct of a virtuous householder consumed by poverty; and like the mind of one renowned for learning when it is possessed by envy. (99)

Like the beauty of one born of a noble family when deprived of learning, like the wealth of a base man when devoid of charity and enjoyment; my human birth—purified by a radiant lineage, sacred knowledge, and virtuous conduct—having become overwhelmed by calamity, is truly pitiable. (Tilaka) The sequence [of similes]: Like the orb of the full moon swallowed by Rāhu, like the body of a young woman broken by a terrible disease, or like [a body] entwined by a python.
Like sandalwood paste smeared by traitors; like the foot of a king besmeared with *hālāhala* poison; like the water of the great milk-ocean obstructed by a massive sea-monster;

like the bank of the celestial river scorched by poverty; like the conduct of a virtuous householder made base by envy; like the mind of one renowned for sacred learning rendered devoid of knowledge; like the beauty of a coward lacking generosity and enjoyment; and like wealth that provides neither charity nor pleasure.
Though this human condition of mine was pure through a brilliant lineage, sacred learning, and virtuous conduct, it has become pitiable, overwhelmed by calamity.

Looking back and forward and examining every direction, I see the wretched, cruel Kṛtānta with a serpent-noose in his hand. I fall to the ground, I lament piteously, and I roll at your footstool like a rogue; why are you so hard? 101.

O All-pervading Lord! Having looked behind me, before me, and in every direction, and beholding the cruel, wretched Yama—the Destroyer—who holds a serpent-noose in his hand, I fall upon the ground and lament piteously; I roll at the base of Your feet. Even so, why are You as hard as a rogue?

"Ah! Why do you not protect me? This Antaka (the Ender) is carrying me away. O Maheśa, is this a time for the arrogance of indifference? Let there be no pain for your heart through compassion; yet there is no shame in your abandoning one who has come to you for refuge. (102)

O Great Lord! This Antaka (Death) is forcibly carrying me away; Ah, why do you not protect me? Is this a time for playful arrogance? Let there be no pain to your heart out of compassion; yet, is there not even shame in you for abandoning one who has come to you for refuge?
Like a rain-cloud spreading its thunder, this Yama has indeed arrived with noose in hand. O Compassionate One! Who can be my refuge?
Have mercy upon me, your wretched servant. Are you ignorant? Are you weak? Are you distracted? Are you preoccupied?
Are you merciless? Are you incapable? Are you overcome by the lethargy of sleep? Or are you reeling from intoxication, that you thus neglect me as I cry out, tormented by the fear of Death?
O Lord of lineage, are you ignorant [unaware of the suffering of others]? Are you powerless [lacking the capacity to protect one who has sought refuge in such a crisis]? Or are you distracted?
Are you merciless? Or are you incapable? Or are you overcome by sleep? Or are you reeling with intoxication—that you [should ignore me] even as I am thus crying out?

You are indifferent to one afflicted by the fear of death—O Lord, are you asleep? Are you distracted in the task of protecting the created world? Or are you surely merciless? Or perhaps you are intoxicated? Or are you acting according to your own whims? Or have you become dull-witted and speechless due to the misfortunes of helpless and wretched ones like me? Why do you not listen to me?

That you do not grant an answer to this lamentation—O Lord of All, O Destroyer of Time, you whose pride can be dispelled by a mere "huṃ" sound—is this hatred for one so wretched? Is it perhaps an incapacity, or is it sheer cruelty, or even a total lack of power? Why such indifference toward me? (104)
"O Lord of All! Is this malice toward me, a wretched creature? Or is it this intolerance? Is it cruelty?
Or is it simply incapacity? That such indifference is shown even toward this wretch of Time, whose pride can be dispelled by a mere *huṃ* sound?
Speaking thus with harsh words like one possessed by evil, he was reckless, as if seized by a planet, out of sheer distress.
Again and again I speak even what is improper, yet even then, O pitiless one, you do not break your seal of silence. 105.

Like one whose lineage is corrupt, speaking harsh and coarse words; like one possessed by a demon, devoid of all restraint—I, out of agony, repeatedly utter whatever comes to mind, even that which is improper.

Yet, O pitiless one, do you not break your seal of silence even for this? When I am terrified, distressed by the pain of existence, clinging to your feet with my desires shattered, seeing no other way of escape—why, toward me who have committed not the slightest offense, do you remain thus?
O witness of the universe, though your heart is anointed with compassion, you have turned your face away.

O Witness of the Universe! Why are you even slightly turned away from me—who am innocent, terrified, distressed by the pain of worldly existence, clinging to your feet with my desires shattered, and seeing no other recourse—though your heart is steeped in compassion?
O Lord, I am naturally impure, crooked, and fickle; such indeed is my enemy, the noose of death, and even your sprout-like eyebrow is of that very same nature.
For its pacification, indeed, poison is the remedy for uneven poison.

Anvaya: O Master! I am by nature impure, crooked, and fickle; my enemy, the noose of death, is likewise such. Indeed, your sprout-like eyebrow, being of that very same nature (impure, crooked, and fickle), is capable of quelling it (my enemy, the noose of death); for in the case of virulent poison, poison itself is the remedy.

What is the use of these incessant, repetitive, and empty prattlings, which cause only distress and yield no fruit? Even though I know this, I speak again and again so vociferously; for I see no other supreme refuge but You.

O Lord! What will even intense suffering do to one who is already afflicted by a multitude of accumulated sorrows? Just as opium can never be more difficult to digest for one who is already consuming opium. Thus, what is the use of these incessant lamentations—repetitive, harsh, distressing, and fruitless?
Though I am aware [of this], I speak repeatedly and loudly, for I see no other supreme refuge but you.

If you are well-disposed toward me with favor, what is the use of words of affection? If you are intent on disregard, what is the use of words of affection? When good fortune has dawned, effort toward virtues is in vain; when it has not dawned, effort toward virtues is likewise in vain. (109)

Anvaya: O Lord! If you are well-disposed toward me with favor, then what is the use of affectionate words? Likewise, if you are intent on disregard, then what is the use of affectionate words? And this is observed: when good fortune has arisen, effort toward virtues is indeed in vain; and even when it is absent, effort toward virtues is likewise in vain.

O Maheśa, though I know this, I do not desist from this prattling out of distress; such is the majesty of your very glance, which turns night into day, darkness into light, fire into snow, and even poison into nectar. 110.

O Great Lord! Even though I know this (in the manner previously described), that I do not cease from this prattle is surely the power of my own affliction, which— like Your glance— turns night itself into day, turns darkness into light, turns fire into snow, and turns poison into nectar.

An enemy may become a friend, poison may become wholesome, and unrighteousness may attain the status of righteousness; when the Lord of the World is favorable, all things are reversed. Conversely, when He is adverse, the opposite occurs.

The mere hearing of the piteous cry of the distressed constantly produces compassion within you, just as the flame of fire consumes the *śamī* wood; yet once born, this very compassion burns him up—what can we say of such a great, unrestrained power of the Lord? (111)
O Lord of lineage, the mere hearing of the suffering of the wretched produces compassion incessantly within you, the compassionate one, like a flame of fire within a *śamī* tree;

and that very compassion, as soon as it is born, utterly consumes that distress of the miserable folk. For this reason, what can we say regarding the great unrestrained power of the Lord in this matter?

Whatever impropriety has been stated here that is unseemly and fit only for common folk—even in that regard, the pleasing whim of a master is enough to cause wonder in the minds of lords, even if it be as trivial as a monkey’s leap. 112.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O All-pervading Lord! Whatever impropriety (*asamañjasa*) or lack of decorum (*aucitya-mukta*) fit for a vulgar person has perhaps been uttered here in this *Stutikusumāñjali*, even in that—namely, in the words of praise composed by a vulgar person like me—the Master’s (*bhartuḥ*, i.e., Your, the Lord’s) pleasure is entirely appropriate (*ucita*).
And this is observed: even a mere monkey-leap (*kapi-jaṃpikā*) becomes a source of delight to the minds of lords (*īśvarāṇām*, i.e., independent masters).

Though seized by thieves, bitten by double-tongued serpents, swallowed by malevolent planets, or even obstructed by enemies; though harassed by tigers pouncing with speed, or sought out by wrathful royal officers; || 113 ||

Even one who has been overcome by spirits, submerged in the waters of the ocean, defeated in battle, fallen into a forest fire, and—what need of more—who is being dragged away even by the messengers of Yama; who is able to save such a person except for Maheśvara? (Yugma) *Anvaya:* Even if seized by thieves, bitten by double-tongued serpents, or swallowed by *grahas* (such as Brahmarākṣasas, Vetālas, and the like);...
Even when obstructed by enemies, or assailed by furious tigers that suddenly pounce, or pursued by wrathful mountain-dwellers,

or overcome by spirits, or submerged in the waters of the ocean, or broken in battle, or likewise fallen into a forest fire— what more need be said? Even when being dragged away by the messengers of Yama, [the Lord] exists solely to protect the afflicted person from such extreme peril and great fear.
Who else besides Maheśvara, that ocean of compassion, is worthy [of being sought]?

Alas, though I am a knower of that [truth], I long for imperishable happiness, yet I crave a transient body which is the sole abode of suffering! Or rather, I shall take refuge in the ancient, fierce-natured Puruṣa, who bears the crescent moon, in order to cross the ocean of worldly existence. 115.

Alas! Am I truly a knower of that [Truth]? Am I truly discerning? For, desiring imperishable bliss, I crave this unstable body, which is the sole abode of suffering! Or rather, for the sake of crossing the ocean of worldly existence, I take refuge in the Ancient Puruṣa of fierce nature, who bears the crescent moon as his vessel!
Even the Moon, the Sun, and the Fire, upon merely falling within the range of his vision, suddenly met their end; alas, am I so wise as to seek him alone?
I, fearing the agony of death, take refuge with devotion in that Lord Sadāśiva. || 116 ||

Anvaya: Alas! Even the moon, the sun, and the fire, upon merely entering the path of his vision, suddenly attained the state of the five (the number five, as well as death). Yet I, though wise, am afraid of the pain of death and take refuge in that very Lord Sadāśiva—wherein the omnipresent Sthāṇu resides, wherein his consort Aparṇā dwells, and wherein their son Viśākha abides. Oh, how great is my wisdom! Translation: Alas! Even the moon, the sun, and the fire, upon merely falling within the range of his sight, instantly met their end (the state of the five elements, as well as death). And yet, despite being wise, I—who am terrified by the agony of dying—take refuge in that very God Sadāśiva, where the omnipresent Lord Sthāṇu dwells, where his consort Aparṇā resides, and where their son Viśākha stays. Oh, how marvelous is the wisdom of those like me!
I desire to enter that most excellent abode for the sake of attaining my desired fruit. || 117 ||

In what abode does that omnipresent Sthāṇu reside, where his consort Aparṇā is, and where their son Viśākha dwells— in that very place I wish to enter to obtain my desired fruit; am I not, therefore, the foremost among the wise?

Though possessed of great intelligence, I am exceedingly timid; yet I desire to enter the terrifying abode of the Lord, which is crowded with hundreds of Vetālas and Bhūtas having the fierce faces of cats, pigs, and jackals, and resounds with the cries of night-stalkers and Piśācas.

"Though I am exceedingly timid by nature, I desire to enter the abode of the Lord, which is crowded with hundreds of Vetālas and Bhūtas with faces as terrifying as cats, boars, and jackals, and is made fearsome by the cries of night-stalkers and Piśācas— and yet, I consider myself wise. For a wise man [is not afraid] of the thousand-headed serpent, the king of serpents, who supports the world upon his thousand hoods while trembling from the noose of Death, which has three coils and ears as long as eyes."
I take refuge in the Puruṣa who has a thousand eyes and a thousand feet. || 119 ||

The wise one reflects: "I am wise because, trembling with fear from the noose of Death—which has ears for eyes, lacks feet, and possesses three hoods—I have taken refuge in the Supreme Person, who bears a thousand-hooded serpent king, and who possesses a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. I am terrified of Śiva, the Lord of Life, who is skilled at seizing all people and whose blazing eyes are fierce like fire. Thus the wise one.
I take refuge in you, the Lord of Life, who boldly removes the suffering of all people and whose gaze is as fierce as fire. || 120 ||

Anvaya: O Śiva! Terrified of Kāla—the Lord of Life, who is skilled in seizing all people and possesses eyes as fierce as blazing fire—I, being wise, take refuge in You, the Lord of Life, who are skilled in removing the suffering of all people and whose gaze is not like that of fire.
The moon, having abandoned its deer-mark, took refuge in You, who have cast aside the deer of the sacrifice, because it perceived You to be the enemy of Kāma.
I have indeed approached you with desire; therefore, I am superior even to those of keen intellect. || 121 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! The moon, having abandoned the deer that serves as its mark, has resorted to you—who have cast off the deer of the sacrifice—under the pretext of its crescent phase (or, by way of increase).

This is indeed fitting. But as for me, having recognized you as the enemy of Kāma, I have resorted to you while still possessing desire (still full of longing); am I therefore superior among the wise?
Since even the four-faced Śatadhṛti, though seated upon a lotus, suffered an indescribable humiliation— abandoned by Śrī, deprived of his fortitude,
and with his face rendered soft and pale— I, being wise, pray for the grace of that Lord.

Even the four-faced Śatadhṛti (Brahmā), who rests upon the lotus of his lineage, suffered an unspeakable defeat at the hands of that Lord; therefore, I— though wise, yet the opposite of him, abandoned by fortune, devoid of fortitude, and with a soft, downcast face— entreat that Lord for his grace.

I worship that Lord who, having taken away all the fruits of the actions performed since birth—which were to be enjoyed over a long period—bestows them upon his devotee in a single moment so that they may never return; oh, how truly wise I am! 123.

Having performed actions from birth, whatever fruit—whether auspicious or inauspicious—has been obtained, he seizes all of that which was to be experienced over a long period of time in a single moment;
and having taken it from the devotee, he accepts them so they shall not return. Oh! I serve that Lord, who is the wisest of the wise!
O You whose body has the nature of fire, Brahmā went above and Hari went below with effort to measure Your sovereignty, yet they were utterly unable to do so. Therefore...
O Lord of the Mountains, does your compliance not bear fruit for those two who stand before you themselves, burdened by the weight of devotion and faith as they offer their praises?

Devoted to dwelling alone in cremation grounds, with eyes leaping like fire, wearing a coil of crooked serpents whose hair is the flame of poisonous light, and bearing a formidable crown of rows of skulls—the wise man who, despite a cowardly heart, takes refuge in such a pervasive and terrifying Lord, is an object of laughter for those of perfected intellect. (124)

Taking refuge in the Lord— who is terrifying (and most fearsome), whose sole delight is the cremation ground, whose eyes are as flickering as fire, who wears a ring of crooked serpents with crests of poisonous flames, and who is crowned by a formidable garland of skulls— how can I, a coward at heart, not be laughed at by the wise?

Ah! I am a knower of reality; terrified of Time, who holds a single serpent in the palm of his hand and devours living beings one by one in succession, I seek refuge once and for all in Mahākāla, whose every limb is covered with numerous serpents and whose mind is intent on swallowing the entire universe at once.

Anvaya: Aho! I, who am terrified of Time—which has a single serpent resting in its palm and which devours living beings one by one in succession—take refuge in Mahākāla, whose every limb is graced by numerous serpents and whose mind is intent upon swallowing the universe all at once; therefore, I am a knower of reality.

Where there is the horned crystal-peaked mountain, where the horned Pināka bow, and where even that beloved horned bull of my master shines— there, terrified, naturally simple, of few words, and lacking in boldness, I, though wise, pray for the proper time of service from my lord.

Where the Lord’s beloved, the Crystal-Peaked Mountain, is horned (both possessing peaks and being proud); where the Lord’s beloved, the Pināka bow, is horned (both fashioned from horn and being arrogant); and where the Lord’s beloved, that Bull, is also horned (possessing two horns and being haughty)—there, at the gate of the Great King, I stand terrified, naturally simple, of few words, and lacking in confidence.
O Wise One, I pray that you attend to the proper time for serving your Lord.
For one whose mind is scorched by the fierce summer heat of calamity, there is no rest anywhere; wealth slips away and past misdeeds bear their fruit.
Therefore, since I have fallen utterly blind into the deep well of long-lasting suffering, who else but you, O Ocean of Compassion, is able to lift me up?

O All-pervading Lord! When wealth has vanished and evil conduct, previously established, bears fruit; when the mind is scorched by the terrifying heat of the summer of calamity and finds no rest anywhere—then, O Bhava, who else but You, the ocean of compassion, is able to lift me up, who have suddenly fallen into the blind well of long-lasting suffering?

O magnanimous one, cast your gracious glance upon those people who are worthy vessels of compassion, whose minds are entangled in the snares of hope, and for whom this wretched rags-clad beggar’s cry for a mere fragment of wealth and body provides no path to attain the supreme state of bliss. (128)

O merciful one! Cast your desired glance upon these people— who are the objects of your compassion, who are characterized by us, whose minds are entangled in the snares of hope, and for whom this wretched ragged garment of begging for a mere fragment of wealth and property does not point out the path to attain that state of supreme bliss.
Lift up your face slightly and proclaim the cry of fearlessness; bestow a clear glance and comfort him who is bereft of his way [or bereft of fortitude].
What else? This one has arrived with an angry look, neck outstretched—he is Death himself. Do not remain thus, sluggish in your abundant pride.

O Lord! Turn Your face even slightly upward; proclaim the cry of fearlessness; grant me Your clear vision; comfort me who am bereft of movement. What more shall I say? Do not remain indifferent due to the intoxication of Your habitual pride, thinking, "Here has come Death with neck uplifted and eyes full of wrath. What else can I repeatedly say to one who beholds before him the furious servant of Yama, with serpent-noose in hand, as if he were leaping forward?

My fortitude falters, my gait stumbles, my form trembles, my stability burns with agitation, my peace vanishes, and my memory fades away. (130) The connection [of the verse]: O Lord! What more shall I say repeatedly? As I behold before me, as if throbbing, the wrathful servant of the Sun-god who holds a serpent-noose in his hand, my fortitude falters, my gait stumbles, my form trembles, my stability burns, my peace vanishes, and my memory fades.

O Ocean of Compassion, uniquely skilled in uplifting the three worlds, O you whose mass of fame is renowned for granting white [safety] and fearlessness, if you do not protect this person, I— terrified by the fierce "huṃ" cries of the wrathful God of Death— being utterly helpless, shall cry out loudly for the violation of dharma; O Lord, in my distress, to whom shall I turn?

That power of yours which makes the inaccessible easy to traverse, that which brings the distant into close proximity, by whose power the desert becomes a pleasure garden, and the enemy acts as a friend—O Lord, may that irresistible power of yours, which manifests as compassion when I cry out in distress, likewise impel you toward my consolation. *Anvaya:* *yat* (by the efficacy of which) *durgam* (the inaccessible) *sugamatvam eti*; *yat* (by the efficacy of which) *dūram* (the distant) *abhyarṇatām bhajate*; *yat* (by the efficacy of which) [the desert] *krīḍopavanatvam eti*; *ripuḥ* (the enemy) *mitrāyate*; *yasyāḥ* (of which) *sā* (that) *bhuvi* (on earth) *śaktiḥ* (power) *apratihatā* (is unimpeded); *sā ārttiḥ* (that distress) [when I cry out]; *svāmin* (O Lord), *mām* (me) *anudat-kṛpā api* (compassion also following me) *nudatu tvām* (may it impel you) *matsamāśvāsane* (to my consolation).
That power which causes even the desert to become a pleasure grove, and by which an enemy acts as a friend on earth—that irresistible and unyielding power is my distress;
it drives me to cry out to you, O Lord! May compassion for my consolation also impel you.
Both Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī dwell at your door, O Lord, yet they are free from anger toward me; however, Lakṣmī dwells beneath the seat of your feet.

Because of my hatred for even a slight acquaintance with Sarasvatī, I have abandoned that which possesses an eternally flourishing state; thus, languishing like the ocean, I carry within my heart this fire that is difficult to bear.

Anvaya: O Lord! Śrī and Sarasvatī dwell at your door; however, Śrī has abandoned me—who have maintained a perpetually flourishing presence upon the surface of your footstool—out of a hatred for even the slightest acquaintance with Sarasvatī. Therefore, languishing like the ocean, I carry within my heart a fire that is difficult to bear.
O Lord, my first age was devoid of discernment like that of an animal;

my youth has been ruined by the commencement of efforts to win the confidence of my wife, which only served to offend her. O Master, now that I am worn out by old age, before this running Death reaches my ear, protect me, who am helpless and have taken refuge at your feet. (133)
O Lord! My first stage of life passed away like that of an animal, devoid of discernment;

my youth was ruined by the commencement of attempts to win the confidence of my wife. O Master! Now that I am worn out by old age, before this death reaches my very ears, protect me, who am helpless and have taken refuge at your feet.
As long as my form was delightful with a multitude of gestures born of unabated pride, for that long I, struck by the darkness of delusion, did not perceive the abyss before me.
Now, my mind terrified by this sudden downfall, whom shall I beseech? Whom shall I take refuge in? What am I able to do? What shall I do? Have mercy on me, you who have betrayed yourself;
protect me!
O Lord! As long as my form was delightful with a multitude of limbs that produced immense pride, so long did I, blinded by the darkness of delusion, fail to see the abyss standing before me.
Now, my mind terrified by this sudden downfall, whom shall I beseech? Whom shall I take refuge in? What am I able to do? What can I do?
O All-pervading One! Have mercy; protect me, who have betrayed myself.

If a man blind from birth, wandering on a narrow path without the support of a hand, should fall into a pit and meet with disaster, what fault is there in him? Fie, fie upon me! For while the eye of the scriptures exists, while the lamp of wisdom exists, and while there is a loving master who shows the way, that rogue who nevertheless falls into the abyss—him alone do I blame.

Anvaya: O Lord! If a person born blind, wandering on a perilous path without the support of a hand, should fall into a pit and meet with disaster, then what fault is there in him? (The meaning is that he is not deserving of reproach. Fie, fie upon me, that rogue who, despite having the eye of the scriptures, the lamp of wisdom, and a gracious master to show the way, falls right into a chasm!
Where there is no protector at all on a perilous path, and if enemies lie in wait to strike, what remedy can possibly be effective?
But where you, the Lord, the ocean of compassion and expert in protecting the three worlds, are present—if they still strike there, whose fault is this reproachful defeat? (136)

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: Wherever on a treacherous path there is no protector at all, there the enemies stand before one; if the executioners have not even noticed the pit ahead, what remedy (*pratividhi*) can be effectively applied there? Yet, where You—the ocean of compassion, the Lord expert in protecting the three worlds—are the protector, even there [the internal enemies] such as desire, anger, and the rest [persist].

If those who cause harm strike one who has sought refuge, then whose pride is bolstered by this humiliation? (O Lord! the meaning is: you yourself must deliberate on this matter. Is it not the case that for one who is powerful, the mind is drenched in the nectar of perfect compassion; or is he, being merciful, unable to accomplish the welfare of others?

Since you possess both power and compassion, the Lord himself will know [the truth], for this wretched person, though terrified by the fear of Yama, has come before you, the Supreme, seeking refuge. || 137 ||

What is the use of that powerful man whose mind is not moistened by perfect compassion? And what is the use of that compassionate one who is unable to bring about the welfare of others? O All-pervading Lord! Both power and compassion belong to You alone. Even a person who is wretched, helpless, and terrified out of fear of Yama has come before You; beyond this, the Master Himself will know.

In the water-pot, which is like a gushing waterfall from the celestial river and is dear to the hand, filled with the essence of compassion, vast and full; and in the moon, which possesses nectar that is sweet, cool, easily accessible, and a destroyer of the heat of affliction— since my beloved lord has arrived before me, he himself shall know what is best.

Anvaya: O Lord! There is nectar—sweet, cool, and easily obtained—in the vessel held in [your] lotus-like hand for cutting the fever, in the waterfall of your own river, in the full ocean of the essence of compassion, and in the full-orbed moon; furthermore, this supplicant has arrived, so beyond this, Your Lordship will know for yourself.
This pain, like a piercing thorn, torments our hearts as long as it remains unrevealed; yet, once disclosed before a wicked person, it produces nothing but humiliation.

Therefore, we have reported this matter to the Lord, the omniscient one who is an ocean of the nectar of compassion; whatever is appropriate will be done by Him, for the Master Himself shall know best.

As long as this pain, resembling a splinter lodged within, has not been disclosed before those possessed of a sensitive heart, it indeed torments the heart; yet once revealed in the presence of a wicked person, it produces only the speaker’s own insignificance. Therefore, that pain has been reported by me before you, the All-Knowing Lord and ocean of the nectar of compassion. Whatever was appropriate has already been done; henceforth, the Master himself shall know what is fitting.
May my writings be well-received in the assembly of the wise; may there be the attainment of the pure scripture; may false views not arise;

may the enjoyment of the stainless one be long-lasting. May all members of the assembly grant their approval, yet even so, there is no liberation through mere logic, for you, O Lord Bhavānī, are the true seer and the valid knower who does not engage in such deliberation.

May the gods in the assembly of the wise (the divine council) be pleased; likewise, may there be the attainment of purity in the assembly of scholars (the learned council). May false views (ignorance and nihilism) not arise; may there be enjoyment that is free from worldly attachment, unassailed, and long-lasting. May all members of the assembly practice conformity (following that path); even through that, liberation (mokṣa) shall be attained by way of justice.

There is no one who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśin*), for you, O Lord Śiva, are yourself the supreme knower; yet if you do not bestow your consideration, who, with broken feet, could climb Mount Meru by crawling on his knees? Who, leaping from the vault of the sky, could seize the orb of the sun? Or who, by the words of a fool, is able to obtain the grace of the Lord? Even though I reflect thus within myself, I have been made speechless by the force of my suffering, O Lord.

O Lord! Who, with crippled feet, would approach Mount Meru by crawling on his knees? (No one. Who, having leaped from the surface of the sky, could seize the dark orb of the moon? Or who is capable of obtaining the favor of the Master through the speech of a fool? Even while reflecting thus within myself, I have been forcibly made talkative by my distress [in praising you].

Even *pauṇḍraka* sugar, when chewed for long in the throat, acquires a pungent taste; even an excellent woman, when pursued with excessive passion, produces distaste; even the celestial river Ganges causes agitation through repeated immersion within; and even a sweet story engenders distrust if it is too long—therefore, one should rest. 142.

Just as even *pauṇḍraka* sugar-candy, when chewed for a long time, produces a pungent taste in the throat; just as even an excellent woman, when excessively indulged with passion, creates a sense of distaste within; and just as even the celestial river Ganges causes agitation from repeated immersion—likewise, even a sweet story, when it becomes too long, fosters a lack of faith. For this reason, I shall take my rest.

Thus, when this piteous lament was uttered by me, whose mind was prostrated by the calamity of delusion extended by hundreds of intense and varied thoughts, O Treasure of Compassion, place it within your heart; for you are the inner self who knows everything dwelling within, and therefore you ought to forgive the transgression of me, your devotee. 143.
Thus, with a mind overwhelmed by the calamity of delusion—protracted by hundreds of various and endless streams of false thoughts—I have uttered this piteous cry:

"O Treasure of Compassion! Place all of that within Your heart. For You, as the inner self (*antarātman*), know everything that exists within; therefore, You ought to forgive the transgression of me, Your devotee.

Thus ends the eleventh hymn, titled "The Lament of the Wretched," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flower-Tributes to the Blessed Maheśvara), composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*.
The twelfth hymn.

I take refuge in that God of inconceivable power, who, though worshiped through sacrifices, is to be served by those skilled in policy; who, though free from all affliction, is renowned for his fierce trident; and who, though fond of the Vedas, is not beloved by the Vedic scriptures.

I take refuge in that God of inconceivable power—who, though worshiped through sacrifices, is served by those who know the right policy; who, though free from all affliction, possesses a celebrated fierce trident; and who, though beloved of the Vedas, is not a lover of the [mere] Vedic texts. Śiva is free from the six waves of worldly existence: cold and heat for the body, and greed and delusion for the mind; having cast aside both hunger and thirst.

You alone are the object of praise, you alone are the praiser, and you alone are the praise; apart from you, nothing else exists. This notion that "I am praising you" and "you are the one to be praised" is ignorance—an illusory perception of separate entities. (2)

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! You alone are the one to be praised; you alone are the one who praises; and you alone are the praise itself. Apart from you, there is nothing else whatsoever by which I might praise you with praise. This notion of separate objects is false; it is indeed ignorance (ajñāna). Nevertheless, I praise you again and again; therein, ignorance perishes through ignorance itself—just as dust growing on a mirror is wiped away by dust.
For indeed, there is no other means apart from this. || 3 ||

Even so, I praise you again and again because ignorance is destroyed by ignorance itself; for there is no other means to wipe away dust settled upon a mirror than dust. Just as when dense darkness prevails, I remain with my mind attached to worldly existence, so too, even when that [darkness] is destroyed, awakening has arisen.
May my mind be attached to existence. || 4 ||

While darkness, bold in its pervasion, is spreading, just as I have remained with a mind attached to worldly existence (*bhava*), so too, even when that [darkness] is destroyed, may I, possessing awakened consciousness, remain with a mind attached to *bhava*—that is, with a mind attached to Sadāśiva.

O Lord of the universe, you who govern all including gods and demons, you are the one to be entreated by me through your compassion; that compassion is to be invoked by those who bow down in their wretchedness.
"She has come to me quite effortlessly. || 5 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! The world, including the gods and demons, is subject to you; you are subject to compassion; that compassion is subject to the wretchedness of those who bow before you; and that wretchedness has come upon me without any effort on my part. O Lord, although I know that you will certainly not fail in the destruction of my suffering, nevertheless, I am making this request so that the burden of action may not fall upon me.
"Your [mind] is subject to both favor and aversion. || 6 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! I know that You certainly do not fail in Your effort to dispel the suffering of me, who am wretched; nevertheless, for the sake of [ensuring] that my own karma does not cause resentment in You toward me, I address You. Having playfully opened Your gracious speech—which is wholesome, truthful, capable of bearing weight, affectionate, charming, and captivating—[I pray].
O Moon-crested One, grant comfort to me who has sought refuge in you.

Anvaya: O Moon-crested Lord! Unfold your speech—which is wholesome, truthful, capable of bearing weight, affectionate, charming, captivating, playful, and serene—and comfort me who has sought refuge in you.
We swallow poison moistened with honey; we swallow a hook hidden within a ball of meat; [we swallow] that which contains a mass of fierce thorns lodged within.
We seize Pauṇḍraka, that morsel of a lump [of a mere fragment]. || 8 ||

O Lord! Since we constantly indulge in sense-objects that are sweet to the taste at first but harsh in their ultimate consequence, what can we do about it, even though we know better? This wretched mind does not relinquish its attachment.

(A pair of verses. *Anvaya*: O Lord! [We] that [constantly] enjoy sense-objects which are sweet to the taste at first (*āmukhe kāmadhurān*) but harsh in their ripening (*vipākarūkṣān*), [what can we do? (Note: The term *yugmam* indicates that these two verses form a single syntactic unit.)
We swallow poison moist with flowing honey; we gulp down a hook hidden within a baited lump;
we devour a piece of a sugarcane ball filled with a mass of fierce thorns. O Lord! Even though we know this, what can we do in this matter?
This wretched mind does not abandon its attachment to sense objects.

How is it that the virtuous—consisting of pearls, possessing long virtues, well-rounded, partaking of purity, and bearing the excellence of fruit—do not, like necklaces, attain a place in the heart of the Lord of Beings, being full of devotion? (10)

How is it that those who possess devotion to the lineage—saintly, free from impurity, long-armed in virtue, well-rounded in conduct, endowed with purity, and bearing the excellence of fruit—do not, like necklaces (which are likewise possessed of beauty), find a place in the heart of the Lord? By Your grace, may I become like You: one who dwells in the cave [of the heart], delights in Dharma, bears the renown of the Lord of the Mountain, possesses true affection, and is endowed with undiminished devotion.
May I become a Blessed One! 11.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! By Your grace, when shall I become like You—residing in a cave (*guhāśrita*), delighting in Dharma, bearing the renown of the Lord of Mountains (*girīśa-prathām dadhānaḥ*), possessing love for the True [Brahman], and endowed with undiminished devotion (*ahīna-bhakti*)? Having propitiated whom alone, the devotee is undoubtedly liberated from the company of great enemies; how shall I come to be near Him by Your favor?
Hara’s encounter with the fierce Mahāri was [terrible]. || 12 ||

Anvaya: O Ugra! By worshipping that one [Lord Hari], the devotee is undoubtedly liberated from the company of great enemies; how has the company of that Hari—the company of the Sudarśana discus—come to you by Your grace?
This [discus] is very difficult to obtain; yet here it is present even in Your mouth, and Sarasvatī is also close at hand. This Kurukṣetra is exceedingly purifying.
For what reason do you delay with one who is worthy and seeking [your favor]? 13.

Anvaya: O Lord! This intense devotion toward You (this attachment of mine) is very difficult to attain; moreover, this Goddess Sarasvatī is also present within my mouth. Therefore, O Blessed One, make this field exceedingly purifying for me. Why do You delay with one who is a worthy petitioner?

Who would not be struck with wonder by this fortunate Sarasvatī, who bestows her grace even upon the Lord who has conquered all afflictions, making him—who was once clad in a steady deerskin—possess a deerskin that is no longer steady? 14.

Whom does this *Sarasvatī*—endowed with lineage and fortune, this hymn—not fill with wonder? For she brings even the Lord—who has conquered all afflictions, who is clad in steady deerskin yet remains unsteady in his sovereignty—face to face.
He, the Lord, when pleased, makes those whose minds are perpetually devoid of all-knowledge and whose wealth of unsurpassed generosity has been abandoned, free from the exhaustion of untimely fear.
And when provoked, [it afflicts] embodied beings. || 15 ||

He for whom the equality of those two shines in his vision— those two who long ago established their abode within the forest depths, where the moon cultivated a friendship with the deer, and the sun, though ever a plunderer of others' property, dwelt there as well.

O Lord, how could there be even the slightest disregard on Your part—who are ever subject to compassion for us and others who are worthy recipients of grace—toward those whose selves have been cast upon a path unfit for the virtuous? (Tilaka) The connection [of the verse]: That Lord, being gracious, [makes] embodied beings such that they never abandon the wealth of supreme generosity, are always possessed of all knowledge, and are not devoid of consciousness.

When enraged, he likewise causes embodied beings— who have never abandoned their supreme generosity and whose minds are forever devoid of all-encompassing knowledge— to be withered by untimely fear. That Moon who formerly for a long time established his abode within the depths of the forest (or waters), and that Sun who always seizes the property of others— of those two [the Moon and the Sun], he [Kali] is the one who causes them to be withered by untimely fear.

O All-pervading Lord! How could even the slightest disregard arise toward those such as ourselves—who have fallen onto a path unfit for the virtuous, yet are worthy recipients of Your grace—when You, who are ever subject to compassion, perceive equality in Your vision?
O Lord, with tears in Your eyes and a trace of perspiration, as if by the smoke produced from the fire of the eye on Your forehead, [You look upon us].
As if by the mass of rays from the fierce splendor arising from his right eye. || 18 ||
The sprouts of horripilation grew densely upon you, as if from the rays of the crescent moon on your crest,
or as if from the waters of the celestial river flowing through your head, cooled by the mass of snow-like teeth.

May I, with my limbs trembling as if from the winds of the hissing of the serpent-king flashing from your armlets, become completely immersed in the nectar of bliss upon beholding you, gracious, before me. (The Tilaka) *Anvaya:* O Lord! Having beheld you, gracious, before me, being completely immersed in the nectar of bliss, [may I become so].

With eyes full of tears as if by the smoke produced from the fire of the eye on Your forehead; with beads of perspiration as if by the mass of rays from the fierce sun risen in Your right eye; with dense sprouts of horripilation as if by the clusters of moonbeams from the crescent moon in Your crest-lock;
and with the lute of Your teeth sounding as if by the waters of the celestial river flowing from Your head, cooled by the multitude of snows.
May I have my limbs trembling as if by the winds from the hissing of the lord of serpents flickering upon your arm;

for this sandalwood tree, which endured the agony of wounds from the axe because it was dear to its Lord, surely bears a resemblance to the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, whose neck is embraced by a serpent.

Because this sandalwood tree endured the agony of the axe in the hope that it might become dear to its Lord, it surely bears a resemblance to the Lord of Girijā, even as its neck is embraced by serpents.

That the trees (*sumanas*) brought joy to their Lord while enduring the pain of being struck by the tips of his fingernails—that is the very nature of the virtuous-minded (*sumanas*). For they do not cause distress to their Master, even when he is in the midst of burning them.
Having prostrated, he abandoned even his service and devotion toward his guru, as well as his reverence for him. || 22 ||

That the *sumanas* flowers, though suffering the pain of being crushed by the tips of the nails held [by the Lord] at the time of gathering blossoms for worship, brought joy to their Master— that indeed is the true "good-mindedness" (*sumanastva*) of the *sumanas*. And that the *aguru* resin, even when falling into the fire, did not abandon its devotion to serving its master—
that is the true "gravity" (*gaurava*) of the *aguru*.

O Lord, that grace born from a single particle of the dust of Your lotus feet is like the arrows of the virtuous in the forest; for while wicked men first display supreme straightness, they do not, upon piercing the vital organs, strike with such sharpness as these. 23.

O Lord! That grace which arises from a single particle of the dust of Your lotus feet—that grace by which the wicked, having first displayed supreme straightforwardness and then entering within like sharpened arrows, do not pierce the virtuous who dwell in the forests;
that grace by which Your name, even when sung by the most vulgar of men, bestows bliss upon the hearts of those possessed of devotion—O Lord, [that grace is present] in all the limbs of Amāna.
Surely, this [joy] breaks forth externally under the guise of horripilation. || 24 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! That bliss which Your name—sung even by common folk such as the Hālākas—bestows upon the hearts of those possessed of devotion, surely, though not present in all the limbs (the body), breaks forth externally under the guise of horripilation. At the final stage, states such as perspiration, trembling, horripilation, stammering, and so forth, manifest for those whose minds are fixed on You through the sight of You.
O Blessed One, may you bestow upon others an unswerving joy that dispels the fear of death. 25.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! For those of perfected intellect who experience intense bliss from the sight of You, at the final hour, states such as perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and faltering speech arise; whereas for others (those of unperfected intellect, the sinful), these same states arise from the fear of the Ender (at the moment of death).

At the final moment of existence, some who are devoted to the service of Your lotus feet place them upon the surface of their throats; others, having attained the coils of the Lord of Serpents, assume the state of being Your attendants, even as they are dragged by the tips of the hollows of Yama’s hands.

Anvaya: O Bhava! Some [rare and meritorious souls], being intensely devoted to the service of Your lotus feet, attain the state of Your attendants at the final moment and wear the coils of the Lord of Serpents upon their necks; others [the sinful], however, wear that which is dragged by the millions of hollows in the hands of Kṛtānta.

Indeed, he who is incapable of destroying Time even for a moment when it comes to the granting of fearlessness to the terrified—[how can He be so] toward one intent on granting white (spotless) fearlessness?
O Lord, how indeed did you come to possess such capacity to destroy Death himself? || 27 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! You who, indeed, are never able to spare even a moment for the destruction of Kāla in the act of granting fearlessness to the frightened;

how then did you come to possess the capacity to destroy Kāla while bestowing white (pure) fearlessness? O Lord, that glance of yours which is soft with the nectar of compassion and cannot at any time overcome desire, is indeed harsh with unrestrained wrath.
O Maheśa, how did he previously accept the destruction of his desire? || 28 ||
O Lord! That glance of yours, gentle with the nectar of compassion, is never able to frustrate the desires of those who bow before you.
O Great Lord! How is it that this very same glance of yours, when harsh with unrestrained anger, previously accepted the frustration of desire?
Do these mountains, headed by Meru and Mandara, bear an immense pride with their exceedingly lofty peaks? But this [pride] was crushed by the prostration of the one adorned with the moon.
Victorious is my head, which bows low before the world. || 29 ||

Do these mountains, headed by Meru and Mandara, truly possess such immense pride with their exceedingly lofty peaks? This, however, is my head, bowed in salutation to the ornament of the moon, which triumphs over the world.
O Lord, it is fitting for you that this head bears the name "Uttamāṅga" (the highest limb), as it proclaims its superiority over all other limbs. Therefore, this is appropriate for you.
Of this one who is worthy of salutation and intent upon prostrating at the pedestal of your lotus feet. || 30 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! O Bhava! That this head—which bears the lofty name "uttamāṅga" (the highest limb) because it excels all other parts of the body—is fit to be saluted by him who is intent on prostrating at the footstool of Your lotus-feet. Is Śrīghana not Sugata? Or is Mādhava never the Janārdana? O Master, is even Gajāri [not Viṣṇu]? Translation: O Lord! O Bhava! This head of yours, which bears the exalted title "uttamāṅga" (the supreme limb) because it surpasses all other parts of the body, is indeed worthy of being saluted by one who is devoted to bowing at the footstool of Your lotus feet. Is Śrīghana not Sugata? Or does Mādhava never assume the state of Janārdana? O Master, is even Gajāri [not Viṣṇu]?
You are the beloved of the Mountain-born Goddess; if you possess independence, what else could there be? || 31 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Though you are Śrīghana (the embodiment of prosperity), are you not Sugata (the Buddha)? Though you are Umādhava (the husband of Umā), do you never assume the state of Janārdana (Viṣṇu)?
Though you are Gajāri (the enemy of the elephant, Gaṇeśa), are you not the beloved of Nagajā (Pārvatī)? Or rather, since you possess absolute independence, what else can we say?
Beholding your forehead-eye, which reveals the lotus-like face with the cool-rayed moon eclipsed by the light of Aruṇa, my morning twilight, as it were, resorts to you.
When indeed will this uneven darkness come to rest? || 32 ||
Just as the morning, having revealed the lotus-face of the sky while the cool-rayed moon has been dimmed by the light of the dawn,

brings an end to the formidable darkness, when indeed will my formidable darkness come to an end upon beholding your eye on the forehead— which reveals the face of the sky while the cool-rayed moon has been dimmed by the light of the dawn?

Thus ends the twelfth hymn, titled "The Dispeller of Darkness," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*.
[The thirteenth hymn follows.]
Now, with these hymns of praise consisting of unhurried syllables, which serve as snares for the deer-like minds of the virtuous,
we reverently propitiate the Lord, the granter of fearlessness, who is intent on the vow of destroying his enemies.

Now, with these hymns of praise— whose syllables are slow and measured, and which serve as snares for the deer-like minds of the virtuous— we reverently propitiate the All-pervading Lord, who grants fearlessness and is intent upon the vow of destroying his enemies.

Place upon your heads the pair of lotus-feet of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), which are beautiful with the sprout-like nails and filaments inlaid by the radiance of the jewels from the crests of the gods' crowns.
What is the use of the desire for a crown?

Anvaya: O seekers of the divine, place upon your heads the pair of lotus-feet of the Destroyer of Cities—feet which are beautiful with the filaments of their sprout-like nails glistening with the radiance of the jewels from the crests of the gods. What is gained by the desire for a crown?
Let the well-spoken mantra "Hara Hara Śaṅkara Śaṅkara," which possesses unbroken rhythm, attain the status of a constant ornament upon your throats.
Why do you have such a desire for a string of stainless pearls? || 3 ||

(Oh connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, oh seekers of the divine! May this pure utterance—"Hara, Hara, Śaṅkara, Śaṅkara"—which possesses an unbroken continuity, attain for you the status of a constant ornament upon your throats through your desires for strings of spotless pearls. What is gained by that?
Wear jeweled earrings; abandon your longing for pure jasmine flowers. Constantly perform the sequence of praises for the deeds of Hara.
The grace of the ear-ornament of fresh lotus stalks.

O devotees! Cast off pride regarding your jeweled earrings; abandon your longing for spotless jasmine flowers. Constantly, through the sequence of hymns to the deeds of Hara, create the grace of fresh ear-ornaments.

Here, the wise man does not bow to one who is intent on bestowing joy upon the pride of mortals, but rather to that which destroys the torment of worldly existence, is capable of pacifying calamities, and is the cause of the destruction of misfortune.
Who else could be the remover of [suffering]? || 5 ||

In this world, what wise person does not bow down to Hara—the supreme one who has destroyed the afflictions of worldly existence, who is capable of pacifying calamities, who is the cause of the destruction of misfortune, and who is intent upon the performance of superhuman delights? Indeed, the meaning is that everyone does so.
He alone, trained in the eradication of evil, occupies the foremost position among the wise throughout the three worlds.
He who bears upon his head, long and steadfastly, that which is devoted to bowing before the crest-jewel of the crescent moon.

He alone whose head is devoted to bowing before the crest-jewel that is the crescent moon, and who has been disciplined by the destruction of his misdeeds, bears it for long and remains at the forefront of the wise even within the three worlds. Victorious is that descent of the power of the Lord of the Universe upon you, O poet, whereby the Goddess of Poetry— who grants unimpeded liberation— bestows a rasa born of incomparable wonder.
By which one attains the accomplishment of gold.

Anvaya: O Lord of the World! Victorious is that descent of Your power (śaktipāta), by which the Goddess of Speech bestows upon the poet that aesthetic flavor (rasa)—the effortless source of incomparable wonder—through which he attains every possible perfection (siddhi), such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Indeed, in this world, others may grant the perception of a master to common folk who offer them obeisance; yet they do not prevail in shattering the fear of death.
O Lord of Immortality, there is no one other than you.
On the contrary, others—those base people who offer salutations—may indeed produce the perception that you are their master (the thought, "This one is our lord").

But here in this entire world, O Amṛteśa! there is no one capable of shattering the fear of death except for You, the Lord. He by whom black soot has been killed and mercury brought under control has opened the door of Kubera.
And of Yama:

Who, while the great orb of the sun shines in the sky, is able to restore activity to this world—which has become blind through a continuous mass of most intense darkness—without [the aid of] one who possesses compassion? (9)

When this vast circle of light has taken its place in the sky, who— save for the Compassionate One— is able to render the world, blinded by the most oppressive mass of darkness, free from disease and with its activities unimpeded?
O you who have shattered all thirst, who manifest supreme joy, and who are mounted upon the great bull, direct [your gaze]!
A clear, boundless grace, white as the flowing waters of the celestial ocean, which transcends all existence.

The splendor of the stars does not prevail, nor does it bestow its gaze, lovely with clarity; for while the sun shall spread forth his light, there is no room for the majesty of the stars. (11) [Yugma] [Anvaya:
O you who have shattered and overcome thirst! O you who possess excellence! O you who manifest joy! O you who are mounted upon a great bull! O immeasurable one...
When the Lord bestows a clear vision, delightful through His grace, which is pure, white like a cloudless sky or the flow of the Indus, and capable of crossing over worldly existence—
then the splendor of the enemies (such as desire and the external foes) does not prevail; for when the Sun spreads its light,
the power arising from the greatness of the night cannot exist.

In this Kali age, who other than I is more skillful in the practice of discerning between what is appropriate and what is not? For he alone serves Bhava himself as the Supreme Śiva in order to conquer this world, which is otherwise the Supreme Śiva.

In this age of degeneration (*anvaya-kala*), who other than I is more adept at the practice of discerning between right and wrong? For it is he alone who, in order to conquer this supremely inauspicious existence (*bhava*, *saṃsāra*), serves the Supreme Auspicious One (*paramaśiva*). Indeed, fire alone is capable of extinguishing fire; snow alone can dispel increased snow; and water alone can digest water—what else can remove these?
For those who possess devotion, you are indeed existence itself. || 13 ||
The logical sequence is as follows: Alas! Only fire is capable of quenching a blazing fire; only snow causes intense cold to fade;
and water [heated by fire] cools water itself. What else? For those who possess devotion, only Bhava (Śambhu) removes Bhava (the cycle of worldly existence).

Better is the life of a beggar for a man who wears the deerskin and matted hair and holds a skull-cup in his hand, provided it is devoid of service to the lotus feet of the Destroyer of Smara; but not the status of a universal emperor.

The life of a mendicant for a man who wears the skins of deer and matted hair, and whose hand is devoted to holding a skull-bowl, is better than the sovereignty of an emperor that is devoid of service to the lotus-feet of the Destroyer of Smara. Better is a single frog in a desert land, its body tormented by the mass of rays from the hot-rayed sun, than [the aforementioned sovereignty].
A man is rendered distraught by the calamity of the waning of his fortune of devotion to you. || 15 ||

In the desert of worldly existence, a single frog, its body tormented by the mass of rays from the hot-rayed sun, is better; but, O Lord, a human being who is disfigured by the calamity of the exhaustion of the fortune of devotion to You is not better.

For the thick veil of the impurities of the Kali age brings a mirror-like intellect—already stripped of pride—to a state of defilement. Thus [ends the verse] beginning with "O Blue-throated One, white as the spreading rays of the cool-rayed moon."
We request you to grant us the essence. || 16 ||

O you whose pride has been destroyed! Because this [intellect] of mine leads even the mind—which resembles a mirror for the mass of the filth of the Kali age—to a state of defilement, O Śitikaṇṭha, we pray for your roar, which is brightened by the spreading rays of the cool-rayed moon. When this decree of yours comes to pass—that my mouth shall become the recipient of his grace, made resonant with hymns—then does he, who has swallowed the inhabitants of the seven worlds, truly prevail?
This is not at all my destiny. || 17 ||
O Lord! If this is your established conclusion— that a person whose mouth is made resonant with hymns of praise becomes an object of my grace—
then even this Kṛtānta (Yama), who has swallowed the worlds of the seven realms, has no power over me (meaning he is not capable of terrifying me).

Victorious is that supreme deity, Kṛśānu (Fire), who formerly appeared intent upon serving you— while your gaze was fixed upon the arrow and the trident for the destruction of Ravi’s son (Karṇa) and Andhaka.

O Lord! He who formerly appeared as fire (*kṛśānu*), having placed his trust in your eye, your arrow, and your trident—respectively used for the destruction of the cities of Ravi’s son (Tāraka), Andhaka, and Prahlāda—and who was intent upon your service, that supreme deity Kṛśānu is victorious. O Moon-crested One, he alone in the three worlds became the source of longing; your skin became the object of his utility, while the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) became yours. Thus, he was born with desire aroused, and he alone in the three worlds [remains so]. Your skin attained the status of an instrument.
By means of the sequence of his foot-steps. || 19 ||
O Moon-crested Lord! That black antelope alone has become truly enviable in the three worlds, whose skin has attained the status of an accessory by serving as a rug for Your feet.
Victorious indeed is the birth of that preeminent serpent, who, having cast off his jeweled bracelets, became a fit offering for You. May you be gracious to me.
The serpent’s coils attain the graceful movements of your limbs. || 20 ||

O Bhava! In this world, even the birth of that preeminent serpent is victorious, for his body—casting off its precious jeweled hood—attains the beauty of your own armlet. O Lord, that bull among serpents has obtained a fruitful birth within the three worlds, since your foot, smeared with the ashes of the corpse of Śiva, rests upon his head.
By him who was held [in check] by one bowed down in discipline. || 21 ||

O Lord Bhava! In the three worlds, he alone was the preeminent bull who attained a birth not in vain—he by whom your foot, smeared with the ashes of a corpse, was placed upon his head while bowed low in humility.
Whom does even the very birth of that Kuñjaraśekhara not inspire with longing in this world—he whose skin, O Bhava, is honored throughout the three worlds?
It bears the grand display of the expanse of existence. || 22 ||

Anvaya: O Bhava! Even the birth of that Kuñjaraśekhara, who is worshipped by the three worlds, in whom does it not generate longing (*spṛhā*) among [devoted] people in this world? He whose skin bears the very pomp of your garment; he who has conquered Time; he who is the Kalakūṭa poison; he who purified the innocent Ocean of Milk with his own birth; and who, having swiftly attained the state of being your morsel, manifests [his power]. Translation: O Bhava! Even the birth of that Kuñjaraśekhara, who is honored by the three worlds, in whom among the devotees does it not engender longing? He whose skin carries the splendor of your own garment; he who is victorious over Time; he who is the Kalakūṭa [poison]; he who sanctified the charming Ocean of Milk by his very birth; and who, having quickly become the object of your consumption, displays [his majesty].
He whose throat-pedestal is dark-blue. || 23 ||

Anvaya: O Conqueror of Time! O Blue-throated One! Victorious is that Kālakūṭa poison, which, having purified the charming Ocean of Milk with its own birth, reached the range of your mouth with speed and now rests upon the terrace of your throat.
Your face possesses the beautiful luster of the full autumnal moon, and your throat resembles the cloudless sky; thus, both are auspicious.
I bow to the Lord, who mocks both the celestial river Gaṅgā and the Yamunā by being non-different from them.

I worship that auspicious pair which imitates the Gaṅgā and Yamunā—[the Lord’s] face, which possesses the beauty of the full autumn moon, and His neck, which resembles the cloudless sky; both are auspicious and indivisible from the All-pervading One.

Likewise, by the grace of the Lord, this auspicious pair is like His very body: the water of the Gaṅgā, captivating as the snow-white moon, and the water of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), lovely as the blue water-lily.
I take refuge in the excellent Harihara. || 25 ||

When shall I, by the grace of my Lord, attain that auspicious and excellent dual form— like the body of Harihara— which, on one side, possesses the water of the Gaṅgā that steals the frost of its lineage and the water of the Kālindī that rivals the beauty of the blue lotus;
and on the other, is captivating and formidable, possessing a crooked voice and bearing the coils of dark, lustrous, and soiled serpents, just as I am when you suddenly turn your face away from me?
His power broken by the great Kali age. || 26 ||

O Śiva! Just as I am now—having swallowed the fatigue of unevenness, bearing a form that is the constant enemy of the stars, and possessing a crooked throat like the moon—you were when you turned your face away;
may I likewise become such as you when you are facing me.
(Yugma) *Anvaya*: O Śiva! When you have just now turned your face away, just as I am like you—one who has assumed a crooked throat and is darkened—[may I become so when you are facing me].

May I, whose union with the coils of the serpent Śeṣa is stained by impurities, and whose power has been shattered by the Great Kali age, likewise come to possess, while standing before You, a crown of lordly serpents, bearing a form that eternally destroys the enemies of the stars (or the foes of the Tāraka demon), and having swallowed the distress of adversity—just as You do; and may I, O Conqueror, at some time become the Lord of the Twice-born (Brahmā).
Victory! Victory! O Giver of Victory, release Your speech, which is sweet like honey and bold in delighting the people. O Madhya-Bhava (the Destroyer of Madana), remove, remove my sins this day!
May you be one whose appearance is both terrifying and not terrifying.

Anvaya: O Jayada! You who are skilled in delighting people, release sweet speech; O Hara! Cast away my intoxicating sin today; O Bhava! Be one whose appearance is both terrifying and fearless. You, who are eternally consecrated for the grace of the three worlds, are manifesting this expansion of your own power—a thing never seen before anywhere, O Blessed One! Translation: O Victorious One! Release words that are sweet and bold in pleasing the people. O Hara! Cast away my intoxicating evil today. O Bhava! Be one whose appearance is both formidable and free from fear. You, who are perpetually initiated for the sake of blessing the three worlds, are manifesting this display of your own power, which has never been seen before anywhere, O Blessed One!
That you display such arrogance toward me while I am so distressed. || 29 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! You, who are eternally initiated in the grace of the three worlds, that you display such unprecedented arrogance (the disregard of one who has sought refuge) toward me, who am thus distressed—that indeed is the manifestation of my own past misdeeds. While I stand before you, prostrate and helpless, you violently employ your mace against me; why then do you show such compassion, moist with the nectar of mercy, toward your other attendants?
You cast upon us a gaze that seems as if it were full of malice. || 30 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! While the distressed [Gada] bows before You, and while I, Your servant, bow down forcefully while bearing the application of the mace as if I were an offender—why do You not grant me that look moist with the nectar of compassion?
[Your] eye, which is like a necklace of great serpents whose hoods are clearly wide-open, expanded, blazing, and flaming.
Quickly abandon this mine of success, which brings about the destruction of powerful passion, pride, time, and desire. || 31 ||
O you who wear the king of serpents as a necklace! (To the wretched person: Cast off that eye which is like the fire blazing with clearly manifest and formidable flames;
which destroys the pride of the powerful and the desires of Death; which is the source of all accomplishments; and which is unsurpassed.
It possesses neither the form of the moon nor of the god of love, nor the intense wisdom of Bṛhaspati, nor the eloquence appropriate for him, nor the redness of the dawn or the speed of the wind.
For one who desires victory, there is no splendor in merely imitating or even in stealing [the enemy's] brilliance.

Neither the moon nor the god of love can emulate the form of this conqueror of lineages who delights Hari; neither the two gods of speech (Bṛhaspati and Kavi) can emulate his intense intellectual fitness; likewise, neither Aruṇa nor the Wind-god can emulate the battle-skill and splendor of this devotee of Śiva.
His beauty, smiling with the lovely white chowries fanning out like white lotuses blooming under the rays of the sun—O Śrī, do not leave his abode for even a moment!
I bow to that power (or devotion) of yours, which belongs to those who have performed meritorious deeds. || 33 ||

O Bhava! I bow to that power of yours, which is the abode of those who have performed meritorious deeds and which the Goddess Śrī—smiling beautifully with chowries as white as blooming white lotuses under the rays of the sun—never leaves even for a moment;

for when you, the Giver of Fearlessness, reside within, our minds, though possessed of all majesty, do not become free from sorrow, but instantly become dejected in the mire of their own pure and stainless actions.
From what has this despondency arisen? || 34 ||

O Giver of Fearlessness! O Despair! Indeed, while you were dwelling within me, our mind was free from sorrow; yet that very same mind of ours, having suddenly entered the mire of impure actions, has become despondent—by what means this occurred, I do not know. Make my mind pure through right conduct and humility, with its rising internal fire of anger extinguished, and restrained by self-restraint and observances.
Averse to playful women full of coquetry. || 35 ||

O All-pervading Lord! Make my mind pure through discipline and humility; make it free from the fault of anger that blazes like a rising fire within; make it restrained by the observances of *yama* and *niyama*; and make it detached from charming, playful women. (1) Compassion, forgiveness, truthfulness, non-violence, mercy, lack of worldly desire, meditation, serenity, sweetness, and straightforwardness—these are the ten *yamas*.
(2) Purity, sacrifice, austerity, charity, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, observance of vows, fasting, silence, and bathing—these are the ten rules of conduct (*niyamas*).

His mind was shaken by the sweet words of his young bride, who was languid with the fresh joy of their union; he, whose form was polished like refined gold, possessed a most wonderful consciousness that surpassed all measure in its devotion to bowing before you. (36)

O All-pervading Lord!
