O You whose creative artistry is beyond measure—whosoever is devoted to Your prostration becomes one whose mental anxieties are shaken off by the sweet words of his wife, who is languid with the passion of the moment; whose body is polished as if by every kind of silver; and who, having internally resolved upon the proper time for rising to attain joy and to utterly destroy even the slightest impurity, becomes free from stain.
This is the support, the very foundation of all joys [and virtues], consisting of the praise of Mahāmahamahā-Īśvara. || 37 ||

Ah! Having internally (within my own mind) resolved upon the appropriate time for my rise, and being fully capable of dispelling no small impurity, I have taken refuge in this festival consisting of the praise of the Lord—the very source of all joys—in order to attain delight. O you who are praised by the virtuous, the wise, and the foremost among the gods led by Hari, may you, the enemy of the foe that is worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), spread what is beneficial for you.
Through grace, even one who takes the lives of enemies becomes a benefactor to those who possess merit. || 38 ||

O Bhava! By your grace, even an enemy who takes away the lives of the meritorious brings about their welfare—such is the case for you, the foe of the enemy that is worldly existence, who are praised by the virtuous gods headed by Indra and Hari. O Lord, even from Janārdana Viṣṇu, who is renowned as Vaikuṇṭha, [welfare comes] if he is more enraged than you.
Instantly, there occurred the attainment of the Sudarśana [vision]. || 39 ||

(Verse 40, Yugma) O Lord! Even for Viṣṇu—who is Janārdana, who is renowned as Vaikuṇṭha, and who possesses excessive wrath—how is it that [this] was not done by You, even though You are virtuous? Or rather, since You are the all-pervading Lord of the Universe, what more can be said of You? *Anvaya:* O Nātha! [This was not done] even by Viṣṇu, who is Janārdana, who is celebrated as Vaikuṇṭha, and who is exceedingly full of rage.

The attainment of the Sudarśana [discus] occurred for you instantaneously from [your] very presence. Then, why does that same attainment of the Sudarśana not occur for me even now—though my intellect is not opposed to all people, though I am as sharp [as a blade] yet [unsharpened by] being blunted, and though I have conquered anger?
Or rather, since you are the Lord of the World and the All-pervading One, what can be said by me to you?

My mind does not find such delight in heaven—where flowers are easily obtained and where the fragrance of blossoms is beautiful—as it finds in Your stories; nor does it find such firm resolve in nectar-sweet flowers as it finds in Your narratives, which moisten the heart with ambrosia.
Anvaya: O Lord! The mind of a devotee does not find such attachment even to heaven (*nāka*), which is easily accessible to the gods (*sumanas*);

nor does it find such attachment to the fragrance that is beautiful to the gods (*sumanas*). Nor does it find such attachment even among the gods (*sumanas*) as it finds in Your stories, which are moist with nectar (*sudhārdra*).

Victorious is the Goddess Śrī, by whose glance the accomplishment of all desired objects comes into the hands [of those favored]. How indeed can that God be described, from whom she was born, and who gave her to the Ocean as a child? 42.

Victorious is that Goddess Śrī, by whose glance the attainment of all desired objects becomes as if held in the palm of one's hand; and how can that Lord be described, from whom she was born and who gave her to the child [Viṣṇu]? Nectar, obtained through the effort of churning the ocean with Mount Mandara, could not rival her; nor could the earth, though boundless. He is this very Śiva, the ever-new.
May it, which is the vessel for honoring the assembly of the wise, be for your welfare. || 43 ||

May this new Śivanava—named *Prabhuprasādana*—who is the worthy recipient of honor in the assemblies of the learned, and who is not rivaled by that ancient Śivanava (Śiva) who possesses boundless nectar obtained through the effort of the Mandara mountain, as well as the earth itself; may he be for your auspicious welfare.
Thus ends [the commentary] titled *Premamakaranda*, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmad Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, on the [work] of the Blessed One...
The thirteenth hymn, titled "Propitiation of the Lord," from the *Stutikusumāñjali* of Maheśvara.
The fourteenth hymn:
That lunar radiance, which dispels affliction and is enchanting, by which the Lord destroys the inner darkness with His hand that touches His crest-ornament.
May there be for you the crushing of the pride of desire. || 1 ||

May that lunar radiance— the crest-jewel upon the eye of Anvaya (Śiva), which destroys the internal darkness called ignorance within the devotee— be a cloudless, desire-granting light for you, charming and dispelling all affliction. To one whose majesty consists of speech profound with overflowing devotion, the world of existence appears like parched grass.
He is seized by the grasping of the dwelling-place of Vāsava. || 2 ||

Anvaya: O Bhava! For that fortunate person who possesses the majesty of speech profound and overflowing with devotion toward Your forms, the grasping for the acquisition of Indra’s throne appears like withered grass.
A body marked by quivering horripilation, eyes with lids filled with tears, and a faltering voice uttering "Hara, Hara"—these arise [in him].
For those who are endowed with devotion to existence. || 3 ||
For those who possess devotion born of spiritual lineage, there arise a body marked by bristling horripilation, eyes with lids filled with tears, and faltering speech crying "Hara! Hara!
As one speaks with devotion in a choked voice—calling him "Blue-throated One," "Crested with the New Moon," "Three-eyed," "Three-faced"—the world becomes as insignificant as a blade of grass.
The entire surface of the earth was filled with gold.

O Blue-throated One! O Lord whose crest is the young moon! O Three-eyed One! O Three-faced One!—protect me! For one who speaks thus with devotion in a faltering voice, even the entire surface of the earth filled with gold becomes like a blade of grass. Where has that [wealth] gone now, which was employed at every step for the sake of consoling the heart of Yama, agitated by the fear of his frown?
Your nectar of compassion. || 5 ||

O Lord! Where has that nectar of Your compassion now gone toward me, who am rendered useless at every step—that nectar which served as a consolation for the heart overwhelmed by the fear of the frown of Death?
O Protector, the fire, the moon, and the sun residing in Your three eyes appear to me, who am afflicted by cold, heat, and darkness, as if they were merely painted in a picture.
They remain. || 6 ||
O Lord! To me, who am afflicted by cold, heat, and darkness, the fire, the moon, and the sun residing within Your three eyes appear as if they were merely painted in a picture.
With a voice as deep as the Ocean of Milk when Mount Mandara was slowly and forcefully whirled in agitation, You ought to protect me.
I am being swiftly assailed by the messengers of Death, who bring no happiness.

O Lord, you ought to swiftly protect me, who am being pursued by the messengers of Death accompanied by their followers, with a voice as deep as the ocean of milk churned by the Mandara mountain during its frantic and whirling dance.
O Master, who else but you could venture to release my neck, which is encircled by a serpent whose coils quiver in the grasp of the servants of Time, were it not for your "huṃ" cry?

O Lord! Who else but Your own roar (*huṃkāra*) would dare to liberate that person whose neck is encircled by the serpent of worldly existence flashing from the hands of the servants of Time? (The meaning is: no one at all.

That humiliation which kings suffer at their own gates—caused by the gatekeepers of fearsome appearance with their fierce knitted brows, who have been humbled by the roar of [Your] command—is endured [only because of You].
By the thirst for even a small portion of wealth.

O Moon-crested Lord! On the threshold of your abode, he makes some person—eager for your worship and holding a flower-vessel and a leaf-cup in his hands—tremble before those [guards] who have been humiliated by the "huṃ" roars of the doorkeepers, whose appearance is terrifying due to their fiercely knitted brows.
(A yugma. [Anvaya:
O Moon-crested Lord! By those people who have been rendered powerless by the "huṃ" roars of the doorkeepers, whose looks are fearsome due to their intensely knitted brows... [of kings].

That humiliation which is endured at the door out of a craving for even a tiny fragment of wealth—that very humiliation, O Lord, afflicts some poor man who, eager to worship you, holds a flower-vessel and a leaf-cup in his hands upon the threshold of your temple.
O God, this is merely a mockery without the service of your feet; for it is as unstable as a drop of water trickling from a lotus leaf.
The manifestations. || 11 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! That prosperity of men which is as fleeting as drops of water trickling from the petals of a lotus is, without the service of Your feet, merely a mockery. But that wealth which consists of dwelling on the banks of the celestial river together with the fawns of the deer of friendship, and regarding kings like blades of grass—this alone is true prosperity.
May you exist [for me] through your grace. || 12 ||

This wonderful glory—friendship with the fawns on the banks of the river Nirjarā, and the viewing of mountains as if they were blades of grass—O Bhava, comes about through your grace! O Lord Maheśvara, if I, being utterly helpless, have approached you for refuge, this is my own fault; for a fish, even when thirsty, seeks the waters of the Gaṅgā.
By their own evil deeds. || 13 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! If, having approached You, Maheśvara, as my refuge, I were to depart turned away indeed without refuge, that fault would belong to me alone;
for a fish in the waters of the Ganges becomes thirsty by its own misdeeds.

[O King,] describe some indescribable state of the devotee who utters "Śiva, Śiva"—the name of Śambhu—which serves as a touchstone for the gold of long-enduring love, while his voice rises in a faltering stammer.
He instructs me. || 14 ||

With voices faltering with emotion, as they praise the name of Śambhu—“Śiva, Śiva!”—which serves as a touchstone for the gold of their long-enduring love, they describe an indescribable state. Upon your exceedingly white head shines the light of the moon, which wards off the affliction of worldly existence; therefore, grant to us embodied beings the removal of our distress through prostration before you.
Taking the hand [in marriage]. || 15 ||

O Lord of the lineage! Upon your head, which is exceedingly white with the light of the moon, water that removes the afflictions of worldly existence shines resplendently; for that reason, we bow to you to extinguish our forest fire of suffering.
Therefore, grant us the support of your hand to living beings.

O Enemy of Andhaka! Grant me—a fool, a vessel of delusion and calamity, blind with grief, and burdened by sins—the state that destroys the darkness [of ignorance], the Tāraka [the Savior] who brings an end to the gloom of Tamisra.
Deliver [us]! || 16 ||

O enemy of Andhaka! O Tārā, the ender of darkness! Deliver me—who am deluded, burdened by calamity, a vessel of sorrows, blinded, crushed by enemies, and fallen into a futile flood of sins—across the ocean of existence.
He whom you yourself behold with eyes that destroy Rākṣasas through sounds as terrifying as their own nature, he shines upon the earth as the slayer of Māra; may he be yours.
The god, radiant with the weight of the sun's rays. || 17 ||

O destroyer of Rākṣasas by your natural and terrifying roars! O Imperishable One! O slayer of Māra! That very deity whom you yourself behold shines upon the earth, radiant with an abundance of solar splendor.

Those people by whom your hymn was composed with devotion through worship performed with showers of arrows—they alone, for that reason, possess true existence. As for others, they are merely non-existent.
The hosts [of attendants], whose masses of fame are praised by bards. || 18 ||

O All-pervading Lord! Those people who, with devotion, have performed hymns of praise to You through offerings of arrows and darts—by that alone do they become Your true Gaṇas, whose hosts of fame are extolled by bards and who follow in Your wake.
Gods, sages, and Indra, who know the difficult paths of coming and going, worship You every single day.
With hymns, [I praise] those who sit in the assembly of the sky-dwellers, those who sit in the assembly. || 19 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! The gods dwelling in heaven—those who have mastered the difficult paths of coming and going, and who are the very essence of the nectar of the abode of the immortals—constantly worship you day after day with their hymns.
Neither the embrace of Anēkapā (the Queen) nor the embrace of my beloved consort brings me such joy as when that omnipresent Kapālin (Śiva), the god of speech, is worshipped by her with her words.
The protector of the world of servants. || 20 ||

The goddess of speech, who is worshipped by that all-pervading Lord Kapālin— the guardian of his lineage and his retinue— brings me such joy as does not my beloved, whose arms embrace many protectors. Having propitiated you, who possess supreme majesty, having brought about the defeat of my enemies, and having conquered worldly existence itself, I shall abandon it.
Having attained the state of Śambhu, they are liberated and do not undergo rebirth.

The devotees of the lineage, having propitiated you, Bhava, who possess supreme majesty, bring about the defeat of their enemies; and having conquered worldly existence (*bhava*) and abandoned rebirth (*punarbhava*), they attain the state of Śambhu and become liberated.
I do not consider them to be of low birth, nor do I praise any other man as being truly noble. [I praise] none other than you, who gladden both gods and demons, and whose nature is ever-new.
I am deceived, even as I constantly compose new [works].
O Blessed One! I do not take into account the thinning of my lineage, nor do I fail to bow before any kinsman who is human.

Creating ever-new [works] that delight both gods and demons, I have not been deceived by Fate. Having recognized wealth—which has Arjuna as its presiding deity, which accomplishes all goals, which was worshipped by Arjuna, which removes mental anguish, and which purifies one from calamities—[I am content].
The fortunate ones praise the Lord, who increases prosperity. || 23 ||

Having recognized that wealth which purifies the calamities of misfortune— namely, the hymn of praise to Śiva— the fortunate ones beg from the All-conquering One (Dhanañjaya), who is the means for accomplishing all goals, who was propitiated by Dhanañjaya (Arjuna), who destroys mental anguish, and who increases prosperity; just as, at the onset of the rainy season, peacocks with their plumage spread wide in intense joy utter the sound of clouds.
May the Goddess of Speech likewise shower nectar upon us, she who bears a clearly bound mass of matted hair adorned with peacock feathers. 24.

Just as the sound of clouds in the rainy season causes the peacock—whose plumage is disarrayed by intense joy—to rain down nectar, so too may the speech of the one who wears a clearly bound mass of matted locks, though it be but a single artful word (*kalā*), rain nectar upon us. Only he possesses a truly blameless human birth whom you, O Bhava, regard as faultless; for even while still unarisen, Death abandons such a person as if they were his equal.
Nor does she bring him joy equal to that of Ramā. || 25 ||

Anvaya: O Bhava! That very human birth which you behold while consuming it becomes irreproachable; for him, there is the birthless, incomparable, and bliss-bestowing Ramā (the Goddess of Liberation), who never abandons him.

Beyond this, what else is there in the world that is devoid of flavor, such that even though it has been spoken and uttered repeatedly, it must be chewed over again and again for thousands of times, even after a long duration?
The praise of Śiva flows with ever-new nectar.

What could be more tasteless than the words uttered by someone in this world, even though they have been spoken repeatedly and again? (Nothing at all; however,) the hymn of praise to Śiva, though chewed for thousands of times over a long duration, flows with ever-new flavor!
O Conqueror of Death, victory! Lead the God of Love—who devours the world—to the state of ashes with the splendor of the intense radiance of Your eyes.

We praise you, whose wondrous deeds are expert in providing protection to those in fear, and who act with such intensity that the wives of noble families—whether destined for fortune or misfortune—raise their voices in lamentation. || 27 ||
O you who shine like the worthy! (O my servant! O Conqueror of Death! (By my grace,) conquer death, the devourer of the world;

by the splendor of the intense radiance of your eyes, surely reduce Kāma to the state of ashes. O you who are expert in providing protection from fear! We praise you, O Conqueror of Death, as you perform such wondrous deeds in many ways, while the wives of agitated families cry out in longing.

May that Light, the cause of all causes, grant me my desired welfare—that Light which, in its aspect as Brahmā, effects the creation and natural manifestation of the universe; which, in its aspect as Viṣṇu, is intent upon the activity of driving away Rāvaṇa; and which, in its aspect as Śiva, brings about the dissolution at the end of an aeon; which is self-luminous and appropriately radiant in the expansion of the origin, maintenance, and absorption of existence; and which is ever-shining with splendor. (Note: The *anvaya*—the grammatical connection—is as follows: *yat* [that] *dhāma* [Light], being *brahmarūpeṇa* [in the form of Brahmā], is *sarganisarganirmitikaram* [the maker of the creation and natural manifestation]; *yat* [which], being *viṣṇurūpeṇa* [in the form of Viṣṇu], is *rāvaṇadrāvaṇavyāpārāvasarāvasaktam* [intent upon the occasion of the activity of driving away Rāvaṇa]; and *yat* [which], being *saṃvartasaṃvartakam* [the bringer of the dissolution at the end of an aeon], is *svābhāsam* [self-luminous] and *bhavasaṃbhavasthitilayasphārocitam* [appropriately radiant in the expansion of the origin, maintenance, and absorption of existence], and is *rocitam* [ever-shining] *bhāsā* [with splendor]).

May that Effulgence—the cause of all causes, which, intent upon the task of routing Rāvaṇa, manifests as Rudra in the form of the Saṃvarta-Saṃvartaka fire; which is self-luminous and appropriate for the expansion of the arising, abiding, and dissolution of worldly existence; and which is graced by its own light—bestow upon me what is beneficial.
Thus ends [the work] composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary named *Premamakaranda*, concerning the Blessed One...

The fourteenth hymn, named "The Beneficial" (*Hita*), from the *Stutikusumāñjali* of Maheśvara. Now follows the fifteenth hymn, which [approaches] the Goddess as if through asceticism, Sarasvatī as if through yoga, the desired Śrī as if through a friend, and the assembly as if through excellence.

Like inspiration through the work of poetry, like fame that reaches those who seek it through wealth, like tranquility in the mind through self-restraint, or like a happy rebirth in the next world through meritorious deeds. || 2 ||

My mind proceeds to offer even this slight hymn of praise in order to worship the Goddess who bears the mark of the moon— the wish-fulfilling creeper that grants all desires, the ender of calamities, and the embodiment of compassion— just as one might approach Sarasvatī with diligent application to worship her through ascetic penance.

(Tilaka) **Anvaya:** *sakalārthārpaṇakalpavallarīm vipadantakarīm devatām tapasā upāsitum iva abhiyogena sarasvatīm upāsitum...* **Translation:** ...to worship, with diligent application, Sarasvatī— as if to worship through austerity the Goddess who is the wish-fulfilling creeper for the granting of all goals and the destroyer of misfortune...

As if to attend upon Fortune through a friend, as if to attend upon the assembly through excellence of character, as if to attend upon creative intuition through the work of poetry, as if to attend upon fame through wealth bestowed upon the needy, as if to attend upon tranquility in the mind through self-restraint, and as if to attend upon a happy rebirth in the hereafter through merit— now, by this mere fragment of praise, [I worship] the wish-fulfilling creeper that grants all desires and puts an end to calamity, belonging to the One marked by the deer’s horn.
My mind inclines toward serving compassion—
compassion that is blossoming through your stainless qualities, O Lord, and which my sweet-speaking speech attends, just as a dark lotus bed attends the sun. 4.

Anvaya: O Lord! Just as a sweet-sounding female bee resorts to a blossoming lotus adorned with stainless qualities, so too does this sweet-sounding speech of mine resort to Your compassion, which is blossoming and adorned with stainless qualities.
Having perceived Your darkened state [of ignorance], my own state of being blinded by darkness places its foot upon me; having beheld Your uneven gaze, my own [vision] becomes distressed.
Vision attains unevenness.

Anvaya: O Lord! Perceiving Your state of being blinded by darkness (*andhakāritā*), blindness (the nature of ignorance) takes hold of me; beholding Your fierce gaze (*viṣamāṃ dṛśam*), my own vision attains fierceness (*viṣamatvam*).

Seeing Your subjugation of the bull (*vṛṣādharīkṛtiṃ vīkṣya*), my own subjugation of virtue (*vṛṣādharīkṛtiḥ*) occurs; beholding Your possession of a curved face (*dhṛtavakrakalatvam īkṣya*), crookedness spreads within me as well.
My crookedness alone [is my ornament]. || 6 ||

O All-pervading Lord! Seeing Your state of being surpassed by the bull (vṛṣādharīkṛti), my own state of being surpassed by the bull (vṛṣādharīkṛti) also becomes possible; seeing Your state of possessing a curved face (vakrakalatva), my own state of possessing a curved face (vakrakalatva) alone spreads forth.

And seeing Your state of having desires shattered (bhagnakāmatā), this state of mine of having desires shattered has arisen. Having observed Your compassion (karuṇā) as well, how could my song not be compassionate (karuṇā)?
May it proceed. || 7 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! Having observed Your state of frustrated desire, this frustration has arisen in me; and having observed Your compassion, why should compassion not arise in my speech as well?

You, by whom the entire world—including gods, demons, and humans—is dependent, are indeed the Supreme Lord; yet that very compassion, by which even the station of sovereignty was surrendered, is truly victorious.
Belonging to you. || 8 ||
The world, including its gods, demons, and humans, is dependent upon you; yet you, O Lord, have been placed at her disposal by her compassion—victorious is this compassion of yours!
O Blessed One, your compassion surpasses even Umā, the mistress of your life; for while only half of you was taken by Umā, you have been taken in your entirety by her.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Your compassion—which effects the upliftment of the three worlds in a mere twinkling of an eye—surpasses even Umā, the mistress of your life; for while Umā (Aparṇā), though afflicted by such extraordinary and peerless penance, took only half of your body (in the form of Ardhanārīśvara), by this compassion you have been taken entirely (you have been made to possess your entire body).
This is the meaning:

Your compassion is praised, by which even you, who have conquered desire, have been brought under control. Furthermore, this is another [wonder]: that she has brought even the goddess Ambikā herself into subjection. [The connection is:
That compassion of yours is praised by us, by which even you, though having conquered desire, have been subdued. And this is another [marvel].
That this [compassion of yours] even brought the Goddess Ambikā under your command— O Lord,
that greatness of your compassion is such that it was sustained by the world-born water, by the earth, by the water, by the white-shining sky, by the wind, and by the sun whose nature is heat. 11.

Anvaya: O Lord! That greatness by which the universe was sustained—by You who bear the eight forms for the protection of the world; by the water-born [fire], according to the Vedic revelation that "fire was born from the waters"; by the earth, by the water, by the moon of white luster, by the sky, by the wind, by the sun, and by Yourself [standing distinct from both cause and effect in the form of the sacrificer]—that greatness belongs solely to Your compassion.
O Lord, I suddenly take refuge in Your purifying river of compassion, whose flow is unimpeded, which is serene, and which has instantly dispelled the mass of my afflictions. 12.

O Lord! I take refuge in Your purifying river of compassion, whose flow is unimpeded, which is gracious, and which has suddenly cast away the multitude of afflictions. O Protector, why does this youthful compassion, long propitiated by my heart agitated with the hope for love, not become firmly established within Your heart?
The Foot. || 13 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! How is it that compassion, which has long been propitiated by affection with a heart agitated by the hope of love, does not take a firm root in Your heart? (Indeed, it surely does.
Just as serpents, though causing distress, lead one to the sandalwood tree, so do my enemies—pride, intoxication, and the rest—though they bring me to a state of ruin, lead me toward You.
Those who cut through steadfastness. || 14 ||

Like serpents that destroy stability and emit poison while withering a sandalwood tree, my enemies— unstable foes headed by intoxication and pride who shatter my steadfastness and vomit forth the venom of their malice— are wasting me away and bringing me to a state of utter ruin.

I go for refuge to the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, who possesses the splendor of Acyuta and whose body—reddened by compassion—is as if it were high and full of partiality toward His younger brother. 15.

I take refuge in the compassion of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, which is partial toward His devotees, which bears the splendor of Acyuta, and which is like the body of Garuḍa— the younger brother of Aruṇa— which is partial toward its wings and bears the beauty of Acyuta. For those who have become harsh-minded and full of wrath strike with bodies that possess throbbing, beautiful, reddish eyes and are covered in profuse drops of perspiration.
Women. || 16 ||
O Blessed One, this is the power of the two— Love and Anger— who have firmly established their roots, possess a thousand branches, and whose unbearable fall causes such agony.

Surely it is your compassion alone that is capable of uprooting these two, just as the powerful childhood play of the destroyer of Naraka [Kṛṣṇa] destroyed the twin *arjuna* trees. (Tilaka) [The verse continues:
That woman, with her beautiful eyes flashing red, with drops of profuse perspiration, and with a body that had become harsh in its intent and full of wrath—whatever [she did]...

"O Blessed One! These are surely the manifestations of the two enemies, Lust and Anger—whose roots are firmly established, whose branches extend a thousandfold, and whose destructive falls are unbearable. Yet, for these two who cause the end of hell, such intense compassion as that of the twin *yama* and *arjuna* trees is certainly capable of cutting them at their very root."

It was not a treasure trove filled with the gain of hidden wealth, nor was it the diversion arising from musk; it was neither the moonlight of the autumnal moon, nor the sweet warbling from the throat of the cuckoo. (19)
The speech of a child is not improper; nor is the playful grace of an embrace with a deer-eyed woman. The eloquence of a lordly poet is not sweet; nor is the expansion of imperial sovereignty. 20.

Neither curiosity for the drinking of elixirs (*rasāyana*), nor the desire to dwell upon the throne of Śakra, would be capable of fulfilling even a sixteenth part of your compassion; O Hara, [take this away]. (Tilaka) Anvaya: O Hara! A ritual (*vidhi*) performed with the acquisition of a treasure would not be capable of fulfilling even a sixteenth part of your compassion.
The delight arising from musk would not be able to equal even a sixteenth part of your compassion;
the moonlight of the autumnal moon would not be able to equal a fraction of it; the warbling of the cuckoo’s throat would not be able to equal it;

the incoherent speech of a child would not be able to equal it; the graceful charm of an embrace with a deer-eyed woman would not be able to equal it; and the sweet eloquence of the lords of poets would not be able to equal it.

The splendor of imperial sovereignty cannot equal even a fraction of your patience; the excellence of drinking elixirs of immortality cannot equal even a fraction of your forbearance; and even the desire to dwell upon Indra’s throne cannot equal even a sixteenth part of filling your compassion.

Neither the fragrant [incense] nor even the southern breeze is an object of my longing; rather, it is the compassion that bestows the desired fragrance of sugarcane to the world that is truly fragrant for me.
Just as it is for you. || 22 ||

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Just as Your compassion is the object of my longing, so too the fragrant spring (*surabhi*), the southern breeze, or even the wish-granting cow (*surabhi*) bestowed by Surabhi—none of these become the object of my longing.
When tears born of sorrow arise, they shine forth as consisting of beautiful joy; that horripilation which spreads through fear proceeds as a source of wonder. (23)

O Moon-crested Lord! That closing of the eyes which arises from the experience of ultimate reality, born of exhaustion—that belongs to the wise who have sought refuge in Your compassion. (A yugma) *Anvaya:* O Moon-crested Lord! That tear born of grief which wells up—that belongs to the wise who have sought refuge in Your compassion.
That thrill which spreads through one out of fear [of birth and death] shines forth as consisting of delightful bliss; that horripilation which manifests is born of wonder and proceeds from it.
That closing of the eyes born of exhaustion arises from the experience of the ultimate reality.
May the speech of Umāpati flow toward me with ease, even though I am gripped by a skeleton of hell; may compassion extend toward you, O Lord of Umā, whose body is marked by the Kali age.

Anvaya: O Lord of Umā! May my speech expand like a virtuous woman (*sādhvī*) toward you, who have seized me by time, whose body is marked by the Kali age, and who am resorting to hell. (Upon seeing me) may your compassion also expand toward him who has seized the skeleton of hell and whose body is marked by the Kali age.

O Blessed One, as long as this body—flickering like the waves of the side-glances of women intoxicated by the wine of passion, and swiftly brought low by old age—does not yet fall into calamity; [so long should one practice virtue].
Mocking the crooked frown of her brows, which was stirred by the servants of the enraged God of Death, the serpent— resembling a mass of thick collyrium—
ascended her neck.
The sensation that arises in hell, fashioned by the ripening of evil deeds, has been described by those who follow the path of tranquility as being like harsh words that pierce the vital organs.
(28) If this river of compassion does not penetrate your heart, alas, what other refuge can there be for those seeking protection amidst the mass of unbearable torments? (29) (Kalāpa)
O Blessed One! As long as this body of mine—flickering like the waves of the side-glances of women intoxicated by the madness of wine—is not swiftly brought to ruin by old age;

as long as the serpent, resembling a mass of thick collyrium and mimicking the crooked frown sent by the servants of the enraged God of Death, does not seize my neck; and as long as the harsh agony produced by the ripening of evil deeds, described by the messengers of Yama in hell, does not arrive.

O Compassionate One! If this river of Your compassion does not plunge into Your heart before these words that pierce the vital organs arise, then alas, what other refuge can there be for those seeking shelter amidst the unbearable mass of their sufferings? (The meaning is: none at all.
For a woman who brings about service to Śiva bestows auspiciousness upon self-restrained men in a way that no other woman, even when united with one of equal status, can bring such joy.
The sinless intellect, tasting [the truth] again and again. || 30 ||

Just as the sinless mind of those who have restrained themselves—which tastes its own sweetness, bestows auspiciousness, and effects service to Śiva—leads to joy, so too does a woman of equal status in union not [lead to such joy].
Might a single great sage, with eyebrows slightly arched, lead the people of Janaka’s city to the city of Indra? Or might he lead them to the realm of darkness?
O Indra among men, if there were not to be compassion from you, which arises from merit, then even the excellence of Padma would not be considered auspicious.

Anvaya: O Bhava! If your compassion, which results in such blessed fortune, were not present, then how could a single great sage (Viśvāmitra), with his eyebrows slightly arched, have sent Janaṅgamajana (Triśaṅku, who had become a Cāṇḍāla due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha) to the city of Purandara? Likewise, how could another great sage (Gautama) have sent Indra to a state lacking prosperity—a dark state (in the form of having a thousand female organs)? The meaning is: how could he have sent him there? How indeed would it have been possible?

Victorious is the imperishable seed of compassion belonging to the Moon-crested Lord: it sprouts in the mind when touched by the suffering of afflicted people, then buds in his auspicious gaze, blooms in an instant in his speech, and bears fruit in his action. 32.

Victorious is the imperishable seed of compassion belonging to the Moon-crested Lord: it sprouts in his moistened mind through contact with the suffering of afflicted people; it buds in his auspicious gaze; it blossoms in an instant in his speech; and it bears fruit in his action—namely, the work of protection.
[He who was] with all his physical excellence dissolving away due to fierce diseases, whose movements were lost, whose limbs were cast about on a bed of filth, and whose every remedy had failed;

For as long as he lives, the fool must perform both beneficial and harmful actions; remembering them again and again, his heart is shattered, and he becomes distressed and flighty, fleeing in all directions. || 33 ||
Afflicted by other severe diseases, with all his physical excellence dissipated and his faculties lost, his limbs cast upon an impure bed,

with every remedy failed and bewildered as to what ought to be done, he— his heart shattered by repeatedly remembering the harmful deeds committed throughout his life— is distressed, terrified, and fleeing in fear, wondering, "In which direction shall I go?"

Having somehow attained this [existence]—which is meager (or "even so," according to another reading)—by means of actions that are turbid and harsh due to the intensity of thirst, and which rob one of happiness after having severely afflicted the body; and seeing before him his entire fortune being plundered by those who seize his inheritance, he loses all his senses and is consumed within by grief. (34)

Having excessively tormented his body with actions that were turbid, harsh, and destructive to happiness due to the intense craving for ancestral lineage, he beholds all that wealth— which was somehow acquired— with its inheritance-seizers plundering it first; thus, with all his faculties failing and burning within from grief, he remains.

He was gazed upon with eyes full of tears flowing incessantly from the excess of his grief by his virtuous wives looking on with trembling looks; and he was tormented by the most piteous lamentations of his sons, friends, natural ministers, kinsmen, and the host of servants, all crying out in deep distress. || 35 ||
Being gazed upon with eyes filled with incessantly flowing tears by his virtuous wives due to the excess of their grief for him,
and being tormented by the sons, friends, natural ministers, kinsmen, and circles of servants who were wailing most piteously with cries of lamentation—

When one is forcibly dragged from the interior of the house by cruel people who, though themselves healthy, are excessively suspicious of impurity—so that even his memory of the inner self is lost—and when he approaches death with his body swallowed by it, who indeed could be a protector at that time, other than the Goddess of Compassion? (36)

(Sandānitaka) At that time, when— dragged by force from the interior of the house for the sake of cremation by his relatives, who are cruel, indifferent to his natural state, and intensely suspicious of impurity— even though his memory has somewhat faded within— he encounters terror as his body is being swallowed by Death; at that moment...
At such a time, who indeed could be a protector without divine compassion? (The meaning is: none at all.
A fragment dwells upon a fragment of the body of the Daughter of the Mountain-King; the crescent moon resides in her crest-lock, and the Lord himself is the wielder of the broken axe (Khaṇḍaparaśu).
Nevertheless, the unbroken activity of the Lord toward one who has newly sought refuge triumphs through compassion in this world. (37)
In one half of the Lord’s body, a fragment of the Daughter of the Mountain King dwells; upon his crest, a fragment of the moon dwells;

and the Lord himself is Khaṇḍaparaśu (the one with the broken axe). Nevertheless, despite this state of being entirely fragmented, the unbroken activity of the Lord’s compassion toward a newly arrived seeker of refuge triumphs throughout the world.

Victory to you, O conqueror of all ailments! Victory to you, O embodiment of nectar! Victory to you, O bearer of the light of immortality! Victory to you, O slayer of Andhaka! Victory to you, O destroyer of Tripura! Victory to you, O annihilator of Death himself!

Victory to you, O supreme and yet immanent! Victory to you, O one devoted to compassion! Victory to you, O path of the virtuous for those who bow before you! Victory to you, O conqueror of Smara! Victory to you, O Great Lord! Victory, victory to you, O Lord of the three worlds! 38.
O Conqueror of Illness! Victory to You! O Essence of Nectar! Victory to You! O You who hold the light of immortality! Victory to You! O Destroyer of Death!

Victory to You! O Destroyer of Cities! Victory to You! O You who have withdrawn the God of Death! Victory to You! O Supreme and yet Immanent! Victory to You! O You devoted to Compassion! Victory to You! O You who grant the true goal to those who bow before You! Victory to You! O Conqueror of Smara! Victory to You! O Great Lord! Victory to You! O Lord of the Three Worlds! Victory to You!
Victory, victory!
Unrestrained by considerations of what is appropriate or inappropriate, causeless and unsolicited, the effort of the ocean is truly for the sake of the welfare of beings;
it is neither the sun, capable of quelling the heat of thirst, nor the cloud, which puts an end to the cold of darkness—it is he who, removing the suffering of all, reigns supreme.
The grace of Maheśvara. || 39 ||

It is true that the effort of both the sun and the cloud—devoid of causal necessity, fixed place, or restriction, and occurring without being solicited—is solely for the benefit of living beings; however, while the cloud is capable of quelling the heat of thirst, it is not so with the sun, nor does the sun bring an end to darkness and cold. But that grace of Maheśvara, which removes all afflictions, reigns supreme.
What need is there for much here? One should worship the [river] that possesses the intense glory brought about by the descent of the auspicious state of the Lord of Umā’s compassion;
she who, like the sovereign power of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, is inclined toward the arrival of what is desired by the heart of Aniruddha.

The Connected Explanation: O seekers of the divine! What need is there for much speaking here? Worship the compassion of the Lord of Umā, which—like the majesty of the Enemy of Kaiṭabha manifested through his auspicious incarnations—is endowed with exalted splendor and is intent upon bringing about the attainment of what is desired by the heart of Aniruddha.
Thus ends [the work] of the venerable Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, together with the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the fifteenth hymn is titled "The Propitiation of Compassion.
The sixteenth hymn begins:
"Victorious through their splendors are those who bear the bull as their mark, the kinsmen of the world who bow down to them, whose matted locks have become the overflowing rivers of the Siddhas."
The drops of nectar from his lotus feet have surpassed the risen moon.

Victorious are the drops of nectar from the lotus-feet of the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva)— those feet which are kinsmen to the worlds prostrate before them in lineage, which have caused the river of the Siddhas to stumble by the weight of their anklets, and which rival the moon with their splendors. Adorned with abundant, pure fruits, and graced by green fields of ripening rice that bow low in reddish hues, your praise appears as bright as straw to those who are worn out.
[He is] the one who praises the Earth, which is adorned with the luster of nectar. || 2 ||

O ornament of the moon’s luster! For one who recites Your praise, even this earth—though adorned with abundant, pure fruits and graced by green and reddish rice crops that bow down—is perceived as mere withered grass.
As You create nectar in the ten directions for those seeking to behold You, O Infinite One, the long-standing darkness that has perpetually exhausted their vision vanishes.
O you who steal away the stains of the Kali age with your eye, steal [this] from me! || 3 ||

O Infinite One! With Your eye—which creates nectar in the ten directions and steals away the taints of the Kali age—steal away my long-standing darkness, which has caused my vision to be perpetually distressed as I seek Your sight. By Your splendors, You bear the full digit of the Moon, which destroys blinding gloom; and You grant a heart whose inner disposition is made pure by light.
With your auspicious form and auspicious flowers, nourish my welfare. || 4 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! May You, who bear a body auspicious with a form that bestows a heart whose quarters are brightened by light—bearing the full digit of the Moon-like One, which has dispelled the blinding darkness of those who have reached [despair]—grant me well-being.
Those whose temple-walls are parched by intense heat and whose lips are distressed by continuous sighing manifest their miserable state before the wealthy.
Deprived of luster, with wretched faces, they are seekers of wealth. || 5 ||

Immediately thereafter, with their faces cast down in shame at being gazed upon by the lords of the earth who had treated them with disdain, they uttered words whose syllables trembled and which were faltering due to the exhaustion of long-restrained joy.

But when their skill in virtue is disregarded by those with long-standing envy and hearts barren of awakening, and is treated with contempt as if it were the fluttering of moths before a flame, they spread such a display only to meet with ultimate humiliation.

Thus, even those of keen intellect—possessing a vast household that is long and difficult to maintain, their minds seized by the obsession of accumulating wealth, and their conduct mocked by forest-dwellers—fall into dense derision. (Cakkalakam) (Through running hither and thither in the hope of obtaining a mere fragment of wealth, due to traveling great distances: Their temple-like cheeks are scorched by intense heat.

With lips distressed by the succession of sighs and faces bereft of luster, those seeking wealth reveal their own misfortune before the wealthy. Immediately thereafter, their gazes met with the contemptuous looks of the lords of the earth, they cast down their faces in shame; those same seekers of wealth then utter words in which the syllables tremble, faltering due to the collapse of long-accumulated joy caused by begging. Then, by those of long-standing envy...
Those whose hearts are barren of awakening disregard and show no respect for the excellence of virtue, treating it as mere idle chatter like the fluttering of moths; thus, though they are wise men,

their grandiosity regarding a long-sustained and burdensome family, their minds seized by the obsession of amassing wealth, and their conduct ridiculed by forest-dwellers, they undergo profound mockery and meet with ultimate defeat.

But the skillful ones have made their dwellings upon the ridges of the snowy mountains— on those charming plateaus where the waves of waterfalls produce sounds resembling the auspicious resonance of soft drums,
and where the grounds are encircled by rows of lush, verdant grass.

On the bank of the celestial river, with a hand whose sprout-like fingers were moving [and crushing] the petals of a ketakī flower, she performed various rites for the lotus feet of the Pināka-wielder, that ocean of compassion, according to the prescribed ritual.

The deer, longing for mouthfuls of the tips of *kuśa* grass, and the young sparrows, seeking nourishment, became their guests; thus, they did not neglect their daily rites, sustaining their bodies with fruits and roots.

At the time of day’s end, they traversed the forest regions for long-lasting auspiciousness—regions made rustling by the dry grass and withered leaves scattered by the wind, and cooled by the spray of the thin waters of the Ganges. 12.

Immediately thereafter, they lie down during nights whitened by the rays of the stainless moon and illuminated by glowing medicinal herbs, where the sounds emerging from the throats of sweet-voiced cuckoos are offered to the ears with natural delight.

Thus, those fortunate ones who wear the auspicious girdle born from the grace of the dust of the lotus-feet of Hara laugh at the fortunes of kings whose minds are deluded and whose positions are as flickering as the flapping ears of an elephant. (A Kulaka of six verses) Anvaya:
Furthermore, [distinguished from those people greedy for even a fragment of wealth and discontented,] the fortunate ones...
Having established their dwellings upon the slopes of the snowy mountain— where the ripples of waterfalls produce sounds resembling the auspicious resonance of soft drums,

and where the grounds are carpeted with lush, verdant grass— they performed various rites of worship at the foot of the celestial river for the Pināka-wielder, the ocean of compassion, using as their hand the trembling sprout-like finger of a *ketakī* flower; meanwhile, deer, longing for mouthfuls of the tips of *kuśa* grass, [remained nearby].

Having performed auspicious rites in the forest glades—which were cooled by sprays from the thin waters of the Ganges; where the daily rituals were not neglected by young *kalaviṅka* birds seeking nourishment as they arrived as guests; where the sustenance of the body was provided by fruits and roots; and which at the close of day resounded with the rustling of old grass and leaves scattered by the gentle breeze—they thereafter dwelt amidst the pure rays of the stainless moon upon the glowing medicinal herbs.

During nights made pleasant for the ear by sounds naturally offered from the throats of cuckoos, those fortunate ones who possess the comforting retinue born of the grace of the dust from the lotus-feet of Hara lie down; they laugh at the fortunes of kings with deluded minds, which rest as unsteady as a flapping elephant’s ear.

O Hara, place before you a powerful force of women, formidable with the arching glances of their tremulous side-long looks; for the voracious God of Love is piercing my heart—already exceedingly emaciated—with arrows that strike those whose eyes are trembling with fear. 15.

O Lord, this anger brings me to a state of ridicule: it produces restlessness in my eyes, causes my eyebrows to quiver with intense agitation, and loosens the tranquility achieved through great effort. || 16 ||

My mind is distressed by the latent impressions of the pleasures amassed through the acquisition of wealth; I am bound by untruthful alliances and rendered helpless by ignoble greed. Even my friends do not touch me when I am thus provoked and have treated supplicants with contempt.

Those who sit in the assemblies of the wise laugh at me—who am devoid of the three appropriate aims of life, obscured, with a mind deluded by dense ignorance, and stained by my lack of discrimination between the real and the unreal. (18)

Thus do the enemies, so difficult to conquer, threaten us, while those of pure intellect avoid us; yet they do not overcome us as we are now distressed. Therefore, O Great Lord, act in such a way that this shall no longer be so; come and grant us Your vision! 19.

O Hara! Before me, the voracious Smara, wielding a mighty force through the side-glances of the city-women, pierces my heart—which is already exceedingly emaciated and terrified by the falling of his arrows. O Lord! This very anger, producing extreme agitation in my eyes, causing my brow to dance with great trepidation, and loosening the peace achieved through effort, leads me to a state of ridicule.

My mind is tormented by the latent desire for the splendors acquired through the gain of wealth; I am attached to the unreal, helpless under a shameful greed, and have provoked and distressed those who seek my favor.

Even my friends do not touch me—how much less other people? Devoid of the appropriate three-fold aims of life, shunned by the virtuous, my mind is stupefied by dense delusion and bereft of the discrimination between the good and the bad. I am defiled; how could I, such as I am, stand before the assembly of the wise in their court?
(The members of the assembly) laugh. Thus, by the manner previously described, my enemies—known as desire, anger, greed, and delusion—are extremely difficult to conquer; they threaten me.
The pure-minded (the wise) avoid me. O Maheśa! Now, act so that they may not again overcome me while I am distressed.
Come quickly to us and bestow upon us your glance consisting of grace.

Where is the bliss born from the remembrance of Maheśvara, which is directly opposed to the fierce heat of the wandering cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)? And where are worldly prosperities, as unstable as drops of water trickling from the petals of a tender lotus, which are the very seat of calamities? (20)

How vast the difference between the words of one who, at the sight of Śiveśvara, speaks with cheeks flushed and voice faltering with the joy of rising horripilation, and the sin of falling onto the wrong path through the prolixity of false praises of kings that lack their true merit! 21.

Where is that tranquility which, through the power of meditative concentration, subdues all afflictions and is incapable of enduring the exhaustion born of worldly existence; and where is this intoxication, which displays every form of physical agitation and whose conduct is censured by those of noble mind? (22)

Thus, O Treasure of Compassion, O crest-jewel upon the peak of the moon, awaken for a moment my heart, which has been rendered devoid of discernment by its inclination toward seeking paths that are improper and unobstructed [by restraint]. (Cakkalaka) Where is that most excellent happiness—born from the remembrance of Maheśvara—which is directed toward the cooling of the terrible heat of the wandering through worldly existence? Where is it? (23) (Cakkalaka)
Where are those riches, as flickering as water droplets falling from tender lotus petals—the very seat of calamities—and utterly contemptible?

Where are those words, O Śiva! O Īśvara!—slow with joy at the bristling of hair on the cheeks of [the supplicant], enchanting to all learned men, crying out "Save me!"—compared to the vast, meaningless, and false praises of kings that result in the sin of falling into the wrong path? Where is the merit of such [true devotion] compared to the transgression of wandering onto a pathless way?

(That which is utterly contemptible. Likewise, where is tranquility (*śamaḥ*)—the mastery over the senses (*jitendriyatvam*)—which, having suppressed the afflictions through meditative absorption, is incapable of enduring the exhaustion born of worldly existence? (It is highly praiseworthy. And where is intoxication (*madaḥ*), which displays its full physical form yet adopts a state despised by wise men? (It is utterly contemptible. O crest-jewel upon the crown of the night! O treasury of compassion! (In this manner [he addresses him].)
Awaken me for a moment—me whose mind is rendered distracted by lack of discernment and who is intent upon seeking the pathless, unobstructed way.
[Consider] young women with eyes reddened by intoxication and slender waists; sons with heads bowed low in reverence; friends who touch the innermost movements of the heart;
and kinsmen whose words are overflowing with the moisture of affection. (24)

May those lords be victorious, whose minds are like the essence of nectar even while bearing the burden of sovereignty sweetened by their grace; who are ever fond of gazing upon the faces of their attendants, and whose followers cry out "Victory! and "Live long! at every moment.

They cannot suddenly destroy the fear arising from the frown of Kṛtānta’s terrifying servants for those who worship You; therefore, O Abode of the Nectar of Compassion, place Your feet—which dispel calamities—within our hearts. (Tilaka) Anvaya: O Lord! [We are] women with eyes reddened by intoxication and slender waists, and sons with all their heads bowed down in humility.

Friends who touch the innermost thoughts with their words, moist with the intensity of affection; kinsmen who bear even the weight of responsibility with a sweetness born of grace; masters whose minds are like the essence of nectar and who at every moment delight in gazing upon one’s face, uttering cries of "Victory! and "Live long!"; and servants—all these are able to instantly dispel that fear which arises from the frown of the terrifying minions of Death. Therefore, O—
O treasury of the nectar of compassion! Destroying the calamities of those who worship you, plant your foot within our hearts.
Alas, that night of delusion—which, like a dark night, brings exhaustion and binds one with the illusion of egoism—spreads a lack of self-awareness that causes the decline of the intellect.
Therefore, casting us into the intensely blazing light flickering from the sun, the moon, and fire, make us joyful through awakened vision, endowed with enlightened and fruitful understanding. (27)

Alas! This night-like state of egoism—which, like the expansive night, binds us to illusion and exhausts our pure tranquility—spreads a decline of our intellect. Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, whose fierce splendor is shaken by the sun, moon, and fire, cast Your joyful eye upon us and make us joyful with fruitful awakening!
Where there is no father as protector, nor siblings for consolation, where the mother’s affectionate efforts become fruitless,
and where kinsmen are barren; for those suffering embodied beings, that which cannot be stolen by thieves and which never diminishes— the one most sweet provision on that path is the name of Śambhu.

Thus ends the sixteenth hymn, titled "Instruction," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with its commentary, the *Premamakaranda*.
The Seventeenth Hymn.

O Bestower of Boons, O Bhāratī, when the mind has become sluggish, attain a state of aesthetic relish and immediately engage in delightful endeavors; may you find your own delight therein. O Mother, at the end of the great sleep of delusion, arouse this person—who has now conceived a longing—to praise devotion to Śambhu with unwearied effort.

Anvaya: O Varade Bhāratī! When my dull mind has suddenly attained a state of aesthetic sensitivity (*rasikībhāva*), may you sport there with heart-stirring efforts; thus your own delight becomes manifest.
O Mother! Know that this person, at the end of the great sleep of delusion, has become free from indolence and has conceived a longing to praise devotion to Śambhu.
Just as the grape is directly a wave of nectar from a hard wooden shell, and the inherently sweet melody emerges from the hollow of the bamboo flute.
Who would not have their face lit with a smile of wonder as this nectar, fit to be drunk from the ear, issues forth from my mouth under the guise of well-spoken verses?

Just as a wave of nectar emerging directly from a wooden vessel that is harsh on the outside, or a naturally sweet melodic modulation (*mūrcchanā*) emerging from the hollow interior of a bamboo cane full of holes— likewise, this nectar fit for the ears, emerging from my mouth under the guise of well-spoken verses, whom among the conscious does it not render with a face smiling in wonder?
O Lord, having reflected that the time for death is close at hand and that life—though appearing as bright as the shadow of a swarm of locusts—is but brief;
and considering You to be one whose heart is compassionate and who is won over by devotion, those who deem themselves refined strive for Your new creation with purified minds.

Anvaya: O Lord! Having meditated upon the terror of the time of death as being imminent, having recognized that life is short and possesses a luster like that of easily caught locusts, and considering You to be compassionate-hearted and won over by devotion, those who consider themselves refined and whose minds are purified strive for Your worship.

From the throat of him whose devotion to the Lord of Beings (Śiva)—who is worthy of praise and from whom the sound of the ocean has emerged—arises, there rises [a song] accompanied by the manifestation of vast horripilation caused by the unfolding of joy, resembling the roar of a noble lion.
He alone laughs at the abode of Indra, bearing no small pride as he utters the unrestrained cry, "Śarva! Śarva! (O Śiva!).

From whose throat—where the hair on his body stands erect like a mountain rising from the ocean at the sight of the lineage of [Śiva’s] devotees, and where devotion to the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa) has blossomed through playful horripilation—there arises an unrestrained sound resembling the roar of a lion:
"O Śarva! O Śarva! (Protect me! That one alone, bearing no small pride, mocks the abode of Indra (Vāsava).

That alone is true humanity wherein the highest birth of the virtuous prevails; that alone is the one true birth wherein fame spreads through the cause of scholarship. That alone is true scholarship wherein speech blossoms with nectar-like sweetness; and that alone is true speech which propagates devotion to Śiva. *Anvaya:* Mānuṣyam tat (eva); yatra satām uttamā jātiḥ prabhavati, sā (eva) ekā jātiḥ (praśasyā); yatra... *Translation:* Only that is [true] humanity wherein the supreme birth of the virtuous arises; that alone is the one [praiseworthy] birth wherein... [fame spreads]. Only that is [true] scholarship wherein speech unfolds with sweet nectar; and that speech alone spreads devotion to Śiva.
Fame spreads because of scholarship; that scholarship alone is blessed wherein speech, full of aesthetic flavor and sweetness, unfolds.
That speech is most blessed wherein devotion to Śaṅkara extends its delight.
In whose mouths do not two or three pure verses—whose conduct is filled with joy and pride, and which terrify even the frowns of Yama’s brow—unfurl? [They do not.]
O Bhava, fie upon those on earth who are empty of the nectar of service to Your feet, even though their hymns pour forth honey-like drops when drenched with devotion! 6.

O Bhava! Fie upon those who are devoid of the nectar of service to Your feet on this earth— those from whose mouths two or three well-spoken words do not blossom, words which dispel the frowns of Yama’s son, which shed drops of honey, which are drenched in devotion, which are pure, and which consist of Your own deeds that bring joy to the intoxicated gods.

O Lord, your devotion shines upon me, constantly distilling nectar— like the beautiful moonlight on a night thick with stars during the month of Kārtika, like a water-station in the heart of a forest that quenches the intense heat of the traveler, and like your own voice, "Do not fear," which dispels the dread of Yama. (7)

O Lord! Like the lovely moonlight of the full-moon night of Kārtika in the thick darkness, like a water-stall in the middle of a forest that dispels the intense heat of the traveler, and like Your own voice saying "Do not fear" amidst the terror of Yama, Your devotion shines for me as a constant stream of nectar.
But for those in whose hearts the path of merit does not exist, and in whom devotion to Śiva (Sthāṇu) finds no manifestation, I do not repeatedly take delight in their smiles. Thus says the world.
I consider that weeping, which is joined with devotion to Him and causes the immediate abandonment of sorrow, to be praiseworthy when it arises from a joyful heart and serves as a cause for healing.

In those smiles of theirs, from which laughter is stirred by joy, wherein the path of merit within them—the devotion directed toward Śiva—does not manifest, I do not repeatedly find aesthetic flavor (the meaning is: I do not desire them). But that weeping, accompanied by devotion to the illustrious Śambhu, in which even the common person suddenly abandons sorrow—that weeping, which is praised when uttered and is the cause of health, I [do desire].
I consider this appropriate:

that sun, which by its rising has instantly dispelled the darkness and possesses the splendor of light that causes the lotuses to bloom, is capable of burning away the fierce defects inflamed by the intoxication of pride destroyed by that [darkness]; yet, in this world, only devotion to Śambhu is able to bring about such a conflagration. (9)

That Sun, who possesses the splendor of the rising lotus through his lineage and who, upon his emergence, did not remove the darkness of worldly tranquility— that darkness which destroys joy and inflames fierce defects within existence (being of the nature of ignorance)— only devotion to Śambhu has the power to consume it.

For those who are submerged in a mass of afflictions that portend the destruction of contentment and tranquility, and whose hopes are shattered by the latent tendencies toward the worship of treacherous sense objects—for them, in this triple world, devotion to Śambhu alone is the path to prosperity, serving as the ground for the realization of the undertaking that shatters the fear of worldly existence. 10.

For those whose hopes are shattered and who are submerged in a mass of afflictions that portend the destruction of contentment and tranquility— afflictions caused by the latent tendencies of serving the treacherous objects of the senses— for them, in this triple world, devotion to Śambhu alone is their refuge; it is the ground for the undertaking of the destruction of the fear of worldly existence and leads to ultimate prosperity.
There are countless men whose progress is obstructed by hypocrisy and pride, their minds bewildered by the playful chatter of women who treat them with disdain;
yet rare are those men who, having fixed their delight on the banks of the Gaṅgā, cherish in their hearts a devotion that is waveless and unbroken. 11.

On this earth, there are countless men whose progress is obstructed by the pillars of hypocrisy and lineage, whose minds are bewildered by the frivolous chatter of those who treat insults with indifference;
yet those men who, finding delight on the banks of the Gaṅgā, maintain in their hearts a waveless, unbroken devotion to Bhārgī, are truly rare.

O Śambhu! Hypocrisy, through its pretensions of undertaking deceptive acts, burns me; this fault of anger, accompanied by malice, diminishes my luster. This heavy burden of egoism whirls me about with arrogance. Only devotion to you has the power to lead me to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence. *Anvaya*: O Śambhu! Hypocrisy, through its pretensions of undertaking deceptive acts, burns me; this fault of anger, accompanied by malice, [diminishes my luster]. This heavy burden of egoism whirls me about with arrogance. Only devotion to you has the power to lead me to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.

The heavy burden of egoism robs me of my luster and, with its arrogance, causes me to wander on evil paths; therefore, devotion to you alone has the power to lead me to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.

Meanwhile, the bodiless god of love swiftly prepares for battle with the beautiful, curved glances from the corners of the eyes of playful women—glances that are as lovely as arrows fixed upon his bow, accompanied by the knitting of their eyebrows.
My devotion to the Blessed One, which spreads forth the descent upon the path of peace capable of burning away all defects, is my refuge and the light for my eyes, like moonlight in the darkness. 13.
The bodiless God of Love immediately prepares for battle with the playful side-glances of wanton women— charming with fixed arrows and knit eyebrows;
therefore, O Blessed One, just as moonlight is the sole refuge for the eyes by spreading a path of peace capable of burning away all defects, so too is devotion to you, O Bhīma, my only resort.
Let Cupid draw his flowery bow at will night after night; let Time place the serpent with its coils broken within the hollow of his own hand.
Devotion to Bhārgī is instantly a wish-fulfilling creeper for all prayers—how many wretched snares of affliction have not been destroyed in this world? 14.

May the God of Love, desiring union, forever conceal his flowery bow (hiding it somewhere); may Time place the serpent within the hollow of his own hand with its coils broken. (Through the ripening of my past merit) I have suddenly obtained devotion, which is a *bhārgī* plant—the wish-fulfilling creeper for all prayers; therefore, how many nooses of affliction, whose hopes were destroyed, have not been snared by me in this world?

Let alone that meager remnant of royal glory, whose splendor is withered by armies commanded to violate the orders of kings, and which consists of the unworthy prayers of those who have fallen from their station;
rather, we praise that devotion to Śambhu, in whom even the foot—though it bears the mark of the fortune of Indra’s vast empire over the conquest of the three worlds—is a mere object of contempt. 15.

Let that meager remnant of fortune remain— the fortune of the armies of successive kings whose splendor was rendered tasteless by the violation of their commands, and which thus entailed improper supplications— even the lotus of Indra, the emblem of the vast imperial sovereignty won through the conquest of the three worlds, became an object of contempt; yet we praise that devotion to Śambhu.

For the wise who dwell on the banks of the Ganges, whose minds are intent on the singular passion for their beloved, who are adorned with bark garments, whose impurities have been washed away by the waters of knowledge, and whose crowns are beautified by masses of matted locks displayed through intense fervor—their devotion to Bharga takes various forms for the sake of liberation. (16)

For the accomplished ones who dwell on the banks of the Ganges— their minds solely devoted to the path of devotion, adorned with bark garments, whose impurities have been washed away by the waters of knowledge,

and whose beauty is enhanced by masses of matted locks made prominent through constant immersion— their manifold forms of devotion to Śiva lead to liberation. Just as a cluster of blossoms spreads its fragrance while the old leaves fall, so too does old age approach the vicinity of the ears as the true messenger of death.

Our form, like a cluster of withered leaves, truly proclaims its fading splendor; old age, the messenger of death, spreads toward our ears. Alas! Now there is no other refuge for us than devotion to Śambhu, for enjoyments—like snakes—coil themselves around the very efforts we exert. **Anvaya:** mūrtiḥ naḥ jīrṇaparṇā mañjarī yathā dhūtim prathayati satyataḥ; mṛtyudūtī jarā karṇābhyarṇam prasarati; bhogāḥ bhogā iva vidadhataḥ ceṣṭitam veṣṭayante; hanta! idānīm śambhubhakteḥ [anyat śaraṇaṃ na asti]. **Translation:** Our body, like a cluster of withered leaves, truly proclaims its loss of luster; old age, the messenger of death, reaches the vicinity of our ears. Enjoyments—like serpents—envelop the very activities of those who pursue them; alas! At this moment, there is no refuge for us other than devotion to Śambhu.

We have no other refuge. Therein, the lunar light—though weak—is incapable of dispelling the thick darkness; there, the heat of the sun does not cause such scorching distress; and there, the flickering flame of fire does not shine with its own brilliance alongside another light. Only devotion to Śambhu provides illumination in that perilous place. 18.
In that perilous state of blinding delusion—where the lunar light, though skilled at dispelling the darkness of succession, becomes weak;
where the scorching heat does not dissolve the dense gloom; and where the flickering fire does not shine alongside other splendors—it is devotion to Śambhu alone that bestows illumination.

May the science known as Ānvīkṣikī—which is easily acquired through repeated study—no longer exist; may the Daṇḍanīti, which shatters calamities, remain far away from the heart; and may even the Vārtā (the science of livelihood), though it brings news of well-being, shine only with stability somewhere else. There is no refuge whatsoever worthy of those in distress other than devotion to Śambhu. *Anvaya:* Bhūyo'bhyasanasulabhā ānvīkṣikī... [Ānvīkṣikī is the subsequent examination (*anvīkṣā*) of that which has been examined through both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*).]

May that science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), which has as its purpose the dispelling of calamities, not even exist; may the delightful science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) remain far away [the meaning being that it too does not exist to remove the fear of worldly existence]; and may the report of prosperity [consisting of agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, and so forth] shine with stability somewhere; for those in distress, there is no other refuge than devotion to Śambhu.
She is not an Arhat.
For the first wave of the ocean of saṃsāra, the woman named Passion—whose desires range from minor to major sins—obstructs the progress of virtuous men who are sinking.
She is the cause of the exhaustion arising from wandering in the whirlpool of delusion; yet this very intellect of ours has become a bridge that leads far away from her. 20.

Therefore, for those whose minds are agitated by fear and anxiety as they seek to cross over this mire of the quagmire of birth, death, and afflictions—for those who, their bodies bound by the noose of hope, cry out in distress at the moment of the departure of life—it is devotion to Śambhu that extends a helping hand. 21.
(A pair of verses:

This intellect—this very intellect—is a dam (in the form of a bridge) that serves as the cause for severing the exhaustion arising from wandering in the whirlpool of delusion; it is a woman whose desires reach to the very brink of sin, the first wave of the ocean of worldly existence for virtuous people sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra, who indeed obstructs their [usual] course. And this intellect... [is the first wave of the ocean of worldly existence].
It moves far away. Therefore, for those whose minds are agitated by fear and anxiety, who desire to cross over this mire of the pit of the afflictions of birth and death,

and whose bodies are bound by the snares of hope— while they are crying out in distress at the moment of the departure of their life-breaths— it is devotion to Śambhu alone that extends a helping hand.
Those crooked side-glances of the fawn-eyed women, terrifying in their prowess like the tips of the flames from the arrows of the God of Love, fall suddenly when drawn forth by passion;
in time, these become beaks as sharp as thunderbolts, mercilessly piercing the inner hearts of the dull-witted—like those of hellish birds.
Those crooked side-glances of the fawn-eyed women, which are terrifying in their prowess like the tips of the flames from the arrows of the God of Love and are instantly drawn forth by passion—

those very glances, when directed toward the lovers attached to them, become in time as sharp as thunderbolts; acting with mercilessness, they pierce the inner hearts of those fools with the beaks and shafts of the birds of hell.
Her pair of arms, which rival the swaying stalks of a young lotus, adorned with ornaments and jingling bracelets, encircle her throat;
I suspect that for those blinded by delusion who fall into the great mire of the terror of suffering, these arms become a noose for the lotus-eyed one. (23)

I suspect that the pair of arms of the lotus-eyed one— which, when compared in succession, resembled the trembling stalk of a young lotus, was adorned with ornaments, and had its bracelets jingling— when it was entwined around the throats of those blinded by delusion, becomes a noose for them as they fall into the great mire of terror and agony caused by Time.

I know that when the slender-limbed woman, her eyes half-closed with intent and her face moist with perspiration, drinks the nectar-like wine fragrant as the ketaka flower, that act— which for those blinded by passion leads to a dwelling in hell with an end so difficult to escape— becomes for her a source of reproach and anger due to the curse of falling back into it again.

I know that very face of the slender-limbed woman— whose eyes were half-closed, which was imbued with the fragrance of the *ketaka* flower, which immediately caused perspiration and flowed with nectar, and which was drunk by those blinded by passion— now becomes for those same passion-blinded ones a source of curses, reproaches, and anger regarding their fall into the abode of hell at its inevitable conclusion, a state otherwise difficult to attain.

That necklace, shaped like a golden pitcher, which was firmly embraced by the doe-eyed woman’s broad pair of breasts due to the intensity of her passion—that very thing, at the time of death, assumes for those fools sinking into the mire of hell the nature of a heavy, firmly fixed stone stuck in a lotus stalk. (25)

That necklace, which had the form of a golden pitcher, was suspended from the broad pair of breasts of that fawn-eyed woman; and because it was tightly embraced by fools out of an excess of passion, at the time of death, for those sinking into the mire of hell, it assumes the state of a heavy, firmly stuck stone upon a lotus stalk.
What is the use of further elaborate displays of speech? Listen well to this final word, which accords with the long-lasting sorrow of the worlds.

Abandoning worldly association—which yields immediate pleasure but results in future suffering—and having obtained the pure water of the Gaṅgā along with its full benefits, devote yourselves to Śambhu.
(A *kulaka* consisting of five verses.
[Anvaya: O people, what is the use of many elaborate displays of verbal composition (namely, the commencement of discourses on detachment that produce discernment)? What [is gained by them]? He...

O people of long-standing sorrow, having heeded these my well-spoken words previously mentioned, listen attentively to this, my final word! Having abandoned worldly association— which yields initial pleasure but results in suffering, and which is accompanied by its constituent bonds— attain the stainless water of the Gaṅgā and devote yourselves solely to the worship of Śambhu.

Blessed are these renunciants who, making the three worlds seem as insignificant as a mere heap of straw, their minds gladdened by devotion to the streaks of the beloved of Rohiṇī (the moon), seek to attain the stainless abode; they vigorously dispel the vast mass of internal impurities with the waters of the Mandākinī and the silken garments of the victory-banner of the matted locks of the Moon-crested Lord.
Counting the three worlds as no more than a heap of straw, their minds gladdened by devotion to the decorative streaks upon the brow of the beloved of Rohiṇī,

these blessed and vigorous renunciants, in order to attain the stainless abode, pierce the thick mass of internal impurities with the waters of the Mandākinī using the silken garments of the victory-banner of Śiva’s matted locks.
O Lord, just as the light of the sun, the master who illuminates all the continents, attains a fierce intensity in shattering the most stubborn darkness, so too, in this worldly existence—
which resembles a prison and is enveloped in the blinding darkness of delusion— only Your devotion is our refuge, bestowing protection upon us who are without shelter. 28.

O Lord, O Destroyer of Smara! While this world—described in the manner stated above—is being overwhelmed by the most intense darkness, attaining a fierce brilliance in the shattering of that gloom, and resembling a prison-house due to the dense darkness of delusion, your devotion alone is our refuge; for it bestows protection upon the helpless, like the radiance of the Sun, the lord and lamp of all the continents.

We praise that devotion, whose power of great majesty is a wonder to the three worlds, and before whom even those three gods who perform the maintenance, creation, and destruction of the universe wait with affectionate eyes, seeking merely a glance from him; he, the Lord of immeasurable greatness, acts like a playful bird toward her. (29)

He, the Lord of immeasurable majesty, whom those three gods— the performers of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe— serve while longing for a glance from His face, seeking merely a sidelong look, knowing that the Supreme Lord will fulfill their desires; that very Lord, for whom devotion acts like a playful bird, possesses a power of wondrous and great majesty throughout the three worlds.
We praise devotion (*bhakti*).

Milk-yielding cows provide but a rasa that is a kinsman to a taste akin to incomparable nectar; whereas devotion toward Śiva is the sole ground for the enjoyment of the wonder that naturally quells all fatigue.

Satisfaction [arising] from the manifestation of one's own Self is the singular cause for the repose of consciousness, which flows with the outpouring of incomparable supreme bliss; thus, it brings calamities under its service.
What shall he do? || 30 ||
