The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is as follows: since I possess devotion to Śiva—which yields a flavor that is a kinsman to the taste of incomparable nectar—and which is the sole ground for the enjoyment of the wonder that naturally dispels fatigue; and since I possess contentment, which is the singular cause for resting in consciousness through the outpouring of incomparable supreme bliss arising from the manifestation of one's own Self—for these reasons, what can calamity do instantly to me, who am its servant?

Thus ends the seventeenth hymn, titled "The Hymn of Devotion," within the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flower-Garlands of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
[The eighteenth hymn follows.]

Victorious is he who has conquered all transformations, who has arranged for the benefit of the world, who has brought about the destruction of calamities, and whose darkness of delusion has been stilled; he whose human effort is incomparable, who has attained supreme authority over the universe, who has humbled the god of love, and who is the one who utters sweet words of endearment to Pārvatī. 1.

Victorious is he who has conquered all transformations through his lineage, who has arranged for the welfare of the world, who has brought about the destruction of calamities, whose darkness of delusion is stilled, whose human effort is incomparable,

who has attained supreme authority over the universe, who has humbled the god of love, and who is the flatterer of Pārvatī. He, the bestower of bliss, makes this vast multitude of bodies and worlds appear minute for the sake of living beings' experience of their karma through his full power.
May that Great Lord, who has commanded the ten directions and whose form is the scripture for the sake of liberation, be the burner away of the defects of worldly existence for you. || 2 ||

May that Maheśa— who possesses full power through his lineage, who bestows happiness, and who, as the all-pervading Lord, manifested this vast multitude of bodies and worlds for the living beings to experience the fruits of their karma— and who, for the sake of their liberation, pointed out the direction of the scriptures free from doubt— may he be the burner away of the defects of worldly existence for you.

O Giver of Boons, conqueror of the supreme heat of afflictions, by your grace, the pure wave of Sarasvatī— residing in the lotus-face of the best of sages, which is stainless with the appearance of true arts and endowed with tireless activity— prevails upon your head like the celestial river.

Anvaya: O Giver of Boons! Just as the celestial river (Svar-dhunī), possessing stainless waves and conquering the affliction of supreme heat, flows upon your head—which is endowed with fire (analasahitavṛtti) and purified by the appearance of the true arts (satkalābhāsaśuddha)—so too, by your grace, does Sarasvatī (Bhāratī), possessing stainless waves and conquering the affliction of supreme heat, manifest in the lotus-face of the best of the wise (Budhavara), which is endowed with tireless activity (analasahitavṛtti) and purified by the appearance of the true arts (satkalābhāsaśuddha).
I take refuge in your footstool, which is like a rain-cloud that brings relief from the exhaustion and fever of the weary wanderer through the cycle of existence;
it is a great celestial bow flashing with the mass of rays from the jewels set in the crowns of the gods as they bow down. 4.

O Bhava! I take refuge in your footstool, which is like a rain-cloud that extinguishes the intense heat of the weary travelers wandering through the cycle of existence; it is the great celestial bow flashing with the mass of rays from the jewels set in the crowns of the gods as they bow down.
With her cheek resting upon her hand, her body withered and delicate as a lotus stalk crushed upon a bed of young moss, she remains sleepless due to long separation.
Terrified by the god of love, she gazes in every direction at night, becoming a vessel for the fall of Rudra’s wrathful glances.

With her cheeks marked by the lines of constant weeping, her form withered and delicate like a lotus stalk tossed upon a bed of young moss, sleepless due to long separation and terrified of the bodiless god of love, the woman gazes in every direction at night, becoming a target for the glances of Rudra—
she who now wanders playfully above the finest elephants, by virtue of the grace obtained through devotion to the pair of lotus-feet of Śiva.
They listen intently to the swelling song of swarms of bees, stumbling in their flight due to greed for the abundant fragrance issuing from the weight of thick intoxication. || 6 ||

By the grace of devotion to the pair of lotus-feet of Hara, those devotees of Śiva who walk with ease upon the backs of noble elephants hear the songs of swarms of bees stumbling in greed for the intense fragrance exuding from their abundant rut.
O Lord, he who bowed to Your pair of lotus-feet with his body thrilled by the seizure of sincere devotion dwells [in bliss].
The footstool, caressed by the bakula garlands slipping from the crests of the vassal kings who bow in service. || 7 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! He whose body is thrilled by the touch of sincere devotion who bows down to Your pair of lotus feet—that fortunate one—inhabits a footstool cherished by bakula garlands falling from the crests of tributary kings bowing in service.
O Moon-crested One! By Your grace, the blessed ones shine with fly-whisks as white as the moon, appearing as if on both sides.
His face was adorned by two streams from the celestial river, which served as omens of his future attainment of the state of Rudra.

Anvaya: O Śaśiśakalaśikhaṇḍa! By your grace, the blessed ones shine on both sides [on both flanks] with chowries as white as the moon, which, like two cascades from the celestial river, are indicative of the manifestation of their impending attainment of the state of Rudra.
O Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain King, by your grace, the fortunate ones in this world bear the washed parasol upon their heads;
it is as if you yourself have bestowed this entire orb of the cool-rayed moon to establish your own preeminence.

O beloved of the daughter of the mountain-king! By your grace, those who bear the washed royal parasol upon the crest of the world are fortunate; for this very reason, you have bestowed upon them the entire orb of the cool-rayed moon, as if to establish their superiority even over yourself, who bears but a crescent moon—thus it is an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
O heart, moist with compassion, the Moon—bearer of the celestial river’s stream, holding a jar of nectar in his hand—dwells within you.
If he, whose crest is the crescent moon, is not enough for you, tell me: what other cooling remedy is there to alleviate the fever of worldly existence? 10.

Anvaya: O heart! If Śrī Śiva—the one moist with compassion, who bears the stream of the celestial river Gaṅgā, who holds a jar of nectar in his hand, and whose crest is the crescent moon—sports within you, then tell me, what other cooling remedy is there for the cessation of the forest fire of worldly existence? Those whose fortitude is praised by the best of gods, whose heroic power is irresistible to enemies, and whose conduct as teachers is established through various scriptures in this world, uphold the governance of the universe.
In former times, millions of the most excellent Rudras constantly performed worship for Śaṅkara.
In ancient times, those who performed constant worship of Śaṅkara became meritorious men, their fortitude praised by the best of gods,

possessing irresistible power against enemies, acting as teachers who introduced various scriptures into the world, and being the most excellent among the Rudras— worthy of being chosen like Rudra himself— they uphold the governance of the universe by the millions.

O Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain, O Lord of tranquil renown, when even the multitude of hands and feet has grown feeble, and when the noose of Yama hangs with its opening wide open—who other than You could be the protector of living beings in this world? (12)

Anvaya: O Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain! when the mountain has reached a state of tranquility in its advanced age, and even the collection of its hands and feet has attained emaciation—or when the noose of Death has gained access to its throat—O Bhava! who else besides You can be the protector of living beings?

With her face resting upon her couch, her cheeks pale, and bearing a languor born of separation from you, the proud lady—her slender vine-like body appearing emaciated—speaks out; yet, alas, she does not destroy the fortitude of the wise who are absorbed in meditation upon you.

O Hara! Even though she is a proud woman who, with her slender creeper-like body, bears a face resting upon her arm—its cheeks pale from extreme separation—and who bears a mind overcome by exhaustion and voices her distress, she does not rob the steadfastness of the wise during their meditation on you.
O Infinite One, enter within my heart, which is tranquil within, as its gross discernment falls away and its excessive sorrow becomes manifest. Be present, be present.
He is a rain-cloud for the destruction of the burning heat of existence, bringing relief to all living beings afflicted by the diseases of the Kali age. 14.
O Infinite One! Enter our hearts—our minds which possess a discernment that grows ever more refined, from which the excess of sorrow has vanished, and which are luminous and profoundly tranquil.
O Bhava! Become for all living beings, along with their progeny, a rain-cloud that extinguishes the burning heat of the diseases brought on by this Kali age.

Burn up the long-lasting, futile flood of sins with an unfailing fire; shine with a beautiful and intense light, the root-source of exquisite bliss. Bestow upon us the instruction that grants liberation.
It has destroyed even the slightest trace of afflictions; it is as sweet as honey, noble, and the very essence of the nectar of speech.

O Lord! Bestow upon me that instruction which burns the long-accumulated flood of sins, which is exceedingly radiant, not dull, the root of beautiful bliss, and which destroys even a trace of affliction; bestow that sweet as honey, noble, and essence of the nectar of speech!
For the hero Māra, whose internal passion is voracious, moves about, and my intellect, like a creeper, trembles with swelling fear—O Lord, [grant this] to me who have sought Your greatness.
Casting down your gaze, bring peace, bring peace; by this the world shall become joyful.
Anvaya: O Lord! The voracious Māra-vīra moves within; great fear stirs like a creeping vine. O Master!
Casting Your eye upon that Kāma whose power is harmful, pacify him, so that this world, filled with joy, may attain peace.
She, whose loveliness rivals the beauty of the hips, serves [the Lord] with a face whose splendor surpasses the lovely lotus accompanied by bees, her passion having risen in delight.
O Lord, the women, with their playful gestures that intoxicate even the God of Love, have taken refuge in you.

O Lord! The woman—whose thick loins possess a dense splendor, whose face has a luster that surpasses the end of her tresses, who rivals a lotus accompanied by bees, and who is flushed with passion—serves you, who have sought refuge in her, delighting you with playful charms that intoxicate even the God of Love.
O Protector, she causes the ocean of worldly existence to swell, generating wave after wave; like a dark cloud-bank that brings forth lightning flashes, she captivates Hara.
The fainting fit of delusion, which crushes fortitude and increases the distinction between the esteemed and the despised, [obscures] the radiance of pure awakening. || 18 ||

O Hara! Like a rain-cloud that has gathered a mixture of lightning and mist, this increase of hostility—which agitates the ocean of worldly existence already stirred by its own creator—destroys the celebrated light of pure awakening, causing a swoon of delusion for living beings.

O you whose desired success is nourished by the excellent intellect of those who have performed meritorious deeds, resort to the side-long glance that bestows desired grace; it veils [the enemy] while [granting favor].
O Lord, O Master, who else besides You is capable of pacifying these unbearable calamities? (19)

O Lord! Bestow upon me, who worships you, that downward glance which grants the fulfillment of desired goals through well-performed merit and excellent wisdom, and which bestows cherished grace. O Protector! Apart from you, who is capable of quelling the onset of unbearable calamities?
[I am one] whose heart is filled with the dust of battle, desiring to strike down the delusion that causes separation from the beneficial.
I take refuge in that Lord, who is praised by those yogis liberated from existence and non-existence, and whose greatness is worthy of honor and praise. || 20 ||

I take refuge in that Lord, whose praise is unassailable and worthy of honor; he who is approached by yogis who have abandoned the power of worldly existence (*bhava*), who are free from passion (*arajas*), who carry within their hearts a state of equanimity, and who desire to strike down the delusion (*moha*) that causes separation from what is beneficial.
He is one whose greatness is immeasurable, who has destroyed false pride, who bestows a consciousness that shines like nectar, yet who makes manifest his own humility—[a humility] difficult to bear.
O Vardhamāna, who shines forth from the cycle of existence, shatter the affliction that oppresses me! 21.

O Lord! Bestowing upon Your devotees that consciousness which is of unfathomable majesty, which has destroyed false pride, which is like nectar, and which shines forth, You—who have manifested Your own humility—shatter my unbearable, increasing, and agonizing contempt for worldly existence.
What need is there here for jewels, or for mantras, or for collections of various medicines, or even for other remedies?
Even nectar generally is not capable of pacifying the torment of sin; therefore, go for refuge to the one Hara, who is supreme in compassion.

What indeed is the use here of jewels, or what use of mantras, or even of collections of medicinal herbs? What purpose is served by various other remedies as well? Even nectar is generally incapable of pacifying the torment of sin; therefore, O seekers of welfare, go for refuge to Hara alone, who is supreme compassion itself.

For here, among mountains, the Snowy Mountain (Himalaya) is supreme; among great lights, the sun; among gurus, the mother; among mantras, the single-syllabled [Om] is the highest state; among friends, merit; among enemies, sin; among rivers, the celestial river (Ganges); and among lords, the Lord whose crest-jewel is the moon. 23.
For indeed, among mountains here, the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya) is supreme; among great things, fire is supreme; among gurus, the mother is supreme;

among mantras, the single syllable is the supreme state. Among friends, merit is supreme; among enemies, the day is supreme; among rivers, the celestial river (Gaṅgā) is supreme; and among lords, the Moon-crested God (Śiva) is the supreme master.

As long as the burden of fortitude is not cast down by the ravages of old age, as long as eloquence does not decay and the intellect does not crumble, and as long as the limbs are not helplessly embraced by the serpents of disease—O wise ones, worship the Imperishable Lord for the sake of conquering worldly existence. (24)
O wise ones! O mindful ones! As long as the burden of fortitude is not cast down by the ravages of old age; as long as Sarasvatī does not decay;

as long as the intellect does not crumble; and as long as the limbs are not helplessly embraced by the serpents of disease—so long, for the sake of conquering worldly existence, worship the Imperishable Lord.
Compassion was repeatedly aroused, and flatteries were offered again and again to the Lord; with a heart gladdened by the contemplation of worldly existence, he was repeatedly brought inside.
His crown was repeatedly placed at the footstool of his feet; what more need be said? Everything has been conquered, and all supernatural powers have been placed in the palm of his hand. (25)

Before the Lord, I wept piteously again and again; I offered repeated flatteries to the Lord with a heart gladdened by the internal contemplation of His being. My crown was cast down upon the seat of His footstool. What else could I have hoped for? By me the entire universe has been conquered, and all supernatural powers have been placed in the palm of my hand.

Thus ends the eighteenth hymn, the Siddhistotra, in the *Stutikusumāñjali* dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
The nineteenth hymn begins.

O Giver of Boons, who here is capable of describing that supreme form of yours which transcends the very path of words? Yet, that mark of the young moon which you assumed to show favor to the world bowing before you—that is what I shall now proclaim.

O Giver of Boons! Who is capable of describing here, by means of words, that supreme and transcendent form of Yours? (The meaning is: because its further shore is unseen, even Brahmā and the other gods are not able to describe Your majesty. However, O Compassionate One! That form marked with the crescent moon, which You assumed to grace the world that bows before You—that alone do I describe.

Let alone that which is supreme; even that which is inferior, O Maheśa, Your own divine form is not capable of being contemplated by those who possess the affliction of worldly existence (*bhava*). For whatever else is conceptualized through the process of mental construction (*vikalpa*), even that is but a dwelling place of bliss for those here afflicted by *bhava*. (2)

Anvaya: O Maheśa! Let Your supreme form remain [beyond reach]; even that other divine body of Yours is not fit for contemplation by those with divine vision—what then to say of people like us who possess only physical eyes? However, whatever is being conceptualized by the fluctuations of the intellect, even that here in this world becomes an abode of bliss for those suffering from the afflictions of worldly existence.

Your form is surely a wick of the nectar of Śiva; for upon reaching it, a few drops of tears fall, the mass of the veil of sins perishes, darkness departs, passion subsides, the eyes become tranquil, and clarity expands. (3)

Anvaya: O Śiva! Surely Your form is a wick of nectar (an *amṛtavarti*); for having obtained it, a few drops of tears fall, the mass of sins perishes, darkness departs, passion is pacified, and the clarity of vision expands.

Truly, this body of Yours is a repository of highly precious jewels of virtue, a support for those afflicted by calamity; were it not so, how could it be adorned with the filaments of the abundant rays of Your toenails?
What is this pair of lotuses called "feet" that has risen up simultaneously here? || 4 ||

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! This is true: Your body is the support for those afflicted by calamity, a treasury of highly precious jewels of virtue. If it were not so, then why has this pair of lotuses named "feet," with their filaments consisting of the mass of rays from Your nails, arisen here?
O Bhava! May Your two feet—whose toes are bristling with the multitude of teardrops of joy arising from the intensity of prostration—[grant us grace].
The fortunate ones enjoy the beauty of a pair of lotuses whose rows of petals are adorned with sprays of frost. || 5 ||

O Bhava! Blessed are those who worship Your two feet, which possess the beauty of a pair of lotuses whose rows of petals are adorned by droplets of frost, and whose fingers are bristling with drops of tears born from the intense joy of prostration.
We bow to the pair of Your lotus-feet, radiant with ashes and reddened by the brilliant luster of the rubies upon the crowns of the gods.
It was as if sprinkled with camphor dust, containing within it the pollen of saffron powder, belonging to the Enemy of Smara. || 6 ||

We worship the pair of lotus-feet of the Enemy of Smara, radiant with ashes as if sprinkled with camphor dust mixed with the pollen of saffron, and reddened by the brilliant luster of the ruby from the crest-jewel of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
We worship that which bestows desired fruits upon Śambhu, possessing a pair of shapely calves and a fresh basin made beautiful by the coils of the King of Serpents resting at the base of the ankles.
I take refuge in [him] who is capable of pacifying the calamity that brings an end to the suffering of existence. || 7 ||

I take refuge in the pair of Śambhu’s shanks— the two creepers that grant desired fruits, capable of pacifying the exhaustion of worldly suffering, and possessing a beautiful, fresh basin at the base of the ankle like the coils of the serpent king— to quell my misfortune. I salute the world-transcending belly of Īśvara-Bhairava, which has held the seven worlds since the time of the end of the age, wherein the cavity of the navel is the primordial source of the universe.
The manner of breaking the path for the departure of the flood of the waves of worldly existence.

I bow to the supramundane belly of Īśvara-Bhairava, which has resided through the succession of world-ages and contains the seven worlds; wherein the cavity of the navel assumes the appearance of a path for the fresh emergence of the flood of beings born from the primordial creation of the universe.
I bow to that [navel], which shines like the frontal globes of the celestial elephants smeared with vermilion, and resembles an autumnal cloud reddened by the twilight. I bow to it.
The chest of the Destroyer of Cities, radiant with a mass of ashes, possesses a beautiful luster reddened by the glow of the jewels in the hoods of the Lord of Serpents.

I bow to the chest of the Subduer of Cities, which shines with a mass of ashes; it is as beautiful as the frontal globes of the celestial elephant streaked with vermilion, it resembles an autumnal cloud reddened by twilight, and it possesses a lovely luster like the gems upon the hoods of the Lord of Serpents.
O Lord, these arms of yours—whose bodies are embraced by the coils of the King of Serpents—truly gladden my heart!
Like the branches of a sandalwood tree, they provide relief from the scorching heat of terrible existence. || 10 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Alas, these arms of Yours, whose bodies are embraced by the coils of the King of Serpents, delight my heart—by extinguishing the terrible heat of worldly existence—like the branches of sandalwood trees whose bodies are embraced by the coils of the King of Serpents.

This [lineage], situated in the middle and extending to both sides of the hand, shines forth like Meru, which is devoid of contact with other mountains; it possesses the perfection of yoga attained through the power of unimpeded planetary influence.
O Lord, your rosary is like a row of stars.

Anvaya: O Lord! This rosary of yours, situated in the middle of the hand and extending on both sides, devoid of contact with Mount Meru, and possessing the perfection of yoga through the power of unimpeded grasping, shines like a row of stars situated in the middle of the sky and extending on both sides of the hand, devoid of contact with Mount Meru, and possessing the perfection of yoga through the power of unimpeded planets.

O Lord, assuming the form of Kālabhairava, you bear a trident that is encircled by the movement of your flickering fingers which possess the splendor of blazing fire; as you desire to dance during the nights of universal dissolution, it takes on the beauty of a fresh cloud kissed by the rising sun.

O Lord! Wielding a trident encircled by the movement of your flickering fingers, desiring to dance during the nights of universal destruction, you assume the form of Kālabhairava and take on the beauty of a fresh cloud kissed by the rising sun.
Victorious is your dark-blue throat, O Śitikaṇṭha, possessing the luster of a freshly polished sapphire cleansed upon a whetstone.

In which [mountain], the serpent, possessing the luster of thick collyrium, assumes the graceful form of Kāliya as he is submerged within the heart of the daughter of Kalinda. O beloved, the fifty letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Kṣa' are doubled by way of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and thus possess eight forms.

One hundred and eight beads are proclaimed for them [the rosary] (*Tantrarāja*). **Anvaya:** O Śitikaṇṭha! Victorious is that neck of yours, possessing the luster of a fresh sapphire polished on a whetstone; upon which neck the serpent, with the hue of thick collyrium, assumes the grace of Kāliya when submerged in the depths of the Yamunā’s pool.
O Lord, although this throat of yours carries a most dangerous poison, it instantly bestows prosperity upon those who take refuge in your words;
therefore, the name Śrīkaṇṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds, is truly fitting for you.

Anvaya: O Lord! Although this neck of yours carries a virulent poison, since by its word it instantly bestows prosperity upon those who have taken refuge in you, therefore your name "Śrīkaṇṭha" (the one with a beautiful neck), whose fame is celebrated throughout the three worlds, is indeed most appropriate. Having reflected within myself, I rejoice—alas!—that the pure face of the Moon-crested Lord is playfully embraced around the neck by the poison. Translation: O Master! Even though this neck of yours bears a deadly poison, because it immediately bestows prosperity upon those who take refuge in your word, your title "Śrīkaṇṭha"—whose renown is spread across the three worlds—is truly fitting. Having reflected inwardly, I am filled with joy that the stainless face of the Moon-crested Lord is gracefully encircled by the poison at His throat. Alas, how wonderful!
[By him] who was skilled in mocking the grand display of bees that had momentarily approached, mistaking it for a lotus. || 15 ||

Anvaya: Hanta! Having reflected within that the face of the Moon-crested Lord—which was sportively embraced by the poison, skilled in mocking the pride of the bees seeking it under the delusion that it was a lotus—has repeatedly caused me to rejoice;

for just as the poison on Your head is well-known to be nectar and the pure water of the celestial river of flowers, so too, O Blessed One, do I believe [the embrace of the poison]. Translation: Ah! Having reflected within that the face of the Moon-crested Lord—which was sportively embraced by the poison, skilled in mocking the pride of the bees seeking it under the delusion that it was a lotus—has repeatedly caused me to rejoice; for just as the poison on Your head is well-known to be nectar and the pure water of the celestial river of flowers, so too, O Blessed One, do I believe [the embrace of the poison].
This nectar resides in your throat when it comes to the consoling of those who bow before you. || 16 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! Just as the water of the celestial river (Sumanaḥ-sravantī), though poison, is well-known as nectar upon Your head;
even so, O Blessed One, I consider this poison residing in Your throat to become nectar when used for consoling those who bow before You.
This is fitting, O Lord, that fire fell from Your mouth—which possesses a luster as pure as nectar—upon the body of Smara, who had committed the transgression of leaping across it.
Does not even a meteor fall upon that moon, the sole preceptor of the three worlds, when he desires to act? 17.

O Lord! It was only fitting that fire fell from Your face—which possesses a luster as pure as nectar—upon the body of Smara; for does not a meteor fall even upon the moon, who seeks to transgress the one Teacher of the three worlds? By good fortune, O Lord, this very Damayantī, though belonging to a people opposed [to You], bears within her sight a state of being enveloped in fire. By good fortune...
O Lord, treasure-house of wonders, salutations to you who, though delighting solely in the forest, are uniquely devoted to the protection of the world. 18.
O Lord! By good fortune (in this joy), even this Damayantī, who belongs to a hostile class of people, has become the object of your gaze, thus bearing the state of being dependent upon fire;
by good fortune, you too, though finding sole delight in the forest, are intent solely on protecting [the world]. O Blessed One, treasure-house of wonders! Salutations unto you!
For that fortunate one whose body is emaciated by penances, your fierce glances fall, O Master; they plunder [his sins].
The eyes of those with the gaze of innocent fawn-eyed maidens are treacherous; they are not the treasury of his fortitude. 19.
Anvaya: O Lord! Upon the body of that blessed one which has been emaciated by austerities, your three fierce eyes fall;
yet even the fierce glances of women with the eyes of innocent fawn-fawns cannot steal away his entire store of fortitude.
O Master, this was accomplished while your own play of the eye—cool with a flood of the nectar of compassion and removing old age and death—was indeed present.
The gods and the ignorant alike have exerted themselves in vain and without limit during the churning of the ocean of milk.

Anvaya: O Lord! While your glance alone—which is cool with a flood of the nectar of compassion and which removes old age and death—is present, the ignorant gods (vibudhas) have performed an endless effort in vain during the churning of the ocean of milk.
That it produced nectar from the white [ocean] and fire from the black is simply its own inherent power; likewise, it produces sugar from sugarcane.
And when it grows together with the poisonous muṣāṇa fruit, what fault does the rain commit therein? || 21 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! That your single eye produced nectar in the moon and fire in the sun—that is simply their own inherent nature.
(This is observed)—when nectar grows in the sugarcane and poison in the *uṣāṇa* fruit, does the rainwater commit any offense therein by growing along with them?

Surely, O Supreme Lord, at the time of churning the ocean, that nectar was drunk by you and not the Kālakūṭa poison; for even today it abides within the flow of your speech, within the play of your glance, and within the essence of your youthful compassion.
Anvaya: O Supreme Lord! Surely at the time of churning the ocean, that nectar alone was drunk by You, and not that Kālakūṭa poison;
for even today it dwells within the sequence of Your speech, the play of Your glance, and the fresh essence of Your compassion.
Truly, at the moment of Your favor, this eyebrow of Yours becomes restless and assumes an exceeding crookedness; [for] without it—
Furthermore, once the noose of Time has fallen unimpededly, there is no other recourse for those overwhelmed by fear. || 23 ||

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Truly, at the time of Your grace, this eyebrow of Yours attains excessive fickleness and assumes a state of great curvature; for without it, there is no other refuge for those overwhelmed by fear when the unobstructed noose of Time descends.
O Master, this matted lock of Yours, filled with the waters of the celestial river, possesses the luster of molten gold for the sake of nectar.
To whom was he not like the ocean of milk embraced by the mountain of the horizon, copper-red with the rising sun? || 24 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Filled with the waters of the celestial river (*surasarit*), possessing the golden-red luster of molten gold, this braid of yours (*jūṭa*), embraced by the twilight mountain (*velāśaila*) copper-red like a fresh cloud, is like the Ocean of Milk; for whom does it not become a source of immortality (*amṛta*)? (Indeed, for everyone—this is the meaning). O Lord!

This garland of human skulls on your crown shines, alas, with a brilliance as pure as nectar (*sudhā*); [it shines] upon the shore of the celestial river (*surasindhu*) shimmering within the midst of your braid.
Like a row of swans delighting in the pleasure of playful sport. || 25 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! This garland of human skulls, possessing a luster as pure as nectar, shines upon your crown like a row of swans sporting on the banks of the celestial river (Ganges) that plays within the midst of your matted locks.
O Supreme Lord, those very heads which were offered at the footstool of your feet by Brahmā and other teachers of the world now rest upon your own head.
That you make it an ornament—this is some peerless maturity of gratitude that triumphs. || 26 ||

Anvaya: O Supreme Lord! Those very heads which were offered at Your footstool by Brahmā and the other world-teachers, those same heads You make into ornaments for Your own crown; that certain maturity of Your gratitude is truly triumphant.
Even where fire does not go out despite water, where this great-flamed fire does not cook them, and where the moon does not find dullness—[in that state of Yours, Your gratitude shines].
Yet, O Śitikaṇṭha, even though it is slender, this crest of yours surpasses those two.

Anvaya: O Śitikaṇṭha! That tuft of hair of yours, wherein even by means of waters fire does not attain extinction, and wherein this very fire, though possessing great flames, cooks those waters of the Gaṅgā—by means of both those [water and fire], the moon, though diminished, does not experience languor; that tuft of yours is victorious.

Carrying fire upon the forehead and both water and the moon upon the head, and a formidable fragment of a skull on one side while a jar of nectar rests in the hand on the other—this wondrous attire of yours shines forth in its singular splendor. (28)

Anvaya: O Lord! This attire of Yours shines wondrously—You who bear the fire upon Your forehead and the water of the Gaṅgā, who bear the moon and a formidable fragment of a skull upon Your head, and who carry a severed head in one hand and a jar of nectar in the other;
You who provide for the rivers with gifts, who joyfully seize the earth and have attained an incomparable state, and who possess a great army gathered by the lord of serpents.
O jewel among kings, whose excellence could be praised here without you? (29)

O Lord! Among those who joyfully provide the ocean of milk as a gift for the rivers, who have attained an incomparable state by treading upon the earth, and who possess great armies gathered like lordly elephants—who else here besides you could be praised for the status of being the crest-jewel of kings? (The meaning is: none at all.
Even for those bearing poison, there is poison in their throats yet ornaments on their limbs; on their heads is the poison of the celestial river. Thus...
Even for you, whose abode is poison, the name of the Lord of Nectar shines as nectar for the ears of the virtuous.
Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Poison shines upon Your throat; ornaments shine upon Your limbs; the poison-bearing serpents shine upon Your body;
and the poison of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) shines upon Your head. Thus, although You are the sole abode of poison, the name "Lord of Nectar" (Amṛteśa) is nectar for the ears of the virtuous.

With our special wealth destroyed and nothing remaining but mere life-breath, we experience this calamity; for the ripening of karma is indeed adverse. Therefore, in this world, He alone is the refuge—the one whose necklace is a serpent, who has fashioned away delusion, and who has utterly severed the excess of sorrow.
With our specific wealth destroyed by adverse fate and with nothing remaining but mere breath, we experience calamity; for our ripening of karma is unfavorable.
Therefore, in this situation, that one who wears the serpent as a necklace—having dispelled delusion and removed excessive sorrow—is the only refuge for those like me.

Thus ends the nineteenth hymn, titled "Description of the Lord’s Form," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flowers of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmad Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
The Twentieth Hymn.

We worship with hymns that playful smile of Śambhu, which, through its auspiciousness, renders fruitless the dense, unerring mass of clouds born from a multitude of clouds; it is skilled in shattering the exhaustion of wandering in the desert of worldly existence. || 1 ||

We worship with hymns that playful smile of Śambhu, which—being fruitful through its auspiciousness and arising from a mass of clouds that are never empty—is a dense downpour that subdues [all else]; it is expert in shattering the exhaustion of wandering in the desert of worldly existence for embodied beings.
Or rather, we worship that which consists of speech—the immeasurable and unfathomable majesty of the Lord, whose boundaries transcend all speech and mind—for one such as I, of meager vision...
O Blessed One, as I touch [this] deeply and reflect within, it dawns upon me. || 2 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Lord! O Blessed One! Having reflected within ourselves—meager of vision though we are—upon Your glory, which is immeasurable and whose limits transcend all speech and mind, we worship with hymns that which emerges from You as the playful smile of Your speech.
This is the connection with the preceding verse.

By means of one who was like a radiant, great fruiting flower shining with the gift of never-failing, noble, and flowing rivers, you yourself brought joy to Upamanyu— who was free from pride, who had no other share, who was born of a mother whose thirst was constant, and who was perpetually afflicted by the exhaustion of ascetic toil.

Anvaya: O Unborn One! We worship with hymns that [Vilāsa] by which You Yourself gladdened Upamanyu—who was free from pride, devoted to none other, born of lifelong thirst, and constantly afflicted by fatigue—through Your playful smile, which resembled a shining flower on a great fruit from a noble tree that bestows gifts upon the lowly;
as before.
O Lord, it was by that very same grace which was so auspicious for Bhagīratha, and by which you first removed the calamity of his heat,
that you again brought relief to his ancestors through the great torrent of the celestial river held upon your head.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Lord! That playful smile, auspicious through its grace, by which you first removed the calamity of suffering from Bhagīratha, and again, by extinguishing the great torrent of the celestial river (*tridaśasindhu*) held upon your head, removed the calamity of suffering for his ancestors—that smile we worship with hymns; thus it connects with the preceding verse.

For the purpose of mocking Śamana, whose prowess was paralyzed by the suppression of his immense surge of pride, and for the sake of consoling the lord of men, who was helpless in the snares of Kīnāśa, he manifested simultaneously.

We worship with hymns that [Buddha], who simultaneously conceived in his mind both the means to quell the excessive pride of Śama— who was paralyzed by the onset of no small arrogance— and to console King Śveta (the Lord of Men), who was rendered helpless by the snares of Death; [and we worship him] who,
through the abundant splendor amassed by the weight of devotion to you, has caused the discernment of one whose heavy pride has grown to slip away.
When you were observing that [person] who was blinded by delusion, possessed of blind darkness, and filled with reckless audacity and passion. || 6 ||

We celebrate with hymns that laughter of yours which arose while you observed Andhaka— who was blinded by delusion, whose discernment had slipped away due to the heavy pride rooted in the vast abundance of wealth gathered through the weight of his devotion to you,

and who was driven by reckless audacity. That laughter of yours, which was irreproachable even at the moment of your wrath, [arose] as you embraced the Daughter of the Mountain, who was terrified by the fury growing upon Mount Kailāsa when it was shaken by the Lord of Laṅkā.
It rose up from his heart, which was brightened by serene clarity and a cheerful countenance.

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "We worship with hymns that smile which arose even at the time of his wrath from him whose face was bright with faultless and charming grace, he who was embraced by the Daughter of the Mountain—who was terrified by the rising fury of Mount Kailāsa shaken by the Lord of Laṅkā.
"Seeing Viṣṇu uprooting his own eye out of anger because you had deceitfully taken one of the thousand lotuses offered for worship, [he struck you]. This is the connection.
The sages, with serene minds, were intensely joyful.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Lord! Having observed Viṣṇu—who had deceitfully (under the guise of testing devotion unattached to anything else) plucked out one of the thousand lotuses presented by him for your worship—digging out his own eye, you, with a mind inwardly delighted, smiled intensely; all this, beginning with that smile, is as explained previously.

Seeing the young women whose self-restraint was shattered by the god of love arising from the sight of their peerless beauty, when the sages raised their hands in the month of Āṣāḍha and prepared to strike them out of anger, that which arose intensely within you—[that is what we seek]. (9)

We worship with hymns that smile which arose from you when the sages, their hands bearing the *āṣāḍha* grass, prepared to strike you in anger upon seeing their own wives— their mental composure shattered by the god of love born from the sight of your peerless perfection of form—
when your lower lip was darkened by the mass of light from the peak of the *kālakūṭa* poison situated near your hand.
That which formerly appeared, mocking the brilliance of the mass of rays from the cool-rayed moon resting upon the peak of the eastern mountain; || 10 ||

The smile that appeared— darkening his lower lip, which was already blackened by the mass of radiance from the peak of the Kalakuta poison situated nearby— and which mocked the splendor of the clusters of rays from the moon resting on the crest of the eastern mountain, is as described before;
[the smile] of the infant elephant-faced one, whose eyes were squinted by the particles of vermilion dust from his temples shaken by the wind from the flapping of his ears.
As soon as he saw this dramatic performance, which was so dear to his heart, it came to pass within your mind. || 11 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! When You beheld the desired performance of the dance by the child Gajāsya (the elephant-faced one), whose eyes were narrowed by the particles of vermilion dust from his temples shaken by the wind of his flapping ears—that smile which arose in Your mind, etc., as described before.

[This occurred] upon seeing Guhavāha (Kārttikeya) engaged in a dance accompanied by the rhythm of mṛdaṅga drums played by the mountains and others—O Master, [beholding him] who possesses the form of Bhairava at the time of the great dissolution... (Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a hymn to Śiva. The translation reflects the available portion.)
It manifested itself during the grand displays of your *tāṇḍava* dance. || 12 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Lord! during the grand displays of Your *tāṇḍava* dance—which assumes the form of Bhairava at the time of the great dissolution—that smile which manifested upon beholding Guha’s mount, the horse, as he engaged in a dance following the rhythm of the drums played by Śailādi (the son of the sage Śilāda, namely Nandin, a specific leader of the *pramatha* attendants), and so forth, is as described previously.

O Lord, the sky—whose darkness was intensified by separation from the clusters of stars as they were shattered by Your fierce staff-like arms—is made to appear once more with abundant light during Your dramatic enactments at the time of the end of the aeon. (13)

Anvaya: O Lord! That [laughter] of yours, by which even the sky—darkened by the separation of the clusters of stars being shattered by your fierce staff-like arms during the dramatic performance of the end of the Yuga—is again rendered full of abundant light;

that [laughter], which imitates the deep roar of the monsoon clouds capable of making the entire circle of the quarters resound; O Lord, what fear can there be for one whose heart is hard? (Note: The word *api* is understood from the context of the commentary as qualifying the sky, indicating that even such a vast expanse is illuminated.)
Which is capable of simultaneously ordaining [destruction] for the enemy and granting fearlessness to the timid. || 14 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! That [laughter of yours], which resembles the deep sound of the monsoon clouds capable of making the entire circle of the quarters resound, is simultaneously able to produce fear in one of hard heart and to grant fearlessness to the timid; that [is as described] previously. It is pure and settled upon the sandy bank of the throat, which possesses a dark hue intensified by the swallowing of the Kālakūṭa poison.
It spreads a mockery of the lunar disc clinging to a mass of clouds thick with water and free from gaps. || 15 ||

O Lord! That pure smile which rests upon the sandy bank of Your throat—its deep blue hue intensified by the swallowing of the Kālakūṭa poison—and which imitates the orb of the moon clinging to a mass of dense, water-laden clouds, [shines forth] as described previously. O friend, with my heart fixed on no other, I spent today, which felt like an eon, meditating upon the lord of my heart; and now, for the sake of union with the master of my life... [The rest of the verse continues: ...I shall spend this night, which feels like an eon, meditating upon the lord of my heart; and now, for the sake of union with the master of my life... [and so forth].
At dawn, sleep came before me like a friend. || 16 ||
(Anvaya: [Śrī Girijā], being greatly distressed by separation from you, related the account of her dream to her friend Jayā:

O friend Jayā! With a heart devoted to no other, meditating upon the lord of my heart, I have passed this night as if it were an entire aeon; then at dawn, for the sake of union with the lord of my life, sleep came before me like a friend.

At that moment, the Lord of my life appeared before my eyes, proclaiming with his very sweet glance the clarity of my mind; he set foot within me, who had been closed like a lotus by darkness, just as the sun enters a lotus-pond of its own accord.

Immediately at that moment, my Lord of Life, having approached me of his own accord with a gentle gaze that proclaimed the serenity of his mind, took his place before the path of my eyes— which were like a lotus pond closed by darkness— just as the sun appears before the path of a lotus pond.
"O lady with a face like the white-rayed moon, what is this that you have undertaken for my sake, which is exceedingly difficult even for sages, during these sports of wandering in the garden?"
Tell me, how can that slender frame of yours, which grows weary, endure such hardship? 18.
O lady with a face like the moon! Why has this deed, which is exceedingly difficult even for sages to perform, been undertaken by you for our sake?
O lady of delicate limbs! Tell us yourself, how can that slender frame of yours—which grows weary from the sport of wandering in gardens—endure such hardship?

Where is this form, as tender as the leaf of a young plantain tree, and where is that intense austerity which is beyond even the reach of the mind? Where is the slightly blossomed flower of a jasmine creeper, and where is the crushing by the harsh trunk of a mad elephant? (19)

O moon-faced one! Where is this form of yours, tender as the leaf of a young plantain tree, and where is that intense penance which is beyond the reach even of the mind? This is seen: where is the slightly blossoming flower of a creeper of choice blooms, and where is the crushing by the trunk of a rutting elephant?

How was the grasping of rough kuśa grass endured by her hand, which is as tender as a fresh sprout? And how did her feet, resembling the interior of a lotus, experience the exhaustion of traveling to sacred fords upon the ridges of rocky mountains? (20)
O fair-faced one! How was the grasping of the rough *kuśa* grass endured by this hand of yours, tender as a fresh sprout?
How did these feet, resembling the interior of a lotus, experience the fatigue of traveling to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) upon the rows of rocky peaks?
And how did that pair of breasts, upon which even a necklace felt like a burden, endure the flame of the bark-garment as hard as a thunderbolt? How is this possible?
Her body, born from delicate lotus stalks, became the site of suffering from the heat of the five fires.

Anvaya: *Yatra* (in which pair of breasts of yours) even a necklace (*hāraḥ*) is like a burden (*bhāra iva*), causing distress; how then did that pair of breasts of yours endure the flame of the bark-garment as hard as a thunderbolt? O slender-limbed one! How was this body of yours, born from delicate lotus-stalks, a target for the calamity of being scorched by the five fires?

With words such as these—interlaced with the moonlight of his teeth, dispelling the spreading darkness both within and without, sweetened by the nectar of a hidden smile—he seemed to offer consolation, having turned back her intense distress. (22)
With words— beginning with "Anvaya" and so forth— which were interwoven with the moonlight of her teeth, which dispelled the spreading darkness both outside and within,

and which were sweet with the nectar of an inward smile, she seemed to console me as I was being turned away from my intense distress; while I remained overcome by shame, gazing at the ground, with drops of perspiration rising like pearls, [she spoke] with a slight gesture of her hand.
Lifting up his face, he seemed as if to rain down a shower of nectar once again. || 23 ||

As my beloved, seeing the earth and overcome by the shame of his lineage, was raising my face— marked by rising drops of perspiration like pearls— with his hand, he desired once more to shower forth words like a rain of nectar;
at that very moment, O friend, that rogue, awakened by the cries of the cock, performed that act wherein he alone is my refuge.
Or rather, he is the Lord of Life, who takes away the entire multitude of living beings.

Friend! Just then, that rogue Creator, who awakened me with the cries of the cock, performed that deed wherein this very Lord of my life (Śrī Śambhu himself) has become my refuge; or else, in his absence, that other Lord of my life (Yama), who carries away the entire multitude of living beings, is my refuge.

Thus, as you listened to that account of her dream—which was told by the daughter of the Mountain King to Jayā while she suffered from the intense fever of separation—you, whose mind was overflowing with a weight of joy, stood concealed by a forest creeper. (Twenty-five verses form a *kulaka*.
*Anvaya*: Thus, as you listened to that account of her dream which was told by the daughter of the Mountain King to Jayā while she suffered from the intense fever of separation...

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: we celebrate with hymns that playful smile which arose from you, whose mind was overflowing with the weight of joy while you were concealed by forest creepers.

This [smile] is the life-restoring elixir for the flower-armed god [Kāmadeva], whose body was consumed by the flames of the fire of Hara’s roar; O young girl, it is a moment [endowed] with the essence of nectar.
For what purpose is this body, the ornament of the three worlds, being cast away? || 26 ||

Anvaya: O young girl! Why do you come at every moment, even though this body of yours—which is like nectar—has been licked by the flames of the fire of Hara’s *huṃkāra*, and which is the life-restoring herb for the flower-armed god [Kāmadeva] and the ornament of the three worlds? For you, who are adorned with wish-fulfilling trees, treasures, medicinal herbs, the cow of plenty, the thought-gem, and so forth, what is difficult to obtain?
That you seek through austerities a dwelling place that surpasses the splendor of your father’s abode. || 27 ||

Anvaya: O child! In the abode of your father—which is adorned with Kalpa-trees, treasures, the wish-granting cow, the thought-gem, and so forth, and which is a repository of glory surpassing the entire world—what object is difficult to obtain that you should seek through penances?

She, who is dearer to your father than even life itself, will surely not give rise to anger toward you, for she is well-versed in the science of policy; nor can it be imagined that this [hostility] was caused by anyone else.
Who would dare to commit such an insult as to forcibly pull the mane of a lion? || 28 ||

O child! You are dearer to your father than even his own life; therefore, having studied the science of ethics (*nīti*), he would not provoke your anger. An insult inflicted by another is not even conceivable for you, for who would dare to forcibly pull the mane of a lion?
Are the fruits of one’s faith, observance of vows, fire-sacrifices, charity, Vedic study, and pilgrimages to sacred sites ever borne by anyone but the fortunate?
O Gaurī, the meritorious deeds performed in the past are as white as a necklace of frost. || 29 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Gaurī! for which fortunate man have those previously performed meritorious deeds—which are white like frost or a pearl necklace and are rooted in vows, fire-offerings, charity, Vedic study, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and so forth—borne fruit, that you bring about grace through his penance? This is to be connected with the words "that you" (*sā tvaṃ*) at the end of the *kulaka* section.

Beholding the entire world being tormented by the humiliations of an unavoidable and miserable state of existence, who was it—possessed of vast resolve, supremely compassionate, with a body as radiant as the moon—that immediately caused a rain of gold? (30)

Beholding the entire world being tormented by the humiliation of an inescapable and miserable destiny, who was that supremely compassionate and magnanimous one, whose splendor was like the radiance of moonlight upon a moonstone, who immediately rained down gold— him whom you seek to propitiate through asceticism? They sing of whose pure [glory], arising from the protection of those who sought refuge when their power was obstructed by the fierce and terrible Time, [overcoming] the dualities...
In the nights of the great Kaumudī festival, washed by the moon, which are the constant abode of Nandana [the celestial grove], || 31 ||

Whose glorious and wondrous deed (*apadāna*)—arising from the protection of those who have sought refuge when their power was obstructed by the fierce and adverse times—is it that you, through your asceticism, bring to fulfillment for the sake of the gods in the Nandana grove? It is that deed which the couples sing of during the nights of the great Kaumudī festival, when everything is washed by the moonlight.
By what great Lord, bearing a body whose splendor is born from the three eyes and adorned with wondrous majesty, [is this achieved]?
The despondency caused by the arrows of unrestrained desire was suddenly dispelled by the great light of joy.

By which great Lord of blazing splendor—who bears a body possessing the beauty born from the eye of Atri and adorned with wondrous majesty—has the dejection and distaste caused by the arrows discharged by unrestrained Kāma been suddenly dispelled? You bring that very one to grace through your asceticism.
Blessed are those who, by their unerring manliness, have shattered the vast pride of Andhaka and thereby utterly dispelled the world's spreading despair!
Poets praise him who, by the fire of his unequalled prowess licked with ease, has reduced the cities of his enemies to ashes. || 33 ||

Anvaya: O Gaurī! Which person do the blessed poets praise—him whose abundant pride was shattered by unerring prowess, who caused the world’s despair to sprout forth as darkness, and who reduced the cities of his enemies to ashes with the fire of his valor and energy consumed by the sportful licking of the uneven flames of exertion? Him whom you seek to propitiate through penance?

Who, maintaining a body purified by bathing in the fire of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā) while never abandoning the practice of begging for alms, and whose limbs were covered with the skin of a deer, spent his time devoted to the practice of perfectly pure dharma as the crown jewel of the twice-born? (34)

Who was that lord of the twice-born, wearing his body purified by bathing in the Ganges, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī, who—never abandoning the practice of begging, devoted to the performance of pure dharma, and with his limbs covered in deerskin—spent his time? He whom you now seek to propitiate through your penance;

he who for a long time wandered about, his peaks made formidable by a garland of unbroken skulls and his body smeared with the dust of funeral pyres, being addicted to dwelling in the terrifying cremation grounds.
Who could [maintain] even an extremely severe vow while holding a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff in hand? || 35 ||

Who is this one who has long practiced such an exceedingly severe vow—he who is smeared with the dust of funeral pyres, whose crest is formidable with a garland of unbroken skulls, who is devoted to dwelling in terrifying cremation grounds, and who carries a skull-bowl and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his hands—whom you seek to propitiate through your penance?
I believe he is the fruit of a tree of merit accumulated over hundreds of previous lives, which remains unattainable for those lacking fortune. Of whom...
A mere glance from the corner of the eye is sufficient; indeed, verbal praise is beyond the scope of words. (36)

Anvaya: O Gaurī! I consider that even the mere glance from the corner of your eye is unattainable for those devoid of fortune, being the fruit of the tree of merit nurtured over hundreds of other births; yet its full appreciation through words is beyond the reach of speech.
You are the shore of the ocean of highly precious jewels of virtue, a river of loveliness, and born of a stainless lineage.
Through the power of your austerity, you bring about that grace which is the very ground of the abundance of pride arising from good fortune, prosperity, wealth, and the like.

"O you who are a shore of the ocean of loveliness for the waves of the sea of highly precious virtues and jewels, born of a stainless lineage, and the very ground of pride in the abundance of good fortune, prosperity, and power— who is he that you seek to win over by such asceticism? Thus, as he was eager to converse with the Queen through a sequence of witty and charming discourse, the youth— under whose pretext this was described— [was revealed].
Though restrained by your concealment, it overflowed due to its excessive weight. || 38 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O Lord! since that playful smile—which, though restrained by dissimulation, arose with great intensity in you who were thus eager for conversation with the Goddess through this sequence of stories smeared with clever wit and who were describing a young man under some pretext—has arisen with such intensity, may it remove my piercing heat and my thick darkness.
This is the connection with what follows.

Displaying his form and speaking words of compassion, he manifested a divine splendor imbued with the essence of nectar; by which he made his face like the edge of the unbroken white moon and the body of the Goddess radiant with the edges of her garments bristling with horripilation. (39)

O Lord! With that white smile of yours—resembling noble camphor, frost, a necklace of pearls, a white lotus, and the moon, the lord of the autumnal night—please effortlessly dispel my intense heat and darkness. (This pair of verses. *Anvaya:* O Lord!

Having displayed a divine form that possesses the essence of nectar and is compassionate toward the mountain, you who bring compassion to the peaks of the mountain... by which [smile]... (Note: The provided Sanskrit fragment for the *anvaya* appears to be incomplete or corrupted; the translation above interprets the intended meaning based on the context of the preceding verse and standard poetic conventions.)
With your smile, you have made the Queen’s face radiant with the splendor of the unbroken white moon, and you have made her body radiant with the splendor of a garment bristling with horripilation.

O Lord! With that smile, which is playfully manifested and resembles noble camphor, cooling snow, a pearl necklace, a white water-lily, and the moon—the lover of the autumnal night—please destroy my fierce fever and my dense darkness.
Having reflected that the thousand-rayed Sun resides within the lotuses of his eyes, and the thousand-eyed Hari resides within the lotuses of his feet,
and having beheld the Blessed Lady filled with wonder, may the smile of Śarva arise for me to attain my desired object.

Having reflected that the sun, who traverses a thousand paths, resides within the lotus-eyes of the Lord; and having reflected that Hari (Indra), who possesses a thousand eyes, resides within the lotus-feet of the Lord; and beholding the Blessed Lady filled with wonder—may the laughter that has arisen from the Lord Śarva lead to the attainment of my desire.

Thus ends the twentieth hymn, the *Hasita-stotra*, within the *Stuti-kusumāñjali* dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
This is the twenty-first hymn.

We pay homage to the Lord whose crest-jewel possesses stainless rays, and who is named Sarvamaṅgala (the Embodiment of All Auspiciousness); we honor the two halves of his body, which are joined together as one form with Umā, and which bear matching, unblemished marks of bracelets upon each other. 1.

We worship the two halves of the body of the Lord—each resembling the other—who has Uma occupying half his form; they are adorned with the jewel of the crown of stainless moonbeams, manifesting all auspiciousness, and marked by the bracelet of the serpent Śeṣa.
For the sake of liberation from rebirth, I revere that body of Śiva which is united with the daughter of the Mountain King, wherein the [Lord’s] face joins the severed fragment of [Uma’s] face.
The crescent moon situated upon his crown shares the same characteristics as the Goddess.

I bow for the sake of liberation to that body of Śiva, half of which is the Daughter of the Mountain, wherein the crescent moon resting upon the crown establishes a resemblance with the severed moon-like face of the Goddess;
on one side it is as pure as a crystal slab, while on the other it is radiant with freshly melted gold.
It assumes the grace of a peak of the snowy mountain, its one portion turned tawny by the mass of the rising sun's radiance. || 3 ||

The form of Ardhanārīśvara, in one half as pure as a crystal slab and in the other half radiant with freshly melted gold, possesses the beauty of a peak of the snowy mountain turned tawny by the mass of light from the rising sun;
wherein one side has eyes with the grace of startled deer, a chest adorned by blossoming jar-like breasts, and a waist—
His head was emaciated, yet adorned with a mass of hair as beautiful as a swarm of bees. || 4 ||

Beholding for a moment that hip-circle, which was full of effort and densely firm, and the feet, clearly beautiful with jeweled anklets, even Nandin suddenly experienced a supreme wonder such as had never occurred before. (A yugma. In that [half-part of the Goddess's form], one eye possesses the grace of a startled deer; the chest... [is]... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be fragmentary; the translation reflects the available portion of the verse and its commentary.)*

Beholding her waist adorned by blossoming jar-like breasts and endowed with slenderness; her head graced by a mass of hair as beautiful as a swarm of bees; her rounded hips broad and firm; and even her feet delightful with clearly visible jeweled anklets—Nandin too was suddenly struck for a moment by a supreme, unprecedented wonder.
There arose [a form] which,

with one half white with abundant ashes, possessed the splendor of Mount Kailāsa streaked by moonbeams; and with the other half, having applied saffron unguent to its body, bore the likeness of the Golden Mountain (Meru) with its crimson luster spread abroad.

Where one half, brilliant with abundant ashes, produces the splendor of Mount Kailāsa as if sprinkled by moonbeams, while the other half, its body colored with applied saffron, produces the impression of a golden mountain with its reddish glow spread abroad;
where [the Lord], though possessing a luster as beautiful as gold, bears a form embraced by the auspicious limbs of a serpent whose beauty is unfolding.
The crown, bearing a beautifully risen moon, instantly provides a mutual comparison with [his face]. || 7 ||

Although it possesses a golden and delightful luster, it is embraced by the auspicious limbs of a serpent that is emerging; and while bearing a crown that reflects the beautiful moon, it suddenly establishes a mutual comparison with it.
It is a marvel how your beloved possesses such extraordinary boldness in bestowing welfare upon those afflicted by the torments of worldly existence; thus they have come together with one another.
Wherein a single sentence, emerging from a single mouth, brings about a state of aesthetic harmony (sāmarasya). || 8 ||

The *anvaya* (syntactic connection) is as follows: [Where the Lord speaks to the Goddess: "O beloved! To bring about the welfare of those suffering from the afflictions of worldly existence (*bhava*), you have attained a certain extraordinary boldness. [And where the Goddess speaks to Śiva: "O beloved! It is a marvel that to accomplish the desired aim of those suffering from the afflictions of worldly existence, you have attained a certain boldness. [Thus it is said by the two, Śiva and Pārvatī, who are united.]
Where the words emerging from their single mouths bring about a mutual state of aesthetic fusion;

where the left half of the body, through the pressure of a firm embrace, trembles as if out of fear of the serpent [Śeṣa]; and where the right half likewise shines with manifest horripilation, as if bathed in the cool waters of the celestial Ganges.

Wherein one half [of her body] trembles limb by limb from the embrace of the cloud as if out of fear of a serpent, while the other half likewise shines with manifest horripilation from the embrace of the cloud as if bathed in the cool celestial river;
where on one side there flashes the coiled form of a serpent’s hood, while on the other there is a garland of blue lotus petals; where on one side the ash manifests as a cosmetic ointment.
Whiteness and the application of sandalwood paste belong to the next world.

In one place it deposits the poison of blackness upon the throat, even though a sectarian mark made of musk is applied elsewhere; in one place there is the stainless luster of bone garlands, while in another there spreads forth a string of pearls. 11.

In one place there is the elephant’s hide dripping with blood; in another, the imperishable saffron-colored garment. Indeed, even such mutually contradictory things as these attain unity in that which possesses manifold splendors. (Tilaka) The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: where, on the one hand, the coiled form of a serpent’s body flashes forth, and on the other, a garland of blue lotus petals flashes forth; likewise, on the one hand, [there is] ashes...

On one side, the body-unguent spreads a whiteness that is actually the staining of sandalwood; on the other, the white mark made with musk likewise spreads a whiteness. On one side, the blackness of the throat bestows a dark hue upon it; on the other, the forehead-mark made with musk likewise bestows that same blackness.
On one side, the stainless luster of bone-garlands radiates forth; on the other, the stainless luster of pearl necklaces radiates forth. On one side, there is the elephant-hide dripping with blood.

In that place of manifold splendor, even things that are mutually contradictory— such as a garment that is imperishable in the next world and a garment dyed with safflower— attain unity. There, while the whiteness of the teeth and the blackness applied as collyrium to the eye on the forehead coexist, there is yet another [quality] in the redness of the hands, feet, and lips.
No new distinction arose between them. || 13 ||

In this [maiden], although there was whiteness in her teeth, blackness produced by collyrium in her forehead-eye, and redness in her hands, feet, and lips, no other new distinction arose between them. Did the luster of her neck, resembling a bee, leave half its portion and take up residence in half of her hair? Or did the golden-hued luster leave one half and remain in the other?
Having abandoned her hair, did she settle upon a certain part of her throat? || 14 ||

Just as there was a golden water-pot in his left lotus-hand, so too was there certainly a jar in his right; the Lord, whose mind is solely intent on play, surely carries that very same one upon his chest out of his own free will.

That very world which existed at the end of the age, and whose fullness was appropriate here in the middle portion, has surely flowed down from that intensity and come to rest upon her firm and solid hips.

In that very place, the lords of the Gaṇas formed such intentions at their first encounter as follows: they remained there until Bhr̥ṅgīśa withdrew his gaze from Ambikā’s lotus feet during the act of prostration. (Cakkalaka) Anvaya: Did the luster of the neck, resembling a bee, leave half its portion and take up residence in the other half of the Goddess’s hair? And likewise—

Did the golden luster of his matted locks (in the form of *kaparda*), having abandoned half of itself, settle upon the region of his throat? Just as there was a golden jar in his lotus-like left hand, surely there was likewise a golden jar in his right; does the Lord, whose mind is intent solely on play, bear that very same jar upon his chest out of his own free will? It was here, at the end of the Yuga, that the entire world existed.

Did that very fullness which was appropriate for her waist, having flowed down with such intensity, come to rest upon her firm and rounded hips? Such were the thoughts that the lords of the Gaṇas formed even at their first encounter,
until Bhṛṅgīśa withdrew from his prostration before Ambikā’s lotus feet.
In that act of salutation, whether it be "Is this Śiva?", or "Is this Śivā?", or "Are these both Śiva and Śivā?"—the speech of the wise remains truly indistinguishable;
the speech of the wise remains truly indistinguishable. (18)

In this context of worship, the question "Is this Śiva? Or is it Śivā? Or are they both Śiva and Śivā? becomes truly inconceivable even for the learned; therefore, in this matter, the speech of the wise is indeed beyond comprehension. "One breast with its natural fullness, one eye marked by collyrium, and a body endowed with slenderness"—by these three signs, she is determined [to be the Goddess].
Even where there is grammatical analysis, its status as an indeclinable shines forth entirely unimpaired. || 19 ||

Inference (*anvaya*): Where one breast possesses its proper elevation, where one eye is marked by collyrium, and where even the body is endowed with slimness—by these three signs, although the distinction between them is determined, their state of non-differentiation (*avyayatva*) shines forth unimpaired. Where there was certainly oneness in the heart itself, that very same oneness has fallen again into speech and body; for whatever exists in the heart of the virtuous, that alone manifests externally.
Whatever is appropriate for speech, that alone is also appropriate for the instrument of speech.

"O beloved Śivā, this mind of mine has taken root in you, and my physical form grants joy to your heart"—wherein such mutual address bestows upon their faces a loveliness made charming by a shared smile. (21)

May that non-duality—which is faultless and heart-pleasing, which is intent on the possibility of the unsurpassed mutual aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) of the two Śivas, and which is the means for achieving the highest wonder—be for the sake of uniting you with Śiva and Śivā. (The *tilaka*) *Anvaya*:
Certainly, that very unity which existed in the hearts of the two Śivas has now descended even into their speech and bodies.

For that which exists in the hearts of the virtuous is the very same that manifests in their speech, and what is in their speech is likewise appropriate for their actions. O Beloved! O Śivā! This mind of mine is rooted in you, and this body of mine, which grants joy to my heart, is likewise rooted in you. Thus, "O Śivā, O Beloved, my mind is rooted in you, and my body, which bestows delight upon my heart, [is rooted in you]"—in this way they address one another.

May that faultless and heart-pleasing non-duality (the state of Ardhanārīśvara), which spreads the common quality of being delightful through smiles upon the face, and which serves as the means for the supreme wonder of Śiva and Śivā— who are intent on the possibility of their unsurpassed mutual aesthetic fusion— be for your auspicious union.

Wherein the characteristics of the two Lords are indeed distinct from one another—some perceptible and others imperceptible—that most wondrous literary artistry (sāhitya) would cause whose hair to stand on end? 23.

Indeed, where else but in the presence of the Blessed One could unobservable characteristics be perceived as distinct characteristics? Who would not have their hair stand on end at this most wonderful union of Śiva and Śivā—
[a union] which bears the upper portion darkened by the luster of the sapphires in the matted-hair crown, while the lower portion is tawny with the flames of fire in the middle?

With a complexion as white as nectar, that cloud of yours—which bears the beauty of Indra’s bow because the curved crescent moon is reflected within it—may it rain down the nectar of joy for you two, O Blessed Ones. 24.

May that breast of the Blessed One shower the nectar of joy upon you— wherein the crescent moon, reflected therein, assumes the splendor of Indra’s bow: its upper portion dark with the luster of the sapphire in the crown of the serpent Ananta, its lower portion reddish-brown with the flames of fire, and its middle possessing a brilliance as clear as nectar, appearing curved.

Thus ends the twenty-first hymn, the *Ardhanārīśvara-stotra*, within the *Stutikusumāñjali* dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
[The twenty-second hymn follows.]

He was celebrated out of curiosity by groups of poets skilled in the arts of poetic composition; he was longed for by those who perform virtuous deeds, whose fame is like the moon to the night-lotus of Kaumudī.
He whose tawny neck was once the dwelling place of the serpent Kāliya on the banks of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) in Kerala;
he who wears the hide of an elephant as his garment, which served as the means for exhausting the sacrificial rites that destroy all sins. || 2 ||

By the Kinnaras—those who are like fire to the forest of the Kekayas, and who are like poets, Kubera, and Keśava—he was made to cry out as he was capable of drawing away the impurity during the process of swallowing the Kālakūṭa poison. || 3 ||

With his earrings resting upon his temples like door-bolts, he has blunted the impurity of even the sharp-edged discus of Brahmā; he is the destroyer of Death and Desire, and the hollows of his matted locks are variegated by the moon, the lover of the night-lotuses.
In the forest, he sported out of curiosity with the sweet warbling of amorous women intoxicated by *kāpiśāyana* wine, and with the tumultuous chorus of warbling cuckoos and whistling bamboo;
amidst clusters of jasmine buds, *kadamba*, *ketakī*, and *kāñcanāra* blossoms; and with the flower-buds of *karṇikāra* and *karabīra*, as well as white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses.

With *kiṃśuka* flowers possessing the luster of a monkey’s cheek, with *kesara* flowers as tender as the bud of a lotus, and with *kovidāra*, *kuṭaja*, and *kaṇeraka* flowers, his hair was entirely strewn and disheveled. (A yugma) With black *kuṇḍalika* flowers serving as stiff bodices, he fashioned lovely bracelets from *kubjaka* flowers.
He was like a young lion cub, cruel with his claws upon the hollows of the frontal globes of elephants torn open in rage.
With his throat-socket adorned by his beloved, who was lovely with her golden girdle and tinkling bells, he feigned the guise of a Kirāta in sport, provoking Arjuna (Kirīṭin) through his artifice.

While the place was defiled by crows, vultures, and kurara-birds, and rendered foul by the performance of cruel deeds, he— desiring [to help] those whose bodies were wounded— drew out their bitter agony with compassion.
May he, who is skilled in creating compassion for those terrified by the afflictions of the servant of Death made harsh by anger,

be capable of performing the work of an axe that cuts away the very root of the sprout of the stain of the Kali age. (11) [A group of eleven verses] He is celebrated out of curiosity by the assemblies of poets, experts in the arts of poetic skill, whose fame is like the moon to the night-lotuses of the Kaumudī.
Longed for by those who perform virtuous deeds, he whose tawny neck is like that of the serpent Kāliya on the banks of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) near the hair-like forests of Kerala;

who brings an end to the exhaustion of the sacrifice that destroys sin; who wears the hide of an elephant as his garment; who was praised by the Kinnaras—who are skilled in the fire-rites at the abode of Fire (Mount Kailāsa)—as well as by poets, Kubera, and Keśava; he is capable of removing all impurity.
With his earrings resting upon temples that served as door-sockets, having blunted the impurities of even the whetted saws of the Creator, the destroyer of Time and Desire,

with cavernous matted locks variegated by the moonlight of the night-lotus, he sported out of curiosity in the forest amidst the warbling of flute-like bamboos and the sweet, tumultuous cries of cuckoos, which were like the playful cooing of amorous women intoxicated by *kāpiśāyana* wine.

With clusters of buds from the *kundaka*, *kuḍmala*, *kadamba*, *ketakī*, and *kāñcanāra*; with *karṇikāra* and *karabīra* shoots; with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and day-blooming lotuses; with *kiṃśuka* trees possessing the luster of a monkey’s cheek; with filaments as tender as the calyxes of lotuses; with *kovidāra*, *kuṭaja*, and *kaṇeraka* flowers—[he was] one whose hair was scattered and bound, wearing black earrings and stiff bodices, and fashioned lovely bracelets upon his bent arms.
