He whose throat was once a thorn to the cruel young lioness dwelling in the hollows of the frontal globes of elephants slain in his wrath; whose neck was embraced by the lovely Girijā, who shone with golden girdles and tinkling bells; who, feigning to be a Kirāta for the sake of sport, provoked Arjuna (Kirīṭin) through that very ruse;
and who is now sought as a refuge by those whose bodies were mangled and who were defiled by crows, vultures, and ospreys during that cruel deed—[to him, I bow].

May the skillful Maheśvara—who, out of compassion, draws forth the bitter torments [of the world] while appearing compassionate yet fearful toward the afflictions caused by the servants of Kṛtānta (Yama) made harsh by anger—be capable of performing the task of an axe for cutting down the root-stalk of the plantain tree that is the stain of the Kali age. May he, whose crown-tip is formidable, fashioned from the skeletal remains of the family of crooked night-lotuses in the river of time; and who is being scattered upon by the hands of Kātyāyanī...
May the particles of camphor and saffron produce compassion. || 12 ||

May that Lord, whose terrifying crest-tip is fashioned from the skeletal remains of the family of night-lotuses in the winding river of the lineage [of his devotees], and upon whom fall the scattered particles of camphor and saffron offered by the hands of Kātyāyanī, bestow compassion.
Thus concludes [the hymn] composed by the great Kashmiri poet, the illustrious Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary titled *Premamakaranda*. Of the Blessed One...
In the *Stutikusumāñjali* of Maheśvara, the hymn consisting of verses beginning with the letter 'ka' is complete.
This twenty-third hymn,
which awakens the world from its distress and adorns the beautiful crest of Vidhu (the Moon), I praise Giriśa— who bestows supreme bliss— with trembling awe.

I praise Giriśa, who in the world of the lineage has awakened the distressed, whose beautiful crest is adorned by the crescent moon, who is filled with intense compassion, and who is supremely intent on bestowing bliss; for among the great,
no other refuge prevails when the mind has been treated with contempt, yet he indeed swiftly takes refuge in you, the Great One.
The speech of Bharata is sweet.

It follows that when the mind of the great has been treated with contempt, even their supreme refuge is not able to prevail suddenly; for your sweet speech, O Great One, possesses a majesty that is sweet. A woman with eyes as lovely as a red lotus, most skillful in the art of captivating the eyes, was like a blade of grass to you when you were delighted by her, having risen to offer yourself to that joyous woman.
For those who worship [him]. || 3 ||

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! When You have arisen for the sake of bestowing joy and are delighted, that woman—whose eyes are sweetly reddened and who is most skillful in the act of captivating the eyes—becomes as insignificant as a blade of grass to those who worship You.
May I obtain Your compassion, which is pure and full of flavor, and which, marked by the moon upon Your crest, indeed offers words of mercy with ever-new freshness.
Let it be attended to. || 4 ||

O you whose crest is marked by the moon! For my sake, alas, resort to that compassionate, pure, and eloquent mercy which, through its novelty, bestows upon those who take refuge in it a voice of compassion. Let your speech, which washes away sin, be skillful in the act of bringing about newness; for in it, even the sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans, once attained, is seen as something merely to be abandoned.
Of the virtuous. || 5 ||

O All-pervading Lord! May my speech, which has washed away my sins, take delight in the clever exposition of Your new [teachings], wherein even the sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans falls into the category of things to be abandoned by the virtuous (meaning it is as insignificant as a blade of grass).
O Lord, may fear never again be taken away by You, whose form is auspicious; for You have fashioned for the wise only that auspiciousness which is intent upon benefiting others.
It has been explained. || 6 ||

O All-pervading Lord! By You, who possess an auspicious form, has that which is beneficial for the future—not consisting of mere worldly assistance but rather true welfare—never been fashioned for those virtuous ones who tremble before You?

And as for me, have You not long ago ordained what is beautiful, excellent, and pleasing? O You whose splendor is illuminated by stainless light, come now and bring about for me the pure fruition of that [past deed], since I have fallen into a state devoid of discernment.

Anvaya: O you whose speech is resplendent with stainless brilliance! When I have entered into the state of discernment (*viveka*), why was that which is beautiful, delightful, and pleasing not performed by you for a long time? O All-pervading Lord! Having considered my ripening [of karma], come to my desire;
just as the sun, whose body shines with unvanquished splendor, causes the lotus to bloom, so do you act. By that path, do not be, do not be averse; direct your gaze toward me.
to me || 8 ||
Anvaya: O Aparājita! Just as the sun makes the lotus possess a radiant and blossoming form, so too, O Bhava, do not turn your face away from me; look upon my gaze.
I do not find a direction free from the serpents of sense-objects; always lamenting like Nala for his peacock, and surrounded by serpents like a serpent-lord.
By darkness. || 9 ||

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Like a snake (bheka) that incessantly hisses, and like a serpent (pannaga) ever shrouded in darkness, this I, deprived of sense-objects, find no direction free from anxiety.

Therefore, may people quickly take refuge in the Compassionate All-pervading Lord—who is free from the quarrels of darkness, who is always accompanied by the speech of the swan-like Lakṣmī, and who is endowed with the essence of sung melodies.

May this song of mine, its passion aroused, quickly take refuge in that Lord—who is ever accompanied by Umā, who is free from strife through his own nature, who is full of compassion, and who possesses a melodious voice like that of a swan;
for, O God of noble mind, people find delight only in doing what you, being compassionate, do. O Protector, do not abandon us to our helplessness; we bow to You.
Sequence: O noble-minded one! O Lord! This person finds delight only in performing that which is real (the true reality).

O All-pervading One! You should turn toward us with compassion; do not turn away from us. Let there be salutation to you! When shall my mind, which is stained by blemish, hear your roar—which spreads like the splendor of Bhava and is like nectar—and [thus] cast off all fear of Bhava?
I release. || 12 ||

Anvaya: O Bhava! I, whose mind is defiled by blemish, having heard your sound—which is white with the expansion of your splendor and comparable to nectar—when shall I cast off all fear of you [from saṃsāra]?
O Lord whose light is immeasurable, show me your face, which is like the moon; tell me, who is the Lord of the World capable of gladdening the world? Who might become such a Lord of the World?
The others have different names. || 13 ||
Anvaya: O Amitābhāsa! Having displayed a face resembling the moon, bestow your glance upon me. O Lord!
Tell me, who else indeed in this world is capable of gladdening the earth? Surely no other;
for his fame eclipses that of even the wise, or rather, it eclipses his misfortune. His body does not appear as a misfortune during this time of splendor.
One passes away before one's allotted lifespan has run its course. || 14 ||

O Hara! I bow to that very one of unassailable fortune, O Lord, who remains ever free from dejection amidst your hymns of praise—which always extinguish the burning dust consisting of the noose of afflictions—and who thus possesses a truly noble mind.
(A yugma) *Anvaya:* O Hara! He who is never despondent amidst your praises—which always pacify the burning dust consisting of the noose of afflictions—is a person of excellent intellect.
He does not become dishonored, for his glories obscure his misfortunes; at this time when his body is filled with grace, his youth does not pass away into calamity.
O Lord! I bow only to him whose fortune remains unassailed.
Now, O Destroyer of Madhu, the forest alone is my refuge for the sake of propitiating you. Since my heart is restrained, it is fitting for me to bow, having shattered all delusion. 16
O destroyer of Madhu! Since my heart is now restrained, for the sake of propitiating you, the forest alone—characterized by *nameru* trees—is my refuge.

It is not a palace of serpents, nor is it the Nandana grove of boundless great prosperity; rather, it is a fresh forest, possessing excellent qualities, intended solely to bring about your excellence.
O God, I delight [in you]. || 17 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! To me, whose great prosperity is eternal and boundless, the abode of serpents is not pleasing; even the Nandana grove, with its eternal and boundless splendor, is not pleasing. (I), however, delight only in making Your new abode straight and endowed with radiant virtues.
O Dispeller of Obstacles, grant me the name that is most excellent, enchanting, stainless, and beneficial. Do not lead me even to a honored station; rather, honor me with Your sorrow-stricken glance.

O You who have transcended all obstacles! Grant me Your stainless, auspicious, and boon-bestowing name, which removes sin. O All-pervading Lord, do not lead me away even from that highly honored state;

look upon me with Your pure gaze. I consider Your name—which delights the heart, is free from disease, and removes fear—to be like the Malaya breeze to one distressed by heat, or like fragrant flowers to a forest of white blossoms. 19.
O Anāmaya! Just as one perceives the fragrant Malaya breeze through its flowers, or a pure forest through its blossoms, I perceive your name—which removes fear of Yama and gladdens the heart.

O Lord of those bowed down by the gods whose crowns are adorned with the light of the crescent moon, O You whose intent is the destruction of sin, gradually destroy my calamity; [grant me] Your state.
Lead me! || 20 ||

O Lord adorned by a digit of the moon! O You who are bowed to by which gods whose crowns are decorated? (Indeed, by all! O Lord! O You whose heart is the destroyer of sins! Gradually destroy my calamity; do not [leave me], lead me to Your own abode.

If You, who are worshipped by sages, do not mercifully protect me—who am exceedingly distressed—then [I have no hope] in Yama, who is skilled in granting grace and capable of pacifying various fears. If You do not protect me with compassion, [what can be done]?

O Lord, you who are skilled in bestowing grace! O you who are worshipped by sages! If you do not protect me with compassion, then Yama will not be able to provide manifold peace for the pacification of the fear instilled in me.

For the lord of the earth, having subdued his subjects whose natural dispositions were provoked by intoxication, protects the circle of the world while restraining his enemies by force. He who [protects] you—[he alone can grant such peace].
From here, [attain] serenity. || 22 ||
Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! He who has obtained Your grace from here becomes a sovereign of the earth with his enemies subdued by force;

gladdening his subjects whose adversities have been conquered, he protects the circle of the earth without decay. For by him Yama (the God of Death) is restrained, and by him even the Moon is surpassed; filled with joy, he performs noble deeds through the path of virtue.

They praise the stainless one. || 23 || Indeed, in this world, even Dhanvantari and others have always been unable to remain effortless regarding the objects of their own or others' memories; for how else could this most treacherous epilepsy of worldly existence be cured, except by a mere fragment of the compassionate glance from the eye of Śambhu?

O Lord, I bow to You, who have adorned the world with Your body that blossoms with beauty and delights the people; may he who is skilled in Your beloved hymns of praise be free from fear. (Yugma) Indeed, by him [the hymn], Śamana (Death) was subdued; by him, whose luster is unceasing and who has attained joy, even *śama* (tranquility) was attained. His conduct, noble and well-established, was practiced upon the auspicious path.

People praise that stainless one—O Bhava! O Īśa! O Abhayastava!—that man who becomes proficient in your beloved hymns; him, whose body is adorned with the blossoming of devotion, who has embellished the earthly realm and gladdened the world, I bow to.

I worship that pure and radiant form of yours, which brings the virtuous to the state of being recipients of perfection, like a lion-king among deer that wards off the elephant of worldly existence, and which leads the multitude of people toward stainless excellence.
Repeatedly with fresh [offerings]. || 25 ||

O Lord, who is like a lion to the elephant-like hosts of obstructors! I, a man of merit, repeatedly worship Your stainless, white, and radiant form, which leads all people to the state of attaining perfection. O Destroyer of the insatiable Smara (the god of love), this hymn of Yours, which creates aesthetic delight and is unimpeded, always makes the hearts of the virtuous—who dwell in heaven—free from fear.
With intense surges of emotion. || 26 ||

Anvaya: O devourer of Smara who is without obstruction! That hymn of yours which always produces aesthetic delight for the virtuous—this very hymn of yours, which removes fear, causes even the hearts of those dwelling in heaven to be filled with intense longing.
I, whose mind is now free from defect, worship your two feet, which cause the agitation of the Kali age and are the refuge for the removal of sin; alas, [I worship them] completely.
Possessing the gait of a noble, boon-granting elephant king. || 27 ||

Anvaya: "Alas! I, whose mind is now free from blemish, take refuge in your two feet—which cause the trembling of the Kali age, which are the sole sanctuary against sin, and which possess the gait of the king of excellent elephants.
Thus ends [the hymn] to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.

The hymn in the form of a *śṛṅkhalā* band composed as a handful of flowers of praise is complete. O Sarasvatī, manifest the power within my speech, which has become the very essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). O Goddess, worship [the Lord] with hymns that are the essence of the hearts of all the gods, and [thereby] dispel fear. (24)

Anvaya: O Sarasvatī! You, whose essence has fully arisen, manifest your power within my speech. O Goddess! Praise Bhava with hymns—the essence of the hearts of all the gods. Worship the Lord who is white as the dust of unceasing ashes, who has attained great auspiciousness, who is as white as the bull of Agaja (Śiva), and who is the stainless dispeller of fatigue. Translation: O Sarasvatī! You, whose inner essence is fully awakened, reveal your majesty within my words. O Goddess! Honor Bhava with your praises—he who is the very core of the hearts of all the deities. Worship the Blessed One, who is radiant with the white ash of smearing, who has achieved the attainment of supreme auspiciousness, who is as fair as the bull of Agaja (Śiva), and who is the stainless queller of weariness.

O Blessed One (Vāṇī)! You should worship Him who is white with the dense dust of ashes, who has assumed the great form of Śiva, who is the queller of fatigue, whose luster is stainless, and who is as white as a mountain-born elephant; that Lord of the rivers who was capable of granting a supreme and great body—worship that Lord, O Goddess, who is not distressed by those who are wretched. Anvaya: He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahāśamalābham, śramaśamanam, vimalābham, agajādhavalam bhaja; yaḥ nadīnām nātham anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ dātum prababhūva, tam anuttamahāvapuṣaṃ na dīnaṃ devi bhaja. He bhagavati! tvam aviralabhasmarajodhavalam, vihitamahā
Anvaya: O Goddess! Worship that Lord who was capable of bestowing upon the young Upamanyu a body possessing unsurpassed grace and who is neither wretched nor lacking in majesty.

The sentiment of devotion toward You, O Goddess, triumphs as a great nectar for the virtuous, and it is pleasing to the hearts of those dwelling at the soles of Your feet, cleansing the mire of the Kali age. Sloka: The sentiment of devotion toward You, O Goddess, triumphs as a great nectar for the virtuous; it is pleasing to the hearts of those dwelling at the soles of Your feet, [cleansing] the mire of the Kali age. (4)

Anvaya: O Lord! Victorious is that essence of devotion to you, which is as delightful as the great nectar and which removes the mass of impurities for the virtuous dwelling at the soles of your feet. Casting forth your eye, destroy the darkness within me—you who have struck down the great poison of the god of love—so that, with delusion destroyed, I may rejoice among enemies and never again in adversities. Translation: O Lord! Victorious is that essence of devotion to you, which is as delightful as the great nectar and which removes the mass of impurities for the virtuous dwelling at the soles of your feet. Casting forth your eye, destroy the darkness within me—you who have struck down the great poison of the god of love—so that, with delusion destroyed, I may rejoice among enemies and never again in adversities.

Anvaya: O destroyer of delusion! Having raised your third eye—which has struck down the great and formidable [god of love]—remove my darkness, so that I may never again take delight in "viṣameṣu" (difficulties or enemies). When you, the granter of boons, are present, beautiful women with chowries waving in their hands attend upon the person in the assembly; yet even he, though surrounded by such women, finds delight only in solitude. Translation: O destroyer of delusion! Raising your third eye, which has struck down the great and formidable god of love, remove my darkness, so that I may never again find pleasure in "viṣameṣu"—that is, in enemies or difficulties. When you, the bestower of boons, are present, beautiful women with chowries waving in their hands attend upon the person in the assembly; yet even such a person finds true delight only in solitude, away from them.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! While You, the Giver of Boons, are present, the women with beautiful smiles, their hands moving the chowries, attend upon the people in the assembly; and those people, in turn, delight them in private. O Blessed One, bear a smile upon Your face that is as white as the mass of moonbeams and mocks the waters of the celestial river; let it not be a mockery here [of our own joy]. Translation: O All-pervading Lord! While You, the Giver of Boons, are present, the women with beautiful smiles, their hands moving the chowries, attend upon the people in the assembly;
and those people, in turn, delight them in private.
O Blessed One, bear a smile upon Your face that is as white as the mass of moonbeams and mocks the waters of the celestial river; let it not be a mockery here [of our own joy].
O Blessed One! You bear upon your face a smile white as the mass of moonbeams, rivaling the waters of the celestial river; in this matter, may you not be mocked (or delayed).

Having effortlessly cast aside my eyebrows, which have been compared to the fickleness of the God of Love, I shall utterly destroy the dense clouds of the glances of those women with sun-like eyes; I cannot endure them any longer.
O Lord! Having playfully cast aside the eyebrows of those sun-eyed women—which possess the fickleness of Cupid—dispel the dense clouds; I cannot bear them any longer.
O Lord, as I remember the path of the Sun’s son (Yama), my heart breaks slightly while listening to the words of the servant of Yama; what shall I do, O Destroyer of Cities? 9.

Anvaya: O Purahara! I, whose speech has become like that of a servant of Yama, remember the path of the son of the Sun (the Yamunā)—[here there is no use of the genitive case because the path is remembered merely as such, and not for the purpose of going upon it, just as in the phrase "I remember [him] sleeping in the reed-huts"]—and as I remember it from afar, my heart breaks; O Lord! what shall I do?
O Lord!
Alas, him who proclaims your greatness with beautiful words of praise— him, the bringer of the accomplishment of hundreds of auspicious things, I shall carry upon my head before long.
Worship Him, the source of the universe, who is capable of shattering the fear of worldly existence for those possessed of devotion, and who ordains welfare even when fate is adverse.

Worship that Source of the World, who, by showing the exceedingly auspicious path to those devoted to him, is capable of shattering the fear of worldly existence; who ordains welfare even when fate is adverse;
who is a forest fire to the tree of passion; who bears the moon, the nectar-rayed one, upon his head; and who consumes the poison of endless sorrow for those who offer their devotion at his feet. 12

Anvaya: O fortunate ones! Worship that Lord—who is a forest fire to the tree of Madana, who bears the moon (the bearer of nectar) upon his head, who is a fire to the poison of worldly misery, and to whom light is offered by those who bow before him.
Bestow the subduer of the ocean; destroy and shatter desire; spread the quelling of fear from Indra; and build a city.
Having slain Kāma. || 13 ||
Thus, whatever was performed by the compassionate Hara for the welfare of the world—revere that great deed of his with words of praise that dispel all suffering.

(Yugmam) [Give the lover of the river to the sage Upamanyu, who is like a child—by the rule "loṭ loṭo hisvau vā ca tadhvamoḥ," the imperative suffix *loṭ* is used for frequency of action, and its substitutes *hi* and *sva* are applied; therefore, one should understand forms such as *vitara* (imperative) and *śakalaya* (causative), etc. He bestowed [the gift]; he shattered the tranquility [he shattered it].

"By all means, destroy desire; spread the fame of Dhananjaya that quells fear; make the city free of lust"—this is the "Great Deed" performed by the compassionate Hara for one who was devoid of the world; worship it with words of praise that remove distress. "O Hara, take away my misfortune; what refuge can there be for those crossing over except you? O Destroyer, do not cause me to fall into cowardice"—with these clever words, he made Hara assume the state of a protector.
The auspicious one. || 15 ||
O Hara! For those crossing over the impurity of this great saṃsāra quickly, what other refuge is there besides you? Abandoning such dejection, make me clever and endowed with auspiciousness.
O Giver of Boons, who else but you sustains this entire world? O Wearer of the Crescent Moon, what person possessed of blemish does not offer salutation to you? 16

Anvaya: O Giver of Boons! Who upholds this entire world apart from You? O Bearer of the Crescent Moon! Who, being possessed of blemish, does not offer salutation to You? (The meaning is: indeed, everyone does. This first birth of ours—among those possessing all other births—is victorious, wherein the All-pervading Lord, manifesting in the heart of the wise, comes to the ground that is to be served. 17
Anvaya: Hanta! Among all those possessing other births, this first birth of ours is victorious, wherein the All-pervading Lord, manifesting within our hearts, becomes the object of our devotion.
O Bestower of Boons to the virtuous, I offer salutations to You, whose stalk is dark; O Great Lord, dispel my indolence, so that I may worship You without delusion. (18)
O Śitināla! O bestower of boons upon the virtuous! I, this very person, offer salutation unto you. O Maheśa! Quell my indolence, so that I may not succumb to delusion.
O Lord, since you indeed bestow compassion for all desires upon every devotee who bows before you, may that compassion of yours, O destroyer of desire, remove all my calamity.
O Lord! O You who have destroyed desire! May that compassion of Yours by which You indeed cherish every person who bows before You, cause my own affliction to come to an end.
O All-pervading One, favor us with those words—sweet as nectar—which, when one’s greed is destroyed, cause people to abandon their sorrow, and which are sweet with the manifestation of Your glory.
O you who have destroyed greed! By that speech of yours, sweet as nectar, people abandon their sorrow; O Lord, favor us with that speech which is manifestly sweet with its splendor.
With that mouth and its sweet voice by which you delight all people, direct toward me at least this one word, playful yet full of grace.
Anvaya: O Lord! With that very face, with its sweet voice, by which you delight all people, direct toward me words of jest.
Grant me that clear eye which brings calamity upon the wicked, which removes vast misfortune, and which dispels the pride of the god of love.
O All-pervading Lord! Grant me that pure eye which, by removing calamity, has taken away the abundant misfortune of the virtuous and which destroys the pride of Madana.
If you gladden the entire world with your voice that dispels darkness, why do you not show compassion toward this person as well with that voice white as snow?

O All-pervading Lord! If you gladden the entire world with your thundering roar that dispels the darkness, then why do you not show compassion to this person as well with that same roar which is white as frost?
In the destruction of sins, nothing of yours is ever cause for despondency; may that [roar], which is beautiful and capable of quelling fear, pacify even my terrible distress.

O Śiva! That hand of yours, which was beautiful and never faltered in removing misfortunes, has now become a hand that causes despair; may it, though exceedingly terrible, pacify even my fear. Since you, O Mahitābha, extend your essential power in the removal of fear, protect me too from great terror, O Purahara, for I am of a timid nature.

In the case of *yamaka*, *śleṣa*, and *citra* figures, there is no distinction between dental and labial sounds, nor between *va* and *ba*, nor between *na* and *ṇa*, nor between *na* and *ma*. Furthermore, there is no difference whether a single consonant or two consonants follow a vowel, nor is there any distinction regarding the presence or absence of the *visarga*. || 25 ||

Anvaya: O Mahitābha! Since you manifest a state of being whose essence is the removal of fear, therefore, O Purahara, protect me, who am of a timid nature, from great terror. I worship Māyāśabara, who bestows excellent boons, who leads the wicked to their end, and who, having conquered Bhava—the source of all worldly activity—brings about existence. Translation: O Lord of great splendor! Because you spread forth a nature that delights in removing fear, therefore, O Destroyer of Cities, protect even me, who am of a cowardly disposition, from this great dread. I adore Māyāśabara, the supreme boon-giver, who leads the one of evil conduct to his destruction; he who, having utterly defeated Bhava, the source of all ritual actions, brings about the manifestation of the world.
The supreme one, who has utterly shattered the succession of afflictions.

Leading the lineage of the virtuous to its conclusion and having conquered worldly existence which arises from ritual action, I worship that Supreme Bhava, the bestower of boons, who subdues the Śabara of Māyā and has utterly destroyed the succession of afflictions.
O Bhava, by your grace, may my impurity be destroyed; O Śiva, I am yours, and this hymn of praise to you, Śiva, has been composed by me. Therefore, deliver me!
Lift me up from this perilous distress; for if the son of the Sun touches you—whether he be present before your eyes or not—why do you not tremble? 27.

O Bhava! By your grace, I have experienced the destruction of my impurities; O Śiva! It is for that very reason that I have composed this hymn of praise to you, the Auspicious One. O Hara! You have lifted me up from the perilous distress of calamity. O Compassionate One! If Yama, the son of the Sun, who is not equal to you, touches me in your very presence, then why are you not ashamed?
There are other faultless words of the learned; which among them is not slow to bring joy to the hearts of the wise, whether real or unreal? And what praises do they not offer?

Yet this speech of yours, fallen from the heights of both the "well-done" and the "ill-done," because it has uttered both the "well-done" and the "ill-done"—I believe that its very stability brings honor to your greatness and produces bliss.

O Anāmaya! What other words of the wise are not indeed slow-moving? (On the contrary, they certainly are. Or what true praises of You do not spread joy in the hearts of the learned? (Indeed, they surely do. But as for this speech of mine, fallen upon the path of extreme trepidation, whatever it has uttered—whether good or bad—in its effort to praise You, I consider that to be the name of Your glory which produces bliss and stability.
He brings [it].

Thus ends the twenty-fourth hymn, titled "The Twin-footed Yamaka," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flower-Praises) to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
May this Lord—

who, it is said, has his heart taken refuge in compassion through the great glory fashioned by her [the Goddess], and from whom the Master attained supreme sovereignty over heaven— protect you in the face of the greatest calamity. 1.

Anvaya: Aho! May this Lord (Parameśvara), whose heart is indeed inhabited by compassion that has fashioned a great exaltation, and by whom the Lord of Heaven (Indra) attained supreme sovereignty, protect you in the midst of supreme calamity.
O Supreme Lord, even Yama does not dare to slay the mind of your servant; therefore, O Blessed One, I bow to Your form which appears devoid of moisture.
It resembles the nectar of the river of the Siddhas. || 2 ||

Anvaya: O Supreme Lord! Śamana does not even set his mind upon killing me, your servant; therefore, O Blessed One, I, who am like one devoid of passion (anīrasadṛk), praise your form which is like the river of the Siddhas (siddhadhunīrasadṛk). That tongue by which a girdle (sārasanā) is fastened is offered to you like a garland; may that tongue, which utters "Victory! unto you, be triumphant. O Mahēśa, the giver of boons, my heart is fixed upon you.
That alone is beneficial, O bestower of boons. || 3 ||

Anvaya: O Maheśa! That tongue (*rasanā*) which, having assumed a beautiful girdle (*sārasanā*), offers speech like a garland unto You—may that tongue be victorious! O Varadeva! That heart which is fixed upon You, the Giver of Boons, is itself truly beneficial.

Your glance, compared to a digit of the nectar-rayed moon, falls like a calamity upon those who do not conform to it. O Blessed One, by Your very glance, Kamalā [the Goddess of Fortune] suddenly comes to Your lap.
The impurities have become yours. || 4 ||
Anvaya: O Blessed One! Your eye, comparable to a digit of the moon, has fallen upon [Your devotee]; thereafter, calamity has vanished like the end of a lunar phase. O All-pervading Lord!
By Your very glance, Lakṣmī suddenly becomes free from blemish and comes to Your lap.
O Lord, keep these words in Your heart: "Your speech is my beloved; I am not Your instigator. Or rather, O Great Lord, do they not cry out with intense longing?
By means of the thought that [the world] is broad. || 5 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! You should take my words to heart, for speech is dear to you, O All-pervading One; therefore, I am not merely your prompter. Or rather, O Great Lord! Do not children cry out with great desire due to their abundant longing? O Giver of Boons! I am rendered helpless by sense-objects that are sweet as the cow of plenty; O Maheśvara, accept me who am devoid of joy, and grant [me] direction.
The nectar of his speech is noble and free from defects. || 6 ||
O Giver of Boons! Accept me—who am rendered helpless by sense-objects that are like the vessels of desire and who am devoid of joy—and bring me under your control.
O Maheśvara! Bestow upon me the nectar of speech which is noble and beneficial.

The entire world has been conquered by me through non-delusion, not through anger; my self-restraint has not been destroyed by that [anger]. Even the great mountain of the gods was made as light as a blade of grass by her [anger], O Maheśa.
By [her] planted in the heart. || 7 ||

O Maheśa! By me, through freedom from delusion (*amoha*), the world was conquered; yet by that same [delusion] when destroyed, my self-restraint (*dama*) was not impaired. Though she was planted in my heart, even the mountain of the gods (*surakṣitidhara*) was rendered like a blade of grass by her. Like the wind from the Malaya mountain, my fortitude was scattered by the trembling Lakṣmī. Therefore, hear this compassionate plea of mine, intent upon propitiating you.
Utter a supreme word of compassion.

O All-pervading Lord! Just as my stability was destroyed by the wind blowing from the Malaya mountain, so too has it been destroyed by my own trembling at the thought of Kamalā. Therefore, listen to these supreme and compassionate words of mine, which are intent upon seeking Your grace, and show me Your great compassion.

For those who have attained Your glance, sweet with favor, the great ones attain a stability that is the very essence of peace; and having cast aside [all else], Lakṣmī herself attends upon those who shine thus.
It attains an extreme state of sluggishness.
Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! For the great ones who have attained Your glance, which is sweet with grace and unblemished, there arises a steadfastness characterized by peace;
for those great ones who shine (sport), the supreme Lakṣmī, casting off her sluggishness, becomes easily accessible.
Alas, in battle where the ranks of lordly elephants were scattered, his undecaying power was manifested—by him, through whom [this power] was swiftly [attained] in the act of serving You.
The intellect, having been offered to another birth, has its essence transformed.

O All-pervading Lord! Alas, the power of that person whose mind—its passion for other births quickly dispelled—was swiftly offered to the service of You, manifested undecaying in battle against a scattered host of elephant-kings. That noble person, whose pride is subdued as he strives toward the objects of sense, brings his own mind—which was once full of pride—under control by Your teaching; therefore, seek refuge in Him.
He brings about new tranquility. || 11 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! This noble person brings this mind of mine, which is striving toward sense objects, under control by Your command; therefore, it seeks refuge with those who possess new tranquility (the virtuous).

Perceiving my heart to be darkened by the dust [of passion] like the son of the Sun (Saturn), I am struck with fear; yet, for me wandering on the path, Your speech—which has conquered the essence of nectar—is a source of joy.
Bestow [yourself] with haste upon those in distress. || 12 ||
O Śiva! Beholding my heart as if darkened by the dust of the son of the Sun (Saturn), it becomes filled with trepidation. O Lord!

Grant me words that have conquered the essence of nectar, for I am wandering in confusion upon a perilous path. O Īśa! When Your eye casts its glance for even a moment upon one who has committed an offense, that person’s transgression is shattered; indeed, the power of others, whose bodies are radiant, is surpassed by those whom You have taken as Your own.
She has been sent to your city. || 13 ||

O Lord! When You, who have destroyed all harm, cast Your eye for even a moment upon her whose offenses were shattered, that supreme Śakti of blazing form entered his body, by whom the people were led to Your city.

The body of the son of the Sun (Karṇa) was suddenly fashioned by You as one incapable of enduring the fire of destruction; yet even so, it did not attain the state of being a consumer of the god of love (Madana).
The state of being free from fear, sin, and greed. || 14 ||
Anvaya: O Lord! The body of the son of the Sun (Kārttikeya), which was not fashioned with courage, has been suddenly reduced to ashes by You. O Sinless One!
Your body attained the state of being a consumer of passion (Madana); nevertheless, that body of Yours does not become terrifying to those who remember it.
Compassion, having attained an increase beyond measure—unbounded—has been acquired by me, surpassing even You, just as the moon, though waning, attains a greater increase for its lineage.
The creeper-like waves of the celestial river are most unimpeded. || 15 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Just as the celestial river was reached by the moon—which was exceedingly distressed and whose body was wasting away—with its wave-like creepers flowing without restraint; even so, by me, compassion—whose increase is limitless yet which has been diminished—has been obtained from you (from your presence).

That the poison was swallowed by Garuḍa, though he possessed wings that were not poisonous, is the greatness of your grace and nothing else; for the Lord does not [despise] one who is bowed down before him.
For one who is intent on pride [is indeed] an adversary. || 16 ||
O Great Lord! That even poison was swallowed by Garuḍa—who, though possessing uneven wings, is now wingless—is indeed the greatness of Your grace alone;
for a supreme lord does not remain intent on pride toward one who has bowed before him.

To attain the state that pacifies all affliction, I fervently pray to the Lord, who is difficult to reach and who utterly destroys the torment of love. Just as a garment removes cold, so may You remove my suffering at this time.
In that very same way, he is indeed my refuge. || 17 ||

I fervently entreat the Lord, the Destroyer of the Bodiless One, to attain His profound state which pacifies the suffering of transmigration; for just as clothing wards off distress during the season of endurance, namely the winter, even so is that Lord my refuge.

She who is most beautiful among the celestial nymphs by virtue of the excellence of her own form, that most delightful woman, O Unaging One whose essence is undecaying, approaches and attends upon Your devotee.
Swiftly by old age. || 18 ||

Anvaya: O Ajara! Among the celestial beauties (*surasundarīṣu*), whichever woman (*ramaṇī*) becomes most delightful (*ramaṇīyatamā*) by the excellence of her own form (*svavapurguṇena*), she, being full of unabated passion (*akṣatarasā satī*), having approached with speed (*tarasā*) even your devotee who is marked by old age (*jarasā*), worships him.

Alas (*bata*), by that very speech (*gīr*) consisting of words which I have uttered regarding you, I conquer the entire world; what then [is there] for you, who are delighted by the nectar of devotion (*bhaktisudhā*) yet filled with fear?
May you be [endowed] with the earth. || 19 ||

O Lord! Alas, by that speech which was uttered by me concerning You, I conquer the entire world; what indeed is gained even by the earth for You, who are already delighted by the nectar of devotion toward one who is fearful of worldly existence?
O Śiva, let Your feet be placed upon my head with a glance fit for a widow, and upon my heart with a thought fit for a widow; thus, with such wisdom, may You endure my calamity.
She who always endures without limit. || 20 ||

Anvaya: O Śiva! May You place Your foot here upon my heart along with that intellect (the intellect of grace)—an intellect which, like a garland suited for the distressed, is suited for the distressed by Your word—and which always endures the boundless misfortunes of the devotee (meaning, it does not tolerate the misfortunes of the devotee).

I fear that inauspiciousness which falls from the limbs of the All-pervading One, who is worthy of refuge; yet He, having cast off the unpeaceful noose falling from His throat, indeed brings about the cessation of my fear as it falls away.

Since I, with my limbs failing due to fear, am terrified of misfortune, I take refuge in that All-pervading Lord; for that Lord, having released the noose of unpeace from my throat, brings peace to the fear in my throat.
Just as the two feet of Murajit were unable to bear the weight of the earth because of its humility, so too have I, seeking protection, bowed down before you.
With an intellect possessing well-developed forbearance. || 22 ||

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Just as the Earth (Kṣamā), unable to bear her burden, took refuge at the feet of Murajit, even so, O Protector of those who bow to You, have I taken refuge at Your feet with a mind possessing appropriate humility (kṣamā). O Blessed One, darkness departs upon reaching the rising light of the sun, and likewise, those who have attained joy abandon their delight when they obtain Your vision. O Lord, having uttered this speech out of devotion... (Note: The final line of the provided text fragment—"bhagavan rasādgiramimāmuditā"—appears to be incomplete, likely leading into a description of how the Lord responded to these words.)
Making me hear it, he gladdened the quarters of the world. || 23 ||
Anvaya: O Blessed One! Just as [devotees] abandon darkness upon obtaining Your glance, which is joyful like the radiance risen from the sun; O All-pervading Lord!

Lending Your ear to these words of mine arisen from rasa (the aesthetic sentiment of devotion), bestow that same glance upon me who am filled with joy. Since You are praised by the gods through compassion for being ever-prostrate at every step, why do You not favor me—who am overcome by fear—because of my lack of prostration?
She did not have her calamities dispelled by that [action]. || 24 ||

O You who are bowed to by the gods! That compassion of Yours which is praised by people for its constant accessibility—do You not, through that very compassion which dispels calamities, favor me who has been seized by the fear of my own lack of accessibility?
May Your eye, which has rendered the slender form of the radiant Madana devoid of luster, surely grant dense prosperity to the virtuous who shine with excellence.
May she also diminish my lack of tranquility. || 25 ||

O All-pervading Lord! That gaze of Yours which extended the bodilessness of Madana—victory indeed to that gaze, which is the very essence of brilliance and grace! May that gaze, which brings about the welfare of the virtuous, bestow intense peace upon those who shine with excellence. By that gaze, human beings on earth attain beneficial prosperity and, in the end, are borne aloft in celestial chariots; and by that same gaze, Yama, who was once terrifying, has been reduced to pieces. Anvaya: He vibho! yā tava dṛk madanasya atanutām vyatanuta, sā lasatām alasatām jayati kila; sā dṛk satām kuśalāya lasatām nibiḍam śam api tanutām | yayā bhuvi mānavāḥ hitām vibhūtim bhajante, ante ca vimānavāhitām; yā ca bhayānakam yamam dalaśaḥ adhāt, tayā... [may I be blessed].
Whom would she not drink in with her wide-beaming gaze?

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! By that glance of Yours, by which human beings on earth enjoy beneficial prosperity and at the end attain the state of being borne by celestial chariots (vimāna), and which shattered the terrifying Yama into pieces—that glance of vast splendor—whom do You not protect? Indeed, [the answer is] everyone.
To me, who am devoid of supreme delight (parama-ramā), You have fashioned this body which is not pleasing; therefore, O Hara, I entreat You with fervor: grant me long-lasting [bliss].
Come to me with beautiful collyrium. || 27 ||
"Since my body was devoid of the supreme *anvaya-ramā* (the lineage-consort), it did not possess this beautiful luster; therefore, O Hara! You were fervently entreated by me.
O All-pervading Lord! Come and make my body eternally radiant with collyrium.
Thus ends [this hymn] dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the illustrious Kashmiri great poet Śrī Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, accompanied by the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the twenty-fifth hymn is titled "Rucirañjana.
The twenty-sixth hymn begins:
"He whose inexhaustible grace is ever-present is the destroyer of calamities and misfortunes, like a fountain that removes the heat of suffering."
And whose tongue is as beautiful as a forest grove. || 1 ||

I praise that Lord, adorned with compassion, who is the protector of the world suffering from the darkness of ignorance, whose mind is such as to grant light and benefit to the world on all sides for those of great stature—(this pair of verses). *Anvaya:* Alas! The unfailing grace of that Imperishable One is the destroyer of calamities and misfortunes; and his tongue is a fountain...

I perpetually praise that Lord, adorned with compassion, who is like a beloved woman in a wilderness—removing the torment of heat and providing light on all sides—who is esteemed as a giver of vision to the great and is beneficial to the world; whose gaze is such that it protects the world afflicted by deep darkness. He is dear to the heart, a true friend, and he satisfies even the lowly without deficiency those who are exalted by their good deeds. He is free from ailment... [and so forth].
By the mere grasping of its name, it removes the suffering of one who is afflicted by suffering. || 3 ||

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "May that God—who is the beloved friend of those whose merits are strengthened by good deeds; who satisfies even the lowly without exception; who, being the Lord free from affliction, dispels suffering merely by his name being uttered; and who appoints [his devotees] to the supreme station—fulfill your desire. This is the connection with the fourteenth verse.
He whom Ceta, Pracetas, and others bear as their sole focus, possessing infinite virtues; he who is celebrated in songs by renowned Siddhas as "the Yogin," the Lord who has been attained. || 4 ||

Even though they possess infinite virtues, those headed by Anvaya and Pracetas direct their minds one-pointedly toward Him; and He who is celebrated in songs as the "Lord of Yogis" and is attained by renowned Siddhas—[the rest is as before]. He who is worthy of honor humbles those of low status, and with His lofty impetuous strides He casts down those of wicked conduct; even the name of one devoid of light He causes to vanish.
He whose [darkness] is the darkness of the world. || 5 ||

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: He who, by means of his exalted and impetuous strides, casts down the base ones whose conduct has been discarded—He whose very name, even for a world devoid of light, obscures its darkness—and so forth, all [the details] are as before.

His prosperity (*bhūti*) is vast majesty (*vibhūti*); the quarters of space are his garment, his dwelling, and his abode; and both the lowly and the noble are his ornaments. His glance is never lacking.
Karālā and Kalikā are on the crown of the head. || 6 ||

The grammatical connection is as follows: May that God fulfill your desire—he whose prosperity (*bhūti*) is his vast majesty (*vibhūti*), whose garment is the quarters of space, and whose abode is the dwelling place of the ancestors; he for whom even those who are deficient [such as spirits] and those who are not deficient serve as ornaments; and upon whose head is a curved, formidable bud (*kalikā*).
He who sports playfully in the sky, who truly laughs with crests that dispel all obstacles, who is the pure Lord of auspicious rays,
and who bears those stars within his eyes.

He who is the abodeless one (the Sun) sporting in the sky with rays that dispel darkness; he who truly laughs (the Fire); he who is pure and the lord of auspicious lights (the Moon)—he who, the All-pervading Lord, bears these unimpaired within his eyes;
he who, even in countless battles, is the cause of the bitterness of enmity for warriors, a ground for reproach, and a forest fire to wrath—[that Lord].
Indeed, he who wipes away harshness. || 8 ||

He who indeed wipes away that harsh anger—which is the source of enmity for warriors even among the countless and the numbered, the very cause of hostility, and a forest fire upon the ground of reproach—that Lord [is here].

He who was not previously invited by Dakṣa, though he was skilled in the auspicious rite of sacrifice, because of his lack of knowledge regarding sacrifice; to him, who is bowed down to, [I offer] the sinless... [offering].
The ocean of compassion bestowed both dejection and grace.

That ocean of compassion, who had previously not been chosen for the auspicious sacrifice by the skillful Dakṣa— who was himself well-versed in the method of logical succession— later bestowed upon that prostrate man a sinless favor, free from all dejection;

he who is unattainable through worldly policies or through the austerities of those who are both disciplined and undisciplined, yet [granted his grace] even to the young sage who was sluggish in service.
His grace rendered [the world] both honored and dishonored. || 10 ||

He who, though unattainable through ascetic practices—whether they be steady and effective or ineffective—that are practiced both in policy and non-policy; he who bestowed his grace upon the child-muni Upamanyu, who was free from pride yet sluggish in service—he alone, and no one else, directs the world toward application in action or inaction. For it is he who provides the purpose for leading beings, whether they possess strength or are devoid of it.
For from that, he arises as one who is capable. || 11 ||

Without this lineage, this world, being incapable of action, would not apply itself to work; it is capable of inspiring even the weak-hearted with resolve. From that source from which prosperity arises—through dharma appropriate to oneself, through desire accompanied by freedom from fear, at the proper time, and through that wind which brings comfort and bows in submission.

He who is served by his own life-force, by the poetry offered by that life-force which is captivating, by a friend who is a friend to those shrouded in darkness, and by one who is gentle and gentle; (this pair of verses).

*Anvaya*: He (the Lord), by means of dharma appropriate to himself, by means of desire accompanied by the granting of fearlessness, and by means of Time (Kāla) that has arrived at the proper moment for bowing down...
He is served by a wind that brings happiness, by the life-force (jīva) offered by Him, by poetry that is enchanting, and by a friend who is gentle; he is served by one who is mild.

He is the Creator, the Ordainer, the All-pervading Lord who created the worlds with their inhabitants out of compassion, the God who bestows desired objects, and who shall appoint you to the highest station according to your wish.

May He fulfill your desire! (14) [A Kulaka of twelve verses] The grammatical connection (*anvaya*): May that compassionate, all-pervading Lord—the Creator who fashioned the worlds along with their inhabitants, and who appoints them to the supreme station—surely (*kāmam*, meaning "certainly") bring your desire to fruition.
The virtuous, shining with graceful words, honor him who is himself honored by bards; and the world extols the playful prowess of that unconquered one in battles with a tumultuous roar.

The prosperity of that steadfast man, which follows the course of his sharp and continuous application, gladdens him as it bestows joy, just as a beloved wife, out of passion, delights her husband while giving him gifts.

That auspicious and pure radiance—devotion to the Lord—which the leaders of the gods bore as the foremost means for achieving all perfections and successes, has become the ornament of the fearless one. (Tilaka) Anvaya: That devotion to the Lord, which the leaders of the gods bore as the foremost cause for the attainment of all perfections and successes—that radiance is auspicious and pure.
Devotion to the Lord becomes an ornament for that fearless one whom bards praise; the virtuous, shining with graceful words, honor him.

The world praises with loud clamor the lofty sport of that steadfast man, earned in battles. His sharp intellect casts away worldly activity followed by the chain of bondage, and Fortune, like a beloved wife, bestows joy through her giving to those in need.

Giving to him out of passion brings joy; why then such intense apprehension? If Śambhu is fond of his servants, he will not abandon a servant who stays close to him. O mind, do you waver for no reason, as if the worshipper's devotion were in vain? 18.

O Auspicious One, that land of Nandana is but a blade of grass to you; where could the auspicious mountain [Kailāsa] be counted? That compassion of yours, which dispels the coldness of the moon-crested Lord, surpasses even his own compassion by its splendor. (19)
Like the light of the rising sun born from the mud, like the fresh moonlight of rivers, that devotion to Śaṅkara— full of apprehension yet providing supreme protection against fear— will gladden you.

He who, though worshipped by enjoyers, does not abandon his own bliss even when faced with fear; that Śambhu, who removes the wretchedness of laziness and the abode of sloth, shall protect you and cast away all that is inauspicious. (Cakkalaka) Anvaya: O mind! Why do you have such great apprehension? If Śambhu is fond of those who serve him, then he does not abandon even a servant standing near him; he protects the one who worships him.
Therefore, that devotion is not false; so, O mind! why do you seek even the slightest restlessness? O joyful one!

that Nandana grove is but a blade of grass to you; and thus, O auspicious one! where is that Kalyāṇagiri mountain to be counted? O mind! that compassion of the Moon-crested Lord, free from trembling, dispels your dullness with its own splendor. O fearful one! the radiance of the young sun is like [the clearing of] mud-born [impurity].
Like the unceasing flow of rivers, that devotion to Śaṅkara— providing high and unwearied protection— will gladden you, O anxious mind! That Lord,
who is honored by those possessed of worldly enjoyments (those craving sense-objects), who bestows happiness and does not abandon those who possess it,
and who removes indolence, the abode of misery, and dejection— that Śambhu shall protect you and cast away all that is inauspicious.

Though she has issued forth from faults and vices, she remains attached to the essence of service like a courtesan; fearless and full of passion, she comes to you to meet you in the darkness of illusion.

(23) [Yugma] O mind! That speech—which, though set loose by the onset of faults and the evening of vice, is intensely passionate, fearless, and attached to the essence of service—is like a young courtesan bound to a new tethering post; having reached the vicinity of your throat, it shall not leave you for a long time. (23) [Couplet] *Anvaya:* O Citta! That Vāṇī (speech), which—though emitted during the evening of defects and the night of vices—is full of passion, fearless, and devoted to the flavor of service, is like a courtesan (vāra-vilāsinī). [She will not leave you. (Note: The provided text fragment ends with the description of the speech as a courtesan, but the commentary implies the completion of the thought regarding her staying with the "mind.")

As if through the darkness of illusion, she has come to seek you; having grown through the influence of her inner being, this speech, having reached the vicinity of my throat, shall not leave you for all time— like a young woman who has reached the vicinity of her husband's neck, like a new mare tied to a fresh tethering post, or like a female elephant that has reached the vicinity of the male elephant's neck.
O Lord of Gaurī, if your celestial, far-reaching splendor and the digit of the moon are both fair, why am I still afflicted by that obstacle called darkness which they have not destroyed?

O Lord! If your divine rays of far-reaching luster, as well as Gaurī and a digit of the moon—these [three]—obstruct the obstacle known as darkness, then am I afflicted by that [darkness] which remains unstruck?
Those who possess effort apply themselves with effort; those free from doubt praise and grant peace. Your devotees are divided [from others], yet they are divided from calamities.
Why have I alone suddenly sunk down? || 25 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Your devotees who possess diligence practice diligence, praise peace, are free from doubt, and are liberated from calamities; if so, why am *I* alone suddenly submerged [in the ocean of calamity]?
The auspicious words of You, whose inner impurities have been washed away, are never in vain for those who bow to You. With those uplifted words, lift me up, for I am helpless and submerged.
One who is of noble birth [is lost] in the darkness of bad times. || 26 ||
O Lord! For those who bow before You, the floods of Your auspicious words—which wash away all sorrows—never go in vain;
therefore, with those exalted collections of speech (which strike terror into the messengers of Yama), rescue me, a man of noble birth, who am helpless and lost in the darkness of a wretched fate!

"Whosoever here is worthy of protection, I protect him, I protect him—even one possessed by the fear of the end of an aeon or the end of the world. By that policy of yours, O Lord, grant me a gracious glance here, which removes all incomparable terror. (27)

Anvaya: O Lord! You possess this policy: "I shall protect him who deserves protection here, even if he is possessed by the fear of the end of the world. By that [policy], bestow upon me here Your gracious glance, which removes incomparable terror. O Kandarpa, why do you assume pride? Your entire power has suddenly set; O coward, why does Your deep [lake] overflow? (Note: The final line appears to be a fragment or a play on words involving *gabhīra* [deep] and *galita* [overflowed/disappeared]).
The protection from the multitude of Rākṣasas is the grace of the Blessed One. || 28 ||

Anvaya: O Kandarpa! What pride do you assume? Your entire power has suddenly gone to its end. O coward! Has the profound grace of the Blessed One—which protected you from agitation—fallen away? (Have you forgotten it?

May that Māyā, by which I have become happy after propitiating you—who are yourself to be propitiated—through both knowledge and ignorance, come to me; let not that Māyā, which has removed fear, depart.
In order to worship you, who are so humble... || 29 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! I know even that ignorance (*avidyā*) by which, having worshipped You, the object of worship, I become happy, as being indeed knowledge (*vidyā*). May that Māyā, which did not become thin (*tānava*) when worshipping You, and which has dispelled fear (*yāpita-bhīḥ*), come to me. By whom—possessed of wealth and enjoyments—is she held in half [of his body], she who is beloved by Rāma and delightful; and who is the destroyer of Death (*antaka*)? She is Lakṣmī, the abode of all splendors (*dhāmāni dhāmāni*).
The vision sustains it. || 30 ||

O Lord! By whom other than You has this delightful and beloved Rāmā been held in half [of Your body], she who is endowed with the enjoyment of pleasures? Whose gaze brings an end to Death himself? And whose dwellings bear the abodes of Lakṣmī?

Who is the pillar for the Conqueror (Viṣṇu), who resembles a pillar? Who is the tormentor of Smara, the maker of torment? And who in this worldly existence, which is experienced as resembling a prison, is the one...?
Jīvaka is the life-sustainer of all living beings, except for you.
Anvaya: O Lord! Without You, who is there to restrain Jiṣṇu, who resembles a pillar? Who is there to cause torment to Smara, the bringer of torment?
Likewise, in this worldly existence, which is experienced as a mere imitation of a prison, who is there to sustain the lives of living beings? [The meaning is: no one at all.
She, through whose praise of devotion to Śambhu, and whose delight in every action toward Smara, remains unimpaired—[she is one whose treasury of merit is inexhaustible].
Who else, being generous, would carry such a body? || 32 ||

That body, which through its very existence proclaims devotion to Śambhu and proclaims delight in the beloved activities of Smara—who else but another [the Lord] could bear that unimpaired body from a treasury of inexhaustible merit? Alas! That body, which by its own power produces an unbroken pride of contempt even toward the King of Gods, yet is itself helpless even in departing because of its devotion—[how pitiable it is! Hā! Niḥsahā! Niḥsaraṇe’pi bhaktyā sā.
Speech has come near to you, O so-and-so.

[Anvaya: Alas! O Lord, that very speech which, generating unbroken pride, produced even contempt for the King through [her] egoism—alas, that same speech, now unable even to escape, has come into your presence out of devotion!

Since the Goddess of Speech thus praised the Great Lord with rhymes appropriate to the occasion of his satisfaction, this [praise], which is praiseworthy and conducive to fame, has arrived before us; may it be for the destruction of our sins.
The favor desired is not obtained. || 34 ||

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: This speech, being satisfied, has thus praised the Lord Maheśa with *yamaka* verses at a fitting moment; this is praiseworthy, conducive to fame for us, and a desired favor from this (Maheśa) that dispels our sins has arrived.
Furthermore, Śrī (Prosperity), whose flickering tips vie with the most tremulous [leaves], who bestows beautiful, radiant, and steady joy, abandons her instability and moves about.
In the lotus-face of those whose hearts are filled with the longing for the destruction of the beloved’s passion, her speech is exceedingly sweet and moist with nectar.

Though she vies with the tips of the most tremulous leaves of the *anvaya* tree, Fortune— possessing a beautiful luster and bestowing intense joy upon those men who possess a devotion to the essence of praising the Destroyer of Rati’s Consort—
abandons her fickleness; and likewise, Speech, moist with the essence of sweet honey, moves within the lotus-face of those whose hearts are fixed on praising the Destroyer of Rati’s Consort.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth hymn, the *Pādādiyamaka-stotra*, within the *Stutikusumāñjali* dedicated to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
[The twenty-seventh hymn follows.]

Victorious is Hara, who assumed the guise of a deceiver in battle by seizing the weapons of the assembled Pāṇḍavas; he whose firm fame was maintained while bearing a body as fierce as fresh wood, and whose arrows were endowed with great speed. || 1 ||

Victorious is Hara, who, in his alliance with the Pāṇḍavas during the battle, employed deceptive stratagems by seizing their weapons; whose body was as fierce as fresh firewood; who maintained steadfast fame; whose arrows were swift; and who is the Destroyer.
His feet, which purify the world, cannot be assailed even by Indra or by those possessed of sin, yet they are craved by the sages for the sake of testing their own conduct.
We praise that which has performed the pure sport of absolute liberation. || 2 ||

We praise him whose feet purify the world through their lineage, who was unassailable even by Indra, yet was desired even by the wicked; who, while testing the conduct of the multitude of sages, engaged in the pure sport of solitary meditation;

who, though his body was a stable abode, was resorted to by the daughter of the mountain; and who turned his back on the blossoming of the transformations of passion—[we praise him] who is like a garland of flames from the poison-fire of the king of serpents.
[He is] one who bestows a terrible appearance and trembling. || 3 ||

Among those who seek peace, those who seek pleasure, or those who are compassionate, we always worship the Supreme Lord—who is most steadfast, the sovereign master, who is excellent, non-terrible, capable of pacifying all evils, and ever-ready to bring about the destruction of the calamities of the deeply distressed. (Yugmam) Anvaya: [We worship Him] who is resorted to by the daughter of the mountain, whose abode is firm, and who is averse to the expansion of the transformations of passion.

We worship the Lord, who—though possessing a formidable appearance like a mass of flames from the poison of the king of serpents—is free from trembling; who is most excellent, non-terrible, and capable of pacifying sin for those seeking peace, those filled with desire, or those possessed of compassion; who is ever supremely steadfast in bringing about the destruction of the calamities of those deeply distressed. Alas, young women of slender waist, though their sons have mastered the Vedas, have had their hearts stolen by yogis; yet that which is the destruction of the affliction of sin and disease cannot be found except through the Lord Amṛteśa.
What do they pacify? || 5 ||

Alas, for embodied beings, what can sons who have mastered the Vedas, daughters who have captivated the minds of yogis, and slender-waisted young women do to alleviate that calamity of sin, nameless and dense with disease? (The meaning is: none of these are capable of pacifying that suffering.)

Neither by Hari, nor by the Moon—the crest-jewel of the gods—nor even by Brahmā, despite his ritual worship, was your form perceived in the past; for where are we, whose minds are shrouded by worldly experience? (6)

O crest-jewel of the moon! Formerly, even the deer [who bears your mark] did not perceive your form; likewise, even the Creator, while performing his ritual worship, did not perceive you. As for us, whose minds are shrouded by the experience of worldly existence, where indeed can we stand in the composition of your hymn?
Only the clever horses, the elephants born of the mountains, and the army of steady, noble, and exalted strength offer their service when you, the sovereign, ordain what is beneficial.
[He went] to the direction that is as pure as a lotus.

Anvaya: O Lord! when welfare was accomplished through Your power, the clever horses, the mountain-born elephants, and the steady, noble, and exalted strength—all these things point toward the direction that is as stainless as a lotus.

You, being skilled in seizing the kingdom of Rāvaṇa—who was intent on tormenting the assembly of the twice-born—became one whose strength was fit for battle at Your feet, having bowed down from the forest.
The elder brother of Bharata.

O Lord, crowned by the moon! Grant me that firm and fierce grace, having obtained which even Bharata—who was devoted to virtue—became one whose great enmity toward his enemies was destroyed, and who was skilled in seizing the kingdom of Rāvaṇa, who was intent on the excessive torment of the assembly of the twice-born. (Yugma) *Anvaya:* O All-pervading Lord! Having obtained which [grace], [Bharata] became skilled in the seizure of the kingdom of Rāvaṇa, who was intent upon the excessive torment of the assembly of the twice-born... [and so forth].

Bharata’s elder brother, though prostrate at your feet and dwelling in the forest, became possessed of strength fit for battle; likewise, O Lord, O crest-jewel of the moon! Grant me that steadfast and fierce grace—which, having obtained it, even Bharata became devoted to auspiciousness and possessed great majesty that destroys the pride of his enemies—and come to me.

Does your beneficial radiance not bring joy day after day to one who is utterly powerless, situated on the path of bad policy, rendered helpless by intoxication, and overwhelmed by calamity—[a radiance] that removes your intense sorrow? (10)

O Hara! Does your benevolent grace not gladden me day after day—me who am utterly powerless, straying from the path of righteousness, rendered helpless by intoxication [and overwhelmed by enemies such as desire], and tormented by intense grief?
O destroyer of Madana, console me with your wealth, you whose tongue emits nectar that removes the pain of the virtuous, and whose eyes are beautiful, gentle, and soft.
Come to me, who have taken refuge in every calamity and every misfortune. || 11 ||

O destroyer of Madana! You whose eyes are gentle, skillful, and soft; you who remove the suffering of those seeking refuge; with your tongue emitting nectar, come and console me, who am fallen into calamity—the very absence of prosperity.
O crusher of Madana, why do you not tolerate me, who am helpless and innocent, standing so near? O creator of the world, the universe shines [only] because of you.
Who is capable of rescuing those who have no other refuge? || 12 ||

O crusher of Madana! Why do you not forgive me, who am innocent and helpless, standing before you? O creator of the world! Without you, who shines in this universe as one capable of uplifting those who have no other refuge? (The meaning is: none at all. If you, who are devoted to compassion, do not place your harsh foot upon my sinful heart, then what is the most beneficial [remedy] for me, whose soul is so defiled? O Hara, take away my great suffering!
The course of events is consistent. || 13 ||
O you who are devoted to compassion! If you do not set foot within my harsh disposition, which is intent on sin, then, O Hara, what most beneficial course remains for me, whose soul is defiled?
If your compassion—which, like the steady radiance of the sun, destroys the intoxication of pride and dispels the surrounding darkness—does not arise, tell me, what hope can there be?
Alas, how does it close for me? || 14 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! If Your steady radiance, which shines like the light of the sun, does not subdue this peerless, intoxicating darkness of madness—just as the sun destroys it—then, O All-pervading One, tell me: how can my fear of You ever close? For the Sun, who is capable of dispelling the night, who has destroyed the mass of the sharp darkness of the night, and who is radiant with the abundance of the light of dawn, has not yet appeared.
When it brings about its arising. || 15 ||
When the moon, the ornament of the sky, does not delight in its supreme compassion, it cannot swiftly dispel the pure darkness that has long descended and remains firm and boundless. (16)
When the serpent born of the sun, devoid of pity, swallows my body emaciated by the fire of emaciation—O Śiva, alas, then who else besides you could grant me steadfastness?

Who else is so devoted to compassion? (The *tilaka*) *Anvaya*: O All-pervading Lord! When [the moon], capable of dispelling the darkness of night and destroying the mass of the sharp nocturnal gloom...

O Lord of supreme compassion! When the sun, radiant with the splendor of its own dawn, does not rise; when the moon, the ornament of the sky, finds no delight in the heavens; when the pure fire does not dispel the long-fallen, stable, and boundless darkness; and when the serpent born of the sun (the noose of Time), devoid of mercy, devours this body emaciated by the fire of suffering—alas, O Śiva! who else besides You could there be? Who else indeed?

Who, devoted to compassion, will grant steadfastness to me who am without refuge? How can Yama, whose hand is seized by a great serpent made terrifying by the thick, shimmering poison that is the instrument of death, run toward my abode with longing for even a moment’s restraint? 18.

O Lord, while You are full of compassion and desire [to help], how can Yama— whose hand is made terrifying by a great serpent held in his grasp and whose poison-fire blazes intensely as the instrument of death— run even slightly toward my abode to restrain me? O Lord, my Love, having fashioned a body that is clever yet distressed and covered in grey hair, will become all-powerful over me when You, who possess mighty strength, are intent on showing no mercy.
How can it be a producer of existence? || 19 ||

O Lord! While you, possessed of dense power and intent on being free from pride, remain, how can Smara—who, fashioning my body grey-haired, closed-eyed, clever, and afflicted, was once a bringer of torment—now prevail?

Even though he is now joined by Madhu and carries Rati, his most beloved, how can he conquer me, who have taken refuge in the All-pervading Lord, the protector, whose strength is never in vain? He alone is victorious over me.
Smara is the destroyer of pride in asceticism. || 20 ||

O Lord! Why does Cupid—who, though joined with Madhu, carries away even the most cherished fearlessness and joy, and who robs the self-restraint of ascetics—now triumph over me, who have taken refuge in You, the all-pervading Protector whose power is never in vain? How can he prevail before You—he who casts the intellect onto the path of the enemy of uneven anger (the Destroyer of Death), leading it toward unrighteousness and away from the perceived true path, and who utterly destroys Your self-discipline?
My intoxication vomits forth its own body. || 21 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! This intoxication of yours—which casts my mind, which has not seen the true path, onto the road of injustice and which violently suppresses self-restraint—how is it that it consumes my body before you? My enemies, who have caused me excessive humiliation and possess uncontrollable wrath, have vainly attained a physical form; for they do not consume that [body] which has already been scorched by you, since they are indeed intent upon your welfare.
The intellect [is directed] toward those who are bowed. || 22 ||
O All-pervading Lord! My enemies—who have repeatedly committed insults and whose wrath is irresistible—have rendered my body (which belongs to Your devotee) useless.

For they do not devour that body of mine which has been subjected to burning; for Your mind, intent on the welfare of those who bow before You, is ever devoted to their well-being. If the light of Your splendor does not shine in the heavens, and if the day consisting of Your essence does not dawn for me, tell me, how can the great darkness that steals away all joy be dispelled?
The intoxication of the uneven humors ceases. || 23 ||

O Śiva! If your light does not shine in the sky (both in the external ether and the ether of the heart), and if the day consisting of you does not come to me, then tell me, how shall this darkness—which steals away great joy and possesses the defect of poison—be dispelled? Grant me that [light] by which even the lotus is made dark, which persists despite the destruction of continuous, dense gloom, and which is fashioned even by the fire of Smara.
A gaze that is a cow of plenty for the timid. || 24 ||

O All-pervading Lord! Grant that eye which is the cow of plenty for the wretched— the eye consisting of the three luminaries (the moon, sun, and fire), upon which the moon-like eye situated on the left side darkens the lotus, the eye situated on the right side dispels the dense and continuous darkness, and upon which the third eye situated on the forehead was fashioned by Smara.

In this month of Sahas, when the mind is delighted by the forceful wind born of fresh clouds, your beloved with her warm breasts does not please you on her chest as much as the song of praise that accords with your virtues.

Anvaya: O Lord! Just as the hymn of praise to You, which accords with Your qualities, delights the mind, so too does a passionate beloved with warm breasts, clinging to the chest during the force of the wind born from the flow of snow, not delight the mind in such a way.
This one here—whose heart-city is seized by the excellence of Yama, whose actions nourish harsh prowess, and who possesses a fruitful alliance with the enemy—is manifesting before me.
Maheśvara attained delight. || 26 ||

He who captivates with the excellence of his lineage, whose actions nourish harsh prowess, who is a kinsman in adversity, and whose acquisitions are never fruitless— this very person (I am such a one), that Maheśvara appears before me,
