having inspired my delight by means of inexhaustible wealth, high-mindedness, most weighty and corresponding virtues, noble birth, a blameless retinue, and unblemished strength.
It increases. || 27 ||

For that person who, being noble-minded and joyful, begins this new and ever-fresh hymn of praise to Śiva, Hara—the bestower of prosperity and the remover of the defects of worldly existence—extends auspiciousness to him as he remains attentive. (28) (A yugma).

*Anvaya:* He who, being noble-minded and joyful, begins with this new and ever-fresh [work] the hymn of praise to Śiva—that man, by means of the imperishable... (Note: The provided source text for the *anvaya* appears to be incomplete at the end; the translation reflects the available portion.)

Through wealth that is agreeable to the wise, through noble lineage, through people of excellent character, and through strength untainted by evil deeds, Hara—the bestower of prosperity and the remover of the defects of worldly existence—increases for him who is attentive; he bestows peace upon that focused one.
He is proficient in all the arts, possessed of intelligence, and loftily exalted in mind; yet he offers no praise to anyone other than the moon-crested Lord Śiva.
He who has performed good deeds is one who has done so for another. || 29 ||
The man who, being virtuous, has offered praise to none other than the one whose crest is the crescent moon—he is an expert in all the arts;
he is wise and exceedingly lofty in mind.

O Lord, by uprooting the separation of the quarters from the sun, You arise for the joy of the birds of the chariot; for through the praises of the Master, the world—though overwhelmed by the poison of despondency—is rendered free from the darkness of non-existence.

(With the Sun rising in the morning: Ah! Just as the Lord Śambhu, through His hymns of praise, has rendered the world free from the affliction of the poison of despondency and devoid of darkness, so too does the Sun rise for the joy of the birds of the chariot [the *cātaka*], bestowing courage by dispelling the pain of separation. Furthermore, the mind of the Lord, adorned with humility and devoted to glory; His stainless intellect, intent on the welfare of others; and His body, the source of vast auspiciousness—all these reflect back upon Him.
The fruit of the creeper of praise. || 31 ||

When it is adorned with the discipline of logical consistency (*anvaya-manas-vinaya*), it becomes delighted by fame; when the intellect is stainless, it becomes intent on the welfare of others; and the body becomes a vessel of abundant auspiciousness—these are the fruits that reflect back from the creeper of praise for the Lord.
Possessing renown amassed through the power of speech that excels the essence of nectar itself, the wise poets, being meritorious, [praise] him who is worshipped by the lords of the gods.
The wise praise Śiva. || 32 ||
The virtuous and skillful poets and scholars, whose fame is accumulated through the power of their speech— a wealth of nectar-like essence won by following the traditional lineage—

praise Śiva, who is worshipped by the lords of the gods. For those great ones of vast and stainless consciousness, the attainment of a beloved wife does not bring such delight as do these verses, which possess a sweet flavor and are moist with the essence of meaning, being composed with poetic constraints (*sayamaka*).
The Praise of the Enemy of Kāma in Yamaka Style || 33 ||

This hymn to the Enemy of Mara (Śiva), possessing *yamakas* and composed of words made sweet by their internal connection (*anvaya*), is as follows: The attainment of a beloved wife does not intoxicate those great ones whose consciousness is unblemished and undiminished; rather, it is [the realization of truth] that intoxicates them.

What woman indeed is not a non-wife to one who has cast aside his beloved? What night is not a lovely night for a man? [To such a one], the glory of the Lord of Night (the Moon) belongs to the illustrious Foe of Death (Śiva).
He approaches him who praises the cause of the foremost of elephants with an unceasing cry.

What celestial nymph (*amaravadhū*), beloved of an ascetic (*avadhūta-kāntā*), would not approach with incessant cries that man who praises the illustrious Antakari—the cause of the destruction of the elephant-like lineage of rebirth? Likewise, what night of humanity (*narajanī*) would not be graced by the beauty of the Lord of Night (*rajanīpati*)? (The meaning is: indeed, all of them.
Thus ends [the hymn] to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the *Śrī-Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the twenty-seventh hymn is titled "The Middle-of-the-Foot Yamaka.
The twenty-eighth hymn:

"By what doubt has the bliss within the heart not been led to destruction? This [bliss] does not flourish because of that; therefore, the Goddess of Speech, whose movement is restrained, possesses a splendor of beauty."
But devotion unfolds within me just as light does from the sun by its own nature; therefore, I shall now speak something every single day.

By what doubt has the inner tranquility in my mind not been destroyed? For that reason, this speech of mine, its movement restrained, does not flourish in beauty. (Anticipating the objection, "In that case, you should remain observing silence," he says: But just as the radiance of the sun unfolds by itself, so too does my devotion unfold; therefore, at present, whatever it may be—high or low—I shall speak something every day.
He spoke: "Bearing a face with pure, long-reaching flames of fire, causing fear, holding aloft a serpent in his hand as he performs a mighty leap—
seeing Death approaching, how could the Lord not utter these words to me, who am so well-known for my accumulated and expansive splendor?"
May Citrā protect us; may she protect us! || 2 ||

Anvaya: O Compassionate One! Having heard these words—accumulated, vast, appropriate, pleasing, and wonderfully extensive—"Death approaches me, bearing a mouth with a massive, long, burning flame, instilling great fear in living beings, and holding aloft in his hand a serpent that leaps forward with its neck outstretched"—how could the All-Pervading Lord not protect me?
I consider that long night to possess the quality of enviable dignity, filled with the savor of serving you—a night which, like nectar, is comparable to a day;
for therein your exceedingly beautiful conduct, the lord of the worlds, is extolled by Nandin, who stands nearby and gladdens him with fitting words.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! I consider that night—during which Your exceedingly beautiful conduct, the conduct of the Lord of the worlds, is praised with appropriate words by those who bring joy to Nandin standing nearby—to possess desirable qualities of dignity and to be long-lasting; and likewise, I consider that day—during which Your conduct is praised with the aforementioned words—to be like nectar, as it bestows upon me the delight of serving You.
I believe that within the lotus-face of that assembly-member, there arises a speech that is overflowing with the destruction of all weariness— pure, tender, and ripening to its full maturity;
and Fortune never deserts him, nor is he ever illumined by worldly riches, for you yourself reside within the lotus of his heart.
He who was satisfied by those rescued from the fear of existence was himself satisfied. || 4 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! He who, out of fear of worldly existence (*bhava*), has protected you and has caused you to dwell within his heart-lotus and has gratified you—for that fortunate one, a pure, tender, and overflowing abundance of words arises from the lotus of his mouth, which dispels the exhaustion of those seated in the assembly and reaches its full maturity; moreover, the splendor of prosperity, ever radiant with wealth, never abandons him.

O Blessed One, those whose intellects have been directed toward You alone since childhood serve You, casting aside the intoxication of pride that brings swelling joy, while bearing a state of perfect prosperity; they are fanned by young women who speak sweetly and captivate the heart with their beauty, as well as by the immortals in heaven with chowries as radiant as moonbeams— those for whom the faculty of discernment was fixed solely upon You from their very youth.
Anvaya: O Blessed One! Those by whom, from childhood, a *śemuṣī*—[that which steals (*muṣ*) delusion (*śi*, so called because it lies in the mind]—which has You alone as its object, was established;

they, bearing great joy, having cast aside their pride (the conceit of thinking, "Whom else shall we, as proud women, follow?"), are now served by young women who are charming and sweet-spoken. Moreover, those very same ones...
People in heaven are fanned by the gods with whisks as radiant as moonbeams;

yet, O Lord, having attained that wealth which is service to you—the very source of all suffering—I shall destroy it, for the fierce-eyed servant of Yama repeatedly leaps there, his face made terrifying by a frown, in order to quickly pulverize their bodies. To avoid that place, I abandon it.
Evil deeds are brought forth by a corrupt mind. || 6 ||

O Lord! Having attained the wealth of service to You— which wards off that place where the messengers of Yama, their faces made terrifying by fiercely arched eyebrows, repeatedly cause terror as they strive to leap with great force to crush my body— I shall destroy the evil deeds committed through my own wicked intellect.

Before the servants of Yama, making a great and terrifying gurgling sound as they release it, display their fierce faces— faces as dreadful as crushed saffron— come quickly with all your might and grant me such a vision as that which dispels the longing for an unceasing flood of nectar!

O Lord! Before the servants of Yama—who have performed great yawning and are emitting a terrifying roar—display their fierce faces, red as saffron powder, with wrath, come quickly; grant me that vision which is the abode of such splendors, which utterly dispels the longing for an incessant flood of nectar.

O Blessed One, as long as I do not constantly resort to that hell which brings torment to living beings and where vast calamities are wrought by the unbearable weapons of fire, so long, O Ever-Blazing One, release Your word— like the life-giving water for those traveling on a desert path, who run with bodies tormented by the distress of a fearsome summer heat.

O Blessed One! As long as I do not take refuge in You— who, until the very end of hell, always inflict burning torment upon living beings whose great calamities are wrought by the weapons of unbearable fire— so long, please utter those words which are like a life-giving elixir for those running on a desert path, their bodies tormented by the distress of a scorching summer heat.

That divine host of celestial women, whose splendor blossoms with playful grace, attends upon that radiant god in the Nandana grove—the very garden of the well-disposed—which delights those of noble mind; for by that [divine state], he has cast this mind of his into you with great enthusiasm, while that [worldly] state of "I-ness" causes intense agitation and brings weariness to the virtuous.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! That egoism (*ahaṃtā*) which causes intense agitation to the virtuous and brings about suffering to the wicked—by that very egoism, this mind, its enthusiasm unimpaired, has been placed upon You; and by that fortunate one, that radiant and divine being, the host of celestial women, with their splendor blooming in playful charm, serves with enjoyments in the Nandana grove, which gladdens the gods.

Alas! That beautiful woman, whose playful charms—rendered lovely by the intoxication of her glances—are like wine that causes the speech to falter, destroys my fortitude and the laughter born of discernment;
she, that great weapon of Kama, bestows upon me a delusion so dark that the expansion of suffering in my mind, consisting of ignorance, has spread abroad.

Anvaya: O Lord! That beautiful woman—whose playful charms have been diminished by discernment (*viveka*), whose speech has faded, and whose lovely eyes are reddened by the intoxication of wine—which destroys the composure of the innocent; alas, that delusion (*moha*) by which her mental expansion of distress has ceased and the darkness consisting of ignorance has spread—that very delusion, the great weapon of Kama, he bestows upon me.

I am ashamed; abandon this kinship that has been shaken off by me with such impetuosity! It was by my delusion that I maintained this sense of "I" through which I have done what is harmful—what, indeed, has not been done that is harmful by one intoxicated by the pride of fortune and established in power? Since I do not resort to it again, O Excellent One, bestow upon me that which is beneficial even if it causes pain.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! By me, who was utterly deluded by that [ego-sense], I feel ashamed even upon seeing You; therefore, abandon it quickly and from afar. Thus has kinship been cast aside. I have maintained this very ego-sense; therefore, what harm has not been inflicted by me, who am intoxicated by the pride of wealth and established in power? O Compassionate One! Grant me that beneficial boon by which I shall never again resort to this [ego].
Bestow [this favor]!
Menakā has been brought by Kāma to the state of intimacy at his feet; what need is there for Rambhā, who is full of exertion in the performance of elaborate enjoyments?

My beloved is the Supreme Goddess, in whom the possibility of misfortune is destroyed, whose nature is some indescribable delight in the heart, and who extends herself as a multitude of beneficial truths.

What need have I for Menakā, who was brought to my side by one desiring lineage? And what business have I with Rambhā, who is so intent on the accumulation of dense enjoyments? There is a certain indescribable delight that extends within my heart, through which it is protected; that devotion to the Supreme Lord, which destroys the possibility of calamity, is my beloved.

I offer this new exposition of the words of praise to that Great Lord, whose matted locks bear a multitude of skulls— disturbing the noble lineage like the river Gaṅgā obstructing the flight of swans amidst her waves— and through which [exposition], with unwavering devotion, I have honored my entire human birth.

We honor this entire human birth with this unwavering devotion, having applied it as an expression of praise for the form of that Great Lord, who bears the divine Gaṅgā— obstructing the mass of skulls like a flock of swans amidst the turbulent intervals of waves— and whose matted locks are auspicious.
May Fortune make some person a vessel for her abiding with her blossoming splendor; may the host of bards praise another who has attained joy through affection as he comes and goes.

But I consider renunciation alone to be the complete pacification of all sorrow—renunciation which is peerless—in which I worship the Conqueror of Death with my mind, speech, and physical action. (14)

May Fortune, whose splendor expands through her lineage, make someone a worthy recipient of her residence; may the host of bards, having attained joy through their affectionate generosity, praise someone; but as for me, I consider that renunciation alone—which is peerless among all things, which pacifies every sorrow, and which I worship with my mind, speech, and desired actions—to be the one who has conquered death.

Though they assume a form that bears the serpent-like trappings of worldly existence and, being mobile, are attended by those whose minds are captivated by prosperity, the steadfast prefer the immobile; for how could the luster of the virtuous not shine forth, having forcibly obtained that brilliance which, like the sun—the cutter of darkness—is the natural light of the noble? || 15 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! Your mobile form, which bears a retinue of serpents, and likewise Your immobile form, the bestower of fortune—both of these are served by those who are self-composed and firm-minded. Having obtained Your form, which forcibly destroys darkness like the abundant light of the sun that cuts through the gloom, how could the innate luster of the wise not shine forth? (Indeed, it must shine.)
O mind, do you desire to praise the auspicious throat of the Lord— dark as emerald and the refuge of Vāsuki— who is intent upon service to the Blessed One?
If you possess devotion that plunges into a state unassailed by the force of pride and passion, then you too shall find steadfastness in the essence of serving the Lord of Serpents as his garment.

Anvaya: O Mānasa! Do you wish to praise Vāsuki—who has resorted to the emerald-green throat of the Blessed One and is intent upon his service—in order to obtain auspiciousness? (With an interrogative intonation: O Mānasa! If devotion to the Lord takes root in you, who are already struck by the force of the wind of pride, then will you also fix your resolve upon the essence of serving the king of serpents as a garment?

Seeing Rāvaṇa, Maghavat abandoned Airāvata and fled; seeing him, he turned pale with fear, imitating the dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇa. All this is the greatness of your grace. Alas, O you whose resolve has been rendered futile, for whom does service not lead to success, yet it leads to a new kind of emaciation for you?
*Note: The term *anukṛta-śyāmādhavam* is a complex pun: it refers both to the pale (anukṛta) Madhava (Kṛṣṇa) and to the one who imitates (anukṛta) Śyāma (Kṛṣṇa).*

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Seeing Rāvaṇa in battle and observing Mādhava—who, out of fear, has become pale and thus resembles Śyāmādhava—Maghavat abandoned Airāvaṇa and departed; this entire new expansion of yours is the greatness of Your grace. O You who have destroyed vain resolves! To whom does Your service not lead to success? (Indeed, it leads to the success of everyone.)

Having slain that lord of night-stalkers along with his army, and having driven him from his abode in Laṅkā, Rāma attained the distress of the gods and the formidable, yet magnificent, sovereignty of Vibhīṣaṇa; how indeed could he have recovered the blameless Vaidehī, who had been carried away by that deluded one, were it not for the extensive and radiant devotion you performed toward the Victorious One?
O Lord! If that Rāma, who was praised by the radiant and victorious [Viṣṇu], had not indeed performed devotion unto you, then how could he—
having slain the lord of the night-rangers (Rāvaṇa), the dweller of Laṅkā, along with his army, while inflicting suffering upon the gods, and having attained the formidable sovereignty of Vibhīṣaṇa—
have recovered that sinless Vaidehī who had been deluded?

O You who are the supreme remover of the world's sorrow, why do You not show me that compassion which grants the dawn of wisdom and destroys the constant, agonizing illusion of those embodied beings who are deeply skeptical and whose vision is deluded by the darkness of Māyā— a compassion for whom even the thick, vast stream of nectar is not worth a fraction? (19)

That compassion of Yours, which arises from the dawn of wisdom to destroy that very illusion which always brings exhaustion to embodied beings— whose vision is deluded by the darkness of ignorance and who are deeply skeptical regarding the world beyond (doubting whether the next world exists or not)— do You not exercise it toward me? That compassion, whose abundant and vast stream of nectar does not even deserve to be called "slavery" in this world.
It is not fitting for the faults to suddenly manifest their rise; let that darkness now bring about the destruction of my own sight, lest it afflict the eyes of those like me.

Alas, this hand of Śiva—renowned like the planet Venus (Pauṣṇa) for forcibly bringing about the blooming of lotuses—does not reveal its power by dispelling the pain of desire, but rather brings it to ruin.

Is it now appropriate for faults to arise? It is not fitting. Let that darkness which destroys the self-illumination of the vision of those like me not prevail! Alas! Does this celebrated hand of Śaṅkara—not like the hand of Pūṣan—by forcibly causing the blossoming of the lotus (the production of the Fortune of Liberation), not dispel all suffering and manifest every hope? (Indeed, it manifests them all.)
p.

610) [The lotus] is cool and smooth, pleasant with its fragrance, and the very essence of the nose; yet it possesses neither substance nor the unrestrained play of affection born of love. Therefore, having conquered worldly existence, may I repeatedly worship you, O Hara, who are free from pride and ever intent upon the welfare of others. (21)

The cool, smooth, fragrant essence of the nose is not the essence; nor is the playful, unrestrained sport fashioned by love the essence. Therefore, O Hara! having conquered this worldly existence which is otherwise invincible due to its unarisen arrogance, I shall worship you—who are ever intent on the welfare of others—again and again.
The gaze of women, shimmering like a snare, obstructs my mind as it dwells within the inner chamber of the night, just as a net traps a young deer.
O Lord, through contact with him, like me, he too has become indifferent to honor and dishonor; now, with joy, he has come for refuge to you, the noble one.

O Lord! While I dwell in my home at the end of the night, when all troubles have subsided, the glance of women obstructs my mind—just as a snare traps a young deer with its flickering appearance. O God! Because of that contact, I must endure here both honor and dishonor; therefore, being greatly distressed, I have now joyfully sought refuge in you, the magnanimous one.
She possessed a vast kingdom whose sovereignty was shared by vassal lords, and whose feet were bathed by streams of rays effortlessly emerging from the jewels in the king’s crown;
yet she bore a face beautiful enough to disturb the minds of sages with a mere knitting of her brows, while her passion for the voracious God of Love increased ever further.
At the gateway there is the agitation of elephants born in the vast caves of mountains; what indeed is the number of riches that manifest the affliction of calamities?
In this way, how could Fortune ever resort to one devoid of splendor? It would be devoid of splendor, were it not for your singular grace, which swiftly bestows favor upon your enemies.
(24) (A yugma).

Anvaya: O Blessed One! If even this one favor of Yours—by which Your enemies have been subdued—were not granted, then [the world would be lost]: the earth, its splendor diminished; the king, whose feet are bathed by streams of rays effortlessly issuing from the crest-jewels of the rows of tributary princes; the vast kingdom, where the conciliation of rival vassals has ceased;
and the lovely woman at the gate, her passion kindled by the laughing God of Love, bearing a face with a knitting brow that agitates the minds of sages.
What indeed is the count of the elephants born in the vast caves of the mountains, whose agitation causes such manifest calamity and destruction of wealth?
How then could Fortune ever attend you,
who bear upon your head— a head devoid of auspicious hair— the terrible garland of human heads, which is like a second wave within the waves of the river of the gods?
That very lotus row, O King, spreads its excellence through association with you; does it not bring about both the attainment of auspiciousness and the destruction of misfortune? 25.

Anvaya: O Lord! You bear upon your head that very row of skulls—terrible, with hair interwoven, and situated within the waves of the celestial river—which, like a line of lotuses, spreads prosperity; O All-pervading One, by contact with you, what auspicious attainment or destruction of misfortune does it not accomplish? (Indeed, it accomplishes everything.)
Having prepared their beds at the edge of caves where the remaining garlands of *kalikā* flowers are strewn, honoring all their prosperity found within the young creepers dripping with honey,

those devoted to you— O Lord of the moon— enjoy the unceasing dalliances of beautiful women within the mountain caverns during the most excellent night of the dark fortnight, illuminated by the rays of the white-rayed moon. 26.

O Lord! Alas! Those who honor the abundance of creepers whose tender shoots are shedding blossoms, having prepared a complete bed at the edge of those very creepers—leaving nothing but a garland of buds—and who are devoted to you with uninterrupted passion, are served by throngs of beautiful women within mountain caves where the darkness is dispelled by the rays of the moon.
O Destroyer of those veiled by egoism, like the great night that eclipses the sun, the hope for wealth—which destroys the bliss of knowledge—diminishes even that uniform knowledge which shines forth.

To those who have rendered you eloquent with their speech through mere praise, yet devoid of reality, may You, the bestower of ultimate good, become the source of welfare for those people who are vessels of calamity. 27.

Alas! For those shrouded in egoism, the hope for awakening is lost; their wealth is the hope for [worldly] riches. O Bhava! Just as the night dims the shining light, so does [ignorance] cause the knowledge that bestows bliss—even when it appears equal [to worldly things]—to fade away. Yet, for those people who have rendered you eloquent through speech and true praise, though they are vessels of misfortune, you alone are the one who brings about their ultimate welfare; indeed, that alone is true welfare.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth hymn, the *Pādāntayamaka-stotra*, within the *Stutikusumāñjali* dedicated to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
[Now begins] the twenty-ninth hymn.
Then, with words of noble sound, harmonious, joyful, and endowed with auspicious characteristics, I approached the Lord Maheśvara with loud-sounding steps, as if with excellent horses. (1)

Then, with joy, I approached my lord, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), on excellent horses that were of noble color, well-bred, galloping, endowed with auspicious marks, and making a loud sound— just as one approaches a sovereign on such steeds.
When Śiva took the hand of the Goddess, which was reddened by the flow of blood and further stained by saffron paste, then his praise, which was red like the sun, fire, and moon, became manifest.
May he be your benefactor and the granter of fearlessness. || 2 ||

When Śiva took the hand of the Goddess—which was reddened by saffron paste and trembling due to its kinship with him—at that time, may that hymn of his (the Blessed One), which is reddened by the sun, fire, and moon, grant you fearlessness and be for your welfare.

May it bring about [the attainment of] collyrium-less [vision], the cause of the blossoming of the eyes; the unrestrained [restraint] of the elephant-like ears; and the fulfillment of the mind’s cakora-birds even without moonlight. May it act thus.
Worship of the Lord destroys all suffering. || 3 ||

May the worship of the Lord—devoid of collyrium yet causing the eyes to blossom, unrestrained yet warding off the elephants that are [noisy] ears, providing sustenance to the *cākora* birds that are the minds, and devoid of moonlight yet shattering the pain of distress—bring you prosperity.

Just as the month of Mādhava (Vaiśākha) brings happiness, dispels fatigue, and delights the gods even in a grove, so too does the month of Mādhava (Spring) bring joy; yet, it is the Lord Mādhava (Kṛṣṇa), who has taken half the body of his consort, who truly brings such bliss.
The Blessed One, the Lord of Mathurā, was being praised.

Does the springtime, which removes the fatigue of the journey, not bring such happiness? Or does the Dhava tree in the grove not bring such happiness as the Lord Umādhava—who has Mādhava (Kṛṣṇa) joined to half his body—brings when being praised?
Or rather, the union of Umā and Rāma, who desire each other, is like the meeting of day and night, or like the confluence of the celestial river Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
May the White and the Dark [deities] destroy your suffering and sin. || 5 ||

May the meeting of the white and black [streams], like the union of the day and the coming night, or like the confluence of the celestial river Gaṅgā and the stream of the Yamunā, or like the meeting of Umā and Rāma’s beloved [Śiva], destroy your fever and sin. May that great ocean, having reached the one named Umā, which has gone to its dear treasure and attained the great joy of happiness, grant you days through its union.
The auspicious ones are pierced by this great one through necessity.

May that Lord of radiant majesty—who, having arrived at the beloved treasure known as Umā, spent his days in happiness—by his command and through his yoga, bring auspicious days to you all. He bears upon his head, which is crowned by the lord of the twice-born, those great arms that have taken up the burden of the earth; and he possesses a body ever supported by compassion that never falters.
May that auspicious and infallible one bestow prosperity upon you. || 7 ||

May Acyuta Śiva bestow prosperity upon you—he who always bears a body whose crest is presided over by the Lord of the twice-born (Brahmā), whose great arms are ever entrusted with the burden [of the world], and who is the refuge of unyielding compassion;

he in whom dwell the atoms of the fire of time, white as nectar, which are like great elephants for the destruction of the tree of sin, and which are the minute particles that grant fearlessness. May he grant it.
May Hara grant you well-being with that hand. || 8 ||
May Hara grant you peace with that hand in which reside the great elephants that destroy the tree of sin, as well as the atoms of nectar-white ash and the particles of purifying fire.
"My steadfastness arises from your Sudarśana; what more need be said, O Hari, regarding our inseparability?"—this was the dialogue between Śaṅkara and Kṛṣṇa.
May that which arises from a single opening [of the lotus] be for your happiness. || 9 ||
Anvaya: O Hari! By your Sudarśana, my steadfastness arises; what more need be said of our non-difference? Likewise, O Śambhu!

By your Sudarśana, my steadfastness arises; what more need be said of our non-difference with Hari? May this speech, uttered from the single mouth of both Śaṅkara and Kṛṣṇa as they addressed one another, lead to your happiness.

O dweller of the mountain, that fire whose birth is not from wood burns cruelly and perpetually in your eye; yet why does it not burn Yama, whose head is always reddened by it? Is that cruel fire devouring those who have taken refuge in you? 10.
O Dweller on the Mountain! That fierce fire whose birth [is not from wood]—that Aruṇa, the crested one—always blazes in your eye. O Lord!
Why have you not, by means of that [fire] ever present on your head, hidden Yama? Let that fierce [Yama] devour me, who have taken refuge in you!

I constantly praise Hara or Hari with fervor and speed—Hara, whose abode is the mountain-peak, whose splendor is enhanced by the Pināka bow, who possesses great supernatural power, and who is intent upon tranquility; or Hari, who likewise possesses great power and is devoted to peace.

I praise with fervor and speed either Hara— who always has his kinship established with the mountain (Naga), whose glory is augmented by the Pināka bow, who possesses great supernatural power, who is intent on tranquility, and who is honored by those who have attained peace— or Hari— who always has his kinship established with the mountain (Anaga), whose glory is augmented even by the sky (Nāka), who possesses great supernatural power, who is intent on tranquility, and who is honored by those who have attained peace.

The mind of the fool wanders excessively in saṃsāra, and day and night it abandons devotion to Śambhu. What else, then, could bring him well-being in this world, if he were to offer his own actions to Śambhu? (12)

This foolish mind wanders excessively in worldly existence (*bhava*) and day and night in the presence of Śrī Śiva; yet, if it abandons devotion [to Him], what peace could there possibly be for it beyond its own actions, even if it were to offer those very actions to Śambhu? Is he Hara or Hari—who, intent on constantly tormenting Skanda, holds in his hand the ocean-born moon, which is as fit to be placed upon his face as it is to be worn as an ornament?
He shakes off your misfortune. || 13 ||

May Hara—or else Hari—dispel your misfortune: he who, ever intent on crushing Skanda, holds in his hand the ocean-born Kālakūṭa (poison), which is black in luster and fit to be placed within his mouth; or else he holds in his hand the ocean-born Śaṅkha (conch), which is white in luster and fit to be placed within his mouth.

Desiring to conquer the ocean of the succession of afflictions, carrying begging bowls in their hands within the forests, and unable to endure the humiliation caused by an evil king, the virtuous ones resort to us, who are devoted to our praise. 14.

Desiring to conquer existence— which arises from a succession of afflictions— the virtuous, who have endured humiliation at the hands of wicked kings, resort to *bhava* (existence) while dwelling in forests with begging bowls in hand, intent on praising [the Lord]. When shall I attain a state worthy of being beheld, possessing a body resplendent with profound peace and fit for beautiful garments and ornaments?
Like the moon and like the sun, so are you to Acyuta.

O Lord! When, bearing a body resplendent with profound tranquility and worthy of being adorned with beautiful garments, shall I attain the fitness to be gazed upon by You, O Acyuta, like the moon or the sun? Is it by a mango grove filled with swarms of bees, or by my beloved’s braid of hair with its swarm of bees? Or is it by the beauty of a lake accompanied by young female swans?
For devotion to the Lord is indeed the foundation for the abode of the immortals.
O immortal one! What is the use of a mango grove filled with restless bees? Likewise, what is the use of a beloved’s braid of hair that is not thick?

And what is the use of the beauty of a lake accompanied by swans? For I have maintained devotion to the Lord through non-violence (*ala*) and non-attachment (*alayā*). When shall I carry [my life]—spotless, exceedingly pure, graced by swans, and with garments brightened by the waters of the great rivers?
By the grace of the Lord, [I cast off] my body as one casts off a garment in autumn. || 17 ||

Anvaya: When, by the grace of the Lord, shall I bear a body that is as faultless as autumn, exceedingly pure with the waters of serene great rivers, and whose garment of the sky is adorned by swans? O mind, come to Mount Malaya or Himālaya to take refuge in the Lord; or else, go to Rasātala, where there is a suitable Himālaya.
Seek out those who take refuge; do not go to destruction. || 18 ||

Sequence: O mind! Come to the Malaya region to take refuge in the Lord, or come to the Himalayan mountain; or seek the Lord Śrī Hāṭakeśvara, who dwells in the netherworld (rasātala) as a fitting abode for serpents. Do not go to your destruction through futile exertion.

Having fixed your eye upon Him—who burns the Mind-born (Kāma), yet does not spread the loss of desire through His glance, and who, though possessing an undestroyed form, maintains the state of having eight forms—[seek Him].
Victorious are the manifold manifestations of Śambhu.

Victorious are the manifold manifestations of Śambhu, who possesses eight forms while his own form remains undiminished; he casts the eye of lineage upon the Mind-born (Kāma) as he burns him with his gaze, yet does not extend the destruction of desire, for he is the destroyer of passion.
O King, for one who takes refuge in you, who are devoted to compassion, there is no defeat anywhere in battle; even when enemies begin a mutual struggle against him, they themselves are defeated.
They take refuge in the Protector, who maintains invincibility with his bow.
O Unborn One! O Supreme Compassionate One! For him who has taken refuge in You, there is never defeat in battle.
Others—those whose mutual victory has begun and who have abandoned their own defeat—take shelter of that Protector.
Surely it was Kṛṣṇa who cast down that king of birds, who had long established his position upon two wings and who removes the distress of Vinatā.
But you, who bears [him] upon his head, are indeed the Lord. || 21 ||

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: He who for a long time has established his station upon two wings, who removes the distress of Vinatā—that king of birds (*garuḍa*), Kṛṣṇa (Śrī Viṣṇu) certainly placed below him. But he who for a long time bears upon his head the king of the twice-born (*dvijādhirāja*), who has established his station upon two wings and who removes the distress of Vinatā—that you are the Lord (*īśvara*).

Even Viriñca does not know the name of that All-pervading One; for him who bows before Him, suffering consisting of dense pain and disease is destroyed, and even He becomes free from disease. He shall not experience sorrow, nor shall he suffer from the ailment of ignorance.

Even Viriñca does not know that Lord, whose throat is embraced by the daughter of the ocean, who is eternally devoted to Satī, and who is Acyuta—the one for whom the abundant Sarasvatī, never turning to another, adorns him with the pearls of his ever-new utterances. (A pair of verses) Anvaya: Even Viriñca does not know that All-pervading Lord, whose chest-throat is embraced by the daughter of the ocean, who is eternally possessed of devotion to Satī, and who is Acyuta.

For one who bows down and whose abundant speech, directed toward no other, adorns [the Lord] with the pearls of novel expressions, that All-pervading Lord destroys the suffering consisting of dense agony;

for that bowing devotee, even that which was previously free from disease may become [a source of joy]. Likewise, this one, humble through devotion, shall not experience even the sorrow of non-communication [in the form of not returning].

O Mahodayā, by whose greatness the sound of Yamadhāma became a bestower of desired objects for King Śveta; O Mahodayā, where is that compassion of yours now toward us, which grants steadfastness to those who bow before you? 24.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Alas! Where has that "Mahodayā" (of great prosperity), Your compassion, now gone from us—that by which, in King Śveta, there arose the sound of the abode of Yama granting his desired boon (the cry, "Do not fear")—that Mahodayā compassion of Yours, which bestows courage upon those who bow before You? I am here, [seeking] Acyuta, the Supreme Person, the conqueror of Bala, who has taken hold of Truth, whose glory is unshakable, and who bears the Nandaka sword.
I take refuge in the Lord who bears the Sudarśana [discus]. || 25 ||

Anvaya: I take refuge in this Lord, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the Infallible (Acyuta), the Conqueror of Bali, who has made his commitment to truth, whose glory is unshakable, who brings joy to those who seek him, and who bears the Sudarśana discus.
How is it that you, who bestow equality upon the devoted, who possess a likeness to the wish-fulfilling vine (Kalpalatā), yet bear this form of Samantā?
I utter a hundred years of praise, yet not even that [is sufficient].

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! Bearing this form of equality, how could I not recite for a hundred years this hymn of Yours—which bestows equality upon those possessed of devotion and bears a resemblance to the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā)?

Herein, he who bears the state of being the crest-jewel of the Moon (the lord of the twice-born) with a form as formidable as a battle-axe, is Giriśa, the benefactor of the virtuous in the three worlds.
Bow down even more deeply to that Acyuta of slender form. || 27 ||

O seekers of spiritual welfare! Bow down deeply to that Lord Giriśa, whose form is more radiant than the moon, who bears the crown of the Lord of the Twice-born (Brahmā), who bestows immeasurable benefit upon the virtuous in these three worlds, and who is the infallible Acyuta.

He by whom Yama’s great transgressions were brought to ruin by his very glance—he who possesses the power to destroy [all] and who brings about auspiciousness—is the Great One; if he is pleased, he bestows that supreme state. (Note: *anvaya* refers to the syntactic connection or construction of the verse.)
And obstacles have been destroyed, and those who have frustrated our desires have been eliminated. || 28 ||

Anvaya: O you who have commenced the Great Festival! If you bestow upon one such as me—a worthy recipient of compassion—that very glance by which you brought about the destruction of that Yama, whose misconduct destroys happiness, then a great and auspicious destiny has arisen;
all obstacles have been overcome and desires fulfilled.

May the Blessed One—who always possesses a splendor kindled by fire, whose eye has assumed a beautiful form, and who is fond of performing noble deeds for the wise—be like the Blessed One [Śiva] unto you. 29.

May the Blessed One (Śrī Buddha), who possesses eyes that are ever-lustrous, whose abode is beautifully fashioned, who is tireless, who is filled with splendor, who delights in beautiful deeds, and who is fond of performing noble services— just like the moon, which is tireless, filled with light, beautifully formed, the maker of night, and fond of performing beneficial acts for the world—
may he lead you to excellent understanding.

Those wise ones who know You never strike that [ego], alas, which is indeed the cause of falling into the lower realms; for when You, the one of excellent intellect, are pleased through the realization of non-egoity, I do not go to suffering that brings about hell.

**Anvaya:** O Lord! Those who know that [Truth] and are accomplished do not ever carry this *ahaṃtā* (ego), which is the sole cause for falling into a low state. O Master! When You, being well-disposed, are pleased, I do not go to the suffering that brings about hell because of that *ahaṃtā*. He who bears upon his lips this beloved speech, which carries the fifth note (*pañcama-svara*) and is a sibling to nectar—he, whose delight finds special rest therein, sustains me. **Translation:** O Lord! Those wise ones who possess true knowledge and are perfected never harbor that egoism (*ahaṃtā*), which is the very cause of one's downfall. O Master! Since You are well-disposed and gracious, I do not experience the misery that leads to hell on account of that egoism. He who holds upon his lips this beloved voice—which resonates with the fifth musical note (*pañcama-svara*) and is a kin to the nectar of immortality—and whose joy finds its special repose in it, sustains me.
May that Śiva, the infallible one, prosper you with his beautiful form. || 31 ||

May that Śiva, the Infallible One, who bears upon his body my beloved Umā—who carries in her mouth a voice that is a sister to nectar, whose resonance rests upon the excellence of grammatical derivation, and who holds the fifth musical note—prosper you. This hymn has been composed by me for the benefit of those who worship you; through it, the welfare of the virtuous is indeed extended, and mental exhaustion is dispelled when it is held in the mind.
Since this has been handed down in the collection of the Vedas. || 32 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! This hymn of praise to You has been composed by me for the welfare of those who worship You; indeed, through it, peace is extended to the minds of the virtuous—whether they are expansive, restrained, or disciplined—and even exhaustion is dispelled, since this [hymn], when held fast, acts like a collection of the Vedas (*śrutisaṃhitā*).

May the All-pervading One, whose greatness is immeasurable, whose heart is won over by the daughter of the Himālaya mountains, and whose intellect is strengthened by compassion, destroy the affliction of worldly existence, bestowing that which is flawless, stainless, and beneficial.
May he grant you [blessings]. || 33 ||

May Bhava— the Lord of immeasurable majesty, whose heart was won by the daughter of the Himālayas, who possesses a mind strengthened by compassion, the All-pervading One— grant you complete, stainless, and beneficial welfare, crushing the disease of worldly existence. May Bhava, whose great compassion is noble, whose splendor is ruddy and intense, who is encircled by the great serpent, whose form is free from dissolution, who quells the flood of sins, and whose glory is exalted through the joy held in the minds [of his devotees], bestow blessings upon you.
May it be so for you. || 34 ||

May Bhava—whose lineage is noble compassion, whose great luster is ruddy and intense, who wears the great serpent as a girdle, whose form is free from dissolution, and whose majesty is sublime—be the pacifier of the flood of your sins, bringing joy to your minds.
One [Viṣṇu] bears upon his head the praiseworthy water from the feet of the other [Śiva], while the second [Śiva] performs worship of the other with the lotus of his eye; thus they honor one another.
May Kāma and the enemy of Kaṃsa—who know the inner nature of the Great Elements and the qualities—bestow upon you an indescribable heightening of joy. (35)
One (Śrī Śambhu) bears upon his head the praiseworthy water from the feet of the other (Śrī Viṣṇu),

while the second (Śrī Viṣṇu) performed worship with the lotus-eye of the other (Śrī Śambhu); thus may Kāma and the enemy of Kaṃsa— who know the inner nature of these mutually great qualities— bestow upon you an indescribable height of joy.

May that alliance between two great beings—wherein the lion and the preeminent elephant, though born of mountain and ocean respectively, cast aside their innate enmity and abide in a state pleasing through friendship;
and wherein even the king of serpents and the serpent-eater are joined in sincere amity—secure for you an unimpeded peace.
*Anvaya:* In which [great alliance], the lion and the preeminent elephant, born of mountain and ocean respectively, having cast aside their innate enmity...

May that alliance of the two Great Beings (Śrī Śambhu and Nārāyaṇa)— in which a state so heartwarming with affection exists that even the King of Serpents and the Snake-eater are joined in sincere friendship— secure for you freedom from all obstacles.
Thus ends [the work] of the Lord Maheśvara, composed by the illustrious Kashmiri great poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the twenty-ninth hymn is the "Ekāntara-yamaka-stotra.

This thirtieth hymn is for the purpose of praising my own form as the Sovereign Goddess (*aiśvarī*), who is like the autumnal river— serene and radiant with the white water-lilies (*uccaiḥ-kavasa*) [or, alternatively, the white lotuses].
The opportunity for liberation shines forth, adorned by the absence of old age. || 1 ||

This is my great opportunity to loudly praise the divine form of the Lord, which is serene like an autumnal river, adorned with high white lotuses and red lotuses, tranquil and unsurpassed. "As long as you see the path, as long as your feet remain firm, and as long as the body does not fail, so long perform what is for your own benefit."
Day after day, I bow to the ornament of the region beloved by Rohiṇī, who delights Nandin and others, and whose neck— blessed with auspiciousness and joined by the approaching Kālikā— is held aloft.

Day after day, I bow to the Lord who delights in the lineage [of the Vṛṣṇis], whose throat bears the auspicious mark of the union with Kālikā, and who is the ornament upon the crescent moon that adorns the beloved of Rohiṇī.
I bow to Him who is colored by the sound emerging from the throats of His devotees, who grants desires at any time, and who disregards the God of Death while having conquered it.
[He who wears] the moon, the enemy of the afflictions, as his crest-ornament. || 3 ||

I bow to the Lord, who delights in the sounds emerging from the throats of his devotees, who grants desires out of season, who shows no regard for the god of death (Kāla), who has conquered all afflictions, and who bears the moon upon his crest.

Let my mind wander incessantly in the assembly of the virtuous through its thirst for wealth; yet, without the nectar of your praise, it is difficult to cross the treacherous path of worldly existence.
There is no kinsman on the journey. || 4 ||
O Lord! May this mind, which is daily tormented by the thirst for wealth, wander intensely on the difficult path within the assembly of the wicked;
yet, except for the nectar of Your praise with its melodious sound, there is no other kinsman.
O Noble Master, whatever hymn of praise was composed here by me, a virtuous man, out of a desire to worship You—may that destroy the calamities of worldly existence.
Now, the essence of which shines forth as the passing of time. || 5 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! O You who have been worshipped by me! May that excellent hymn of praise which has now been composed here by me, a virtuous one, with longing—its essence shining as it dispels the disease of worldly existence—dispel my calamity.

For me, who am overwhelmed, there is no father, no mother, nor even kinsmen; they are driven away by the desires for wealth. An enemy besieges one who is separated from friends and devoid of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The one named Mānasamādhi. || 6 ||

Anvaya: O Lord! The mind of one like me, overwhelmed by the latent impressions of wealth (*dhanavāsanā*), is obstructed neither by father nor mother, nor by kinsmen; yet the enemy named mental anguish (*ādhi*) obstructs it—[a state] which the virtuous maintain through an intellect obtained by the grace of Your ordinance, an intellect that shines with the destruction of pride (*adarpakāntakavirājamānā*). Translation: O Lord! My mind, overcome by the desires for wealth, is not restrained by my father, nor by my mother, nor even by my kinsmen; however, the enemy known as mental anguish (*ādhi*) does indeed restrain it. But the virtuous sustain their minds through an intellect acquired by the method of Your grace—an intellect that shines by destroying pride and is radiant with the end of passion.
The burden of the gods.

O Destroyer of Cupid! The virtuous ones bear the burden of the gods with an intellect that shines by having attained the practice of your grace— an intellect shining as the Destroyer of Cupid— and by which,
O Lord who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, a certain multitude of rays, possessing the luster of a lotus, has been acquired through the power of your grace.
O you who have enraged the assembly of the immortals with your majesty! || 8 ||

O you who have the crescent moon as your crest-jewel! That Sun indeed adorns your right eye with a fresh red tint by virtue of your grace; setting aside this innate darkness, please gradually adorn this excellent person with that [redness] as well. (A yugma). Anvaya: O Śītakara-khaṇḍa-śekhara! By which Sun, through the power of your favor, [the eye] became a vessel for the lotus...
That certain, extraordinary mass of rays, powerful as the splendor of the sun-god when provoked, is indeed the Sun;
since it adorns your right eye with its fresh redness, do you, by means of that very right eye, gradually dispel the dense, innate darkness and favor this person.

O Blessed One, for those who have sought devotion to you—whose great body is free from the darkness of ignorance—the hosts of Siddhas proclaim their fame here on earth, [you] whose great body is free from the darkness of ignorance. 10.
Indeed, O Blessed One! Here, the hosts of Siddhas proclaim the fame of those great souls who have sought devotion to you—those of incomparable and great form, free from the darkness of ignorance.

By your grace, this beautiful land, radiant with the splendor of Dāmodara and adorned by charming people, shall be long inhabited by those who enjoy tranquility. [Radiant with the splendor of Dāmodara, it is made beautiful by the people.]
The forest was strewn with soft grass suited to the season.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! By your grace, people who have attained tranquility dwell for a long time in the forest strewn with soft seasonal grass, which is beautiful with its dark pigment and shines with the luster of the moon (Dāmodara), and is further adorned by the splendor of the unconquered (Ajitā). Your playful glance, while striking down the great sage who was killing a deer, brought about a new state of meditative absorption; yet that same glance once again restored him to life.
He attained the concentration that is like a fresh creeper fashioned by Yama.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Your playful glance, slaying the deer-like pride of the great sage (Dakṣa), brought him to a state of new, unprecedented lack of composure; yet this is most wonderful—that your very same glance, its playfulness now stilled, has caused him (the Prajāpati Dakṣa) to regain his composure once again.
The assembly, filled with a multitude of worthy persons, shines brightly through the spontaneous honoring of the king who is devoted to you and whose interest in the gathering is insatiable.
[With the vessel of supreme bliss.

13. [Analysis: O Lord! This assembly of the King—who is devoted to you, who possesses great zeal, and who is a vessel for supreme bliss—shines forth, filled with excellent people who are vessels for supreme bliss and who are ever-ready to honor him.
He who constantly praises you with unrestrained speech that is free from obstacles, Lakṣmī herself approaches him without hindrance and attends upon him most closely.

O All-pervading Lord! Prosperity herself, coming of her own accord, waits upon him who—his speech uncurbed by obstacles—constantly praises you without hindrance; she follows him closely and serves him.

Even Yama, whose restraint is difficult for the likes of Sahasramukha and others to bear, finds him unbearable to hold within his heart; therefore, come with me and Umā, and favor him with your gracious presence.
By her glance, she performed the sacrifice of the arms of the bodiless god of love. || 15 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Yama, whose power even those beginning with me cannot withstand, is difficult for me to hold within my heart; therefore, you, who are capable of enduring Umā, come together with her—who has humbled the shoulders of the bodiless Love—and favor me with your gracious glance. When your flawless, nectar-like speech is uttered to grant a boon, when will this wretched body of mine become like a vessel for that boon? Translation: O Lord! Even for those such as myself, Yama’s power is difficult to endure; thus, he is hard for me to bear within my heart. Therefore, you, who are capable of enduring Umā, approach her—who has subdued the shoulders of the bodiless Cupid—and look upon me with a gracious eye. When your flawless, nectar-like words are spoken to bestow a boon, when will this wretched body of mine become like a worthy vessel for that blessing?
This nourishes my body. || 16 ||

O Lord! When Your flawless, auspicious words—which grant the most excellent boon (*vara*) to those who have taken refuge in You—are uttered, they are like nectar; when will this body of mine, which is like a digit of the moon (*raṅku-aṅka-tanoh kalā*), be nourished by that nectar? Whom does an army that has destroyed the Dānavas—who are like elephants among the clouds of the wicked—never satisfy for the sake of attaining Śiva, an army that is ever-new and in which Śiva is propitiated?
