The speech, ever new, bestows the blossoming of devotion. || 17 ||

For whom does an army—whose followers are ever devoted to Śiva, which brings about the blossoming of devotion, which has destroyed the haughty Dānavas, which possesses new songs, and whose warriors are ever like elephants in the ocean of Hari—not lead to the attainment of auspiciousness? (Indeed, for everyone. I, however, have had my power dispelled by dense enemies who have transgressed through egoism and who carry away stainless bliss; thus, I do not abide in a state of abandonment of faults.
O powerless one, this is not the occasion for your arrogance.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! I am one whose vigor has been dispelled by dense enemies—those who transgress against the ego and who carry away stainless happiness—and whose form bears loss; therefore, O All-pervading Lord, there is no occasion for pride toward me, who am bowed and weak. [Furthermore,] there is a great-speeded, serpent-like, formidable enemy in the mind, which causes excessive despondency even when no fault exists; lead that very end-maker, the sole cause of trembling at the end, to its destruction quickly.
The destruction of evil conduct and impurity. || 19 ||

Anvaya: O you who wear the terrifying hood of a serpent! O destroyer of wicked conduct! Antaka (Death), who brings excessive despondency even to a mind free from fault—lead that inauspicious Antaka, the sole cause of trembling at the end, to swift destruction.

Neither our shields, nor horses, nor new war-cry-raising elephants roar within our palace; for the enemy’s army, its feet wounded, has been defeated by the command of the Lord whose feet are wounded by the blows of the enemy.
For Bhava, when properly honored, is indeed auspicious. || 20 ||
In our home, there are no armor-clad warriors, nor are there horses with fresh manes, nor are there elephants;
yet, while calamity has been warded off by us, our command is subject to the misfortunes of opposition. Therefore, Bhava has been conquered by us;
indeed, Bhava has been properly honored.

Deer go to bodies of water, and swans frequent bodies of water; likewise, the base strike at strength that is difficult for others to overcome. People laugh at one whose impetuous anger has been conquered, even while they themselves remain unrevered in this world of existence.

Just as dull-witted, foolish deer, driven by a desire for water, go toward a pool of strength in an impassable desert, even so do foolish, base people— laughing at the Supreme Lord Sadāśiva, who has conquered the impetuosity of anger— go toward worldly existence (bhava) while abandoning His worship.

Those who were once dependent on intense passion (amanda-rāga) have here become gods with subdued passion (manda-rāga); those who were worshipped by the Siddhas and Sādhyas have become Siddhas and Sādhyas among the gods; those who delighted in new [pleasures] have now attained freedom from decay through that delight.
Anvaya: O Lord! O You who are worshipped by the Siddhas and Sādhyas! Those who are devoted to You here have extended Your unending, ever-new [glory].
Those Siddhas and Sādhyas—people who have resorted to a passion that is not dull, and who have reached Mount Mandara with their passion—have been born into the divine race [attaining immortality].

O Compassionate One! Grant joy; grant liberation which bestows joy; destroy the pride of the emaciated; grant peace, for there is no granting of peace by those who seek their own benefit through the expansion of hostility. Indeed, no such expansion is performed by those who have offered praise.
Your body extends auspiciousness. || 23 ||

Anvaya: O Compassionate One! Delight me; you who grant tranquility to the emaciated, bestow prosperity, and grant liberation—quell that distress! O You whose praise is performed by those who have undertaken protection (such as Viṣṇu and others), does Your expansive benevolence not extend auspiciousness? (Indeed, it spreads great welfare.)

In this time of passion, devoid of restraint, even toward those who were not lacking in wealth and were themselves noble, that which was proclaimed as noble and exalted conduct has now fallen into calamity— conduct that should destroy all affliction.

O Blessed One! That wealth—which was not deficient even among the great kings, which was proclaimed as noble, and which was acquired by me through improper exertion during the season of passion (youth)—that very wealth, destructive of self-restraint, has brought about this calamity.

Indeed, Kamalā (Lakṣmī), whose abode is the desire for the playing of the lute of love, and who is the cause of torment, has, through her violence toward the virtuous, rendered the daughter of the Ocean (Sītā) devoid of her lotus-like beauty.
Lightness of the lotus. || 25 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Indeed, the daughter of the ocean, who brought about the destruction of the Daityas, Lakṣmī—the daughter of the one whose abode is the lotus and whose vehicle is the swan—rendered whom not insignificant? (That is to say, she rendered everyone insignificant.)

O preeminent among the wise, O protector of the earth, may she— who dwells on the Malaya mountain, who is stainless with her lotus-like form, who is compassionate toward the distressed, who is ever-gracious, who brings about the dissolution of existence, who is steadfast, and who destroys the abode of calamities— bestow upon you the state of being free from fear.

Anvaya: O fisherman! O most excellent fisherman! Do not consider me—a dwelling place for calamities—to be like Mount Malaya; for I am stainless, devoid of fear and compassion, merciless, and lacking in steadfastness, yet possessed of a lotus-like [nature] that is free from attachment. Grant even a slight measure of your mind, which is adorned with generosity and capable of bestowing protection and fearlessness; become the granter of my heart's desires in this auspicious forest-abode.
Rama paid her utmost respect with great reverence. || 27 ||

O Bhava! O bestower of desires! O You whose ornaments are generosity, who are capable of providing sustenance and fearlessness, and whose essence is the Supreme Soul—have You not shown even the slightest regard for my auspicious abode, my very home? O giver of fortitude, I have taken refuge in You, who are beyond the reach of the senses (or, who lead one from the path of wrong conduct), and who are free from the afflictions of the Yama-s. He who bestows peace and praises it, and who grants well-being while possessing steadfast joy, [is You]. *Note: The verse plays on the double meanings of "ādaram" (regard/respect) and "adaram" (lack of regard), as well as the various nuances of "yato" (from which/leading to), "yamān" (the Yama-s/afflictions/self-restraint), and "dhṛtamudam" (possessing joy/holding joy).*
Elevate that state of exaltation.

O bestower of fortitude! Since [from this news] one who is devoid of right conduct does not tremble before Yama, the restrainer, and since it proclaims peace (*śam*) to those who proclaim it—reveal that news which brings joy and is firmly established.

By you, the auspicious one, the destroyer of worldly existence, the ground of unmeasured suffering has been shattered. O Hara, remove the end of the end-maker (*kṛtānta*), for we have reached the end of our lives.
What is this "mine-ness" of mine? It is such as that. || 29 ||

O Hara! O destroyer of the Destroyer of the World! By you, who possess auspiciousness and are the savior from worldly existence (*bhava*), has my immeasurable, unreckoned, and all-consuming pride—not even considered by others—been utterly shattered? O you whose fame possesses pure splendor, protect me; O you who are capable of what the three worlds cannot endure, bring me to your own abode; do not lead me away.
O You who are the imperishable one, whose face is like a wound, and who are both the twin and the inexhaustible! 30.

O you of pure splendor and glory! O you who are incapable of being overcome by the pride of the skillful! O imperishable one! Adorn the three worlds; do not lead me to a state of destruction before the eyes of the Yakṣas, but lead me to your own abode—therefore, honor me.

May you, the destroyer of enemies here, day after day, gradually and ever anew, carry away the sins of the world with the destruction of thick clouds of evil, bestowing gifts upon the lowly and the humble.

O Bhava! By me, here, every day, carrying [you] without fail, you—who bestow undiminished gifts, who destroy enemies, who are strengthened by the rising of compassion, and who are united with Umā—have been appropriately won over through ever-new and gentle means (that is, by force or suddenly). O you whose intellect is not unsteady toward what is beneficial and what is harmful, may I strive for your welfare. (32) (A pair of verses). *Anvaya:* O Bhava! By me, here, daily, carrying [you] without fail, you—who bestow undiminished gifts, who destroy enemies, who are strengthened by the rising of compassion, and who are united with Umā—have been appropriately won over (accepted) through ever-new and gentle means (meaning, by force or suddenly). O you whose intellect is not unsteady toward what is beneficial and what is harmful... (Note: The provided text contains a complex *yugalaka* (pair of verses), and the commentary focuses on the first verse. The translation reflects the structure and meaning as presented.)
O Blessed One! With a mind steady and free from enmity, I shall strive for what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful through Your words.
Who would speak of disease in the presence of wealth that removes all affliction? O All-pervading Lord, without You, people are like those afflicted by illness who lack food.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! When wealth—whether internal, in the form of consciousness (*saṃvit*), or external, such as gold—is seized by affliction, who among men, being afflicted with disease and remaining near You, the Compassionate One, would remain without food?

(None at all. By whom has Your power not been established through both praise and blame? [Your] auspicious and swift speech is the destroyer of the calamities of the God of Love. (Note: The verse is structured as a *parisaṃkhyālaṅkāra* [exclusive specification], asserting that no one remains without food when suffering near the Merciful Lord.)
O Destroyer of the Lord of Rati! By whom have your pleasing hymns not been offered? (Indeed, by everyone.
Yet, this auspicious calamity has swiftly fallen upon my speech.

May that state—which is bowed down, devoid of expansion, and which wards off the distress of unobstructed enemies—bring about for me, O Immeasurable One, a peace that is like the very peace of Hara himself. Thus indeed, may it be so for me.

O Hara! I, being free from exhaustion, [approach] Your feet—which grant the removal of the afflictions of enemies without obstruction—to those who are bowed down [in devotion], while immeasurable peace prevails;
thus indeed shall there be peace for me, bringing auspiciousness in both worlds.
The gods and demons, including Indra, along with their kinsmen who have committed great offenses, always take refuge in and go toward Him, who is the source of constant, perfect humility.

"Alas! May he, being composed and well-disposed, protect us from this great and dull ignorance; for he, having no external latent tendencies, is indeed capable of leaping over our dense defilements. (37)
(Stanza in couplet form):

Alas! That very Lord, the kinsman of those who have committed great offenses—the gods and demons, including Indra—who always take refuge in Him and go to Him for protection, seeking His constant grace and honor; may He, the well-composed, the inexhaustible, and the possessor of abundant liberation-glory, protect me, who am His own, for my welfare. Indeed, it is He.
O All-pervading One! May You, who are free from external impressions, be intensely longing for us as we leap over the dense mass of obstacles.
Enough of these dense, unassailable [obstacles] for one practicing austerity, practicing austerity! For my body, though small, has indeed attained a new state of extreme emaciation.
Indeed, O Lord! In the month of Māgha, thick clouds become impossible to cross; therefore, as I perform austerities in this cold season, my large body has reached a state of extreme emaciation.

O Hara, destroyer of Smara—the cause of the destruction of the power of the dark and pale forces of impurity—take away [my suffering], grant [me grace], and, being worshipped, bestow [blessings] in every direction.
A vision resembling the radiance of the radiant. || 39 ||

O Hara, you who are the cause of the remembrance of Smara, whose power is marked by the absence of the *alakṣa* (unmanifested) *lakṣa* (marks)! O Destroyer! As you resort to the quarters, take away my foulness—the threefold impurity consisting of the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* types—and bestow upon me a vision that resembles the radiance of the sun.

O Subduer of the many, unhesitating, and unquelled darkness of delusion accumulated through the arising of worldly existence; O Hara, remove from me this mind, fashioned with its various transformations and full of expansion.
The evil deed has been increased. || 40 ||

O Hara, subduer of the darkness of delusion accumulated through worldly existence! Having rendered this manifold, fearless, unpeaceful, and transformed by various fluctuations of passion, remove this thickened evil of mine.
O Blessed One, grant me that speech which is piteous, repeatedly uttered, highly beautiful, and beneficial; and likewise, O you whose mind is ever-joyful, grant me that which bestows honor.
For that reason, I do not fall away from the virtuous. || 41 ||

O Blessed One! Since I have spoken piteously many times, please grant me Your words, which are exceedingly beautiful and beneficial. O You who delight the minds of the virtuous! O You who have destroyed pride! Grant me that very direction so that I do not fall [into the cycle of worldly existence]. We consider no other path than devotion unto You; by Your glance alone—which removes the darkness of unrighteousness—we consider even the salutation offered to one named Manyā to be a path leading to liberation.
The wise person does not harbor pride regarding those things called "veins" (dhamanīs), for such pride is indeed a source of distress.

O All-pervading Lord! By Your very glance, which quells all darkness, we consider that there is no other refuge for us than devotion unto You; indeed, we regard ourselves as having gone astray. For the intellect, when possessed by pride, does not tolerate bowing down to others—just as the blood-vessel called *manyā* (the neck) cannot endure being bent in directions other than its own. O Lord, may [this devotion] never cease, increasing day by day, surpassing all honor, and being enjoyed by both oneself and others. May it not fail to come to pass.
My intellect is esteemed by the wise, indifferent toward pride, and equal toward both friends and enemies.

Anvaya: O Lord! May that *mā* (prosperity), which has surpassed all pride (*māna*), which increases day by day, and which is incessantly enjoyed by both oneself and others, not be [my goal]? Rather, may my intellect (*dhī*), which is praised by those free from pride (*mānālasa*), be equal toward friends and enemies alike!

Whether it be a snake or a necklace, a bed of flowers or a stone slab, a jewel or a clod of earth, a powerful enemy or a friend, or even a blade of grass... [The verse continues: *tṛṇe vā haye vā bhuvi vā nṛpe vā maṇike vā loṣṭhe vā himakarakiraṇe vā kuśe vā kuśeśaye vā | same vā hṛṣīkeśe'pi ca tulyanijapriyāpriyo vande videhīnandano munirājo yadātmā ||* Whether it be a blade of grass or a horse, the earth or a king, a water-pot or a clod of earth, the rays of the moon or a blade of *kuśa* grass, or even the Lord of the Senses (*Hṛṣīkeśa*)—I bow to that King of Sages, the son of Videha, whose self regards as equal both what is dear and what is not dear.
Or rather, may my days pass in the holy forest, where I look upon all women with equal vision, while repeatedly crying out, "Śiva! Śiva! Śiva! in my lamentation.

The great defects of the humors agitate me; the evening darkness of delusion robs me of my fortitude. When will that night of evil come, with a body marked by the moon of its source of faults, like the intoxicated night when Aniruddha’s throat was seized by the enemy of Doṣā? 44.
Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! The great evils, the enemies in the form of defects, agitate me; the defects of the night of delusion take away my fortitude.

O Compassionate One! When will the dawn—whose body is like the orb of the moon (the vision of Śrī Candramauli)—come to me, just as the intoxicated Uṣā (daughter of Bāṇāsura) [came] to Aniruddha, the throat of whose neck was darkened by the fault [of separation]?

O Goddess whose form emulates the rays of the moon through its loveliness, who possesses celebrated beneficence, and whose crest-jewel is the peak of Mount Rājakhaṇḍa that destroys all darkness—who other than you could be the deliverer from this prison-house called "existence" (bhavana) without your grace? || 45 ||

Anvaya: O you who possess the peak of the crescent moon! In this prison named Bhavana, apart from your grace alone, what [thing] can be a deliverer—one whose form imitates the rays of the moon created for its beauty, which is renowned for its assistance, and which has dispelled the darkness? (The meaning is: none at all.)
Sustained by a mind purified by the *kāśa* grass, it provides space for the path of liberation; it possesses abundant radiance like the sun situated within the limits of the sky;
it has rendered the *kāśa* grass-like barrenness of the world equal to the end of time (*kṛtānta*); and what hope for sustenance is there for a servant, unless he possesses the vision of Śambhu? (46)

Without the lineage-based Śāmbhavī vision, there is no state whatsoever—meaning none at all—that provides space on the path to liberation for those whose minds are held within the sphere of worldly desire; it does not possess abundant light like the sun situated within the limits of space, nor does it dispel the darkness of Death that is scattered throughout the world, nor does it provide shelter for those who serve their masters.
Do not beautiful women, with their hands grasping the hems of their garments as they stumble, reach the end of their distress in the summer heat? Beautiful women indeed [do so].
The wives of the enemies of the kings devoted to you, wandering in the forest, have their tresses forcibly disheveled by wild beasts. || 47 ||

Anvaya: O Blessed One! In the summer heat, what beloved women—dwelling in the forest, lovely, desired, with their hands grasped by their lovers, with the hems of their garments slipping, with the ends of their curls crushed by forest-dwellers, and who are the wives of kings hostile to those devoted to you—do not undergo the exhaustion of torment? (Indeed, they all experience every kind of distress.)

May that sequence of misfortunes—which presents to me the illusion of a mass of sunbeams upon a desert plain—cease; for when will Your compassion, which is the very abode of all illusions and a great darkness-dispelling light, descend here like the rising sun, having assumed its supreme form? (48)

That Māyā, which is difficult to transcend even for Brahmā and the other gods, inflicts weariness upon me like a mass of sunbeams in a parched desert. O Lord! When will Your grace—the dawn that has assumed the highest form—come here to this great darkness, like the light of the goddess Māyā (Lakṣmī)?

Bearing devotion to existence that is served by Rāma and others, she is delightful; like a medicinal herb (oṣadhi) relied upon by Rāma, she has destroyed difficult-to-cross distress (āmā). Like a virtuous wife (satī), she brings an end to the calamities of the good; O Rā! She does not abandon her honorable home, nor is she fickle-minded (mā). 49.

For a person who possesses devotion to Bhava and is served by Rāma and others, the venerable home (the object), wealth (the agent), and likewise the woman— like a medicinal herb dependent on Rāma, virtuous, delightful like Rāma himself, having destroyed difficult-to-cross distress, and having brought an end to the calamities of the virtuous— does not abandon him; indeed, she is stable, and the Fortune of Liberation (*mā*) does not desert him.

Like nectar from the ocean, your gaze—which, like Vārāṇasī, brings about the destruction of sins—is difficult to restrain and possesses constant rays. Like a courtesan and like an army accompanied by cavalry, it rises again and again with a broad beard-like fringe.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Your gaze, which destroys sin and is difficult to resist, is certain to reach [the devotee]; it rises again and again like nectar from the ocean, like Vārāṇasī, like a courtesan, and like an army with its cavalry and long-maned horses.

Like an auspicious elephant, she who has rendered the forehead auspicious through the tilaka-mark honors the Lord upon the auspicious throne; like the auspicious, white lunar day that grants all desires, her body is most excellent and surpasses even Rāmabhadra in its virtues.
For one who has worshipped the Lord upon a *bhadra-āsana* (an auspicious throne), like an elephant named *Anvaya-bhadra*,

his body becomes exceptionally beautiful (*vibhadra*)— removing the delusion of people— and emulates Rāmabhadra through its virtues; it bestows desired objects, just as the lunar day (*tithi*) called Bhadrā— which is white (*sitā*), associated with the bright fortnight, marked by the *bhadra* on the forehead, and whose auspiciousness is uncreated— bestows what is sought.

O steady one, my mind has not reached the depths of your heart; it is like a city of the gods, possessing golden serpents and resting upon elephants. Furthermore, it has not gone elsewhere, creating a state free from affliction, like the eastern quarter where Indra dwells, with its lofty Nandana groves and its elephants.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Just as the city of the gods (Amarāvatī), together with its golden mountain (Meru), is like the abode of the Nāgas, so too this sinless intellect of mine has not reached the unfathomable heart of You;
thus, creating blameless speech (gāḥ), this intellect, resting upon the Nāgas (the serpent-king Śeṣa) and possessing lofty Nandana groves, is like the eastern quarter (Indra’s direction).

(Except for the nectar of praise for Your Lordship) it has not gone elsewhere. Though my intellect is unable to bear the essence, it finds its essence in You; it has undertaken the pursuit of the darkness of delusion through the attainment of the essence.
Possessing the essence of well-spoken verses equal to the cries of the sweet-voiced cuckoo, it is like a string of pearls that removes the heat of heavy suffering.

Anvaya: O All-pervading Lord! This intellect of mine—which has driven away the darkness of delusion, which possesses the essence of refined speech equal to the words of the excellent cuckoo, and which is like the *Sārāvalī* (a medicinal herb that removes the heat of fever) in its removal of the intense torment [of worldly existence]—though it has been cast aside by those who cause heavy suffering, remains devoted to You alone; for in the assembly of ministers and kings, it shares in the excellence of Your well-spoken verses, offers praise beneficial to the audience, and is free from envy toward those who have attained tranquility (*sāma*). It does not follow the common path.
O Lord! May that venerability— which, by its power,

I did not resort to as a common path, which is the essence of well-spoken words witnessed in the assembly of ministers and kings, which consists of praise beneficial to the audience, and which has cast away all envy— may that venerability never quickly abandon me in Your presence.
Like a torrent from a mountain, like a boat with a helmsman, your gaze is a stream that bestows a rain of nectar; like the city of Dhārā, it grants happiness;
like the edge of a sword, it cuts away misfortune; it is a stream that removes the suffering of others and destroys the six internal enemies.

O All-pervading Lord! Your eye, which bestows happiness, is like a mountain peak providing a foundation, like a boat with a helmsman, like a shower of rain upon barren soil, like the city of Dhārā which is the edge of the sword for misfortune, the ultimate limit (the highest excellence) in removing the suffering of others, and one that has destroyed the six internal enemies.

The region of your neck has a luster like black iron; your throat is beautiful black; even your eye is like the fire of time (Kālāgni), burning away time in an instant. Your speech is timely yet not soft, and you have destroyed the time [of suffering] for your servants.
O Infinite One, what gain could there be for me without these? 56.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Your throat-region possesses a luster like black iron (it is beautifully dark); Your eye also, like the fire of cosmic destruction, is "kālā" (dark) in that it burns away time in an instant; and Your speech, though not soft, is "ālā" (a protector) for those who have been wounded [by worldly existence], just as the goddess Kālī is.
O All-pervading Lord! Without these—Your throat, Your eye, and Your speech—who else could be the bringer of gain for me throughout this infinite time?

Filled with compassion for me who has surrendered my own self at your feet, never forsaking me; released from the fear of Saturn by one who delights in worshiping you with pearls and other offerings; as pure as a string of pearls—this speech, released by me through departing from other paths, has been offered to you like a necklace of pearls. 57.

Anvaya: O Lord! By me—who have abandoned the path of other [deities] and who have ceased delighting in the worship of others—this pure speech, like a string of pearls (*muktāvalī*) that has not been released (*amuktā*), which is full of compassion for my feet and has been offered by me out of fear of the sun (*ārki*), has been uttered before you and cast forth (*vimuktā*). It is not small (*analpā*). It is not abandoned (*amuktā*). It is stainless (*vimalā*). It is unreleased (*avimuktā*). It is like a pearl necklace (*muktāvalī*). It has been spoken (*uktā*) unto you. It has been cast away (*vimuktā*). It is not small (*analpā*). It is not abandoned (*amuktā*). It is stainless (*vimalā*). It is unreleased (*avimuktā*). It is like a pearl necklace (*muktāvalī*). It has been spoken (*uktā*) unto you. It has been cast away (*vimuktā*). It is not small (*analpā*). It is not abandoned (*amuktā*). It is stainless (*vimalā*). It is unreleased (*avimuktā*). It is stainless (*vimalā*). It is unreleased (*avimuktā*). It is like a pearl necklace (*muktāvalī*). It has been spoken (*uktā*) unto you. It has been

May my speech, which is like a creeper named Kalpa (the eon), which has washed away the conceptualizations of misfortune, which is fashioned like the Kalpa-tree, which offers praise, which is like the moon, which is seen through the scriptures of the Kalpa-sūtras, and which is an image of the nectar of immortality—may it be inexhaustible for me. 58.

O All-pervading Lord! May this song of mine—offered as praise unto You, which has washed away the fluctuations of misfortune, which is as beautiful as the moon, well-versed in the thread of the Kalpas, conforming to the scriptures, and resembling nectar—be like the *Kalpa* creeper, undecaying until the end of the world-cycle (*ākalpa*).
Suddenly I have been made like the sun by the Self-born Creator, who possesses a thousand powers; he, indeed, who suddenly hurls his arrow [of destruction].
Though she approached with sudden trepidation, she was nonetheless difficult to endure.

Anvaya: O Lord! Just as the sun is suddenly [overpowered] by Mārgaśīrṣa, so have I been suddenly made to bear what I am incapable of bearing by Ātmabhū (Kāma), alas! That woman, who is difficult to endure and full of mockery, approaches me with sudden fear; she hurls that arrow in the form of a woman at me.

Produce sorrow for the afflicted, produce it for those who are not worthy vessels; produce it through the agitation of begging and the lack of delight; produce stainless weariness through the unimpeded application of the self to the nectar of immortality. 60.

O Akhañjanaya! O Aja! (May you) bring about freedom from suffering for me, who am distressed by the lack of a worthy recipient (*abhājanatā*), by begging, by the desire for enjoyment, and by agitation; likewise, through the application of yourself to me, lead me—who am thus born, stainless, and unexhausted—to immortality (*amṛta*).

O Lord of Umā, you who remove even a slight affliction of suffering, O you who have brought fear to the demons (*kṛtabhīśamanā*), O you who are free from disease (*śamanāmaya*), grant me the state of being free from the bonds of worldly existence (*vipāśamanā*).
They are the pacifiers of those who are not pacified, as proclaimed by the people of Śamanātha. || 61 ||

O Lord of Umā! O you who have subdued fear! O you who are free from affliction! You, who with but slight effort bring relief to the distressed, do not become one who fails to pacify my sorrows! O All-pervading One! You, whose subduing of the suffering of the helpless is renowned—grant me peace that is free from bonds and free from destruction. Adored by the destroyer of Madhu (Viṣṇu), you are equal to Madhu (the spring season), born from the flower named Madhu, and like a young bride languid with honeyed wine, you are not [like] Madhu [the demon].
I offer you speech drenched in honey, along with honey itself.

Anvaya: O you who are honored by Madhu—the destroyer of Madhu (Vasanta), and by that which is born from flowers named Madhu (the pollen)—I have now awakened, as it were, the languid speech of a woman intoxicated by honey (sweet as nectar), which was sleeping within you, like a woman overcome by wine. (Note: *Madhunāśinā* refers to Viṣṇu, the slayer of the demon Madhu; *madhunā* here refers to the spring season (*vasanta*). *Madhunāmapuṣpajanuṣā madhunā* refers to the pollen (*kiñjalka*) produced from flowers called *madhuka*. *Madhunā alasām vadhūm iva* compares the speech to a languid woman; *madhunā plutām* means "overflowing with honey" or "intoxicated by wine. The sense is that the speaker has awakened the dormant eloquence within the addressee.)

O you who are worthy of worship by the guardians of the earth, that earth which was once devoid of wealth and grain, and whose surface was not even lush, has now become a ground of wealth through the fame of your complexion as white as nectar;
for to our eyes, your face is like fresh nectar itself.

O you who are worthy of worship by the guardians of the earth! You, whose fame possesses a luster white as nectar, run to abandon wealth (*vasu*) and grain (*dhānya*) among people who have become emaciated due to the lack of such abundance; thus, this new vision of yours regarding the earth (*vasudhā-dṛk*) becomes like fresh nectar (*sudhā*), yet it is not mere nectar (*asudhā*), for it bestows life.

He, who is the Lord of the World, whom those full of expansion reached through their vows, and by whom all things in the world become full of beauty through his timing— he, who is composed of nectar, has been worshipped by me with words full of sweetness.
In this world, where have the words (*samayāḥ*) of those standing near (*samayā*) this Lord of the Age (*samayāpati*) not attained full bloom? (Indeed, everywhere.

Likewise, since the words (*samayāḥ*) of those situated near (*samayā*) this Lord of the Age become full of delight (*vilāsamayāḥ*), that All-pervading One (*vibhuḥ*) is worshipped by me with speech consisting of nectar (*sudhāsamayā*).

In the heart of the other Kali age, there is a fresh longing that is like a sprout of nectar swelling at the withering of the Kali era; she is like a garland of blossoms that has conquered all other flowers, and she, bearing the splendor of the Kali age, is a bud upon his crown.
Anvaya: O Blessed One! In Your heart—which is compassionate toward people distressed by the Kali age and weary of strife with men—there was no room for *utkalikā* (anxiety or longing).

O Conqueror of Śaka! That *kalikā* (the Kali age), which withers even the nectar-like waves of immortality, has been cast out; yet that *kalikā* (flower bud) possessing luster, like a subtle blossom, has been fashioned upon Your crown and garland.

He who is free from disease, resorted to by a single digit; he who, by a digit of the moon that has crushed all feverish distress, is possessed of all parts yet remains partless; he who, through his voice, has brought an end to the accumulation of sorrow.

Anvaya: O Sakalākala! Though you are one who has crushed the fever of worldly existence (*pākala*) by means of the digit of the moon (*ekakalā*), and though that digit is itself devoid of sorrow (*vihita-śoka-layā*)—even so, by that same digit (*kalā*) in the form of your exceedingly sweet speech, you have rendered those who take refuge in you free from disease. (Note: Although in Ayurveda *pākala* is specifically known as the fever of elephants, it is here employed by poets to denote ordinary fever or the fever of old age and death. Furthermore, while the digit of the moon is traditionally associated with sorrow, this verse describes it as being "devoid of sorrow" by way of its poetic artifice.)
O Supreme One!

By Your glance, Ramā has attained that state which brings an end to the supreme enemy [Māra] and is honored by the highest beings. O You who are devoted to compassion! Abandon me, who am supremely distressed, for I am the very succession of the true virtues of the ultimate reality.
Anvaya: O destroyer of the enemy of Pāramāraka! O succession of excellent virtues of the ultimate truth! By Your glance, Ramā has obtained another person who is bowed down;
O You who are intent on compassion, do not abandon me, who am supremely afflicted!
Like a sweet-sounding kalakaṇṭha bird, may we have speech ever-new, fresh, and worthy of praise; O You who shatter the fear of worldly existence, be, be, be! [Obeisance to You].
O Destroyer of the pride of pride, far away! || 68 ||

O Bhava! O destroyer of the intoxication of Madana! Like a sweet-voiced cuckoo with its *kala-kala-kala* notes, protect us—we whose words are ever-new, fresh, and most excellent—by casting far away our pride.
You who are terrified by the fear of worldly existence, become [our] refuge.

Grant us a voice that is perfectly melodious (*avikala-kala*) and a throat that is sweetly resonant (*kalakala-kala-kaṇṭha*), and bestow upon us ever-new and ever-fresh, supreme speech. O Lord of prosperity, arise, arise, for you are the dispeller of the fear of worldly existence.
O Destroyer, take away this pride, pride, pride, pride, pride, and pride! || 69 ||

O you whose digits are complete! O you who are ever-new through your constant renewal! Grant to one such as me your excellent speech, which possesses a throat resonant with the *kalakala* sound. O Lord of all power! O Bhava! Be the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence for us; take away this merciless, intoxicating pride.
When the Goddess Jayā and Vijayā worship her, may your victorious gaze, fixed upon her whose brows dance, be for our victory, like a rain of grace.
Bhūḥ, Divi, Vijayā, she who is called Vijayā by her form, Trasadravijayā, and she named Jayā—[these are your forms].
O Blessed One! For the sake of victory, Your victorious gaze—which bestows victory—is fixed upon the Goddess Śrī Bhavānī, whose eyebrows dance as she is worshipped by Jayā and Vijayā;
likewise, this earth, from which enemies flee in terror, has been protected by Your form known as Vijayā and named Jayā, just as the world is protected by rain that conquers the heavens.
"O virtuous ones, abandon the impure, dense, and base attachment to worldly pleasures; do not expand that which is of small form. Take refuge in the pure, expansive, and honored [state];
take refuge in the truth, and become [that]. Thus was it said.

O wise ones! Do not extend that which is dense, stainless, and delightful, yet involves the transgression of *damala*; rather, take refuge in that which has arisen from our form as it was uttered by us! O seekers of the auspicious! May you take refuge in our speech, which is honored by people and is the truth (*ṛta*). Bow down to him who has pacified the calamities of the company of virtuous men through his union, and who is resplendent with a majesty that humbles desire. Bow down!
It is illuminated by the splendor of the Mahīna [deities] of desire. || 72 ||

O wise ones! Indeed, you should bow to Him who has quelled attachment and the suffering caused by the wicked—namely, Śiva, whose desires are stilled; who is not lacking in splendor, being radiant with full brilliance; who destroys the darkness of the Kali age; who is adorned by the king of serpents; and who bears the crescent moon upon his crest. Remember Hara, the destroyer of Smara, who is graced by the king of serpents and who has mastered all that is enchanting.
Marked by a crest and a moonlet. || 73 ||

O devotee! Remember Hara, who destroys the darkness of the Kali age, who is resplendent with the sound [of his laughter], who is marked by the crescent moon and the peacock, who is adorned by the most beautiful Māra who has been subdued, and who is the destroyer of Smara (the god of love). He is Hara, marked by the crescent moon and the peacock; remember him.
He always strives to block the delusion hidden within the heart; protect your fame from fear and conquer. Therefore, he who removes darkness [is the one] in wealth, free from ill-will.
Join it with that which possesses eternal and imperishable splendor.
Anvaya: O Blessed One! I am always striving to block the delusion hidden within my heart; therefore, protect my fame (the meaning is:

act in such a way that I may attain renown among those of restrained mind). O All-pervading Lord, conquer fear! Then, you who remove darkness, unite me—who am ever-striving—with wealth that shines with inexhaustible splendor and is free from enmity (i.e., devoid of lack of friendship).

He who holds the entire universe along with the skull-bowl, who is adorned by the intoxicated and unstable [goddess], the destroyer of passion; he who is the benefactor in the destruction of the great delusion of worldly existence, the pacifier, the one without a home, and the abode of those whose pride has been humbled. (75)

O crest-jewels of connoisseurs! [You should worship Him who is] all-auspicious, skull-bearing, adorned with joy, the destroyer of unstable intoxication, the annihilator of passion, the one who brings about the destruction of the great delusion of worldly existence, the supreme tranquility, the immersion into the Self, and the abode of humility. (76) (A pair of verses) Anvaya: O jewels among those who relish the aesthetic flavor! [You should worship Him who is] entirely peaceful, possessing a skull, beautifully adorned, joyful, the destroyer of instability, and the vanquisher of desire.

Worship Bhava, who is situated at the destruction of great delusion; who is the pacifier and the immersion [into peace]; who is the abode of all that brings auspiciousness; who is sufficient for the destruction of pride; who is the destroyer of unstable intoxication; who is established in the destruction of great delusion; who is the pacifier and the immersion into peace; who is the abode of those whose pride has been subdued. O Śaṅkara, by means of this devotion which is free from the discord of the body, may you grant me an abundance of bliss through your vastness. May I become thin in my physical form, yet full of joy through your expansive grace. May I attain the essence of peace through your far-reaching power.
"O you who bring about the destruction of the body through the intensity of enmity! || 77 ||

O Śaṅkara! You, who possess infinite and incomparable extension, having made me—who am not extended (not small)—extended (abundant), favor me with the essence that brings peace to the body, O All-pervading Lord! May I bring forth the essence (the flavor of devotion); may you, through your infinite and perfectly balanced extension, make me one whose peace is unbounded, rendering me free from the emaciation caused by desire. (The word *kara* is the second person singular imperative of the root *kṛ* belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*).

The usage in the *prayoga* [of the Vedic language] is as follows: "tebhyo namaskurvan" (*namas* is used with the accusative case ending *-am*); this Vedic usage is employed even in the common language (*bhāṣā*) regarding the object of devotion, according to the statement that "even Vedic forms are sometimes used in the common language" (meaning: use the form *kuru*).

Meditate in your heart upon Śaṅkara, who is beneficial at the time of this worthless world, who is the goal for those seeking essence, whose feet are illuminated by light, whose feet are severed from worldly afflictions, and who is the embodiment of aesthetic bliss (*rasa*).
He who brings to rest the surging waves of passion that have been colored by worldly attachment, and who is the ender of the incomparable darkness of the mind.
O ornaments of the connoisseurs! Remember Śaṅkara— the one who has shattered all calamities, who proclaims the state free from affliction,

who is beneficial at this time of essencelessness (at the unstable moment of the final instant), who is embraced by the aesthetic sentiment of bliss, who is colored within the heart (meaning he shines and sports there), who is rippled with remembrance,
who possesses a mind that is peerless and free from the darkness of pride, and who leads even Death itself to a state of peace.
May this hymn of praise, adorned with manifold beauty, captivating to the mind, and free from all ailments, which I have offered to you who captivate the heart, bring you joy.
Since your mind is gracious and you are the destroyer of the entire mass of delusion, I no longer harbor any desire for that mass of delusion. (79)

Anvaya: O Hara! May this hymn of praise, composed by me—which is free from defects, heart-stealing, and resplendent with variety—delight your mind. O All-pervading Lord! Since you, whose nature dispels darkness, possess a gracious mind, I, who am peerless, no longer entertain any desire for the mass of worldly delusion.

Like a lovely river in the midst of a wilderness upon this earth filled with many mountains, she who—in an instant—by the vision of her pure intellect, reveals the relative gradations [of truth] wherever they may be; like the radiant form of the Sun in the blinding darkness of the night, may that glorious speech of Bharata’s, through its constant praise by the wise, delight the hearts of the learned to the very end of their weariness. (80)

Like a lovely river in the midst of a wilderness, this speech—exceedingly beautiful—is, by the mere glance of one with pure intelligence, where on this earth, including its mountains and forests, has it not attained excellence? Indeed, everywhere.
This venerable speech of mine, worthy of praise through the hymns of Andhaka, is like the body of the sun in the darkness; it dispels the exhaustion of the hearts of the wise.

May this hymn— which rains down blessings upon those who are like peacocks to the clouds of the heart, which bestows welfare upon the assembled and the well-disposed, and which is as skilled at cutting away committed misdeeds as a sickle is at cutting grass— intensely intoxicate [the mind]. May this auspicious praise, which threatens evil and triumphs over the universe, grant prosperity.
May the fragrance of the chariot of the Son of Surabhi spread throughout the entire world.

Acting like rain for the peacocks that are the connoisseurs of literary excellence (*anvaya-sahṛdaya*), bestowing what is beneficial upon those who are well-composed, as skillful at cutting through committed misdeeds as a sickle is at cutting grass, auspicious in granting welfare, and threatening all that is inauspicious— may this hymn of praise to the Lord Śambhu (who rides the bull and dwells in the Nandana grove of the gods) spread throughout the entire world.

Thus ends the thirtieth hymn, titled "The Great Yamaka," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flower-Blossoms of Praise) dedicated to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
The Thirty-first Hymn.

Having made the mind supremely internal within meditative concentration—motionless and free from waves—O wise ones, worship the Lord, the consort of Girijā, in order to bring about the destruction of the fear of worldly existence. 1.

Sequence of meaning—O wise ones! Having made the mind completely internal, waveless, and motionless through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), worship the all-pervading Lord, the Consort of Girijā, in order to shatter the fear of worldly existence. Just as one restrains a great bird with a snare or a great horse with the strength of a bridle, restrain the monkey-like mind through yoga and worship the All-pervading Lord.
O lover of Girijā! || 2 ||
Restrain the monkey-mind through yoga— just as one restrains a great bird with a net, a great horse with the strength of a bridle, or a serpent with mantras,
medicines, and other rites, or a deer with a snare— and worship the Lord, the consort of Girijā, having withdrawn the mind from all attachments by means of the intellect.
Worship the all-pervading Lord, the consort of the Daughter of the Mountain.

Just as one might capture a serpent through the application of mantras and medicines, or as one captures a deer with a snare, even so, having restrained the mind—which is free from attachment—by means of the intellect (in the form of one-pointed concentration), worship the all-pervading Lord who is the serpent of Girijā.

Pierce the forehead, which is marked by the knitting of the eyebrows, where the fire arising from His wrath consumed the bird-like god of love (Ananga); worship that all-pervading Lord, who has thus burnt away the moth of the darkness of delusion.
Worship the lover of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Worship that Lord, the lover of Girijā, who—having split the forehead with its knitting of brows by means of the fire rising from it—impetuously consumed the bird-like Anaṅga;

the Lord who bears a mass of matted hair as thick as the celestial Gaṅgā, whose body is adorned with magnificent serpents, and whose eye is tawny with the flames of fire. Worship that All-pervading One.
Worship the lover of the Daughter of the Mountain.

Worship the Lord, the lover of Girijā, who bears a body with limbs as powerful as serpents, who carries a mass of matted hair that holds the river of the sky in full flow, and who possesses an eye tawny like the flame of fire;
he who delivers those distressed by the bonds of worldly existence, whose ornaments are the blazing jewels of his circle of hoods, and who dwells in the caves of the mountain— go to him for refuge.
Adorned with the moon, the bearer of cool rays.

O learned ones, connoisseurs of the savor of devotional love! Go for refuge to Him who rescues those distressed by the bonds of worldly existence; who is adorned with the blazing jewels of the circle of serpent-hoods; who finds shelter in mountain caves; who is crowned with the moon; who has vanquished the voracious god of love; who swallowed the bitter *kālakūṭa* poison; and who is the refuge for the multitude of those who have sought His protection. Go for refuge to Him!
Adorned with the moon, the maker of frost.

O seekers of the divine! Take refuge in Him who has vanquished the devouring Smara, who swallowed the bitter Kālakūṭa poison, who is the shelter for those who have surrendered to Him, and who is adorned with the moon;

take refuge in Him whose footsteps are traced upon the desert lands and whose feet are ever-present upon the crest of the Lord of the Gods; take refuge in Him, the remembrance of whom removes the threefold suffering.
Adorned with the moon, the scatterer of frost. || 8 ||

Seek refuge in Him whose footsteps traverse the desert lands of the earth, whose feet are ever-shining upon the crest of the Lord of the Gods, whose very remembrance removes the threefold suffering, and who is adorned with the cool-rayed moon;

seek refuge in Him who grants liberation from worldly existence to those who bow before Him, who has conquered old age and death, and who brought about the destruction of the triple city as He marched forth.
Adorned with the moon, the scatterer of frost. || 9 ||

O you who are terrified by the fear of worldly existence and possess nothing! Go for refuge to Him who wears the moon as an ornament, who has destroyed the three cities, and who brings about the crossing over to the state of the True One for those who bow before Him—Him who has conquered old age and death.

Go for refuge to Him who has shaken off the veil of the darkness of delusion, who is clothed in the skin of an elephant, and who is the Lord of the City manifested within the heart. Go for refuge to Him.
Adorned with the moon, the scatterer of frost. || 10 ||

Take refuge in Him whose veil of the darkness of delusion has been shaken off by His followers, who wears an elephant hide as His supreme covering, who is the protector of the city imagined [in the heart], who is adorned with the moon, and who is the true shelter.

Take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, whose neck is dark like a young *tāla* tree, whose forehead is radiant with a mass of flaming crests, and upon whose head shines the skull of the Supreme Being (*Parameṣṭhin*).
The web of impurities has been destroyed. || 11 ||
O connoisseurs, take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, whose stalk is dark like a young *tāla* tree, whose forehead is radiant with a mass of flaming crests,

and upon whose head shines the skull of the Supreme Lord (*Parameṣṭhin*), which destroys the entire web of sins. Take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, who wears a garland fashioned from the heads of men, who has crushed the thick darkness of delusion for those who bow before him, and who has severed the power of Time with hundreds of rays from his eyes.
which destroys the web of sins. || 12 ||

Take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, whose crest-garland is fashioned from the severed heads of the leaders—Brahmā and the others—who were destroyed during the great cosmic dissolutions; who has felled the thicket of delusion for those who bow before him; who has severed Time with hundreds of flames from his eyes; and who has destroyed the web of sins.

Take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, who has destroyed the entire web of impurities; he bears upon the region of his throat a most expansive necklace of serpent-kings, formidable with the flickering flames of uneven poison-fire and adorned with fierce, prominent veins.
Take refuge in the All-pervading Lord, who wears upon his broad neck a serpent-king necklace terrifying with its fangs like the flames of uneven poison; he whose fierce heads destroy the web of sins.
Within the bounds of the three worlds, there is no one else capable of shattering [the cycle of existence] except him. Take refuge in that All-pervading Lord, the swan dwelling in the stainless mind.
[He is] the one who has struck down the web of sins. || 14 ||

Except for Him, there is no one else within the three worlds capable of shattering the foundation of worldly existence; therefore, take refuge in that Lord, whose pure mind is the dwelling place of swans, who has destroyed the web of sins, whose matted locks are tawny with the pollen of lotuses, who gratified the Child [Kṛṣṇa] by offering the ocean, and who is the great sword for the defeat of the enemy that is worldly existence. Take refuge in that All-pervading Lord.
The web of defilements has been destroyed. || 15 ||

Take refuge in the Lord, whose matted locks are tawny with the pollen of the lotuses of his lineage; who gratified the gods by offering the ocean; who is the great sword for the defeat of the army of worldly existence; and who has destroyed the web of sins.

Worship him who is white as the dust of the ashes of the excessively voracious [fire]; whose power of awakening was bestowed upon the prostrate world; and who shines with a great, brilliant whiteness from the splendor of his banner.
The Lord, who is as radiant as the daughter of the mountain. || 16 ||

Worship the Lord who is as white as the dust of the ashes of the fire that consumes the lineage [of sins], whose power of awakening was bestowed by the prostrate world, who is brilliantly white with the splendor of his banner, and who is the consort of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī).

Worship him who, by his radiance, has surpassed the dark hue of a fresh cloud, whose neck is variegated by the crest-jewels of his armlets, and who holds in his mouth a great morsel fashioned from poison.
The Lord, who is more radiant than the daughter of the mountain. || 17 ||

Worship the Lord, who surpasses the dark blue of a lotus petal with the radiance of his body, whose neck is variegated by the tips of the jewels on his armlets, and who holds a great mouthful fashioned from poison;

worship him who is as white as the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), whose crest is shimmering with the waves of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), who bears at the base of his throat a potent, great venom, yet whose heart is as simple as nectar.
The Lord, resplendent with the daughter of the mountain as his consort. || 18 ||

Worship the Lord, who bears a crest as tremulous as the waves of the celestial river, who possesses a neck bearing great poison yet a heart as straight as nectar, and who is as white as the daughter of the mountain;
worship Him who has removed the stain of the impurity of evil deeds, who bestows the great lotus upon the prostrate world, and who grants the pure ripening of auspicious perfection.
The Lord, who is more radiant than the daughter of the mountain. || 19 ||

Anvaya: O friends of the heart! Worship the Lord who is as white as the daughter of the mountain; who has cast off the stain of evil deeds, who bestows the great lotus upon the prostrate world, and who grants the ripening of auspicious success.
Worship Him who gives words as sweet as a dense laugh, who shatters all the sins of those who bow to Him, and who grants the desired fruit to those who worship Him. Worship Him!
The Lord, who is more radiant than the daughter of the mountain. || 20 ||

Worship the Lord, who is as fair as the daughter of the mountain; he bestows continuous and abundant laughter and speech upon those who bow to him, shatters all the sins of those who take refuge in him, and grants the desired fruit to his devotees.

Bow down to him whose feet are polished smooth by the multitude of jewels set upon the peaks of the excellent mountains of the gods who are ever intent on prostration, and whose crown is whitened by the mass of rays from the moon.
The refuge for those who have no refuge, the destroyer of the city of the enemy. || 21 ||

Bow down to Purahara, the refuge of the helpless, whose feet are polished by the multitude of jewels set upon the peaks of the excellent mountain that is the lineage of Anvaya-Avirata, and whose crown is whitened by the mass of rays from the moon;

he whose compassion has matured into the granting of desired boons for those whose minds are restrained by tranquility, self-control, and discipline, and whose intellects are distressed by the agitation caused by the repeated insults of worldly existence.
Bow down to the Destroyer of Cities, the refuge of the helpless. || 22 ||

Bow down to Purahara, the refuge of the helpless, whose compassion has matured into the granting of desired boons; whose minds have been disciplined by the practice of tranquility, self-restraint, and observance, and whose intellects are shaken by the afflictions of birth, existence, and decay. Bow down to him whose mind is exceedingly tender, who possesses an intellect intent on the welfare of others, and who is honored by the fire that has become familiar through the pacification of the god of love, which he regards as no more than a blade of straw.
The protector of those who have no other refuge, the one who destroys the city of the enemy. || 23 ||

Bow down to the Destroyer of Cities, the refuge of the helpless, whose mind is intent on the welfare of others, who honors the fire that is well-practiced in extinguishing the god of love— which resembles a mere blade of grass in comparison to his lineage— and whose heart is exceedingly tender; he whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and the fire, who bears white rays upon the mass of matted hair on his head, and who has shattered the dense darkness of the hearts of those who bow before him.
Bow down to the Destroyer of Cities, the refuge of the helpless. || 24 ||

Bow down to Purahara, the sun to the lineage of devotees, the moon, and the fire; who bears the white rays of the crescent moon upon his crest; who has dispelled the dense darkness of the delusion of bowing beings; and who is the refuge for the helpless.

Bow down to him who wears human skulls resembling a mass of lotuses blooming at the rise of the divine river overflowing with abundant water, and who is a cloud that extinguishes the forest fire of worldly existence.
The refuge for those who have no other refuge, the destroyer of the city of the enemy. || 25 ||

Bow down before Purahara, the refuge of the helpless, who bears upon his head human skulls resembling clusters of blooming lotuses on the banks of the Ganges overflowing with incessant torrents; he is a cloud that extinguishes the fire of the worldly deluge.

Abandon the collyrium that dispels the darkness of the eyes when they are clouded by artificial impurities; cast away the sandalwood paste from Malaya that delights the hearts of those in distress. Worship him!

The worship of the lotus feet of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain-King—the one who has conquered the immersion in the great ocean of worldly existence characterized by its treacherous power—is indeed excellent; so too is the worship of the lotus feet of the Beloved of His Daughter. (26)
Sequence: O foolish people! Abandon the collyrium that destroys the darkness of the eyes of imagined impurities;

abandon also the application of Malaya sandalwood that delights the distressed heart. But rather, resort to the worship of the lotus feet of the Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain King—an act that prevents one from sinking into the great ocean of worldly existence, which is filled with the power of formidable poisons.

Worship that unbroken boat for crossing the ocean of insurmountable sins—the boat that is skilled in shattering the shackles of the serpents of all the impurities of the Kali age; whose crown-ornament is adorned by the beauty of a crescent of the bright moon;
and which grants fearlessness to the heart afflicted by the cruel punishment of the intoxicated king of passion. 27.

O you of dull intellect! Worship the unbroken [Lord], who is skilled in severing the serpent-fetters of the entire mass of the impurities of the Kali age; whose heart is fearless though tormented by the wicked king of intoxicated passion; who is adorned with a crest-jewel beautified by a fragment of the pure moon; and who is a boat for crossing the ocean of insurmountable sins.

O Lord! Grant upon my head Your lotus-feet, which are cherished with affection by the Moon, the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), and the Lotus-born (Brahmā); which are colored by the filaments of the beautiful flowers on the crest of Indra as he bows; and which are served by Brahmā, Mādhava, the Friend of the Night-lotuses (the Moon), and the Sun, the Lord of Day-lotuses—feet that are cool with droplets of nectar.

*Anvaya:* O Lord! [Grant] those [feet] which are cherished with affection by the Moon, the Daughter of the Mountain, and the Lotus-born; which are colored by the filaments of the beautiful flowers on the crest of Indra as he bows...

Place upon my head the lotus-foot, served by the Creator, Mādhava, and the Moon—the friend of the night-lotus—and by the Lord of the day-lotuses; cool with sprays of nectar; the means for shattering the affliction of the threat born from sinking into the pit [of worldly existence]; that which brings delight to the heart of those who have performed prostration;
and the cause for warding off fear and destroying the evil resulting from the slaughter of Tripura. Place upon my head the lotus-foot, cool with sprays of nectar. (29)

O All-pervading Lord! Bestow upon my head Your lotus-foot, which is cool as a spray of nectar; which is the means for shattering the affliction of the threat arising from drowning in the pit [of worldly existence]; which brings delight to the hearts of those who have performed prostration and consists of the long-lasting worship of the Untainted One; and which is the cause for destroying the evil resulting from the slaughter of Tripura and for warding off all fear.
Accept, accept from me this gift consisting of the elixir of praise—a natural flavor, prepared without the labor of gathering various medicinal herbs.
Grant me a boon; grant me a boon that removes the most agonizing pain of fever! Bestow upon my head your lotus feet, cool with the spray of nectar.

O Hara! Accept these sandals of mine—which require no collection of various medicinal herbs as their means, which possess an unartificial essence, and consist of the elixir of praise—and favor me (who have sought refuge); show me grace. Likewise, with supreme joy, proclaim that excellent boon which removes the pain of the highest burning. O Blessed One! Bestow upon my head Your lotus-feet, cool as sprays of nectar.

Thus ends the thirty-second hymn, the *Natopadeśastotra*, within the *Stutikusumāñjali* dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmad Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.

O Hara, deliver this clever one who has come for refuge—this world-sustainer who is helpless; he is distressed by the exhaustion born from the treacherous confusion of wandering in the desert of existence, overwhelmed by the calamity of defeat inflicted by wicked men with hearts as hard as thunderbolts, and terrified by the hideous *huṃ*-cries of the most fearsome servants of Yama. || 1 ||

O Hara! Lift up quickly and skillfully the world-sustainer who has come for refuge—him who is distressed by the exhaustion arising from the treacherous agitation of wandering in the desert of worldly existence; him who is overwhelmed by the humiliation inflicted by wicked people with hearts as hard as thunderbolts; and him who is terrified by the distorted *huṅkāra* roars of the most fearsome servants of Yama.

O Hara, deliver the clever one who has come for refuge—him whose consciousness and self-control have been shattered by the god whose banner is the makara, who is the object of the taunts and threats of beautiful-eyed noble women, and who is afflicted by the intense pain born of the fever of heavy pride arising from even a mere fragment of virtue; O Jagaddhara, protect him who is without shelter. 2.

O Hara! Lift up the clever Jagaddhara, who has taken up residence there; whose consciousness and vitality are shattered by the god of love (Amaraketa); who is the object of the threats and reproaches of beautiful-eyed noble ladies; who is afflicted by the intense pain born of a heavy fever of pride arising from even a mere fragment of his own virtues; who is helpless and has come for refuge. He is enslaved by the snares of sense-objects through the power of the most cruel and wicked violence at its forefront, and his body is tightly oppressed by the great burden of his inherently difficult-to-grasp possessions.

O Hara, deliver the clever one whose agitated mind is being devoured by the blazing, unrestrained forest fire of worldly existence; protect me, the world-sustainer, who am without refuge and have come to you for shelter. || 3 ||

O Hara! Lift up me, the world-sustainer, who am clever [in seeking refuge], who have come for protection, who am helpless, and who am overwhelmed by the noose of objects that are outwardly charming yet inwardly cruel; whose body is intensely tormented by the heavy burden of a wife who is difficult to manage by nature; and whose mind is agitated, being swallowed by the blazing, unrestrained forest fire of worldly existence.

O Hara! Wealth, youth, sons, happiness, and the like—all these are as flickering as water moving beneath the surface of lotus leaves tossed by the wind; they are rendered unstable by the discernment of wisdom, and are overwhelmed by the violent plundering of the deceitful thieves that are the powerful senses. O clever one, rescue me, the world-sustainer, who am helpless and have come to you for refuge! 4 *Anvaya:* O Hara! [All things such as] wealth, youth, sons, happiness, and so forth, are as transient as water shimmering beneath the surface of lotus leaves shaken by the wind. [They are] made unstable by the discernment of discrimination, and are agitated by the forceful looting of the powerful thieves that are the deceptive senses. O clever one, uplift me, the sustainer of the world, who am without refuge and have sought your protection! 4

O Jagaddhara, you who are skillful, rescue this world which is agitated by the instability of its lack of discernment, overwhelmed by the forceful plundering of the thieves that are the powerful senses, and has come to you for refuge without protection.
O crusher of Mada, O destroyer of passion, you who are eager to pierce through evil deeds, O creator of the universe, O supreme purifier, you who are bowed down by those whose devotion is most firm!

O Hara! O destroyer of Madana, the delighter of Samadā! O creator of the world! O supreme purifier! O you who are adorned by a crown marked with the crescent moon! Lift up [me], who am distressed, whose desires are frustrated, and who am clever; protect me, the world-sustainer, who have come to you for refuge and am without protection—[me] who am intent on piercing through sins, whose desires are frustrated, who am agitated, yet possess firm devotion and am bowed down. *Anvaya:* O Hara! O destroyer of Madana, the delighter of Samadā! O creator of the world! O supreme purifier! O you who are adorned by a crown marked with the crescent moon! [You,] lift up [me], who am distressed, whose desires are frustrated, who am clever, who possess firm devotion, and who am bowed down. I am one who is intent on piercing through sins. Protect me, the world-sustainer, who have come to you for refuge and am without protection.

O Jagaddhara, who possesses a form honored by the grace of the world, you who have accepted the true seekers as your own; O subduer of Tripura, whose body is variegated by latent impressions, who are eager for the worship of the unreal; O Hara, who grants profound wonder and yearns for the proper honor of those who offer salutations—save me, the clever one, who am protectorless and have come to you for refuge! Save me, the clever one, who am protectorless and have come to you for refuge! 6.

O You whose form is honored for its grace toward the world! O Punisher of Tripura! O Hara! Lift up me—the world-sustainer, the clever one—who have sought refuge with no other shelter; who have taken hold of You through a firm resolve; whose latent impressions are variegated; who am eager for the worship of the unreal; who offer salutations with intense wonder; who long for appropriate and true honor. (Note: *Jagaddhara* here refers to the author himself, meaning "the sustainer of the world.")

O Giver of Boons, gladden me; O Crusher of Misfortune, why do you remain so merciless toward me, who have offered my petition—a state of incomparable agony, filled with rising distress and calamity? O Lord whose wealth is glory, grant me your glance, which purifies the heart and is a river of stainless awakening; O Hari, the Sustainer of the World, uplift me, the helpless one who has come to you for refuge. (7)
O Giver of Boons! Delight me, who have offered my supplication, whose pain is incomparable, and for whom distress and calamity have arisen; destroy my misfortune! O Lord!
Why is such ruthlessness found in You? O Treasure of Fame! Grant me the vision that purifies the heart and bestows stainless awakening! O Hara!
Lift up me, the world-sustainer, who am clever yet without refuge and have come to You for protection!

Grant fearlessness; diminish your guile; place your foot upon my head; lift up your face; bestow your speech; O Granter of Boons, do not deceive me who am bowed before you! Lift up the clever one who is utterly exhausted by hundreds of ceaseless labors and unable to endure further fatigue; O Hara, protect me, the world-sustainer, who am without refuge and have come to you for shelter. O Hara, protect me, the world-sustainer, who am without refuge and have come to you for shelter—me, who am clever yet utterly exhausted by hundreds of labors performed without rest and unable to endure further fatigue. O Varada, grant fearlessness; diminish your guile; place your foot upon my head; lift up your face; bestow your speech; [release me]. O Hara, protect me, the world-sustainer, who am without refuge and

O All-pervading Lord! Do not deceive me, who am bowed before you (I who am humble). I am utterly exhausted, unable to endure further fatigue from hundreds of labors performed without rest; I am without refuge.
O Sustainer of the World, lift up me, the clever one, who has come to you for shelter!
Thus ends [the hymn] to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the thirty-second hymn is titled "The Deliverance of Those Who Have Sought Refuge.
The thirty-third hymn is "The Melodious Clangor of the Golden Bells at Kāñcī and the Jangling Sound of the Resonant Ankle-bells."

Victorious is the praise of the Moon-crested Lord, which resounds with the tinkling of the rows of jewels adorning all his limbs, and with the jingling of the bracelets on the tossing, swaying, and quivering vine-like arms of Sarasvatī as she moves in her rhythmic steps. || 1 ||

Triumphant is the hymn of praise to the one whose crown bears the crescent moon— a hymn consisting of the tinkling of golden bells on the girdle during the act of walking, the jingling of resonant anklets, the tumultuous chiming of rows of jewels from all the bodily ornaments, and the ringing of bracelets as they clash against moving, swaying vine-like arms.

O Lord, the Goddess of Speech has surely fashioned Your face as a pleasure-garden for the playful strolls of Her own will for one who is devoted to You; otherwise, how could this ever-increasingly fresh and heart-stealing arrangement of radiant syllables and tender words be observed arising day by day in succession? (2)

Anvaya: O Lord! O Bhava! Surely the Goddess of Speech has fashioned the face of Your devotee into a pleasure-grove for her own spontaneous wanderings and playful sports? If not, then how is it that this ever-new, heart-stealing, and radiant arrangement of soft syllables is observed arising here day by day in succession?

O Ornament of the buds of the lily-thicket of the Kairaviṇī family, blessed are the true poets who, by means of their hymns to You, become masters of the Goddess of Speech— made lucid through the expansive and spontaneous grace of Sarasvatī— and who, out of Your praise, bestow cool and gentle drops of nectar to dispel the heat of calamity for those who possess devotion to You. (3)
O ornament of the family of night-lotuses!

Blessed are the true poets, who— by means of the pretext of praising you, O you whose speech-goddess is under their own command through the vast grace of Sarasvatī’s essential power— freely bestow cool and soothing drops of nectar upon those devoted to you, in order to dispel the heat of their calamities.

Salutations to that Blessed Śeṣa, whose wondrous form is the marvel of the three worlds, and by whose hundreds of heads bowing to you, by the sight of your beauty, and by the festivals of hearing your virtuous conduct, his two thousand eyes attain fulfillment; and by whose pairs of thousands of tongues chanting your praises, his two thousand tongues likewise achieve their purpose.

Anvaya: O Blessed One! Salutations to that Lord Śeṣa, whose thousand heads attain fulfillment by bowing to You, whose two thousand eyes attain fulfillment by beholding Your beauty and by the festivals of hearing Your life-story, and whose pair of two thousand tongues attains fulfillment by chanting Your praises—that Lord whose form is a wonder to the three worlds.

"O Śambhu! O Śarva! O Moon-crested One! O Śiva! O Śrīkaṇṭha! O Lord of the Universe! Save me!"—these words of the virtuous, moist with thick nectar, steal away the hearts of the good more than the moon, more than Mādhava, more than the company of the righteous, more than honor from a master, and even more than the enjoyment of the full expanse of a lover's pair of breasts.

O Śambhu! O Śarva! O Moon-crested One! O Śiva! O Śrīkaṇṭha! O Lord of the Universe! Protect me!—these words of the virtuous, moist with the thick nectar [of devotion], steal the heart more than even the moon of the full-moon night, or the springtime, or the company of the virtuous, or honor from one's master, or the enjoyment of the expanse of a beloved’s pair of breasts.

Whose mind do the eloquent sayings of the virtuous— not sprinkled with the nectar of hymns to Śambhu— fail to render distasteful like the springtime for one longing for a dark-complexioned woman, indifferent to musk and saffron from the Nāsīra region, and devoid of pride in anointing oneself with sandalwood paste,
while instead yearning for the firm embrace of a fresh bride?

Do these hymns of praise, which sport upon your mouth— hymns that dispel the arrogance of musk from the vanguard, the pride of sandalwood paste, and the longing for the firm embrace of a fresh bride; hymns that mock the fury of the serpent Kali’s tongue, matted with the mass of flames conquered with ease— not perform this?

O Blessed One! These hymns of praise for You, which effortlessly surpass the fury of the tongue of Time (Kālarasanā) thick with its mass of flames—these which sport upon Your mouth—move before Him whose divine body is the target for the volleys of arrows from the glances of the beloved of Indra’s city (Śacī). This is what is proclaimed by the hosts of celestial bards. **Anvaya:** O Blessed One! These hymns of praise for You—which possess the appearance of the fury of the tongue of Time, matted with a mass of flames conquered by mere playfulness—which sport upon Your mouth; [they move] before Him whose divine body is the target for the volleys of arrows from the glances of the beloved of Indra’s city. This is what is proclaimed by the hosts of celestial bards. **English Translation:** O Lord, these hymns of praise for You—which bear the semblance of the wrath of the serpent Kālarasanā, hersing with masses of flames that are easily subdued by Your playful ease—and which sport upon Your lips, proceed before Him whose celestial form is the target of the showers of arrow-like glances cast by the beloved of Indra’s city (Śacī). Thus do the throngs of heavenly singers proclaim.
The utterances of the hosts of gods and bards leap forth (they shine).
May your auspicious and sweet words of praise, which increase the height of joy and rival the flow of mature honey, remain long in the ears of those who recite them;
for them, the mass of nectar—beautiful with drops of honey emerging from the undoubtedly charming lips of the moon-faced maidens of the Nandana grove—will surely attain a state of languor.
The longing of pregnancy. || 8 ||

O All-pervading Lord! For those fortunate ones who for a long time have held within their ears Your sweet words of praise—which increase the height of joy and rival the flow of mature honey—the longing for the mass of nectar as beautiful as drops of honey emerging from the undoubtedly charming lips of the moon-faced daughter of Nandana finds its fulfillment; indeed, their languor vanishes.

Devoted to the practice of the sixfold knowledge, dwelling in assemblies, seated upon the throne of a palace, consuming pure food, wearing well-washed garments, destroying all fear of the wicked, overflowing with joy, laughing with a serene smile, possessing virtuous latent impressions, addicted to excellent poetry, his tongue moistened by nectar, he has performed the worship of Śambhu. || 9 ||

One who has performed worship of the lineage of Śambhu (i.e., a servant of the illustrious Sadāśiva), who practices true knowledge, who dwells in assemblies, who occupies a throne in a palace, who consumes pure food, who wears well-washed garments, who destroys the fear of the virtuous, who glows with joy, whose laughter is serene, who possesses the impressions of the good, who is devoted to excellent poetry, and whose tongue is moistened by nectar— such a person [becomes].
Those whose splendor eclipses the moon, who have destroyed all sorrow, who pour forth streams of nectar, who remove the exhaustion of the heart, who produce wonder,

and who possess the grace of melodic song— such praises, when contemplated within, cause one here to abandon even the longing for the blissful taste of the joy found in Śambhu’s embrace of his young bride, who was trembling and overwhelmed by the roar of the clouds. 10.

In this world, those who inwardly contemplate the praises of Śambhu— praises which possess the luster of the full moon, which destroy all sorrow, which shed streams of nectar, which remove the exhaustion of the heart, which produce wonder, and which bear the melody of song— those fortunate ones abandon their longing for the pleasure of tasting the joy of embracing young women who are trembling and overwhelmed by the roar of thunderclouds.

O Lord, those who know the essential from the trivial, who destroy the fear of the virtuous, who sever the distress of those bowed down in supplication, whose hearts are moist with compassion, who are gracious friends,
whose consciousness expands infinitely, who are the protectors of all people, who have illuminated the quarters with their fame, who enjoy the earth, and who draw in the nights—
those beautiful-eyed ones are ever attached to touching Your footstool. (11)

Anvaya: O Lord! Those who know the essential from the non-essential, who destroy the fear of the virtuous, who dispel the distress of those bowed down to them, whose hearts are moist with compassion, who are gracious friends, whose prosperity expands, who are the protectors of the entire world, who illuminate the quarters with their fame, who enjoy the earth, who touch Your footstool, and whose beautiful glances are ever fixed upon You—such people captivate the night.

Those whose splendor is invincible, whose bodies are full of joy, who have scorched away the excess of their thirst, who enjoy supreme excellence, whose anger is destroyed in an instant, whose lives are filled with auspiciousness, whose power rises up, whose luster is kindled, who have cast aside formidable time, who laugh within their hearts, who have attained the secret of happiness, and whose sins are washed away by meditation upon you— [for them, there is no fear]. 12.

Anvaya: O Blessed One!
