In the assembly, they cause the eyes of the members to flow with tears; they drive far away the intense anger of their great protectors;
and with their well-spoken verses, they melt the hearts of the virtuous like a lunar gem—O Master, those fortunate ones who make you hear their ever-new utterances!

Those of pure intellect chew their eloquent sayings like betel nuts; they humble the swelling pride of the cruel. The wise call upon them to taste the fresh nectar of Your [teachings], those who bow their heads with joyful hearts at the tips of Your feet. (35)
Those of pure intellect chew upon their well-spoken verses like betel nuts; they diminish the swaying (wandering) pride of the cruel before them;
those wise ones call upon you for the tasting of fresh nectar—those who, with joyful minds, bow their heads at the tips of your feet.
Those gentle ones do not cause even the wicked to suffer out of compassion; they dispel from the hearts of the wise the exhaustion born of calamity.
Even to those afflicted by thirst, they offer their own words, sweet as nectar; they cause you—who have shattered the afflictions of the Kali age—to enter within them. 36.
By your grace, those who are gentle do not afflict even the wicked; they dispel the exhaustion born of calamity within the hearts of the wise;

and to those afflicted by thirst—who long to hear—they offer their own words, sweet as nectar. They cause you, the Lord, who have shattered the afflictions of the Kali age, to enter within (into the mind).

Those who dispatch their speech to your presence for the attainment of their desires quickly disperse the passions such as attachment that have gathered in the mind; though blinded by anger, they do not harbor hatred toward anyone due to their vast discipline; and they utterly destroy the dense darkness of delusion within the sky of their superior intellect. (37)

They quickly dissolve the passions such as attachment that have gathered in the minds of those who follow them; being possessed of immense discipline, they never harbor hatred even toward those blinded by anger.
They utterly dispel the dense darkness of delusion from the sky of their superior intellect, and they dispatch their speech to your presence in order to attain what is desired.

They diminish the world-renouncing detachment in the hearts of the self-controlled, which is otherwise honored there; and having caused calamities to subside for those who were terrified, they constantly provide them with consolation.
Those who terrify Death with words solely intent upon your nature, and who, through their praise of you, cause the heart's fear of those who bow before you to vanish; || 38 ||

Those who, having dispelled all calamities, instill in the minds of the self-controlled an unblemished and constant world-weariness; who constantly reassure the terrified with words solely inclined toward Your nature; who strike fear into Death itself; and who, through their hymns of praise, cause You—who remove the fear from the hearts of those who bow—to exult;
they proclaim their own virtues in the assembly of the knowers of Truth, and within their own hearts, they destroy the terror born of the serpent of the inner controller.
Those who place Your praise as an ornament upon their ears quickly loosen the dense fetters of the passions, even those that have become fully matured. (39)

Those who proclaim their own virtues before an assembly of the wise, who dispel the inner dread born of the serpent Yama within their hearts, who quickly loosen dense afflictions as if they were snares, and who place Your hymn of praise like a crest-jewel upon the ears of the eminent— [they alone truly know You].

They carry out their sinless duty through devotion to You; they encourage their minds to remain steady and unceasing in Your service; and like Yama or Madana, they burn away their own flood of sins by Your very glance—those who daily cause You, being personally attentive, to hear their petition.

But those devotees who, day after day, attentively (having become vigilant) cause you yourself to accept their petition, carry out their faultless actions through their addiction to devotion to you; they incessantly encourage their minds to remain steadfast in your service, and they burn away their own mass of sins with your glance, just as Yama and Madana [are consumed].
Like carpenters fashioning a heavy tree, they carve away your sins; they consume the abundant burden of auspicious fruits until they reach full satisfaction.
With sharp intellect, they perceive even the imminent Goddess of Fortune; those devotees of yours learn your hymn of praise as if it were the Vedas themselves.
They carve you, their teacher, like a tree with an axe; they consume you to their full satisfaction as if you were a fruit-laden tree heavy with auspicious rewards;
and with sharp intellect, they perceive even the prosperity that is close at hand—those who teach your devotees your praise, just as one learns the Veda.
Thus ends [the hymn] to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, accompanied by the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the hymn on the attainment of the fruit of praise is completed.
This is the thirty-seventh hymn:

For here, the wise ones whose pure consciousness has been purified by the contemplation of their own Self as the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) are not stained by external coverings, just as lotus petals are not wetted by water.

For here, the wise whose consciousness has been purified by the contemplation of their own Self as the Great Lord are not stained by external coverings—the three kinds of karma consisting of the auspicious, the inauspicious, and that which is both—just as lotus petals are not wetted by water.

Victorious is the *Sūktikalpalatā*, which makes its abode in the grove of the lotus-faces of poets; it bears fruit in the form of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*) through the sprinkling of the nectar-essence of devotion to Śiva. 2.

Victorious is that Kalpalatā of eloquent speech, which has made its dwelling in the garden of the poets' lotus-faces and bears fruit as both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the sprinkling of the nectar-essence of devotion to Śiva.
Victory, victory! For him who praises Lord Śiva with the words "Hara, protect me from fear; O God, grant me auspiciousness," the essence of Sarasvatī’s grace becomes fruitful.
It is expansive by its own nature. || 3 ||
[Anvaya: O Hara! Victory, victory! [The repetition of "victory" is not a fault due to the overflow of devotion; the same applies hereafter. Protect me from fear!
Thus, for one who praises the god Śiva in order to obtain auspiciousness, his flow of eloquence (*sārasvata*) becomes abundant, excellent, and spontaneously fruitful.
O Śiva, Śiva, Śaṅkara, Śaṅkara, O Source of Existence (*Bhavagati*)—for him whose mouth is made resonant by such lamentation, indeed, the days become fruitful through union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*).
And it has come into his hands. || 4 ||

O Śiva! O Śiva!! O Śaṅkara! O Śaṅkara!! (For you are the refuge) of me who am without refuge; he whose mouth becomes resonant with such lamentation—verily his days become fruitful, and liberation in union with Śiva comes into the palm of his hand. Indeed, he who here passes even a small portion of time in praise of the Lord of Creatures is liberated while living, freed from all the impurities of the Kali age; what more need be said?
Enough with much [talk]. || 5 ||

The logical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: indeed, whatever person (*puruṣa*) here, even for a brief duration—be it a mere moment, instant, or hour—renders himself fulfilled by means of hymns to Paśupati, he, being liberated from the impurities of all the Kali age, becomes one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). What need is there for much speaking? Victorious is the hymn to Śambhu, which is a stream of accumulated merit, the sole ladder for ascending to the supreme state, a great river of nectar that delights the assembly of the wise.
Victorious is the praise of Śambhu—a continuous stream of accumulated merit, the sole ladder for ascending to the supreme state, a great river of nectar that delights the wise.
Is this the vision of a true guru consisting solely of bliss? Or is it the creation of the universe? Or perhaps a rain from a cloudless sky, showering the nectar of the ears?
This is the praise of Śambhu. || 7 ||

Is this praise of Śambhu, raining down the nectar of its recitation, the very vision of the True Guru? Or is it perhaps the creation of the world consisting solely of bliss? Or is it a rain from a cloudless sky?
It is the enjoyment of imperishable happiness, a novel method for attaining Supreme Śiva; or rather, it is liberation while living—a praise that rains down the nectar of its recitation.
Of Śambhu. || 8 ||

Is the praise of Śambhu—which rains down the nectar of hearing its sequence—the enjoyment of imperishable bliss? Or is it a new method for attaining Supreme Śiva? Or perhaps it is liberation while living itself?
That is the sacred field here, that is the purifying holy site, that is the sanctifying temple; that is the sinless grove of asceticism here, wherein resides the praise of Śambhu.
It enters into the Veda. || 9 ||

In this world, wherever the praise of Śambhu enters the ear—be it a field or any other place—that alone is a sacred field, that alone is a purifying holy ford, that alone is a sanctifying sanctuary, and that alone is a stainless grove of asceticism. That is true play, that is true fellowship, that is true rest, and that is the attainment of the supreme ground; that is the cessation of all suffering, wherein the praise of Śambhu resides.
It enters into the sacred revelation (śruti). || 10 ||
That alone is play, that is the assembly, that is rest, that is the attainment of the supreme state, and that indeed is the cessation of all suffering, wherein the hymn to Śambhu enters the ear.
That is meditation, that is absorption, that is the great sacrifice, and that is the complete worship; that indeed is the supreme initiation wherein the hymn to Śambhu is heard.
It enters into the sacred revelation. || 11 ||

That is meditation, that is concentration, and that indeed is the great sacrifice; that is the entirety of worship, and that truly is the supreme initiation, wherein praise of Śambhu enters the ear. If a cluster of *pārijātaka* flowers is not easily available as an ornament for your ears, then lead these hymns to the path of your hearing.
Of Śambhu. || 12 ||

O you who bow down! If a cluster of *pārijāta* flowers is not easily available to adorn your ears, then lead these hymns of praise to Śambhu onto the path of your hearing. (The meaning is that these are even more heart-pleasing than clusters of flowers from the celestial *pārijāta* tree.)
If you desire to restrain the deer of the mind, which is more difficult to seize than even the wind,
then take up these praises of Śambhu, carefully strung upon the thread of firm virtues.

O seeker of the divine! If you desire to restrain that which captivates the mind and is more difficult to grasp than even the wind, then—becoming composed—take up these hymns of Śambhu, woven with firm threads: namely, the three qualities of *ojas*, *prasāda*, and *mādhurya*.
"What indeed is the taste of that nectar which arose from the churning of the ocean?"—if such curiosity arises in your heart, then listen to these praises of Śambhu. (14)

O connoisseur! If there is curiosity in your heart as to what the taste of that nectar produced from the churning of the ocean might be, then listen to these hymns of Śambhu. Liberation is considered by the wise to be an innate bliss devoid of the enjoyment of sense objects; if you wish to know even that, listen with an attentive heart.
Praises of Śambhu. || 15 ||
O you who bow before Him! To the wise, liberation is considered to be an innate bliss devoid of the enjoyment of sense objects;

if you desire to know even that liberation, then listen to the praises of Śambhu with an attentive heart. This impure body, a reservoir of sorrows and turbid with filth, is truly not desirable to anyone as a means for the worship of the Blessed Lord.
This body is impure, an abode of sorrows, and a mire of filth; yet, even though it is such, it becomes a means for the worship of the Blessed One. For this reason, who would not desire it?
If you consider the restraints, observances, breath-control, and so forth, to be difficult to perform, then resort to this easy means—praise—for the attainment of the supreme state.
Of Śambhu. || 17 ||

Anvaya: O man! If you consider the practice of restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth to be difficult to accomplish, then for the sake of attaining the supreme state, resort to this easy means: the praise of Śambhu. The blessings of the virtuous who speak the truth have been perfectly fulfilled; the fruit of merit has been obtained; and this [life] has been brought to its successful conclusion.
For this reason, there is praise of Śambhu. || 18 ||

My desire has been perfectly fulfilled; the blessings of the virtuous who speak the truth have borne fruit. I have obtained the reward of my own merit, since I have brought this hymn to Śambhu to completion.
This worldly existence is my essence; this entire mortal birth of mine is fruitful, for there is no one equal to me, as I am a singer of praises.
It became Śiva’s. || 19 ||

Fortunate am I! My worldly existence has attained its essence; this entire mortal birth of mine is fruitful and purposeful. There is no one like me upon this earth, since I have become a hymnist of Śiva.
I bow, I bow; I praise, I praise the Lord, the Master of the Universe. I meditate, I meditate, and I go toward the stainless, supreme abode.

I bow down, I bow down to the Lord, the Master of the World, with my speech, mind, body, and actions; I praise, I praise Him, being single-mindedly intent upon Him; and I meditate, I meditate upon His pair of lotus feet. And by Your grace, I shall surely go to the stainless, supreme abode.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh hymn, titled "Praise of Praise," in the *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flower-Praises) dedicated to the Blessed Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrī Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the commentary *Premamakaranda*.
Now begins the thirty-eighth hymn.

May the thousand-headed Puruṣa, the blessed one with a thousand eyes and a thousand feet, purify you— He whom these three persons, motionless at the throat, the base of the feet, and the eyes, likewise worship. (1)

The Puruṣa with a thousand heads (Śeṣa), the Puruṣa with a thousand eyes (Indra), and the Puruṣa with a thousand feet (Sūrya)— these three Puruṣas, being motionless, worship Him (Śrī Śiva) respectively at His throat, at the soles of His feet, and in His eye. He is the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet [who is called Puruṣa because He dwells in every city— i.e., in every body].
May the Blessed Lord, in the form of Virāṭ, purify you!

May this Sarasvatī rain down nectar upon you—she who, like the river Sarasvatī, has emerged from a digit of the moon; who, like the goddess Sarasvatī, possesses sounds that are nectar to the ears; and who, like the river Sarasvatī, flows with waves consisting of hymns of praise to the Lord.
Just as the Sarasvatī [river] has risen from the ocean, just as the digit of the moon showers nectar with her rays [her own beams],

just as the Sarasvatī [the lute] showers nectar with notes that are nectar to the ears, and just as the Sarasvatī [the river of that name] showers nectar with its waves— so may this Sarasvatī [of mine] shower nectar upon you through hymns to the Lord.

Wasted away in vain was all my time by me, a wicked man devoid of discernment; yet this alone has been extracted from that which is utterly essence-less: that my mind is now held as the wage for the praise of the Lord. (3)
By me, a villain devoid of discernment, all this time has indeed been spent in vain; yet from that which is essence-less, I have extracted this supreme essence:

that my mind has been held fast in the service of praising the Lord. A foul-mouthed child, with a nose clogged by a running catarrh, does not please others; but to his own father, he is dearer than life itself.
In the same way, even this effort of mine is an object of ridicule. || 4 ||

Just as a child with a foul mouth and a nose thick with flowing mucus does not become dear to others, yet that very same child is more precious than life itself to his own father; even so, I know that this effort of mine, though it may be an object of ridicule, is likewise [dear to you].
I recognize this as a full abundance of fortune, indeed a descent of the Supreme Lord’s power, or perhaps the highly precious grace of the Great Ones.
If the mind is the means for the propitiation of the Lord. || 5 ||

I perceive that this is indeed an accumulation of good fortune; it is truly the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (the casting of His glance); or rather, it is the highly precious grace of the Great Ones, by which the mind becomes a means for the worship of the Lord.

Oh! I am fulfilled by this speech, delightful to the mind and adorned with virtues, as well as by this Rama, who is charming here; and my body, free from disease, is maintained steady in this worldly existence.
That devotion which has been unbroken by me.

Ah! Here I am, made fulfilled by Your speech—which is adorned with virtues, delightful to the mind, and like Rāmayā herself—adorned with virtues and delightful to the mind; for by it this firm and healthy body of mine is sustained, as is unyielding devotion in this world. Such pleasure is not found through priceless learning, nor even through ever-increasing prosperity, as is found through this peerless vow of exclusive devotion to Śiva.
By my speech, which is like thick nectar, [I shall speak]. || 7 ||

Neither by learning that is honored as priceless, nor by prosperity that increases day by day, does such joy arise for me as that which comes from speech— speech that is peerless, like unto thick nectar, and devoted solely to the hymn of Śiva. While reflecting upon Maheśvara manifesting before me, I reach that state in which the sensation of internal objects to be known has dissolved, through the act of composing this new hymn.
Only my all-pervading inner self knows that.

I, who perceive no other object of knowledge because it has dissolved through the process of *anvaya* (successive realization), while contemplating the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) manifesting before me, touch upon a certain state (*daśā*)—the stage (*bhūmikā*)—in the composition of this new hymn; that state of mine, which is absolute (*kevalam*), is known only by the all-pervading Inner Self (*antarātmā*).
Humanhood, manliness, birth in the highest caste, wisdom, true poetic skill, and oneness with Śiva—this is my succession of blessings from the All-pervading Lord.
Through the occasion of this praise, she has attained fulfillment.
Humanity, manhood, the highest caste, wisdom, excellent poetry, and oneness with Śiva— in this manner, this lineage of my welfare has attained fulfillment through the occasion of praising the Lord.
Truly, this series of stainless, dense, and resonant sounds, filled with the essence of the nine sentiments, [praises] Him of vast power who is adorned by the crescent moon.
He will make the blue-throated one rejoice. || 10 ||

[The syntactical connection is as follows:]— Just as a series of fresh, dense clouds, filled with a sound pregnant with moisture, brings joy to the blue-throated peacock adorned with a crest of large plumage, so too does this faultless series of thirty-eight new [verses], filled with a sound pregnant with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), [bring joy].

It will surely bring joy to the one of vast power, adorned with the crescent moon and having a blue throat (the illustrious Śiva). For even though we are unworthy to stand near his feet, nevertheless, these words of ours— though we dwell only within the limits of his courtyard— will cause wonder, like the modes of song of outcasts.

Anvaya: If indeed we are unworthy to cause these hymns to be heard in the presence of the Lord, nevertheless, these words of ours, set to the mode of song, will surely produce wonder even among the groups of sentries stationed at the very threshold of the Lord’s courtyard, like the songs of outcasts.

"Like serving a king through services to others, or like the household life of a poor man through the satisfying of requests—even though this body is full of much suffering, I consider it desirable for myself because of these hymns to the Lord. (The reading "idaṃ vapurbahukleśamapīdamīśvarastavairavaimi spṛhaṇīyamātmanaḥ" is also correct; alternatively: "Even though this body is full of much suffering, I consider this form desirable for myself because of these hymns to the Lord. 12.

I consider this body of mine to be desirable through hymns of praise to the Lord—just as royal service, though fraught with much hardship, is made desirable by acts of assistance to others; or as the domestic life of a poor man, though full of toil, is made desirable by satisfying the needs of those who seek help. Just as the water of a pond is beautified by lotuses, or the head of the king of serpents by its multitude of jewels, I perceive this human form, despite its defects, to be truly enchanting.
Birth [is attained] through hymns of praise to Maheśvara. || 13 ||

Just as muddy water from a pond becomes delightful through lotuses, or as the head of the lord of serpents, though filled with dense venom, becomes beautiful through its multitude of jewels, so too do I perceive this human birth— though it be full of defects— as enchanting through hymns to Maheśvara.
These [hymns] emerge from the mouth of the poet like lion cubs from the interior of a cave, or like heaps of pearls from the temples of a lordly elephant.
Whose praises do they not bear a pleasing quality? (14)

Like lion cubs emerging from the interior of a mountain cave, or like clusters of pearls emerging from the frontal globes of a lordly elephant, do these thirty-eight hymns emerging from the mouth of me, the poet, not possess charm for anyone? (The sense is: indeed, they are charming for everyone.)

Just as a row of swans adorns a lake, or a string of pearls adorns the stainless breasts of fair-browed women, may this series of praises to Maheśvara become an ornament upon the lotus-face of the virtuous. 15.

May this *Maheśvarastavāvalī* (the Garland of Hymns to Maheśvara), composed by me, become an ornament upon the lotus-faces of the virtuous—just as a row of swans graces a lake pure with its currents (for *mānasa*, "lake," is appropriate here), or like strings of pearls upon the breasts of fair-browed women.
May the parrot look up toward it as toward a bank of clouds; the *cakora* bird, as toward the moonlight of Kārtika; and the *rathāṅga* (cakra) bird, as toward the radiance of the sun.
Who would not rejoice upon seeing this collection of hymns? || 16 ||

Who would not rejoice upon beholding this collection of hymns composed by me— just as a peacock at the sight of a row of clouds, a cakora bird at the sight of the Kārtika moonlight, a ruddy goose at the sight of the sun’s radiance,
a honey-bee at a garland of flowers from the celestial grove, a white-winged swan at the pericarp of a lotus, and a cuckoo at a blossom-cluster of mango trees with its sheath opened?
And who chews upon this collection of hymns? || 17 ||

Who would not relish this collection of hymns— which is like a garland of *saumanasa* flowers for a bee that follows its kin, like the pericarp of a lotus for a white-winged swan, and like a blossom of the mango for a cuckoo with its sheath opened? Just as the sidelong glances of proud women or the charming prattle of infants inevitably yield honey, so too must the nectar of these creepers of eloquent speech.
It will moisten the minds of the wise. || 18 ||

The nectar of these creepers of eloquent verses will surely moisten the minds of the wise (the connoisseurs), just as the sidelong glances of noble women moisten the hearts of lovers, or as the charming prattle of sucklings does. This collection of hymns, like the beauty of spring to a pleasure grove, or like the rainy season to a lake parched by heat, shall satisfy the curiosity of the virtuous for poetry.
It will make even that which has been worn out for a long time become young again.

Just as the beauty of spring (the splendor of the season) rejuvenates a pleasure grove worn out by untimely heat, or as the rainy season rejuvenates a lake parched by the sun, so shall this collection of hymns rejuvenate the waning enthusiasm for poetry among the virtuous (making it fresh once more;
the meaning is: upon examining this poem of mine, other poets will also become intent upon it).

With palms joined above my head, I pay homage to those great-souled ones who are free from envy and capable of discerning the true from the false. May they look upon this collection of hymns either out of respect for their master or with a mind of grace toward me.

This *Stutikusumāñjali* (A Handful of Flower-Garlands of Praise) is offered with palms joined at the heads of those great-souled ones who are free from envy and capable of discerning the true from the false. May they look upon this collection of hymns composed by me with great respect; or else, may they look upon it with a mind of grace toward me, a wretched man.

Under the pretext of presenting this offering of a garland of praise, I desire—without hesitation—the touch of the Lord’s feet, which is unattainable even for the gods dwelling in his presence, as I seek that touch.
Even in my boasting, there is no hypocrisy for me. || 21 ||

Although my boasting may seem like a mockery, there is no deception in my desire—under the guise of offering a collection of hymns—to fearlessly seek the touch of the Lord’s feet, which is unattainable even for the gods who follow closely behind him.
Previously, this mirror of my mind, stained by the soot of the impurities of the Kali age, was not capable of perceiving even an object clearly manifest before it; [but now] suddenly...
In this [mind] purified by the clear waves of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma), we behold this entire world as clearly as a jujube fruit in the palm of one's hand. || 22 ||
(Formerly), this mirror of the mind, stained by the soot of the impurities of the Kali age, was incapable of perceiving even a manifest object appearing before it.

Now, however, when this mirror of the mind has been cleansed by the pure waves of the Śabdabrahman (in the form of hymns to the Blessed Lord), we behold this entire universe like a jujube fruit in the palm of one's hand (the meaning is: we realize that the whole world is composed of auspiciousness).
When there was ignorance, born from the latent impressions of the cataract of memory, then this entire world was seen as consisting of women;
now, for us who apply the collyrium of more refined discernment, the vision has become equalized and extends even the three worlds as Brahman.
While Ānandinī and Nandinī were praising [the Goddess] with their hidden meaning, the God, performing a gesture with the flexing of his fingers,
necessarily caused the Goddess— who was seated upon their bodies and filled with laughter— to understand these hymns.
When the daughter of the lineage (the goddess Gaurī), who brings joy to the gatekeeper (the Lord of the Gaṇas), hears the hidden meaning of these praises of mine and rejoices while offering praise,

the Lord Śambhu— displaying a graceful gesture of snapping his fingers in wonder— will certainly cause the Goddess, the Blessed Girijā, who stands beside him and is filled with laughter, to understand the hidden meaning of these praises of mine.

I believe that those wonderful and powerful meritorious deeds performed by me in the past through thought, word, and deed—purified by devotion to Śiva—have now borne fruit as these well-spoken verses, which are nectar for the ears. (24)

I believe that those powerful, abundant, and wonderful good deeds performed by us in the past through thought, word, and action—those very deeds have now borne fruit as these well-spoken verses, purified by devotion to Śiva and nectar to the ears.
May these thirty-eight hymns, which are dear to the Lord, the Master of the Pramathas, grant [fulfillment] to the learned who contemplate them; by that alone, may they be seen in their true light.
Like the digits of the moon that sustains the nectar-rayed orb, or of the seven-flamed fire, they bring about the attainment of all goals.

May these thirty-eight hymns to the Lord of Anvaya, the Master of the Pramathas, bestow the attainment of all desired goals upon the wise who contemplate them— those who, like the digits of the sun, moon, and fire held in the hands of the Lord himself, relish the nectar of the aesthetic flavor of devotion to Śrī Śiva.

This *Stutikusumāñjali* (Handful of Flower-Petals of Praise) for the lotus-feet of the Blessed Lord who bears the young moon, composed here by a servant, has been gathered from the creepers of fresh eloquence watered by incessant devotion; may it, through its fragrance, cause the longing minds of the virtuous to yearn for it. (26)

In this work, this *Stutikusumāñjali*— composed by me, a servant, as a garland of flowers from hymns gathered from the creepers of fresh verses watered by constant devotion at the lotus feet of the Blessed One who bears the young moon— may it, through its fragrance (the perfume that bestows supreme bliss),
captivate the minds of the virtuous.

O leader of the Pramathas, presiding lord of the three worlds, you of gracious countenance, six-faced one, adored by the gods, Lord of Nandin! Through devotion, let this handful of blossoms of unfolding words, offered before you by your servant at your feet, be presented to the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva).
[The connection is as follows: O presiding lord of the three worlds! O leader of the Pramathas! O you of gracious countenance! O six-faced one! O you who are worshipped by the gods!

O Nandīśvara! (Supply "show mercy toward me"). Present before the Enemy of the Cities this handful of flowers of blossoming words, offered with devotion by me, Jagaddhara the poet, who am a servant at your feet.

Thus, having offered this bouquet of hymns as a tribute to Śambhu—while it was being proclaimed and honored by Siṃha, Syandana, Skanda, Nandin, and others in the assembly—may the stainless bliss obtained thereby be for all. 28.

May evil conceptualization diminish on every ground; may pure awakening increase on every front to conquer the flood of misfortunes; may the heat of calamity be dispelled on every path by the crushing of fierce afflictions; and may devotion to Śambhu blossom in fullness within every man. (29)

Having offered this bouquet of flowers of praise— being proclaimed as venerable (praiseworthy) by Siṃha, Syandana, Skanda, Nandin, and others who have been gratified in the assembly (in the manner previously described)— to Śambhu, whatever stainless bliss has been obtained by me through that [offering], may this [which is about to be spoken, beginning with "bhuvi bhuvi"] prevail everywhere on earth (in every region). May there be no ill-conception.

May pure awakening diminish its own slightness; may devotion to Śambhu—which has crushed fierce calamities, dispelled all suffering, and is full of perfection—grow at every step on every path, increasing further and further, so as to conquer the flood of misfortune in every person. May that powerful merit which has been earned through this composition of praise for the deeds of the Blessed One become an unfailing presence in the minds of the virtuous.
The wonder of devotion to Śiva. || 30 ||

The connection [of the meaning] is as follows: by whatever exalted (*ūrjita*) merit (*sukṛta*) has been acquired by me through this composition of praise concerning the deeds of the Blessed One, may there arise in the minds of the virtuous a wondrous devotion to Śiva that never departs.
Thus ends [the work] of the Lord Maheśvara, composed by the great Kashmiri poet, the illustrious Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the *Premamakaranda*.
In the *Stutikusumāñjali*, the thirty-eighth hymn is the "Praise of the Transformation of Merit.
It contains a description of the author's lineage:

"In ancient times, there was one who was grey with the dust of the feet of the Enemy of Pura (Śiva), who was the playground for the free wanderings of Sarasvatī, and who was renowned for his illustrious lineage, sacred learning, and virtuous conduct."
Indeed, Gauradhara was the foremost among the wise. || 1 ||

In former times, there was indeed one named Gauradhara, the foremost among the wise, who was greyed by the dust of the feet of the Foe of Tripura (Śiva); he was renowned for his noble lineage, sacred learning, and virtuous conduct, and served as a playground for the goddess Sarasvatī to roam at her pleasure.

[By way of metaphorical application: The ancient poet, having reflected upon the row of twice-born men standing before him, could not help but compose this first verse in their presence, lest he be led astray by error.
He caused it to be established once more, marked with the sign of a crow's foot.

The ancient poet Brahmā, due to delusion—[that is, because his mind was distracted by the process of creation]—necessarily failed to compose this first verse (of foremost renown) at the very beginning [i.e., at the outset of the entire class of Brahmins]. Then, having reflected [having deliberated], he marked it with a crow's foot above the row of the twice-born; [just as a certain poet might mark something that must necessarily be written first with a crow's foot as a sign of error].
Furthermore, having written the verse, he again placed a "crow's foot" mark above the line of syllables (*varṇānām*)— that is to say, a sign indicating his own error— and then set it down once more.

[This] straightforward description of the meaning of the words of the Yajurveda reveals [the truth] for those who have traversed the paths of infinite philosophical systems and have seen the further shore of the entire ocean of scriptures.
Whose wonderful fame has been heard. || 3 ||

He who followed the path of the infinite established doctrines and had seen the further shore of the entire ocean of scriptures—his commentary on the meaning of the *Yajurveda* (the *Vedavilāsa-bhāṣya*) was straightforward, stainless, and faultless; his renowned learning manifested its wonder. To him was born Ratnadhara, a crest-jewel among the wise and an ocean of a multitude of virtues, upon whom Sarasvatī leaned as if for support.
She is the Goddess Śrī, who rests upon the chest of Ruru, which is adorned with jewels.
The son of this Gauradhara was Ratnadhara— by name— a crest-jewel among the wise and an ocean of a multitude of virtues;
Sarasvatī, having taken refuge in him, rivaled Śrī, who rests upon the chest of Hari, the bearer of the Kaustubha gem.

Having entered his noble, vast, and perfectly stainless mind— whose disposition was firmly rooted and unfathomable— the Goddess of Speech, acting of her own accord, established herself there as steadfastly as she does in the ocean.

Anvaya: Having entered the vast, exceedingly pure, firmly established, and unfathomable inner disposition (the mind) of that Ratnadhara— which possessed noble courage (abundant fortitude)— Sarasvatī, being under his own control, took a firm footing, just as the river Sarasvatī, having entered the vast, exceedingly pure, firmly established, and unfathomable oceanic depth— which is filled with great sea-monsters (makaras) and the like— takes a firm footing, being under its own control (or, quite out of control).
(The meaning is that he took his stand right there.

His words cause the faces of the wise to assume for a moment an expression with earrings swaying against the cheeks, with brows undulating and the forehead furrowed, and with eyes half-closed in contemplation. (6)
The utterances of this [author], when heard by the wise (the connoisseurs), for a moment cause their faces to sway as their earrings rock upon their cheeks,
their brows to ripple with the knitting of their arching eyebrows, and their eyes to be half-closed. Then,
there arose for him an intellect that bestowed its seal repeatedly upon the faces of disputants— a speech that was noble in refinement and possessed of excellent essence.
Jagaddhara, whose lotus-like mouth is pure. || 7 ||

Now, his son Jagaddhara was wise; he had repeatedly impressed the seal [of defeat] upon the mouths of disputants, and the lotus of his face was purified by speech that was noble, refined, and full of essence. Furthermore, having mounted the intellect of others—which, though possessing a firm foundation established by its own great bulk, is sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass—oh, how wonderful! He places his foot there with the playful ease of one wandering at will.
Sarasvatī placed [it] without faltering.

Anvaya: Aho! Alas! Sarasvatī, whose firm footing is not established even among the most gross-minded (sthavīyaḥsu), has placed her step without stumbling through the playful sport of wandering at will upon his intellect—even though it is as sharp as the tip of a blade of kuśa grass. For, in the case of a subtle subject, the act of extending one's foot is truly marvelous. He is free from envy, a connoisseur of aesthetic sentiment, one who has reached the further shore of sacred learning, possessed of a humility that transcends the world, pleasant of speech, and of excellent character. What more need be said? Of the words of the poet— [The verse continues: ...he is the one who has mastered the Vedas, whose modesty surpasses all, who is sweet-spoken and of virtuous conduct. Or rather, what else can be said of the words of the poet? He is one who has seen the furthest limits of learning, whose humility exceeds the entire universe, whose speech is dear, and whose nature is most disciplined. Furthermore, regarding the words of the poet— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a verse praising a king or patron. The translation reflects the available portion.)
He whose intellect is preeminent in its skill at discerning between existence and non-existence is the one and only refuge. || 9 ||

Free from envy toward his kin, possessed of a sensitive heart, one who has reached the further shore of sacred learning, endowed with a humility that surpasses all, sweet-spoken and of excellent character—what more need we say?
He whose intellect was the foremost bearer of skill in discerning the true from the false, he alone was the refuge of the words of poets.
By him, while still a child, being presented [to the Lord] with a curiosity born of devotion that blossomed with joy; [he beheld] this [Lord], whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon...
May the virtuous savor this elixir of the essence of Saṃsāra. || 10 ||

May the virtuous, who have mastered the words of our teacher and possess insight into the inner meaning, taste—that is, relish—this gift being offered by that very youth Jagaddhara, whose devotion and curiosity have blossomed into joy;
may they savor this elixir of praise for Him who wears the crescent moon as His crest-ornament.
May those who have grasped our speech perceive some special excellence within it, for they alone seek out the hidden truths.
The experts [extracted] only a mass of lotuses from the pond-water, which was turbid with a vast network of water-moss.
Let those who have heard our words and understand our inner intent take from this [work] whatever special excellence may exist in its entirety;
for it is observed that experts draw out only a mass of lotuses from the water of a pond, even though it is turbid with a dense network of wide-spreading moss.
Although there is no essence within these words—neither swift, nor sweet, nor expansive—that possesses an internal charm or a core meaning.
Even there, virtuous people ought to bring these hymns of praise to the Teacher of the Three Worlds—which are purified by loving-kindness—to the path of their ears as an ornament. (12)

Anvaya: Although there is not even the slightest essence in these [my words]— whether it be a vast, fresh, and abundant core of meaning, or an internal aesthetic charm consisting of the ultimate reality revealed through the indicated and the suggested— nevertheless, virtuous people ought to lead these [my words], which are purified by friendship for the hymn to the Teacher of the Three Worlds,
to the path of adorning the vicinity of their ears.
O wise ones, direct your minds toward Maṇikarṇikā with love; do not dull them for the sake of a string of pearls, nor touch upon the vanity of betel-rolls.
For these strings of hymns and sacred verses serve as ornaments upon the ear-lobe, the throat, and the lotus-face of the Lord who wields the bow of Love. 13.

O wise ones, diminish your affection for jeweled earrings—that is, those ear-ornaments made of gems; do not set your minds upon strings of pearls, and do not touch even the passion for betel. For these are the hymns and verses from the collection of praises of the Lord who wields the bow of Smara (the illustrious Śambhu), intended for your ears, necks, and lotus-like faces.
(ca) They serve as ornaments.

I have deposited fifty thousand coins along with seven hundred, free from harm, in the presence of the Lord, the unique abode of Dharma, the crest-jewel of the best of the twice-born, who is endowed with virtues.
Since Fate is adverse and does not grant even a single step to me—who am generally afflicted, whose speech is wretched, and whose head is cast down to the earth—I shall act in this matter.

The fifty-seven thousand verses (*anvaya-mayā*)— that is, fifty thousand verses of *suvarṇa* meter (where, although one should have said "fifty thousand verses of *suvarṇa* meters," there is no fault in the omission of words regarding devotion within the narrative of tranquility)— together with seven hundred (meaning a total number of 5,700), were dedicated to the Lord, the sole abode of heat, who is the crest-jewel of the best of the twice-born and is non-violent and virtuous; however—

Now, for one who is generally afflicted and speaks in a piteous voice—even with such piteous words as "Give, O Master!"—and likewise with head bowed to the ground, does this Lord not grant even a single step to me? Since Fate is adverse here, what can I, a wretched man, do?

By these senses whose tranquility has been obstructed and which provide no protection, my mind has been rendered subservient, having repeatedly performed [evil deeds] and being deprived of the enjoyment of the blissful experience of serving Śambhu.

But at some place and at some time, a certain glimpse of that holy vision must have fallen upon me, since I have obtained this grace of the Lord in the form of these verses, which possesses the taste of nectar more powerful than the conquered [nectar] itself. 15.

By these senses— which are like bandits, lacking restraint, devoid of tranquility due to their habitual tendencies, and being unsubdued— this mind of mine has been repeatedly made subject to others, obstructing the enjoyment of the bliss of serving Śambhu; yet, by the power of good fortune, at some time and in some place, that indescribable vision of the Holy One fell upon me, whereby this [work] was composed in the form of elegant sayings.

O Mother, the favor of the Lord has been obtained, which yields a victory over the taste of nectar; yet, O Goddess of Speech, you were led to a state of humiliation by that village leader—devoid of the discrimination between the real and the unreal—who was intent on false praise, and for this you were afraid. Abandon your timidity, for this delusion of yours has become the very limit of good fortune through these hymns of praise to the sole Lord of the World.

Anvaya: O Mother! O Sarasvatī! Since you have been led to a state of humiliation by those like us of dull intellect—like village headmen devoid of the power to distinguish between the real and the unreal—who are intent upon false praises, you are therefore afraid; this is true. But, O Mother! (now once again) abandon that timidity, for by these hymns of praise to the sole Lord of the universe, this [fear] of yours...
The limit of good fortune and luck—delusion (a great surge of supreme bliss)—has arisen.
Thus ends the description of the lineage of the illustrious poet Jagaddharabhaṭṭa.
Where is this [other] abundance of speech, swelling with the mature and radiant eloquence of a true poet?

"How can I, who am thus overwhelmed by hundreds of mental and physical ailments and possessed of such utterly distracted intellect, still remain a devotee?"— even while thinking this, I was impelled in my heart by a certain sky-clad one (a naked ascetic), who was an ocean of the nectar of compassion.

Therefore, may the venerable Guru— the one who is skilled in shattering the fear of worldly existence, whose fame acts as a tilaka-mark adorning the three worlds while uprooting the three-fold afflictions, and whose nectar-like words bring life and stir wonder in the hearts of the virtuous— be pleased with this work of mine, which, though like the composition of a bewildered child, is an elaborate commentary on the handful of flowers that is the *Jagaddhara-kavi-stotra*, and which shall impart the fragrance of the wise.
Victorious is that certain Great Lord, the Guru Śrīpāṇipātra, by a mere atom of grace from the dust of whose lotus feet one attains absolute liberation (kaivalya).

O Lord of the city of Vārāṇasī! O Blessed One, Protector of the protectorless! I make this representation before you: even a child who has fallen through his own hundreds of misdeeds should be gazed upon with eyes full of compassion.
May that certain compassionate deity bestow auspiciousness upon me, who has extended his affection even toward one devoid of learning and virtue.

By Tripāṭhī Premavallabha Śarmā, a servant of the venerable feet of the illustrious Aṣṭottarasahasra (1,008)-glorified, morning-remembered, worshipful, holy Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, Śrī Śrī Hariharānanda Sarasvatī (Śrīkarapātrī Jī Mahārāja).
The *Stutikusumāñjali*, composed by the great Kashmiri poet Śrīmaj-Jagaddharabhaṭṭa, together with the commentary named *Premamakaranda*,
is completed.
